text: Week 2 Treatment Plan 1. Explore the possibility of driving and continued gar-dening. 2. Finalize plans for discharge to home, including order-ing and installing adapted devices. 3. Finalize home program and follow-­ups. The patient was evaluated on some aspects of driving using a modified car. He was able to transfer in and out of the car with moderate supervision. He was discouraged that he was not able to push in the clutch with his left foot. He preferred driving a stick shift but could see that a car with an automatic transmission would be easier for him. He agreed to discuss getting a different car with his wife and son. Other adaptations that might make driv-ing easier and safer were explored. The issue of neglect of his left visual field was discussed and evaluated using a driving simulator. He did have problems (i.e., simulated crashes) because of neglect. It was decided that additional practice with the simulator and other activities to improve his visual scanning were necessary before he could drive again. G.W. continued to use various leisure and ADL activi-ties to increase active use of his left arm and hand. The setup of the activities was structured to require increased visual scanning as he did these activities. Although G.W. continued to improve in his walking and stair-­climbing ability, it was decided that a second handrail should be installed at both entrances to the home and in the basement and upstairs stairways. His son agreed to arrange for someone to do this. In addition, he agreed to install grab bars in the bathroom and in the hallway between the bathroom and bedroom. Sometimes, G.W. needed to use the bathroom at night. Although he was improving in his performance on the driving simulator, he was told that he was not yet safe to drive. G.W. was referred to a regional driving center, which evaluates and trains persons with disabilities in safe driving. His wife or son would drive him until he could drive again. A home program was developed with a variety of tasks and activities that required the use of his left arm and hand. He was now approaching the level of function that made him an appropriate candidate for CIMT. Unfor-tunately, access to this type of program was not feasible for G.W. because of distance and money. The therapist explained the concept of CIMT and developed a modified program that G.W. could do on his own. The modified program was adapted from the “ingredients” of an mCIT described by Page and colleagues. 73 Three outpatient follow-­ups were scheduled to monitor and upgrade his home program.

Client-­centered practice recognizes the autonomy of individuals, the need for client choice in making decisions about occupational needs, the strengths clients bring to a therapy encounter, the benefits of client-­therapist partnership, and the need to ensure that services are accessible and fit the context in which a client lives. 2

Offering the individual receiving services a more active role in defining goals and desired outcomes 3. Making the client–therapist relationship an interdepen-dent one to enable the solution of performance dys-function 4. Shifting to a model in which therapists work with indi-viduals to enable them to meet their own goals

text: 5. Evaluation (and intervention) focusing on the contexts in which individuals live, their roles and interests, and their culture 6. Allowing the individual who is receiving services to be the “problem definer” so that, in turn, the individual will become the “problem solver” 7. Allowing the client to evaluate his or her own perfor-mance and set personal goals Through the use of these strategies, the evalua-tion process becomes more focused and defined, clients become immediately empowered, the goals of therapy are understood and agreed on, and an individually tai-lored intervention plan may be established. The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure 1 is a standardized tool that embraces a client-­centered approach. van den Broek 7 specifically recommends using a client-­ centered approach as a way to enhance neurorehabilitation outcomes. van den Broek 7 states that treatment failure may be secondary to clinicians focusing interventions on what they believe the client needs rather than what the client actu-ally wants. van den Broek 7 affirms that client-­centered goal setting is a key to successful rehabilitation outcomes, stating:

text: Goal setting is of central concern as without goals, reha-bilitation has no direction and the intervention cannot be judged to be effective or ineffective. Moreover, the quality and type of goal setting sets the tone of the interaction between the clinician or treating team and the patient. Goals that are proposed, suggested, or identified by the clinician tend to be those based on what the clinician be-lieves the patient needs. Of equal, if not more importance, however, is what the patient wants to achieve. Patients tend to be motivated toward achieving or satisfying their wants, and may not be so motivated or quite unmotivated toward achieving other goals. The process of goal setting therefore involves arriving at an overlap between needs and wants, or where this is not possible agreeing to work toward wants that represent a reasonable compromise. Goal setting that ends with treatment goals that consist of needs that the patient does not want or is indifferent toward is not client centered but prescriptive, and runs the risk of concluding in an ineffective outcome (p. 468).

text: Another argument for using a client-­centered approach to guide the intervention focus with this population is that interventions typically used for those living with a vari-ety of impairments after stroke are notoriously difficult to generalize to “real-­world” settings and situations. For example, visual scanning training via table-­top activities for those living with unilateral spatial neglect most often will not automatically generalize to the client being able to use the scanning strategy to find items in the refrigerator unless the strategy is specifically taught in the context of the activity. In addition, strategies that are taught to accom-plish a specific task (e.g., using an alarm watch to maintain a medication schedule for those living with memory loss) will not necessarily generalize or “carry over” to another task such as remembering therapy appointments. Finally, there are a large number of clients whose level of brain damage precludes the clients from generalizing learned tasks. 3 This issue of task specificity related to treatment interventions must always be considered by clinicians working with this population. A client-­centered approach will help ensure that outcomes, goals, and tasks used as the focus of therapy are at least relevant, meaningful, and specific to each client as well as their caretakers despite the potential lack of being generalizable for a segment of the population living with various cognitive and perceptual impairments. Indeed, from an evidence-­ based perspective, client-­ centered practice is supported. A systematic review 6 sug-gests that patients consider active involvement in goal setting important to their recovery process after stroke. Additionally, statistically and clinically significant changes in self-­perceived performance and satisfaction with tasks of daily life have been shown to occur at the end of a client-­centered occupational therapy program for those with stroke and traumatic brain injury. 4

text: It happened during breakfast, on a bright December morning, unannounced, almost gently, and absolutely painlessly. I was wearing a thick terry cloth robe, which buffered my slumping to the floor and gave it (at least in my visual memory) a slow-­motion appearance. I ended up on my left side on the parquet floor, reject-ing my father-­in-­law’s offers of help, thrashing my right leg, holding onto the seat of my chair with my right hand, a little embarrassed and miffed that I did not seem able to stand up. I also remember distinctly my irritation at my mother-­in-­law’s plaintive demands that her husband remove a piece of bread I was chewing on when the stroke hit. She, a keen observer with an artist’s eye for detail, had

text: noticed that chewing motions had ceased on the left side of my mouth, and food was stuck under the cheek. Because I was recuperating from open heart surgery—a mitral valve repair that had been performed 2 weeks ear-lier—little diagnostic acumen, especially for a neurologist, was required to conclude that I had had a stroke. Lying on my dining room floor waiting for the ambulance, I rumi-nated about the inappropriateness of the word stroke to describe what had happened to me, which had been more like the gentle snuffing of a candle than a violent hit. Nev-ertheless, the term stroke (from the Latin ictus, which is still widely used in medical jargon) is universally accepted and has equivalent words in most Western languages. I concluded one of two things: either stroke referred to the suddenness of the event rather than to its outward mani-festations or I had had an unusual stroke. Now I know both things are probably true. The fact that I was musing about words minutes after my stroke illustrates the most important “lucky” feature of this unfortunate event: it had spared mentation and speech. Although at times I suspect that my friends and relatives may have welcomed a little aphasia on my part, talking, reading, and, soon enough, working have been vital parts of my recovery, and I am certainly grateful for whatever forces, natural or supernatural, pushed the blood clot into the right rather than into the left carotid artery. Finding myself totally incapacitated in a hospital bed was not as traumatic an experience as it would be now, maybe because it occurred so shortly after a similar post-operative intensive care experience. Or else, unbeknown to me, I was in a slightly stuporous state that blessedly quenched the emotional reactions to what was happening. Although I seemed to remember every detail of those first days after the stroke, later, I discovered some curious gaps. For example, I have no memory of having received a Dop-pler scan. Months later, when a repeat scan was performed and I was shown the results of the first examination, I had to admit to myself that I must have been in that same laboratory, which I did not remember, subjected to the same procedure, which seemed new to me, by the same technician, who greeted me cordially but whom I did not recognize. The question most often asked, especially by other neurologists, is: “What does it feel like to be hemiple-gic?” I had asked myself the same question when seeing patients who had lost various degrees of motor control. The answer, again, at least in my case, is disappointingly simple: it really felt like nothing, like I had never been able to use my left limbs; no exasperating feeling of formulat-ing a mental command and getting no action occurred. Nor do I think that this was because of loss or diminu-tion of left-­body awareness (asomatoagnosia) or sensation because I had neither to any detectable extent. Peculiarly, the frustration and anger with the sluggish and clumsy left limbs, especially in the hand, came later as I was gradu-ally regaining function and continue to this day. I do not remember how many times I have cursed and actu-ally punched my left hand for not performing adequately, knocking things over, being in the way, or simply being ridiculously (and embarrassingly) tremulous in reaching for objects. However, at the time of admission to neurology, my only frustration was related to being totally dependent on others for everything, from turning in bed to performing bodily functions. As an intensely (maybe a bit neuroti-cally) private person, as I had been all of my life, the loss of privacy that comes with major illness was initially a big problem for me. The “silver lining” has been, in fact, the acceptance of my physical frailty as a matter of fact. How does a neurologist live with a neurologic disease? I cannot answer this question appropriately because I lived my stroke as a patient, not as a neuroscientist. I asked few neurologic questions and never wanted to see my mag-netic resonance imaging films. As I had done at the time of my heart operation, I had full trust in the skill of my physi-cians and colleagues first and my physical and occupational therapists later and took a passive, although cooperative, attitude throughout the healing process. I think this con-sciously ignorant and trusting position may have done me more good than a critical, controlling approach did. Of course, seeing my own left toe go up in a classical Babinski sign, witnessing my own excessive knee jerk, and feeling odd paresthesias in the left side of my body and “pins and needles” in my left hand were strangely interesting experiences. Some peculiar phenomena may have escaped an untrained observer; for example, I noticed at some point (perhaps 2 months after the stroke) that a spontane-ous Babinski sign occurred whenever I initiated urination. This happened without exception and consisted of two or three jerky dorsiflexions of the left toe that promptly sub-sided as the stream of urine became steady. This “urinary Babinski sign” persisted throughout the first year after the stroke and continues to occur sporadically to this day. My colleagues in the stroke unit swear they have never heard of a similar phenomenon, but physicians and therapists may find inquiring about this systematically with patients recovering from stroke a worthwhile task. Who knows, perhaps the “urinary Babinski sign” (DiMauro sign?) will be added to the spontaneous Babinski sign observed by H. Houston Merritt on removing a patient’s slippers. As every patient does, I worried about the extent of recovery I could expect. I was encouraged by the fact that I could bend my leg from the very beginning. I would show this proudly to visitors and colleagues with the expecta-tion of rosy prognostic pronouncements. I was concerned by the total lack of movement in my left arm, but I learned later from a good friend, a pediatric neurologist, that he had felt optimistic about my future recovery because from the first day, I could flex my fingers. Wisely, however, he kept his own council about his positive prognosis until much later, when my arm had in fact regained a good deal of function.

text: Another weird aspect of my stroke (and as it turned out, a positive one) has been the complete lack of spasticity, which has greatly facilitated the rehabilitation process. The only hint of spasticity appeared during automatic reactions such as stretching and yawning, when both left limbs would spontaneously and uncontrollably go into extreme flexion.

text: THERAPY

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Foundations of Stroke Rehabilitation
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 4: Client Centeredness:A Survivor’s Perspective, THERAPY, p. 82

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 4: Client Centeredness:A Survivor’s Perspective, THERAPY, p. 82

text: When the editor of this book, who had been my occupa-tional therapist, asked me to write about my experiences as a patient recovering from stroke and suggested the title “Notes of a Survivor,” I asked him whether he meant sur-vivor of the stroke or survivor of physical and occupational therapy. Lest my later comments sound too enthusiastic or be considered self-­serving on the part of the editor, let me start with a few negatives. Both physical therapy and occupational therapy are boring, consisting as they must of highly repetitive exer-cises and activities: the patient soon learns to count “reps,” longing to reach the magic number (usually 10—do thera-pists have a functional rationale for this quota?) requested by the therapist. And no cheating is tolerated; therapists have mastered a secret way of keeping track of reps auto-matically and privately even as they keep up a conversa-tion with you, and they will not be defrauded of even a few reps. Another thing—therapists have a bit of a sadistic trait that may be innate and predisposing to the job or else part of their professional training. As soon as you feel comfortable doing the required number of reps for any given exercise, the number of reps usually goes up by five. The idea, I think, is to keep you challenged, and you are. Furthermore, consider pain: did you know that therapists distinguish between “good” pain and “bad” pain? Good pain is the muscle soreness that comes from those five cycles of 10 reps, a guarantee for the therapist that you are doing your exercises and using the proper muscles. Bad pain is classified in imaginative ways; my occupational therapist, a man, used a scale of severity that ranged from “paper cut pain” to “labor pain,” at which point the secretary on the occupational therapy floor, a woman, invariably reminded us that we men did not know what we were talking about. One other piece of good news and bad news—exer-cise works but only as long as you keep exercising. The moment you stop, you start losing ground, so that you are in fact condemned to exercising for life, which to a Medi-terranean soul such as I is a pretty harsh sentence. My way of surviving this torture is to make exercise part of a highly routinized wake-­up ritual, something I do almost auto-matically, like brushing my teeth. This way I feel slightly guilty when I skip the routine and, conversely, when I do exercise, I enjoy that little heady virtuous feeling I remem-ber from my jogging days.

reference.part_title: Foundations of Stroke Rehabilitation

text: So much for the negatives. The positive side of the ledger is much larger. As a neurologist and a student of neuromuscular diseases, I am ashamed to confess that I had virtually ignored physical therapy and occupational therapy—a never-­never land where patients usually ended up after the physicians concluded their brilliant diagnos-tic workups—and I had a vague notion of physical and occupational therapists as robotlike technicians. A few sessions of occupational therapy and physical therapy suf-ficed to change my views drastically. The first thing that impressed me was their knowledge of muscle anatomy and physiology; I thought I knew muscles! Throughout the rehabilitation process, I was amazed at their understand-ing of movement and lack thereof, muscle coordination, and compensatory mechanisms. Thus, I had at all times the comforting notion that all exercises and activities were rationally planned on the basis of my specific deficits and needs and were not part of a “canned” program. Another encouraging sign was the therapists’ obvious satisfaction at every sign of improvement; far from being automata, these people clearly loved their profession and took plea-sure in a job well done. In fact, I came to admire both the dedication and the professionalism of my therapists so much that I developed the conviction—which I expressed to the chairman of our Department of Neurology—that all neurology residents ought to spend at least a few weeks observing occupational and physical therapists at work. All too often, we neurologists are content with our diag-nostic workup of stroke patients and our intervention in the acute phase, only to lose sight of patients’ progress. I developed a pain syndrome in my left shoulder that not only gave me sleepless nights (partly because of pain, partly because of an exaggerated fear of dislocating my arm by sleeping on the left side) but also resulted in a “frozen shoulder,” a very painful condition that interfered with my occupational therapy. Again, I was impressed by the variety of approaches used by my therapists not just to alleviate the pain but also to resolve the problem, includ-ing slinging, supporting my arm on an over-­the-­shoulder bag, and taping my shoulder in conjunction with pas-sive mobilization and massage. On that occasion, I found myself in another situation I usually experience from the other side; I volunteered to be the subject of a teaching conference for occupational therapy trainees. Although I derived some satisfaction from being materially useful to the medical profession (something akin to but fortunately short of donating your body to the Department of Anat-omy) at our clinical conferences, I am now much more aware of the discomfort caused to the patient by being an object of study.

text: GOING HOME

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Foundations of Stroke Rehabilitation

text: Falling is, of course, the big fear. I had fallen once in my hospital room, and I fell once again a few days after my return home. Finding myself on both occasions next to a

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Foundations of Stroke Rehabilitation
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 4: Client Centeredness:A Survivor’s Perspective, GOING HOME, p. 83
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 4, p. 83
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 4: Client Centeredness:A Survivor’s Perspective, GOING HOME, p. 83

text: wall, I went through the steps my therapists had so care-fully rehearsed with me in the hospital gym, and on both occasions, I got up on my own. However, after my rela-tives left, I had nightmares about falling in the middle of a room and not being able to get up and reach the phone or the intercom. The problem was solved by the acquisition of a portable phone, which I slipped into my pocket every night as soon as I entered my house. I never had to use it, but it served its purpose as a “security blanket.” Showering and getting dressed in the morning also took some adjusting, but I soon learned that what had appeared in the hospital as slightly ridiculous procedures (left sleeve and pants leg first; hook the sock on your big toe first, then slip in the other toes) were in fact precious clues to a highly routinized and reasonably rapid pro-cess. I took several months to remaster the tie knot, but I remember with joy the pride of my occupational therapist when I appeared at a clinic appointment wearing shirt and tie instead of the usual turtleneck. Lest all this appear an exceedingly smooth return to normal life, let me dwell for a moment on the frustrations to which I alluded in my opening paragraphs. Even a mild residual hemiparesis is an endless source of frustration in just about every aspect of daily life. I find dropping objects especially irritating and often remember with new empa-thy my son’s frequent outbursts as a clumsy adolescent— “I hate gravity!” Buttoning shirts, especially cuffs, can be a trying experience, and I have more than a few shirts with ripped-­off buttons to prove it. Frustration at times turns to rage, and I have occasionally punched my slug-gish left hand with my agile right one; even worse, I have punched a table, with the only result of having still a slug-gish left hand and a painful right one. One less disruptive way to deal with frustrating experiences is to curse; I have invented a peculiar English–Italian hybrid curse (unprint-able in either language) that I use as a mantra many times a day. Naturally, the level of frustration and the threshold for the “tantrums” vary considerably from day to day and are influenced by mood; on some “bad days,” I notice that I am almost looking for a frustrating experience so I have an excuse to explode, thus using the stroke as a scapegoat for my bad mood. Although I have never been a sportsman (library mouse would be a more fitting definition), as my rehabilitation progressed, I have repeatedly had vivid dreams in which I ran; I just ran for the sake of running, and it felt both exhilarating and as easy as it had been before the stroke. I actually tried the motions of running while holding on to a shopping cart in the hallway of my apartment building, but somehow the exhilaration of the dream was not there.

text: CONCLUDING REMARKS

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Foundations of Stroke Rehabilitation
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 4: Client Centeredness:A Survivor’s Perspective, CONCLUDING REMARKS, p. 83
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 4, p. 83
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 4: Client Centeredness:A Survivor’s Perspective, CONCLUDING REMARKS, p. 83

text: Although I cannot run, I can walk without a cane, I am independent in my daily activities, I have been able to resume my (fortunately sedentary) job, and I travel around the world. To be sure, this is not the typical outcome of stroke. Every patient is different, and I have been unusu-ally lucky in that I was spared speech impediments and spasticity. This in turn has made my rehabilitation easier and more effective. However, my left side was totally paralyzed only 2.5 years ago (at age 54 years), and I am now enjoying a nearly normal life. Much of my progress has been because of the patient, steady, intelligent, and compassionate work of my physical and occupational therapists. The punch line of these “Notes of a Survivor” has to be that not only can one survive a stroke, but brain plasticity does exist, and good physical and occupational therapy does improve the condition of every patient recovering from stroke to a remarkable degree. Some improvement continues to occur (if you exercise, that is!) for a long time, although at a reduced pace. So, who knows, maybe I will be able to run again before I turn 60.

text: Just as Alexandre Dumas père felt obliged to write “Twenty Years Later,” a follow-­up to The Three Muske-teers, so 10 years after my stroke, I also feel obliged to offer a follow-­up. The good news is that I still walk inde-pendently, work full-­time, and travel extensively. The bad news is that I never ran again—although running remains a recurrent subject of my dreams—and I still have par-esthesia in the left side of my body, mostly in the hand. Additional problems are due to two situations, one of which is totally outside my will, while for the other, I have to take full responsibility. The first has to do with aging and related troubles (still preferable to the alterna-tive, to quote Woody Allen). Thus, generalized arthritis has necessitated a total left hip replacement, adding insult to the injury of the stroke and accentuating my limp. The second has to do with my physical laziness and my weak-ness for the Mediterranean diet (which is the opposite of the Atkins diet): lack of exercise and excessive weight are not what my physical therapist recommended. And I hear about it about every day because my physical therapist and I have developed a wonderful personal relationship. You can call this development a positive side effect of the stroke for me and an occupational hazard for her. But it is a happy ending for both, and who does not like a happy ending?

text: EPILOGUE

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Foundations of Stroke Rehabilitation
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 4: Client Centeredness:A Survivor’s Perspective, EPILOGUE, p. 84

text: In my “Concluding Remarks,” I optimistically stated that I was unusually lucky from my first right brain stroke, when I was spared speech impediment and spasticity. I was unusually unlucky 4 months ago, on a Saturday before Easter, when I was hit again by a bad stroke affecting the left hemisphere of my brain, due to my frequent atrial fibrillation (a-­fib).

reference.part_title: Foundations of Stroke Rehabilitation

text: Unlike what I remembered happening 20 years ago, I was totally unconscious regarding what happened sud-denly to me, vaguely thinking that I was falling to my right side. Fortunately, my physical therapist wife, my veritable custodian angel, came to my assistance, called an ambu-lance, and paramedics quickly took me to the Allen Pavil-ion, where the neurologist on call had the premonition to send me promptly to Columbia University Medical Center, where a providentially clever radioneurologist/interventionist inserted a line into my femoral artery, all the way into my cerebral left middle artery, from which he removed the offending embolus. About 2 hours after the stroke occurred, he returned me to my consciousness and asked me how I felt and did I move my right limbs, which I both could move; I also recognized around my bed a few familiar loved faces. I was again “unusually lucky” in my bad situation, and my left brain showed a remarkable ischemia, which was rapidly restored by a network of blood vessels. However, the dominant brain suffered from aphasia and I noticed a number of amnesic names, which I could barely recall. On the contrary—and to my relief—I remembered the main subjects of my research, mostly mitochondrial dis-eases. One disturbing problem came to my mind, and that required my incapacity of hearing and understand-ing the English language often recurring in conversa-tions or reported in brief news on TV programs. This degree of receptive aphasia may apply equally to mis-understanding spoken sentences in my native language, Italian, and my acquired Spanish idiom. Another prob-lem was discovered by my ignorance of the rich English vocabulary, which I applied to solve crossword puzzles in the Sunday New York Times magazine. An additional problem related to receptive aphasia made difficult for me understanding fully the meaning of humorous op-­ ed articles in the New York Times, which required much abstract thinking. What is the problem of my motility? Contrary to walk-ing dangerously due to the old hemiparesis, the right foot has developed “freezing” or festinating small movements when facing an elevator door, and I feel constantly my vestibular instability. I experienced at least four falling episodes, thus far without fractures. The “parkinsonian” features described above for the right foot and further combined with small right hand movements and micro-graphia were treated with carbidopa/levodopa (Sinemet) at gradually increasing doses: there was more clearing of the visual instability than of the ambulation. Here I stand 4 months poststroke #2, occupying my office and writing my correspondence, reading articles, preparing papers and review chapters. I cannot travel extensively, although my guardian angel and my precious wife has organized my month-­long vacation in Sardinia, a heavenly place of peace, good food, siestas, and sunbath-ing near the sea.

text: Physical therapy and occupational therapy are provi-dential, but the luck in this situation was the saving touch of the radioneurologist/interventionist, who has allowed me to live my professional life, despite all my intellectual limitations. More colleagues than I know tell me repeat-edly that I could get better within a year of therapy. I still hope to improve faster than I did after my stroke #1. Calling this an epilogue, it refers to a late event fraught with many difficulties, but still rich with loving care by my immediate family and by my dear collaborators. As such, it reflects more accurately a “prologue” introducing me to a few more years of activity and to my role as a true grand-father and as a mentor to many young clinical scientists. Long life to them!

text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Understand how to implement the occupational therapy process in a manner that is client centered and is based on top-­down reasoning and an occupation-­based and/or occupation-­focused approach to evaluation and interven-tion. 2. Describe the ADL Taxonomy, a structured self-­report of a person’s strengths and problems with personal and instru-mental activities of daily living (ADLs). 3. Understand how to evaluate the quality of performance of instrumental ADL tasks for a person with stroke. 4. Understand how to write occupation-­focused documenta-tion, including writing client-­centered goals, for each step of the intervention process. 5. Understand the different models of practice that can be used to plan and implement occupation-­based and/or occupation-­focused interventions to enhance a person’s performance of instrumental ADL tasks.

text: Stroke often leads to disability in activities of daily living (ADL), and transitions between ADL independence and dependency has been noted to occur up to 5 years post-stroke. 35 Furthermore, increased independence in ADL is strongly associated with health-­related quality of life. 28 Thus, addressing impairments in ADL performance after stroke is a primary focus of occupational therapy (OT). A recent systematic review of randomized controlled trials found that OT targeted toward improving ADL increased performance scores on ADL measures (e.g., Functional Independence Measure, Barthel Index) and reduced the risk of poor outcome (i.e., death, deterioration, or depen-dency in personal ADLs). The study also found that stroke

text: survivors who received OT were more independent in “extended ADLs” (i.e., instrumental ADLs). 27 There are a variety of models that can be used to guide a clinician’s reasoning when addressing limitations in ADLs. Examples include the Model of Human Occupa-tion, 22 Occupational Adaptation Practice Model, 37 and Occupational Therapy Intervention Process Model. 12 In this chapter, we will present a case for a patient, Astrid, in which the occupational therapist, Maria, uses the Occupational Therapy Intervention Process Model (OTIPM) 12 to guide her reasoning as she evaluates her client and then plans and implements interventions to enhance Astrid’s performance of ADL tasks after a stroke. Maria chose to use the OTIPM because it supports the occupational therapist’s reasoning to ensure that (1) the services provided are client centered, (2) the client is evaluated in a true top-­down manner, (3) the evaluation and intervention methods used are occupation based and/or occupation focused, and (4) documentation is occupa-tion focused. 12,13 The OTIPM is shown schematically in Figure 5.­1. Definitions of the terms occupation centered, occupation based, and occupation focused, as used in this chapter, are shown in Table 5.­1. The OTIPM has been used for more than 18 years at the hospital where Astrid was seen for OT services, and it is the basis for the OT program used for all patients seen in the OT department. More specifically, in Sweden, the context for the OT services described in this chapter, it is common practice to develop an OT program that specifies what services the occupational therapists are to provide for a specific client group in a particular setting. A group of occupational therapists working in a broad variety of settings (e.g., acute care, rehabilitation, home health, other community-­based programs, university-­based edu-cation), with a broad variety of client groups in terms of age (i.e., young children to older adults) and diagnoses (e.g., developmental, neurologic, orthopedic, psychiatric) and a variety of roles (e.g., direct services, consultative services) within Västerbotten County developed a gen-eral OT program from which more specific OT programs could be developed. These programs are based on Fisher’s OTIPM; the general OT program developed in Sweden is also included in Fisher’s text. 12 Specific OT programs delimit what is to be done at each step of the intervention process, as well as how each step is to be implemented. Consistent with the general OT program, the specific OT program includes options for evaluation and intervention methods, but the final decision as to what evaluation methods and interventions to use are based on the needs and priorities of each client and the professional reasoning of each occupational thera-pist. In other words, the specific OT program describes options for “what is to be done” and “how it is to be done” at each step of the intervention process, from the initial referral to discharge from OT services.

text: Although there is evidence within stroke rehabili-tation suggesting that patients benefit from a team approach, 9,24 it remains critical that the occupational therapist contributes to the team approach with his or her professional expertise. Using the OTIPM, as well as specific OT programs that have been based on the OTIPM, to guide the occupational therapist’s reasoning process ensures that the occupational therapist, as part of the rehabilitation team, maintains an occupation-­ centered perspective. 13 For example, recent critical reviews of interventions for stroke survivors 19,32,43 con-cluded that authentic occupation (i.e., occupation-­based interventions, goal-­ oriented activities that provide a just right challenge, and the use of strategies to opti-mize engagement in occupation) is the most effective type of intervention for those living with decreased occupational performance secondary to both cognitive and motor impairments after stroke. Finally, to evalu-ate the effectiveness of the provided OT interventions, sensitive occupation-­based and/or occupation-­focused outcome measures must be used. 12,13,18,19,32,43 For example, at the rehabilitation department where Astrid participated in OT services, the entire interdis-ciplinary team works in a client-­centered manner in which the client* is included as a member of the team. Together with the client, all team members collaborate and formulate client-­centered goals at an initial plan-ning meeting. The occupational therapist’s contribu-tion to this collaborative team approach is to bring a clear occupation-­ centered perspective, stressing the client’s ability to perform the daily life tasks that hold meaning for the client and that he or she wants to be able to perform more effectively given the circum-stances in which he or she lives. In this chapter, we will describe how Maria went through each step of the OTIPM when she worked with Astrid. More specifically, we will describe how Maria implemented client-­centered, occupation-­based, and occupation-­ focused evaluation and intervention services, including how (1) an occupation-­ focused interview guide, the ADL Taxonomy, 38,40,41 can be used to gather information about the client’s perspec-tive on his or her occupational strengths and problems and (2) the occupation-­based and occupation-­focused Assessment of Motor and Process Skills (AMPS) 16,17 can be used to gather information about the client’s observed quality of ADL task performance. These tools will be stressed because the focus of this chapter is on ADL task performance. See Table 5.­2 and Chapter 6 for examples of other tools that can measure ADL per-formance. We will also demonstrate how the occupa-tional therapist can use these occupation-­based and/or occupation-­focused evaluation results when they col-laborate with the client to develop client-­centered and occupation-­focused goals, plan occupation-­based and/or occupation-­ focused OT interventions, and write occupation-­ focused documentation. text: As shown in Figure 5.­1, the first phase of the interven-tion process, as defined by the OTIPM, is the evaluation and goal-­setting phase. During this phase, the occupa-tional therapist must use true top-­down reasoning, in which he or she focuses first on gathering information from the client about the client’s perspectives on his or her daily life, the context of daily life task performances, what areas of everyday life are of interest and provide meaning, and what the client views as most important given his or her current situation (establish the client-­ centered performance context and identify resources and limitations within the client-­centered performance context). In this process, the occupational therapist also begins to develop therapeutic rapport and work collab-oratively with the client; this collaborative working rela-tionship extends and further develops throughout the entire intervention process (depicted by the dotted line in Fig. 5.­1). The occupational therapist then proceeds to enabling the client to identify his or her perceived strengths and problems of occupational performance, having the cli-ent prioritize what daily life tasks are of most concern, and then observing the client’s quality of occupational performance (identify the client’s reported and priori-tized strengths and problems of occupational perfor-mance, observe the client’s performance of prioritized tasks and implement performance analyses, and define and describe task actions the client does and does not perform effectively). Structured interview guides such as the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM), 25 Occupational Performance History Inter-view-­II 23 (OPHI-­II), or the ADL Taxonomy 38,40,41 are often used to support the client in identifying occupa-tional performances of concern as well as those that are perceived as most important to prioritize for further evaluation. Standardized and nonstandardized perfor-mance analyses are then used to observe and evaluate the client’s quality of occupational performance of pri-oritized daily life tasks. 15 The occupational therapist then uses the results of the performance analyses to document the client’s baseline levels of observed quality of occupational performance in a manner that is occupa-tion focused. 12,13 After the occupational therapist and the client have determined what aspects of daily life task performance

text: Recall, Plan and Perform System of Task Analysis, 6,33 are preferred. 18 True top-­down reasoning is a feature of the OTIPM, and such reasoning is differentiated from bottom-­up rea-soning in which the occupational therapist initially focuses on evaluating the client’s body functions and environmen-tal factors. The identified limitations of body functions and environmental constraints or barriers are then inter-preted as the reasons why the client is having problems with everyday life task performance. The true top-­down reasoning process of the OTIPM also differs from more commonly used top-­to-­bottom-­up reasoning processes in which the occupational therapist initially focuses on the client’s occupational profile or occupational performances that are of concern but then jumps immediately to focus-ing on the body functions and environmental factors that may be causing the client to have problems with occupa-tional performance, skipping over the important step of observing the client’s quality of occupational performance and implementing performance analyses. 12,15 The second phase of the OTIPM is the interven-tion phase. During this phase, the occupational therapist selects which type(s) of practice model(s) to use to address the client’s problems with occupational performance. As shown in Figure 5.­1, the occupational therapist may select from among four options that all involve planning and implementing interventions that are occupation based and/or occupation focused. 12,13 In the final phase of the OTIPM, the reevaluation phase, the occupational thera-pist uses occupation-­based and occupation-­focused evalu-ation methods to reevaluate the client for enhanced and satisfying occupational performance. Most commonly, the occupational therapist again uses (1) observation-­based tools (e.g., AMPS) to determine if the client’s quality of occupational performance is enhanced and (2) interview guides (e.g., COPM, ADL Taxonomy) to determine if the client’s level of satisfaction with occupational perfor-mance has improved.

text: As the intervention process progresses, different types of evaluation methods are used to gather information from and about the client during each step of the pro-cess. As we already noted, occupation-­focused inter-view guides such as COPM 25, OPHI-­I I, 23 or the ADL Taxonomy 28,40,41 can be used to facilitate the client’s self-­report and prioritization of strengths and prob-lems with occupational performance, including ADL task performance. When the occupational therapist progresses to the step in which he or she implements performance analyses and defines and describes the task actions the client did and did not perform effec-tively, either standardized or nonstandardized per-formance analyses can be used. 15 If the client reports problems with ADL task performance or social inter-action, existing standardized observational tools such as the AMPS 16,17 or the Evaluation of Social Inter-action 14 can be used. Standardized tools have the advantage of providing the occupational therapist not only with information about what occupational per-formance skills (task actions) were effective or inef-fective; they also enable the generation of linearized measures that can be used as objective indices of the client’s current level of occupational performance or change in level of occupational performance after intervention. Nonstandardized performance analy-ses only enable the occupational therapist to identify what occupational performance skills were effective or ineffective. 12,17 The AMPS is a standardized evaluation of a person’s observed quality of personal and instrumental ADL task performance (collectively, ADL task performance). The AMPS can be used with persons with any diagnosis and at any age from 2 years to older than 100 years as long as the person is interested in and has a need to perform ADL tasks. To become a trained and calibrated AMPS rater, the occupational therapist must attend a training course and test 10 people after the course. When the potential rater demonstrates the ability to score the AMPS in a valid and reliable manner, he or she becomes a calibrated AMPS rater and has full access to reports generated by the Occupational Therapy Assessment Package (OTAP software). 39 The use of these reports in practice is demon-strated in this chapter. When the AMPS is administered, a person is observed performing two or more relevant and chosen ADL tasks. A total of 125 standardized personal and instrumental ADL tasks are included in the AMPS. The tasks represent many different cultures and lev-els of ADL task challenge. Examples of standardized AMPS tasks are listed in Box 5.­1. For each ADL task observed, the occupational therapist rates the person’s quality of performance of 36 occupational performance skills (AMPS items), including 16 ADL motor skills and 20 ADL process skills (Table 5.­3). Occupational per-formance skills are small, observable units of an ADL task performance (e.g., lifting a glass and gathering it to the kitchen counter in the context of pouring oneself a glass of juice), not underlying body functions (e.g., grip strength, shoulder range of motion, memory, praxis) that may help support or limit a person’s occupational performance skills. 2 To implement an AMPS observation, the occupa-tional therapist interviews the person and others in the client’s constellation to find out what ADL tasks are relevant to the person’s life and are perceived by the client to be problems or potential problems of occupa-tional performance. text: therapist has determined what ADL tasks are perceived as problems and have been prioritized by the client for further evaluation, the occupational therapist initi-ates a standardized AMPS performance analysis. After each AMPS task observation, the occupational therapist scores the person’s quality of performance of each occu-pational performance skill (i.e., the 16 ADL motor items and 20 ADL process items) for each observed AMPS task and enters the person’s AMPS item raw scores into the OTAP software. Calibrated AMPS raters may also enter global and specific baseline statements, the client’s goals, and rec-ommendations for intervention that will then be included in the AMPS Results Report. The AMPS Results Report will assist the occupational therapist in planning appropriate interventions focused on improving the person’s quality of ADL task performance. An AMPS Progress Report also can be generated provided the per-son has been evaluated with the AMPS both before and after intervention. The AMPS Progress Report is used to evaluate and document the effectiveness of the imple-mented interventions. 15,16 More specifically, when the results of a standardized AMPS observation are used to their full potential, AMPS Results Reports and AMPS Progress Reports will include two ADL ability measures (ADL motor and ADL process) that will inform the occupational therapist and the client about the person’s quality of ADL task performance in relation to criterion-­ referenced cutoffs that represent varying degrees of physical effort or clumsiness, time-­ space efficiency, safety, and independence; norm-­ based interpretations are also possible. 16 Occasionally, upon interviewing the client, the occu-pational therapist learns that none of the 125 standard-ized AMPS tasks are relevant to the person. On those occasions, the occupational therapist can implement a nonstandardized performance analysis by observ-ing the person perform prioritized and relevant ADL tasks. text: The ADL Taxonomy, 38,40 similar to the COPM, 25 is an occupation-­focused interview guide that can be admin-istered early in the intervention process, when the cli-ent is asked about what ADL tasks he or she performs and perceives as strengths and problems of occupa-tional performance. The ADL Taxonomy differs from the COPM in that it focuses on smaller actions that are part of ADL tasks, and its design minimizes the risk of the client being allowed to identify problems that are not occupation focused (e.g., improved ability to use right hand). The design of the ADL Taxonomy allows for the use of a variety of formats for recording the client’s reported strengths and problems, but one of the most common is conceptualized as a divided circle in which each area of daily life tasks has its own slice (Fig. 5.­2). All slices are then divided into the actions included in each task domain according to a hierarchy of difficulty. The ADL task domains and the ADL task actions included in each domain are listed in Table 5.­4. Located at the top of the circle is a larger blank slice where the occupational thera-pist can add occupational areas of importance to the client that are not included in the listed areas (e.g., leisure tasks). When the occupational therapist records the client’s reported strengths and problems within each ADL task domain, the occupational therapist may choose how to score the ADL Taxonomy. 40 For example, the occupa-tional therapist may choose to record only whether or not the client is able to perform each task action. Another option is to record that the client (1) can perform the task action independently, with assistance, or using an adaptive device; (2) cannot perform the task action; or (3) does not perform the task action. A third possible scoring scheme is shown in Figure 5.­2. More recently, Wæhrens and Fisher 42 developed a ver-sion of the ADL Taxonomy that is scored using a three-­ category rating scale reflecting the person’s observed level of effort, efficiency, safety, and independence performing each ADL task action. Wæhrens and colleagues have since developed two self-­report versions, one based on interview and one based on the person filling in a questionnaire. 41

text: Geriatric Day Rehabilitation Unit: Client Living in Comfort (Assisted) Living In rehabilitation departments in Sweden, as well as in North America and other world regions, it is common to work with interdisciplinary teams. 10,30,38 This means that several pro-fessions are involved throughout the entire rehabilitation process, and members contribute to the team with their spe-cific expertise using profession-­specific evaluation and inter-vention methods. The use of a collaborative interdisciplinary approach, in which the client is viewed as an integral member of the team, allows the team to better obtain a full picture of the client’s needs and provide appropriate interventions. Such an approach requires that the team members collabo-rate closely and assist each other in solving problems that arise during the rehabilitation process. It is also critical that the client’s rehabilitation goals guide decisions about which team members to involve in the rehabilitation process; deci-sions about who to involve can also change over time as the client’s goals change. 21 Using Astrid as an example, we will demonstrate how this interdisciplinary teamwork is imple-mented in the rehabilitation process. Our emphasis will be on the contributions of the occupational therapist.

text: rehabilitation unit 3 months later, Astrid had met her first three goals. When propelling her wheelchair, she was unable to move it more than a few meters before she required assistance. She also continued to require minimal physical assistance with upper body grooming (i.e., wash-ing her face, combing her hair, brushing her teeth) and moderate physical assistance with dressing and prepar-ing her breakfast; persistent cognitive limitations report-edly limited Astrid’s ability to learn new, compensatory strategies. Upon discharge from the inpatient geriatric rehabili-tation unit, Astrid was referred to a geriatric day reha-bilitation unit for continued rehabilitation. At the same time, Astrid moved to a comfort living complex for people 55 years and older. Comfort living is a setting where the person has his or her own apartment within the complex and the residents have access to jointly shared common areas, including a dining room. A comfort living com-plex is similar to an assisted living complex in the United States.

text: Establish Client-­Centered Performance Context Because of a waiting list, Astrid did not start coming to the geriatric day rehabilitation unit until 4 weeks after her discharge from the inpatient unit (4.5 months after her stroke). At her first visit, her new occupational thera-pist, Maria, began the process of establishing the client-­ centered performance context by reading through Astrid’s medical record, which included the background informa-tion from her stays in the stroke unit and the inpatient geriatric rehabilitation unit. Maria then met Astrid and carried out an initial OT interview. Astrid came to the interview with her ex-­husband, Emil. During the interview, Maria asked a variety of open-­ ended questions intended to enable her to gather infor-mation from Astrid about each of the 10 dimensions of the client-­centered performance context defined in the OTIPM. 12 Maria’s goal was to understand Astrid, from Astrid’s perspective, and Astrid’s perceptions of her cur-rent (and past) level of occupational performance. One such question involved Maria asking Astrid to describe for her how a usual day was laid out. Finally, as part of her interview, she used the ADL Taxonomy to help Astrid visualize which daily life tasks she performed well and which ones she was concerned about (see Fig. 5.­2). Maria gathered the following information about Astrid’s occu-pational performance context, summarized below accord-ing to each of the 10 dimensions defined in the OTIPM, not based on the progression of the OT interview.

text: Astrid moved to a comfort living complex 1 month ago. Her apartment has a bedroom, a living room, a kitchen, and a large bathroom. The bedroom has a bed with rails, a bookshelf, and a bedside table with a telephone and a digital alarm clock and calendar. The living room has a sofa, two armchairs, a TV, and a dining room table with two chairs close to the kitchen. In the kitchen, there is a refrigerator, and a microwave oven is located at cup-board height above the kitchen counter. The bathroom has a shower, including a shower stool, and toilet with a raised seat and armrests. The bathroom also has a washing machine and dryer. In addition to her apartment, there are several shared common areas in the comfort living complex where Astrid lives (i.e., dining room, library, TV room, spa unit). Finally, Astrid has a wheelchair and a roll-ing walker. Astrid’s social environment consists of the staff of the comfort living complex who are available 24 hours per day, close friends who visit often, her ex-­husband, Emil, two grown daughters (one living in southern Sweden and one living abroad), and her grandchildren. Before her stroke, she lived alone in her own apartment; she contin-ues to live alone in her apartment in the comfort living complex.

text: Astrid’s interests include being together with friends; she is especially motivated to invite her friends to her apart-ment and wants to be able to do that independently. She also wishes to be able to eat a meal using customary uten-sils because it bothers her that others see her using only her fork while eating (in Sweden, it is customary to use both a knife and a fork during a meal, with the knife held in the right hand and the fork held in the left hand during the entire eating process). Because of this, she does not want to eat in the dining room but instead chooses to have the staff prepare meals for her in her apartment, where she eats alone. Astrid values being independent and doing as much for herself as possible. Her goals include being able to manage her daily tasks herself again (e.g., inviting her friends for coffee, making her breakfast, making sandwiches, going to the toilet, and participating in activities in the shared areas of the comfort living complex). Astrid’s past interests included going for walks in the forest; picking berries and mushrooms; keeping her home “nice and tidy”; decorating her home; going to the theater, concerts, and movies; and gardening. She also enjoyed reading fiction and magazines about gardening and home decorating. Although she cur-rently enjoys reading the daily newspaper, she reports that she is no longer interested in attending cultural events or cleaning her apartment because, “Me…too hard…now.”

text: The tasks Astrid mentioned that are relevant to her past and current situation include personal ADLs (dress-ing, toileting, showering, grooming, and eating), social activities (e.g., socializing with her family, socializing and having coffee with her friends), instrumental ADLs (preparing coffee, preparing simple meals such as oatmeal or sandwiches, shopping), and leisure (reading the news-paper, watching TV, resting). Tasks that were relevant to her life before her stroke but that now are irrelevant because of her lack of interest or are now too difficult for her to perform include walking in the forest and picking berries and mushrooms; attending the theater, concerts, and movies; gardening; house cleaning; and managing her finances (banking, paying bills).

text: During the interview, Maria noted that Astrid seems to have a good relationship and receives a lot of support from her ex-­husband, Emil, but Maria did not ask about their relationship. Maria also did not ask about the quality of Astrid’s connectedness with her friends, daughters, and grandchildren. Although she assumed Astrid has good relationships with all of them, Maria was aware that she might need to confirm that with Astrid later in the OT process. Maria did learn that Astrid often traveled to visit her daughters and spent a lot of time with her grandchil-dren but that they now travel to northern Sweden to visit Astrid. Astrid also did not comment on her relationship with the staff at the comfort living complex, and Maria again reasoned that she likely would want to learn more about that, especially if they became involved in Astrid’s rehabilitation, for example, as recipients of consultative OT services in relation to assisting Astrid.

text: Astrid has several resources available and that she now uses, including the staff at the comfort living complex who are available to help her 24 hours per day; her ex-­husband, who is legally responsible for her finances; home help ser-vice personnel, who come once a week and clean her apart-ment; and the interdisciplinary team at the geriatric day rehabilitation unit. She also has full access to any needed health care services provided by the Swedish health care system. The Swedish health care system will pay for her to take a taxi (mobility service) to the geriatric day rehabilita-tion unit twice a week and will pay for her rehabilitation services at the unit until she meets her rehabilitation goals. This generally includes paying for adapted equipment and assistive technology that might be prescribed.

text: Maria gathered the following information from Astrid’s medical record and through informal observation dur-ing the interview. Maria did not attempt to otherwise evaluate Astrid’s body functions; she reasoned that she would do that later in the OT intervention process when she reached the step in the OTIPM where she would, as needed, clarify the reasons for Astrid’s problems of occu-pational performance (see Fig. 5.­1). She also was aware that the physical therapist’s role is to evaluate Astrid’s underlying physical capacities (e.g., strength, range of motion) and functional mobility. Immediately poststroke, Astrid presented with right-­ sided hemiparesis, aphasia, and low arousal secondary to cerebral edema. She also presented with fatigue and depression (which was treated medically). Currently,

text: Astrid’s biggest limitations are reported to be her mem-ory problems and her decreased ability to use her right arm and hand. During the interview, Maria did note that Astrid can now move her right arm and grip objects with her right hand, but her arm movements still seemed to be “stiff,” perhaps with limited range of motion. Astrid also mentioned that she has pain in her right shoulder, mak-ing it hard for her to reach for objects, especially those that are stored overhead. Astrid has insufficient strength and postural control to be able to walk independently or safely. She also continues to fatigue easily. Finally, Astrid continues to have expressive aphasia. She speaks with many pauses but uses “high-­ content” words and gestures that Maria judged to accurately convey Astrid’s intended message (e.g., “Me…too hard…now”). Astrid also seemed to consistently understand the mes-sages Maria or her ex-­husband, Emil, sent.

text: On an ordinary day, Astrid’s routine starts when a staff member at the comfort living complex comes in at 7:30 am and wakes her up. The staff member then helps to transfer her to her wheelchair, go into the bathroom, and transfer onto the toilet. She then transfers herself to the shower stool and receives help with showering and then dressing. After the staff member makes her breakfast, she eats and reads the daily newspaper. She then lies down to rest until lunchtime. A staff member then returns, helps her to the bathroom, and makes her lunch. After lunch, Astrid usually has a session with a staff member during which she practices walking with her rolling walker. In the afternoons, she often has visitors. On the days when her visitors do not come, a staff member comes and pre-pares for Astrid an open-­faced sandwich and a cup of cof-fee. Astrid then rests again before dinner, when a staff member comes to her room, helps her to the bathroom, and prepares her dinner. In the evening, she watches TV and reads the newspaper. She goes to bed around 9:00 pm when a staff member arrives and assists her with undress-ing and transferring into bed. Finally, Astrid takes a taxi to geriatric day rehabilitation two afternoons every week (between 1:00 and 3:00 pm).

text: Develop Therapeutic Rapport and Work Collaboratively with the Client When Maria met Astrid and Emil, they started to develop therapeutic rapport and identify the persons to include in the client constellation and subsequent collaborative rela-tionship during the intervention process. Although Emil was a source of support for Astrid, he did not have prob-lems with occupational performance in relation to Astrid, so the “client” was determined to be only Astrid. Emil’s role was to confirm what Astrid tried to say and to pro-vide her with moral support. In fact, Astrid managed the interview to a great extent by herself and only occasion-ally looked to Emil for support. To support the develop-ment of rapport and a strong collaborative relationship, Maria keenly listened to what Astrid (and Emil) had to say, and she showed empathy for the situations that Astrid described. Maria was aware that fostering their relation-ship early in the interview process would support their ongoing collaboration.

text: Astrid is a 72-­year-­old woman who lives in a small apartment in a comfort living complex for elderly adults and that provides around-­the-­clock support services. Her apartment is adapted to accommodate for functional limitations (e.g., rails on the bed, raised toilet seat with armrests, shower stool). She has the sup-port of her ex-­husband, who manages her finances. She has a well-­established daily routine and is motivated to be as inde-pendent performing daily life tasks as is possible (e.g., cooking, self-­care). text: prioritize for further evaluation and intervention. Maria chose to use the ADL Taxonomy to guide this part of the OT interview because she thought that doing so would provide Astrid with a structure that would sup-port her in identifying and prioritizing what she viewed as her most important problems with daily occupational performances. Because Astrid has both aphasia and some memory loss, Maria believed it would be too difficult to use the COPM. After administering the ADL Taxonomy during the OT interview, Maria learned that although Astrid is able to eat using a fork, she requires help from the comfort liv-ing staff to cut up foods that must be cut using a knife, and she is unable to eat using a knife and fork. Astrid requires assistance with dressing, toileting, showering, and meal preparation. She also requires verbal and standby assis-tance to transfer to and from her wheelchair when getting in and out of bed or on and off the toilet. She is now able to manage her grooming (e.g., brushing teeth, combing her hair) independently. When her friends visit, they must prepare their own coffee and serve the coffee with cook-ies, in part because Astrid is unable to reach for and gather objects from the cupboards above the kitchen counter or from the upper shelves in the refrigerator. Astrid is unable to manage her own finances, and she cannot clean her apartment or do her shopping. Finally, Astrid is unable to access the shared dining room, library, TV room, and spa unit because of her inability to propel her wheelchair the required distance or walk independently with her rolling walker. When Maria asked Astrid which tasks she wanted to prioritize, Astrid reported that she wanted to be able to make coffee and serve the coffee with cookies for her friends, make her own breakfast (e.g., oatmeal), make an open-­faced sandwich, and eat while simultaneously using a knife and a fork. Astrid also said that she wanted to be able to walk with her rolling walker and write with her right hand. Maria, however, was aware that these were not task performances per se. Rather, Maria rec-ognized that she needed to maintain her occupation-­ centered perspective and enable Astrid to focus on the tasks she wanted to perform that would require her to walk with her walker or to write. When Maria did so, Astrid was able to clarify that she believed that one rea-son she could not make coffee or breakfast was because she could not walk and carry task objects; thus, Maria recognized that being able to walk with her rolling walker while performing kitchen tasks was actually part of those kitchen task performances. Astrid also clarified that she wanted to be able to write short notes to her-self. Maria, with her occupation-­centered perspective, recognized that writing notes may well become possible using adaptive strategies rather than writing with her right hand but that “writing notes” is occupation; using her right hand to write is related to underlying body functions, not occupation.

text: Observe Client’s Performance of Prioritized Tasks and Implement Performance Analyses Now that Maria had learned what daily life tasks Astrid reported as problems and wanted to prioritize, Maria’s next step in the OT intervention process was to observe Astrid perform some of those tasks. Maria, therefore, shared with Astrid that she would like to observe Astrid perform two of the tasks she was most concerned about during their next session together. She also clarified that doing so would enable her to better understand Astrid’s problems with occupational performance so that they could then determine together what interventions might be most appropriate. Astrid agreed. Because many task options were included in the AMPS manual that were culturally relevant and that matched ones Astrid had prioritized, Maria further clarified, “I would like to use a standardized evaluation tool, the Assess-ment of Motor and Process Skills, or AMPS, when I observe you. If you agree, you could choose which two of the tasks included in the AMPS you would like to perform. For example, I could observe you eat using a knife and fork, or I could observe you make a sandwich or as you prepare a bowl of oatmeal. I know that your friends are helping you when you have coffee and cookies together, so it might also be helpful if I observe you making a pot of coffee. text: tized tasks that she had reported to have challenges per-forming, but that they would not be so challenging that Astrid would be unable to perform them without maxi-mum support. Maria was aware, however, that she could still evaluate Astrid’s quality of ADL task performance using the AMPS even if Astrid needed occasional to fre-quent assistance. Finally, Maria reasoned that because Astrid needed help to prepare a pot of coffee and serve it with cookies, the much harder task (AMPS task C-­4) that involved preparing oatmeal, a sandwich, and a beverage might be too challenging. Maria also realized that the AMPS task P-­1 related to eating a meal is much easier than average on the AMPS hierarchy of task challenge. Although the person is expected to use a knife and fork to either cut food or put a spread (e.g., butter, jam) on bread or toast, there is no expectation that the person must eat “Swedish” or “Euro-pean” style. Thus, Maria was concerned that this task might be too easy for Astrid. Maria therefore prepared to observe Astrid performing any of the remaining eight tasks on her list of potential task options that were either aver-age or a little harder than average in task challenge. 16,17 Maintaining her client-­centered perspective, she wanted Astrid to decide which two ADL tasks to perform. Maria’s next step was to ensure that all the needed tools and materials for these tasks were available in the clinic kitchen. For example, she wanted to ensure that there would be both oats and rye flakes in the kitchen so that there would be at least one other option for cooked cereal. Maria also wanted to ensure that there would be (1) several beverages in the refrigerator, including lingonberry juice, orange juice, and apple juice; (2) milk; and (3) a variety of sweeteners (sugar, artificial sweetener). For the sandwich tasks, she wanted to ensure that there would be both soft breads (white, whole grain) and hard bread (rye crisp), a variety of spreads (butter, liverpaste), cheese, meat, and so on. For the coffee tasks, she checked the clinic kitchen to be sure that the coffee maker was available and that there would be ground coffee, coffee filters, and cook-ies. Finally, she verified that the cupboards, drawers, and refrigerator were equipped with typically available tools and materials, including bowls, plates, glasses, coffee cups, and cutlery as well as unrelated food supplies such as boxes of dry cereal and pasta in the cupboards and jars of pickles, mustard, and jam in the refrigerator. When she was done, Maria made a list of things that were not available so she could make arrangements to order them from the hospital kitchen or bring them in from outside the hospital. When Maria and Astrid met at their next visit, they reviewed their plan for Maria to observe Astrid perform-ing two ADL tasks, and Maria offered Astrid the option to prepare oatmeal and a beverage, make an open-­faced sandwich, or prepare a pot of brewed coffee. Astrid chose to make the oatmeal and an open-­faced sandwich. Maria then clarified that Astrid could make any one of a vari-ety of sandwiches, including one with liverpaste or one with sliced meat or cheese. Astrid indicated a preference to make an open-­faced sandwich with cheese. Maria then proceeded to implement her two AMPS task observations, beginning with the setup of the envi-ronment, summarizing for Astrid what she had agreed to do, and then observing Astrid while taking observational notes. These two AMPS observations are summarized in the next sections.

text: When Astrid and Maria set up the environment before her performance of the first AMPS task, Maria ensured that Astrid was completely familiarized with the clinic kitchen, including what tools and materials were available, where they were located, and how any equipment she might use was operated (e.g., water taps, electric appliances). As part of this process, Astrid, with help from Maria when needed, rearranged the kitchen so that objects were placed in loca-tions as similar to how she would have them at home as was possible. This included ensuring that objects located high in the cupboards were placed on lower shelves where Astrid could reach them. Maria also made sure that Astrid opened and closed all of the cupboard doors she could reach, the drawers where the cutlery and other tools were stored, and the refrigerator where the milk and juice were stored. As Astrid became familiar with and rearranged the clinic kitchen, Maria asked Astrid exactly what type of hot cooked cereal and what type of beverage she would pre-pare. text: in a bowl with milk and white sugar over the oatmeal, and she chose to pour and serve a glass of lingonberry juice. Astrid also clarified that she planned to put salt in the water she would use to cook the oatmeal. Just before starting the task observation, Maria sum-marized for Astrid what she had said she would do. She also ensured that Astrid was aware she could ask for help if she needed it. Maria then stepped back and began to take notes to record what she observed. Maintaining her occupation-­centered perspective, Maria wrote down only the task actions she observed (e.g., effort reaching for the spoon), not the reason why (e.g., spasticity in her right arm). The following is a narrative summary of what Maria observed. The relevant ADL motor and ADL process skills (AMPS items) observed are noted in parentheses. When Astrid attempted to move her wheelchair and position herself at the counter, she demonstrated mod-erate to marked physical effort (Moves). She often posi-tioned herself with her left side toward the counter, and when she attempted to reach for task objects with her right hand, she demonstrated increased effort reaching across her body to obtain them (Positions). Although she was stable when sitting in her wheelchair (Stabilizes), she persistently leaned far back in her wheelchair (Aligns), resulting in her demonstrating increased physical effort when she bent forward and reached with her left hand for the bag of oats and the glass that were stored in the cup-boards (Bends, Reaches). Leaning far back in her wheelchair (Aligns) resulted in similar problems bending and reach-ing forward for the milk and juice that were stored in the refrigerator (Bends, Reaches). She generally searched for and located task objects (Searches/Locates) and then grasped and lifted them using her left hand without problems (Grips, Lifts). However, she chose orange juice instead of the lingonberry juice she had said she would use (Chooses), and she slid the bag of oats, the bowl, and the pan along the countertop rather than lifting them (Lifts). Moreover, when she attempted to transport the milk, juice, bowl, and sugar to her workspace, she was only able to transport one object at a time (Transports). When she gathered the things she needed, she placed most of them so close together at her workspace on the kitchen counter (Organizes) that she bumped her left elbow into the milk carton (Navigates) when she reached over other task objects to pick up the jar of juice; the milk carton almost fell onto the floor. She also gathered the jar of juice to her main workspace, and she gathered the glass to another workspace on the opposite side of the sink (Gathers, Organizes), resulting in her having to go get the glass and bring it closer to the jar of juice when she was ready to pour a glass of juice (Adjusts). When she attempted to open the jar of juice, holding the jar in her left hand and trying to turn the lid with her right hand, the lid repeatedly slipped in her hand (Grips, Coordinates); Maria judged that she needed to intervene and provide Astrid assistance to open the jar.
