text: Astrid was also moderately ineffective when she attempted to scoop the oats from the bag with a measur-ing cup held in her right hand; she did not fully open up the bag (Terminates); she did not support the bag, and it tipped sideways (Handles) and some of the oats fell onto the floor (Notices/Responds); and she repeatedly bumped the measuring cup into the side of the bag when she attempted to insert it into the bag (Navigates). She also occasionally hesitated before she started the next step action (Initiates). For example, she hesitated before she started to open up the bag of oats and again just before she reached for and grasped the measuring cup with her right hand. When she did start to grasp the measuring cup, she fumbled it between her fingers (Manipulates) and needed to try again to grasp it more securely (Grips). As she continued to try to scoop oats out of the bag with the measuring cup held in her right hand, the measuring cup kept slipping in her hand (Grips), and her arm and hand movements were somewhat jerky and stiff (Flows). After several tries with her right hand, she stopped, hesitated, and then moved the bag of oats to her right hand and the measuring cup to her left hand (Continues). After she switched the measuring cup to her left hand, she scooped out the correct amount of oats from the bag (Terminates). Astrid then asked where the salt was, and Maria gave her a general cue, “Why don’t you see if you can find it?” because Maria was aware that Astrid had placed the salt in the cupboard beside the sink and knew, therefore, where the salt was stored before the task observation started (Inquires, Searches/Locates). Maria also reasoned that if Astrid continued to not be able to find the salt, she could always step in and help her, but doing so now would pre-maturely result in lowering even further Astrid’s scores on Inquires and Searches/Locates. Astrid proceeded to look for the salt, opening two other cupboard doors before she found it (Searches/Locates). Astrid used her left hand and opened and closed the cupboard doors without observable problems (Moves). When Astrid began to serve the cooked oatmeal into the bowl, she initially tried to scoop the oatmeal with her right hand, but the spoon slipped from her grasp (Grips); she then paused and switched the serving spoon to her left hand (Continues). Because she did not stabilize the pan with her right hand while she was scooping, the pan slid on the counter as she scooped out the oatmeal (Coordi-nates, Handles). Maria cued her because she was afraid the pan might fall onto her lap. When Astrid poured the orange juice into the glass, she held the jar in her left hand and tipped the bottle with so much force that some orange juice spilled onto the counter (Calibrates). She then proceeded to fill the glass so full that more juice almost spilled over the rim of the glass (Ter-minates). Finally, after Astrid had served the oatmeal and the juice at the table, she proceeded to restore all items to their original storage places, but she did not wipe up all of the spilled oats (Restores). text: Because it took Astrid so long to prepare the oatmeal, Maria and Astrid decided to implement the second AMPS observation at Astrid’s next visit. When Maria initiated her observation of Astrid’s second AMPS task, she again began by having Astrid set up the environment and clarify-ing with Astrid exactly what ingredients she planned to use when she made her cheese sandwich. For example, when they set up the environment, Maria made sure that Astrid had tried to open all cupboards and drawers, including the refrigerator door, and that Astrid knew the location of all the things she needed. She also made sure that all tools and materials needed for this task were moved from the upper cupboards down to locations that were within reach when Astrid was sitting in her wheelchair. This meant that Maria obtained the objects from the upper cupboards and gave them to Astrid to put where she wanted them, in locations as similar to her own kitchen as possible. As Astrid put away the cheese, bread, and vegetables, Maria asked Astrid which cheese (Gouda, cheddar, or Jarlsberg), bread (white or whole grain), and vegetable (cucumber or tomato) she wanted to use. Astrid chose to use Gouda cheese, whole grain bread, and cucumber. Maria also ensured that Astrid understood that she was to use butter (as is typical in Sweden) and serve the sandwich on a plate. After Astrid had set up the task environment and Maria had determined what ingredients Astrid would use for her sandwich, Maria again summarized for Astrid what she had said she would do: “You said you were going to make a cheese sandwich with cucumber on whole grain bread, put butter on the bread, and serve the sandwich on a plate. When you are done, put everything away, wipe up any spills, and let me know when you are done. If you need any help, just ask.” Maria then stepped back and took notes to record what she observed Astrid doing. The following summarizes what Maria observed; relevant AMPS items are again noted in parentheses. When Astrid attempted to move her wheelchair within the kitchen, she again demonstrated moderate to marked physical effort (Moves). Each time she went to the refrig-erator to get the ingredients for her sandwich, she posi-tioned herself too far from the refrigerator (Positions). She also sat leaning far back in her wheelchair (Aligns), and when she bent forward and reached with her left hand for the Gouda cheese and the butter from the refrigerator, she demonstrated moderate physical effort (Reaches, Bends). There also was a mild delay before Astrid located the butter when she was searching for it in the refrigerator (Searches/Locates). After she got the cheese and the but-ter, she asked Maria, “Vegetable…which one?” (Inquires). Maria, consistent with the standardized criteria for admin-istering the AMPS, answered vaguely by saying, “Use the one that you said you would use.” Again, Maria reasoned that if she cued Astrid by telling her to use cucumber, it would result in the need to further lower some of Astrid’s scores. Astrid then went to the refrigerator and chose a tomato rather than the cucumber she had said she would use (Chooses). Taking separate trips to the refrigerator to do so, Astrid grasped and lifted the cheese, butter, and tomato without problems using her left hand and placed each of them in her lap (Grips, Lifts). After Astrid had the cheese, butter, or tomato in her lap and attempted to transport each of them to her workspace, she again demonstrated moder-ate to marked effort and moderate inefficiency moving her wheelchair (Moves); she was only able to transport one task object at a time (Transports). When she positioned herself at her workspace, she again sat diagonally in relation to the counter, with her left side closer to the counter than her right side (Posi-tions). She often attempted to use her right hand to place task objects onto the counter, and when she did so, she demonstrated increased physical effort reaching (Reaches), her arm and hand movements were somewhat jerky and stiff (Flows), and the task objects frequently slipped from her grasp (Grips). She gathered related task objects to the same workspace (e.g., butter and butter knife, cheese and cheese slicer), but she placed task objects very close together, crowding her workspace (Organizes). She occa-sionally bumped her hand into task objects (Navigates), and she placed the butter so close to the edge of the counter that it almost fell onto the floor (Notices/Responds). When she tried to spread the butter on the sandwich, holding the knife in her right hand and stabilizing the bread with her left hand, the knife slipped from her grasp (Grips, Coordi-nates). As she continued to spread the butter, she did so with somewhat stiff arm and hand movements (Flows), and she put so much pressure downward on the bread that the bread started to tear (Calibrates). Moreover, she did not always stabilize the bread on the counter, result-ing in the bread almost falling into her lap (Handles). She then paused her task performance, switched the knife to her left hand, and proceeded to finish buttering the bread (Continues). She demonstrated similar problems related to task objects slipping from her hand (knife, cheese slicer) and stiff arm movements when she tried to use her right hand to slice the tomato and slice the cheese while she stabi-lized them with her left hand (Grips, Coordinates, Flows). She often paused before starting the next task action (e.g., starting to slice the tomato, starting to reach for the cheese)

She considered Astrid’s observable overall level of physical effort or clumsiness, efficiency, safety, and independence. Maria was aware that later, after she had scored the AMPS, she would write specific baseline statements and that they would provide a more detailed description of which task actions were effective or ineffective. 12 After discussing with Astrid her overall impressions of Astrid’s quality of ADL task perfor-mance, Maria wrote the following, which she planned to insert into the OTAP software so that it would be included in the AMPS Results Report she would generate using the OTAP software.

text: Define and Describe Task Actions the Client Does and Does Not Perform Effectively Maria reasoned that defining and describing what actions Astrid had and had not performed effectively required that she go through four steps. In the first step, she would score the AMPS items for each task Astrid had performed. In the second step, Maria would select the AMPS items that best reflected Astrid’s strengths and problems with occupational performance. In the third step, Maria would group these AMPS items into clus-ters and write summary statements that she would use to document Astrid’s specific baseline levels of occupational performance. Finally, in the fourth step, Maria would enter Astrid’s data into the OTAP software, generate an AMPS Results Report, and interpret Astrid’s AMPS observation results from a criterion-­ referenced and a norm-­referenced perspective. Maria planned to share a copy of Astrid’s AMPS Results Report with Astrid when she came for her next visit.

text: When Maria scored Astrid’s quality of ADL task perfor-mance, she used the criteria in the AMPS manual to score each AMPS item = 4, 3, 2, or 1. 16,17 More specifically, the ADL motor and ADL process skills Astrid performed effectively were scored 4 (competent) or 3 (question-able, but no apparent disruption). ADL motor and ADL process skills Astrid performed ineffectively were scored 2 (ineffective, clear disruption in her ADL task perfor-mance) or 1 (severe; marked physical effort or fatigue, marked inefficiency, markedly unsafe, need for verbal or physical assistance).

text: After Maria had scored the AMPS and written her spe-cific baseline summary statements, she proceeded to enter Astrid’s data into the OTAP software. More spe-cifically, in addition to her demographic data (e.g., age, diagnosis), Maria entered her AMPS item ratings for each ADL task and the global and specific baseline state-ments she had written. When she was done, she gener-ated Astrid’s AMPS Results Report (Fig. 5.­3). As we will discuss later in this chapter, Maria also entered part of her documentation of Astrid’s goals and her intervention plan into the OTAP software. As a result, they are also shown in Figure. 5.­3. After Maria had generated Astrid’s AMPS Results Report, she was ready to proceed to interpreting the results from both a criterion-­ referenced and a norm-­ referenced perspective. She decided to start by review-ing the Overview of and Interpretation Guidelines for the Assessment of Motor and Process Skills included in her OTAP software (also available from http://www. innovativeotsolutions.com/content/wp-­c ontent/uploa ds/2014/01/AMPSReportSupplement.pdf). This docu-ment describes the AMPS, how it is scored, and how the person’s raw AMPS item scores are transformed into linear measures of ADL motor and ADL process ability. Additional sections discuss how criterion-­referenced and norm-­referenced interpretations of the AMPS measures are made, how to determine if the person’s AMPS mea-sures have improved at time of reevaluation, and how the AMPS measures can contribute to predicting if a person needs assistance to live in the community. Maria focused her attention on the sections describing criterion-­ referenced and norm-­referenced interpretations as well as predicting need for assistance to live in the community.

text: When Maria reviewed Astrid’s AMPS Results Report, she started by looking at where Astrid’s linearized ADL motor and ADL process ability measures were located along the respective AMPS scale (see Fig. 5.­3). It was clear to Maria that Astrid’s ADL motor and ADL process ability mea-sures were well below the criterion-­referenced cutoffs that indicate that the person demonstrated at least some degree of clumsiness or increased physical effort (i.e., below the ADL motor cutoff at 2 logits) or some degree of ineffi-ciency (time-­space disorganization) (i.e., below the ADL process cutoff at 1 logit). But Maria was more interested to know the criterion-­ referenced range of quality of ADL task performance commonly observed among persons whose AMPS mea-sures are at the same location along the AMPS scales as were Astrid’s ADL motor and ADL process ability measures. For example, Maria noted that Astrid’s ADL motor ability measure was in the range along the ADL motor scale where most people are observed to have moderate to marked clumsiness or increased physical effort or fatigue. This matched the overall quality of ADL task performance Maria had observed; Astrid did not demonstrate any fatigue, but she did have moderate to marked physical effort, especially when trying to use task objects held in her right hand and when she moved her wheelchair. Astrid’s ADL process ability measure was located in the range along the ADL process scale where most people are observed to have moderate inefficiency or disorganization when performing ADL tasks. This result also matched Maria’s observations of Astrid.

text: Maria then proceeded to interpret Astrid’s AMPS results from a norm-­referenced perspective. Clearly, Astrid’s quality of ADL task performance was below age expectations. That is, her ADL motor and ADL process ability measures were located well below the vertical bands (to the left of the AMPS scales) depicting the expected range (mean ±2 standard deviations [SDs]) for nondisabled persons of Astrid’s age (see Fig. 5.­3). The table on page 1 of Figure. 5.­3 indicates that her ADL motor and ADL process ability measures (− ­0.3 logit and 0.0 logits, respectively) were both more than 3 SDs below the normative mean. This table also indi-cates that more than 99% of well persons of Astrid’s age would be expected to have AMPS ability measures higher than hers. More information about the AMPS scales and criterion-­ referenced cutoff measures and ranges can be found in the AMPS manual. 16

text: Astrid’s AMPS observation could be used to support Astrid’s likely need for continued support from the Swedish health care system (e.g., home health services for house cleaning; assistance from the staff at the comfort living complex). Maria was aware that her professional judgment, and that of the entire team, was that Astrid needed the help she cur-rently was getting, and they suspected she may continue to need some help even after discharge. Maria also knew that although the AMPS is a test of ADL ability, not level of assistance needed for community living, the results of an AMPS observation only can be used to provide support for other information that might be available (according to the AMPS manual 16; see also Overview of and Interpretation Guidelines for the Assessment of Motor and Process Skills avail-able from http://www.innovativeotsolutions.com/content /wp-­content/uploads/2014/AMPSReportSupplement.pdf.) If a person has an ADL motor ability measure below 1.0 logit (Astrid’s was −0.3 logit) and an ADL process ability measure below 0.7 logit (Astrid’s was 0.0 logits), there is a high likelihood that the person needs assistance for com-munity living. Maria planned to share this information with the rehabilitation team when they next met together with Astrid because they likely would want to take this aspect of her AMPS observation results into consideration when they considered Astrid’s common rehabilitation team goals.

text: Establish, Finalize, or Redefine Client-­ Centered and Occupation-­Focused Goals Now that Maria had interpreted Astrid’s AMPS obser-vation results, she planned to meet with Astrid at their next meeting and share the results with Astrid. She sug-gested to Astrid that if she wanted either Emil or one of her daughters to be there, it might be helpful for one of them to join her. Maria was aware of Astrid’s continuing problems with aphasia and memory, so she reasoned that perhaps it would be important for someone close to her to also hear what Maria and Astrid discussed. Astrid came to the next meeting with her daughter. When Maria shared her observations with Astrid and her daughter, she started by sharing some of her key observa-tions, the ones she had summarized in her global and spe-cific baseline statements. She also asked Astrid about her perceptions of her own performance to see if they concurred overall; they did. Maria then proceeded to use that informa-tion to initiate a collaborative goal-­setting process between Astrid and herself. In this process, Maria supported Astrid to express her goals in her own words, and then Maria built on that, suggesting alternative ways to express Astrid’s goals in a way that would be realistic, attainable, observable, mea-surable, and occupation focused. For example, Astrid continued to express a desire to be able to prepare her own sandwiches and breakfast. Maria, therefore, helped Astrid formulate her goal to perform such tasks independently. text: performance of these tasks (e.g., pan almost falling into Astrid’s lap) and suggested that safety also be an impor-tant part of Astrid’s goal. With her daughter’s encour-agement, Astrid agreed that safety was an important outcome. After they had formulated Astrid’s goal related to preparing simple meals, they also proceeded to discuss important subgoals related to preparing simple meals. Maria and Astrid discussed the specific baseline state-ments that Maria had written, and they collaborated to develop subgoals based on those. Astrid also continued to express a desire to prepare cof-fee and cookies for her friends. Based on what Maria had observed and knowing that preparing coffee and cook-ies would be even harder than the ADL tasks she had observed, she reasoned together with Astrid that a more realistic goal, at least for now, was to manage that task with supervision or minimal assistance instead of doing it independently. Finally, Astrid continued to express a desire to eat independently using a knife and fork held simultaneously in her hands, so they also included that goal. Maria was aware, however, that without first imple-menting a performance analysis and establishing Astrid’s baseline level of performance, it was not appropriate to document these as finalized goals. Instead, Maria would document them as preliminary goals. When they were done, Maria first documented Astrid’s global goal and her specific subgoals related to preparing simple meals because they pertained directly to Astrid’s AMPS observation. Maria also entered that global goal and the specific subgoals into the OTAP software so they would be included in Astrid’s final AMPS Results Report (see Fig. 5.­3). text: Now that Maria had evaluated and documented Astrid’s quality of ADL task performance, she was ready to clarify or interpret the reason(s) for Astrid’s problems of occu-pational performance (see Fig. 5.­1). Maria was aware that the conceptual model of the AMPS (Fig. 5.­4) stresses that many factors may contribute to a person’s quality of occu-pational performance, including the demands of the tasks the person performs, the demands of the environment, underlying person factors and body functions, and soci-etal and cultural influences. In the end, however, Maria knew that she needed to use her professional reasoning to speculate about the most likely causes of Astrid’s problems performing the two ADL tasks she had observed. 12,13 When Maria looked through her notes that summarized the 10 dimensions of the client-­ centered performance

text: context, what she had documented in Astrid’s medical record, and the information she had gathered from the other members of the team, Maria assumed that Astrid’s biggest problems were most likely due to her limited underlying physical capacities and her memory impair-ments that she had acquired after her stroke 5 months earlier (body function dimension). For example, Maria assumed that residual hemiparesis in her right arm limited Astrid’s ability to use that arm effectively when grasping or otherwise interacting with task objects and that poor postural control or weakness in her trunk muscles was the reason Astrid persistently leaned back in her wheelchair. When Maria considered reasons why Astrid asked where the salt was located and then looked into several cupboards to find it and why Astrid chose orange juice instead of lingonberry juice and tomato instead of cucum-ber, Maria’s first guess was that these problems were due to Astrid’s residual memory impairments because such problems with ADL task performance are common among persons with memory impairments, including Alzheimer’s disease 10,16; persons who have had strokes associated with cognitive impairments also can display similar problems. 16 But still, Maria could not be sure that perhaps Astrid “just changed her mind” or perhaps she had gotten the orange juice and the tomato because they were a bit closer to her when she reached for them. Maria also reasoned that environmental factors may have affected Astrid’s quality of ADL task performance, especially her ability to effectively move her wheelchair. That is, although limited use of her right hand and foot may have had some impact, Maria was aware that most clients with hemiparesis are much more effective in mov-ing their wheelchairs than was Astrid. In Astrid’s case, her wheelchair was quite high, making it hard for her to reach the floor with her feet. Finally, Maria was aware that Astrid had been evaluated in the outpatient clinic kitchen and that it would be important for her to arrange to visit Astrid’s home and implement an evaluation of her home environment to see what barriers might be present. Maria documented the following in Astrid’s medical record.

text: • Restorative models: The planning and implementation of restorative occupations focused on the client restoring, developing, or maintaining person factors or underly-ing body functions in the context of performing rele-vant daily life tasks (e.g., increasing grip strength in the context of performing simple meal preparation tasks that require the use of the affected hand to grasp task objects, maintaining memory through engaging in card games that require the use of memory) (see Fig. 5.­7). Restorative occupation is occupation based because the client is engaged in meaningful occupation, but it is never occupation focused because the proximal or immediate intended outcome is improved person fac-tors or body functions (e.g., grip strength, memory). 13 As Maria considered which models of practice to choose, she recalled both what she knew about Astrid and the suggestions available in the AMPS manual regarding what approaches might be most effective with clients who have differing levels of ADL motor and ADL process abil-ity. For example, Maria was aware that Astrid’s previous occupational therapist had reported that Astrid’s cognitive limitations limited her ability to learn new, compensa-tory strategies, but Maria did not know if Astrid’s former occupational therapist was referring specifically to learn-ing compensatory or other types of adaptive strategies. She also was aware that, according to the suggestions in the AMPS manual, 16 when a client’s ADL process ability mea-sure is at or below 0.0 logits, he or she may more readily benefit from adaptive strategies based on the provision of structured supports or assistance from others than adaptive occupation that emphasizes learning new compensatory strategies; Astrid’s ADL process measure was 0.0 logits. Moreover, Astrid’s low ADL motor and ADL process abil-ity measures may indicate that Astrid has limited potential to relearn occupational skill through occupational skills training based on the acquisitional model. Finally, Maria was aware that these guidelines from the AMPS manual are based on a “review of the literature and clinical experi-ence. Thus, each occupational therapist must base his or her own decisions on the available evidence supporting cost-­effective improvements of occupational performance in relation to the clients with which he or she works.” 16 Based on this information, Maria decided to try using both acquisitional occupational skills training and intro-ducing compensatory and other adaptive strategies (e.g., adapted equipment), but she reasoned that she would do so cautiously and carefully monitor Astrid’s progress to be sure she benefited from either or both. Maria believed that the use of restorative occupation was not appropriate, partly because she knew that Astrid and her physical ther-apist were focusing on Astrid’s shoulder mobility, postural control, and ability to walk using her rolling walker and partly because she reasoned that Astrid was unlikely to regain much more underlying functions in her right arm or hand. Finally, Maria reasoned that if there was a need to provide an in-­service for the staff at the comfort liv-ing complex, she might try to arrange a session with them where she could orient them to more effective strategies to use to help residents like Astrid. Maria’s next step was to consider Astrid’s goal related to simple meal preparation and then each of her subgoals. She developed the following preliminary ideas for an intervention plan that she planned to discuss with Astrid in order to gather any ideas that Astrid might have, as well as her opinions about how she preferred to proceed with her OT services.

She especially liked the idea of trying a different wheelchair. Astrid commented, “This [pointing to her wheelchair]…too high.” Maria supported Astrid’s experience, commenting that she had observed that one of Astrid’s biggest struggles during both of the tasks she had observed was propelling herself effec-tively. Moreover, if Astrid could not move around in the kitchen more effectively, it would be hard for her to reach her other goals. text: After Maria and Astrid agreed on an intervention plan, Maria initially changed the seat cushion in Astrid’s wheel-chair to one that was not so thick. When Astrid tried it, she was immediately able to propel herself forward both effec-tively and quickly by using her feet, but she did not like it and wanted to change back to her higher cushion. Maria then suggested and Astrid tried out a wheelchair that had a lower seat, but that too was unsuccessful. Astrid did not like sitting so low, and it remained difficult for her to propel. By this point in her rehabilitation, Astrid had made progress with the physical therapist, and she was now able to walk longer distances with minimal physical assistance using her rolling walker. Because Maria wanted to take this into account, she reviewed Astrid’s current status and what she had learned when she had implemented her initial OT evaluation (through all the steps of the evaluation and goal-­ setting phase of the OTIPM) and reached the conclusion that Astrid might be able to use a rolling work chair, with a brake and adjustable-­height seat (Fig. 5.­8). Maria’s idea was that if Astrid tried and liked the rolling work chair, she could use it within her apartment, including when perform-ing tasks in her kitchen. Maria reasoned that the rolling work chair would likely make it easier for Astrid to reach up into the refrigerator and upper cupboards. Moreover, Maria still found it hard to imagine that Astrid would learn to walk safely and independently, at least in the near future, and if Astrid was going to be able to reach her global goal, to prepare simple meals safely and independently, she would need to be able to perform such tasks from a sitting posi-tion. When Maria shared her thoughts with Astrid, Astrid thought that a rolling work chair sounded like a good idea. Maria arranged, therefore, for Astrid to borrow a rolling work chair from the Assistive Technology Department, and Astrid received the rolling work chair in time for her next visit to the geriatric day rehabilitation unit. The chair needed to be adjusted to fit Astrid, and she needed training in how to maneuver and use it in a safe manner (i.e., lock-ing the brakes before sitting down onto the seat, before standing up, and when raising the seat to the highest level [maximum seat height, 75 cm]). Maria therefore contin-ued to use educational principles within the compensatory model as she oriented Astrid to the features of the roll-ing work chair and provided her with the opportunity to practice and begin to learn how to use it (e.g., moving in it around the kitchen, locking and unlocking the brake when appropriate). text: be able to use the rolling work chair safely and indepen-dently even if she still had to transport task objects one at a time. After this initial practice phase, Astrid was ready to begin to practice and learn to use the rolling work chair in the context of occupation-­based adaptive occupation (i.e., preparing oatmeal, making a sandwich). At this point, Maria had begun to realize that the staff at the comfort living complex was often giving Astrid “too much help,” not allowing her to do as much as she was able. At the same time, Maria reasoned that she would need to provide the staff education and follow-­up supervi-sion related to how to support Astrid when she used the rolling work chair, how to operate the chair, and how to use it in a safe manner while still allowing Astrid to inde-pendently perform the task actions she could perform without their help. Maria therefore arranged for a short in-­service with the key members of the support staff. Dur-ing this session, Maria demonstrated the features of the rolling work chair and how to ensure that the brake was locked when Astrid sat down or stood up. She also dis-cussed with those who were present the importance of not providing Astrid with more help than actually was needed. At the end of this educational session (educational model), Maria arranged a follow-­up visit with the staff so she could provide them with additional consultative support related to using the rolling work chair and providing assistance only when needed (compensatory model). To save time and lower costs, Maria scheduled the follow-­up visit with the staff at the comfort living com-plex on the same day that she would evaluate Astrid’s home environment. In this way, Maria could supervise the staff assisting Astrid with the rolling work chair while also becoming aware of how Astrid had her home orga-nized. More specifically, Maria’s ability to make home visits was constrained by the Swedish health care system. This meant that it was necessary to implement Astrid’s rehabilitation at the geriatric day rehabilitation unit, not in Astrid’s kitchen in the comfort living complex. She was allowed, however, to make one or two home visits during which she, together with Astrid, could evaluate Astrid’s home environment and make subsequent modifications they determined were necessary (e.g., relocating where tools and materials were stored). Then, when she knew exactly how Astrid’s kitchen was arranged, she and Astrid could also further rearrange the kitchen in the clinic to be as similar to Astrid’s as possible (e.g., moving needed objects to locations that imitated the situation in Astrid’s home). If she did return on a subsequent home visit, Maria would continue to consult with the staff members working with Astrid and ask them how they thought it was going when they were working with Astrid and her new rolling work chair.

text: After the home visit and evaluating Astrid’s home envi-ronment, it became obvious to Maria that she and Astrid needed to reorganize some of the cupboards in not only the clinic kitchen but also in Astrid’s kitchen. If Astrid was going to be able to readily reach the objects she wanted to use from her rolling work chair, some changes would be needed. Yet in both the clinic and Astrid’s home, there was limited ability to make all modifications that might be ideal. For example, the location of certain electrical appliances was limited by the locations of the electrical outlets, and the locations of the sinks and refrigerators in each kitchen differed. Nevertheless, Astrid and Maria were able to work together to arrange both environments to be more accessible to Astrid, and in the end, they were quite similar. When they were done, Astrid was able to reach for all of the task tools and materials she needed to prepare oatmeal or sandwiches. During the time they worked together to address Astrid’s second subgoal, her participation in rearrang-ing the kitchen also gave her the opportunity to continue working toward her first subgoal. Although she was able to move about the kitchen in her rolling work chair, she continued to require occasional assistance to position her-self appropriately at her workspaces. It was clear to Maria that Astrid would benefit from occupation-­based adaptive

text: At the end of their session, Maria and Astrid began to address Astrid’s third subgoal. Maria had observed many occupational performance issues related to holding and stabilizing task objects during just two AMPS task obser-vations. Astrid had needed assistance to open the jar of orange juice; many task objects (e.g., knife, serving spoon, cheese slicer) slipped from her grasp when she attempted to hold them in her right hand; and she did not always sta-bilize task objects, resulting in the sandwich and the pan of hot oatmeal almost falling onto the floor or into her lap. Maria reasoned, therefore, that a variety of adaptive strategies may need to be introduced. First, Maria suggested that Astrid try using a nonskid mat, placing it on the counter under the bread when she buttered it. When Astrid placed a slice of bread on the mat and then spread butter using a butter knife held in her left hand, the bread remained in place, and she was able to butter the bread. Maria also had Astrid try putting the cheese on the mat and trying to slice it. When she pulled the cheese slicer across the top surface of the cheese to slice it, the cheese kept sliding and almost fell onto the floor. Astrid commented that although she was very satis-fied with the nonskid mat, slicing cheese was too difficult. She said, “No, can’t…must have help.” Astrid still had a strong tendency to first try grasping the butter knife or the cheese slicer with her right hand, and Maria was aware that the nonskid mat would not solve the problem of utensils slipping from her grasp when she used her right hand. She decided, therefore, to suggest to Astrid that using utensils with larger, nonslip handles might enable her to better grasp them. Again, Astrid remained open to this idea, so Maria had her try using a butter knife with an enlarged, nonslip handle that she had in her clinic kitchen. When Astrid tried the knife, she was able to grasp the handle more securely, but it still had a tendency to slip from her hand. It seemed to both of them that this strategy was not going to work. Maria therefore began to consider trying acquisitional occupation combined with compensatory occupation. Her idea was to engage Astrid in practicing making different kinds of sandwiches, pouring beverages, and making hot oatmeal. The compensatory component would include the use of the nonskid mat and the rolling work chair, and the acquisitional component would be practicing using her left hand as her “lead hand” and using her right hand as her “assisting hand.” Another solution would be needed for the cheese and most likely slicing vegetables.

text: Maria had one more concern, the hot oatmeal pan and the sandwich that Astrid did not even attempt to stabilize; the hot pan almost falling into her lap was a serious safety risk. Maria considered, therefore, that it may be the case that if Astrid did not learn, through practice, to use her right hand to consistently stabilize task objects, she would need to discuss with Astrid the idea of redefining Astrid’s goals. That is, perhaps it was going to be more realistic for Astrid to prepare simple meals with minimal assistance or supervision from the staff at the comfort living complex. For example, they may need to preslice Astrid’s cheese and vegetables when she wants to make a sandwich, and provide her with supervision and, when needed, assistance to pre-vent any risk of injury. As Maria and Astrid discussed this situation further, Astrid said that she wanted to get a nonskid mat, and she agreed to Maria’s suggestion to use presliced cheese. They also discussed the idea of having the staff at the comfort living complex slice her cheese and vegetable (e.g., tomato, cucumber) when they come in the after-noon but for Astrid to then make her sandwich without their help.

text: Over the next 2 weeks (four sessions), Astrid practiced making open-­faced cheese sandwiches with cucumbers or tomatoes, pouring herself a glass of juice, making oat-meal, and preparing yogurt with muesli (another break-fast she often eats). Within 2 weeks, Astrid could make her own sandwiches provided she used presliced cheese and vegetables that Maria had prepared for her; she ate her sandwiches for her afternoon snack at the geriatric day rehabilitation unit. When she practiced preparing hot oatmeal, she persisted in demonstrating problems with not stabilizing task objects, so Maria placed more emphasis on occupational skills training focused on prac-ticing and learning to effectively stabilize task objects using her right hand. Although she could sometimes safely manage the hot pan of oatmeal, Maria believed that Astrid would likely always need standby supervision for safety risks (e.g., a hot pan falling off the counter). Another problem that persisted during all task per-formances was positioning her rolling work chair effec-tively at her workspace, such that she was able to reach for objects without increased physical effort. Maria again introduced acquisitional occupation and encour-aged Astrid to approach the counter facing forward, not sideways. With practice, after a period of practicing during which Maria gradually decreased the number of verbal cues she gave, Astrid did begin to position her-self at the counter or the refrigerator more effectively. As Maria expected, she still was able to transport only one object at a time.

text: Now that Astrid had had an opportunity to practice mak-ing sandwiches and preparing oatmeal, Maria felt it was important to reevaluate Astrid’s quality of occupational performance and document her progress. Reevaluation using the AMPS also enabled Maria to clearly define what task actions were now effective and which ones remained ineffective and needed to be targeted through further intervention. When Maria reevaluated Astrid’s quality of ADL task performance, she observed the same two tasks that she had observed the first time she evaluated Astrid. Astrid was already familiar with the kitchen, so Maria did not need to take the time to familiarize her with it, but she did confirm with Astrid what ingredients she would use for each task (e.g., tomato or cucumber, orange or lingonberry juice). Maria also presliced a cucumber and a tomato and ensured that all other needed tools and materials were available; she had Astrid put the cucumber and tomato slices in the refrigerator to ensure that Astrid knew exactly where they were located. When she observed Astrid, Maria observed many of the same types of problems she had seen during her earlier AMPS observation but with some obvious dif-ferences: problems that Astrid had frequently demon-strated (e.g., “grip slips”) she now only demonstrated occasionally, and problems that had been moderate to marked were now only minimal (e.g., effort moving her rolling work chair). Astrid did, however, continue to demonstrate moderate inefficiency, primarily because she continued to transport task objects one at a time; she had very crowded workspaces; and she occasionally used ineffective search strategies, resulting in delays locating needed tools and materials. She was, how-ever, able to complete both tasks within a 35-­minute time frame. Another important outcome was that when Maria asked Astrid how she felt it went, Astrid indicated that she was very satisfied with how well she could now perform these tasks, saying, “I am happy. It is much better.…New chair. I can do it now.” After scoring Astrid’s quality of performance of each AMPS task, Maria entered Astrid’s raw AMPS item scores into the OTAP software and generated an AMPS Prog-ress Report so she could obtain an objective measure of how much Astrid’s quality of ADL task performance had improved. As shown in Figure. 5.­9, Astrid’s ADL motor and ADL process measures both increased by 0.3 logit, an amount that is clinically observable but not statistically significant. When Maria documented Astrid’s progress to date, she wanted to be sure to do so in a manner that would con-vey the observable differences in Astrid’s quality of ADL task performance. text: Continued OT Services When Astrid and Maria met again, it was the end of the seventh week that Astrid had been coming to the geri-atric day rehabilitation unit. After meeting with Astrid and discussing the results of the second AMPS observa-tion and revisiting Astrid’s goals, Maria planned to share her findings with the entire rehabilitation team. Maria thought that it was time for the team to review Astrid’s common rehabilitation goals and develop an ongoing intervention plan. Over the final 3 weeks that Astrid came to the outpa-tient geriatric day rehabilitation unit, she continued to participate in ongoing OT services related to her goals. That is, she continued to practice simple meal preparation tasks at home, with occasional verbal assistance and sup-port for safety from the staff at the comfort living com-plex. When she came to see Maria, they focused primarily on Astrid’s goals related to eating with a knife and fork and making coffee and serving coffee along with cookies to her friends. More specifically, Maria began by implementing another AMPS observation, but this time she observed Astrid as she prepared a pot of coffee and served it with cookies and as she prepared an open-­faced cheese sand-wich and a pot of coffee. Astrid chose these two tasks because they both involved brewing a pot of coffee. During both observations, Astrid used her rolling work chair and the nonskid mat, as needed. Maria also imple-mented a nonstandardized performance analysis when she observed Astrid eating a meal that required her to

text: cut meat as well as eat holding a knife in one hand and a fork in the other. Maria then proceeded to go through the steps of the OTIPM (see Fig. 5.­1), defining the actions Astrid did and did not perform effectively, working with Astrid to final-ize her goals, considering the reasons for Astrid’s observed problems of occupational performance, and then planning and implementing appropriate interventions. Because her performance of both coffee tasks was moderately inef-ficient, Maria applied the acquisitional model and had Astrid practice strategies to try to keep her workspaces organized so that she stopped bumping into objects. They also explored adaptive strategies to help Astrid more read-ily find the correct tools and materials without illogical searching. For example, they tried placing labels on the cupboard doors and making lists of needed ingredients so she chose the correct ones. Although Astrid made some gains, Maria’s greatest concern remained safety. For eating, Maria applied the acquisitional model and planned and implemented occupational skills training. She graded the task challenge, starting by simulating the task of eating with knife and fork using a slice of bread to imitate a thin slice of beef. Astrid then practiced cutting the bread into bite-­size pieces. When Astrid mastered this simulated task, Maria arranged for another home visit and observed Astrid as she ate a meal. Maria was pleased to see that the staff at the comfort living complex let Astrid cut her own food so she could practice and learn to eat using a knife and fork in a natural, ecologically relevant, context. Maria also used this home visit as an opportunity to observe Astrid prepare coffee in her own kitchen. This enabled Maria to ensure that the adaptive strategies Astrid had learned and used in the clinic kitchen were able to work in Astrid’s home kitchen. Astrid was able to complete the task with occasional verbal assistance and support for safety. Maria shared these findings with the support staff so that they would be able to continue to provide Astrid the ongoing support she would need. Just before discharge, Maria implemented her final AMPS observation. Astrid chose to make coffee and serve it with cookies and to prepare oatmeal. She performed both tasks safely, but she needed occasional verbal assis-tance. She continued to demonstrate a mild increase in physical effort and clumsiness, and her performance was mildly inefficient. Her ADL motor measure increased to 0.3 logit, a change of 0.6 logit since her first AMPS obser-vation at the geriatric day rehabilitation unit, representing both an observable and a likely significant improvement. Her ADL process measure was 0.3 and was unchanged since her last reported AMPS observation; her improve-ment since admission was observable but not statistically significant. At the time of discharge, Maria and Astrid reviewed all of Astrid’s goals. By this time, Astrid had redefined some of her original goals; she had realized that performing simple meal preparation tasks, including preparing coffee, were all going to need to be done with support from the staff at the comfort living complex. Maria documented the following in Astrid’s medical record.

text: Occupational therapy (OT) intervention in stroke reha-bilitation is focused on increasing functional indepen-dence and participation and can vary greatly from one patient to the next. Limited return of upper and lower extremity function can make participation in activities of daily living (ADLs) quite challenging, and interventions must be tailored to meet the unique needs of each per-son. One study found that even 4 years following a stroke, stroke survivors continued to report high levels of activ-ity limitation and participation restriction. 6 Loss of func-tion and disuse of the paretic limb are common, and these upper extremity impairments have been shown to have a negative impact on activity and participation. 3 Evidence suggests that OT intervention can lead to significant improvements in ADL performance and participation (Box 6.­1). Additionally, recent stroke guidelines recom-mend that individualized ADL training should be given to all individuals with stroke, according to each person’s unique needs and goals. 22 While functional recovery of the affected upper extremity is often a priority in therapy, patients with severe hemiparesis may need to rely on com-pensatory one-­handed techniques to be able to perform

text: The World Health Organization’s 2001 International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health 23 provides a useful framework for assessment of health and disability at individual and population levels. Addition-ally, in order to maintain our “distinct perspective and contribution to promoting the health and participation of persons, groups, and populations through engagement in occupation” (p. S2), the Occupational Therapy Practice Framework 1 should be consulted in assessment, both for-mal and informal, standardized and unstandardized. Many assessments have been used in research as well as in clinical practice to assess functional outcomes in patients who have survived a stroke (see Table 6.1). Assess-ment can be performed at an impairment level, activity level, or participation level. When assessing occupational performance, a therapist must consider both the barriers and strengths for the client. Physical factors such as tone, postural control, balance, sensation, vision, etc., all affect occupational performance. Cognition and perception skills such as insight, safety awareness, problem-­solving ability, and neurobehavioral deficits also need to be assessed in relation to functional participation. Additionally, psycho-social factors such as adjustment, motivation, and culture should be considered during all OT evaluations. The environment in which occupations will take place should also be evaluated in order to optimize participa-tion. This includes the client’s home, worksite, classroom, or any other place where he or she regularly participates in meaningful activity. In inpatient rehab settings, the therapist may need to speak with family to obtain infor-mation about home and environmental barriers. Family may be able to provide pictures and measurements so that therapists can set up simulations for practice and provide appropriate equipment recommendations. See Chapter 30 for additional information on home modification in order to facilitate participation in daily activities after stroke.

text: Additionally, caregivers and other social support should factor into assessment in order for a therapist to appro-priately address management of daily activity after stroke. Various levels of assistance may be required, and the type of support needed can vary. Some clients will require physical assistance, while other clients may need supervi-sion for safe performance of ADLs. Additionally, financial resources should be a consideration with regard to home modifications as well as hiring private attendant support. For example, if a client will be living at home with no fam-ily present to assist in self-­care, that client will need to be able to perform his or her ADLs independently. If a client will have caregiver assistance, techniques used to perform ADLs can be altered to utilize caregiver assistance. Client and caregiver goals and priorities should factor into ADL training after a stroke. For example, if a client is receiv-ing assistance for self-­care but has a personal goal to toilet unassisted, the therapist should factor the client’s goals into the intervention.

text: safety. In settings where treatment is provided outside of the patient’s home, such as inpatient or outpatient rehabilitation, the therapist should ascertain details of the patient’s home environment in order to ensure that intervention carries over to the patient’s natural context. Room setup that enables safe positioning and mobility performance in the bedroom is a priority for ADL per-formance. The patient should be able to sit comfortably on the bed with both feet flat on the floor to provide a good base of support. If the bed is too high, the bed frame may need to be removed, adjusted, or replaced. If the bed is too low, bed risers can be used to achieve an optimal height. A firm mattress can improve balance and postural stability when sitting on edge of bed. A bed transfer handle that is positioned on the patient’s stron-ger side can improve ease and safety of transfers in and out of bed (Fig. 6.­1). Bedroom furniture should be arranged to give the patient a clear path from the bed to the door and bath-room. Obstacles and clutter should be removed, and changes in the floor surface should be avoided if pos-sible. Throw rugs and small carpets may be removed to reduce the risk of falls. Room lighting and tempera-ture are other important factors to consider. Adequate lighting is crucial for both ADL participation and safe navigation of the environment. Temperature can also affect participation as colder temperatures may increase spasticity, making movement more difficult during self-­ care tasks. See Chapter 30 for detailed review of home modifications.

text: The therapist may use energy conservation and work sim-plification techniques to teach the patient ways to priori-tize, organize, and limit work in order to save time and energy. The following techniques should be considered: 1. Organize your space. Excess space forces a patient to travel greater distances, draining personal energy resources. For example, if the bathroom is down a long hallway or on another level of the house, a bedside commode and sitting table with a mirror can be set up in the bedroom to enable easier performance of toilet-ing and grooming. 2. Arrange for easy access of supplies by eliminating excess reaching and bending. Shelves are easier to access than drawers. If drawers are used, they are easier to open with a central knob than handles. Closet rods can be lowered to eliminate excess reaching. Heavier items should be stored at counter level to minimize lifting. 3. Place appliances and controls where they can be accessed easily. Lamps, alarm clocks, and telephones should be conveniently positioned. The use of environ-mental control units such as Amazon’s Echo and Alexa devices can be considered along with apps that help manage environmental control (https://www.amazon.com/Amazon-­Echo-­And-­Alexa-­Devices/b?ie=UTF8& node=9818047011). 4. Eliminate clutter. Thorough cleaning and organization are essential to allow for easy retrieval of commonly needed items.

text: Generally speaking, there are various approaches a thera-pist can employ to increase functional participation. Some clients will improve participation through remediation of their impairments. Other clients will need to rely on com-pensatory techniques to achieve independence in ADLs. In addition to hemiparesis after stroke, any neurobehav-ioral deficits (see Chapter 25) that might be present will affect treatment choice and intervention method. For example, flac-cid hemiparesis is very different from a hemiparetic limb with hypertonicity (see Chapter 20), and upper extremity dressing techniques may need to be modified based on the presentation of the hemiparesis. Finally, the psychosocial aspects of managing daily activities (see Chapter 15) will affect choice in treatment approach. Aspiration precautions (see Chapter 29) should always be observed to ensure safety with meals. The weaker arm should be positioned on the table with good alignment to promote proper posture as well as attention to the arm. The follow-ing adaptive equipment can be considered to increase ease and efficiency during feeding.

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 6: Adaptations for Managing Daily Activities with Hemiparesis, Showering and Bathing, p. 123

text: Safety is an important consideration during bathing, and factors such as transfer techniques, seating and position-ing, amount of assistance required, and control of water temperature should all be evaluated. Nonslip mats or adhesive decals should be placed inside and outside the tub or shower. A tub transfer bench and grab bars can increase safety with transfers and stability during bath-ing (see Chapter 7). The patient should be seated with back support and feet stabilized. Plenty of time should be allowed for bathing to avoid rushing, which can lead to accidents. Many patients require supervision or assis-tance during shower transfers and bathing, and the thera-pist should help the patient and caregivers determine the appropriate amount of assistance needed to bathe safely.

text: There are a number of different techniques and approaches for dressing with hemiparesis. text: Pants and Underwear in Bed 1. Bend the weaker leg toward the body using the stron-ger arm or leg to bring the foot within reach. Pull the underwear or pants over the weaker leg and allow the leg to straighten into the clothing. 2. Place the stronger leg into the clothing and pull the pants up as far as possible. Place one or, if possible, both feet on the bed and bridge to lift the pelvis. Pull the pants up over the hip of the stronger side using the stronger arm. Then, while lifting the hips again, reach across to pull up the pants over the weaker hip. It may take several attempts to move the pants up to the waist. If the person is unable to bridge, pull the pants up over the hips by rolling side to side. 3. Elastic pants or pants with adaptive fasteners may make donning and doffing pants easier.

text: Pants and Underwear in a Seated Position (Fig. 6.­10) 1. While seated on a stable surface with feet on the floor, cross the weaker leg over the stronger leg using clasped hands to lift the leg. Nonslip drawer liner can be placed between the legs if needed to keep them crossed. 7 2. Place the pant leg over the weaker foot and continue to pull it on the leg until the foot can be seen. Then place the stronger leg into the pants and pull both pant legs up as far as possible.

text: 3. If able to stand safely, the person can stand and use the stronger hand to pull the pants up over the hips. To prevent the pants from falling down once standing, a pant clip can be used. A pant clip can be made from two small clips with holes in the tabs. The clips can be tied together with a string, with one clip attached to the shirt and the other attached to the pants (Fig. 6.­11) (https://www.performancehealth.com/pant-­clip). This prevents the pants from falling down around the ankles once the person stands up. 4. If unable to stand safely, the person can remain seated and shift side to side to work the pants up over the hips. Looser pants with stretchy fabric, such as workout clothes, will work better for this technique.

text: • To don shoes, the weaker leg can be crossed over the stron-ger leg or a foot stool can be used to elevate the foot, mak-ing it easier to reach. Open the shoe wide to slide the foot into it. A shoe horn may help to slide the heel into the shoe. Alternatively, a small piece of splinting material can be molded to fit around the heel of the shoe so that the back of the shoe does not buckle when the heel is slid into it.

text: Energy conservation and work simplification techniques can also be applied to instrumental ADLs (IADLs). Patients can prioritize, organize, and limit work in order to save time and energy. In general, patients should allow increased time for task completion and take frequent, short rest breaks. Work surfaces should be positioned at a height that allows for maximal efficiency to avoid exces-sive reaching and bending. To allow for easy access to supplies, items that are frequently used should be kept on convenient shelves at the front of accessible cupboards and drawers or at the back of the work surface. When pos-sible, patients should sit while working to save energy.

Some products can be ordered through medical supply companies; however, many companies are now making products that are readily available to a general population. text: Work simplification methods should be applied in the performance of household tasks. Housework requires a great deal of mobility and necessitates getting into awk-ward positions. Her husband is also retired and is serving as her primary caregiver. T.S.’s daughter and grandchildren live nearby and visit often. Prior to her stroke, T.S. was an avid reader, enjoyed cooking and travel, and loved spend-ing time with her grandchildren. T.S. was referred for home care services after receiving a course of acute inpatient rehabilitation. Upon evaluation, she was found to be alert and oriented but noted to have mild left neglect with some difficulty finding things placed on her left side. Her husband was able to safely provide assistance to help her transfer from her bed to her wheelchair. T.S. required minimal to moderate assistance for ADLs, such as dressing, grooming, and bathing. She was able to eat using her right arm, but she was concerned that her plate slid on the table and that she often pushed her food off her plate. She was not able to cut her food very well due to the use of only one arm. She also had some dif-ficulty finding items placed to the left of her plate due to left neglect. T.S. expressed frustration with not being able to read as she could not hold her book. Her husband and daughter assisted her with IADL tasks such as shopping, cooking, medication management, and cleaning. The home occupational therapist used the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure 10 to help T.S. set meaningful goals. T.S. chose the following goals for herself, and her husband agreed that these goals were important. 1. I want to be able to get dressed by myself. 2. I want to be able to eat by myself without making a mess. 3. I want to be able to read a book. 4. I want to be able to cook. The occupational therapist then set to following goals:

text: Environmental Modifications and Adaptations Prior to beginning ADL training, the therapist evaluated the home and the areas where ADLs were performed to ensure safety and ease of participation. 1. Obstacles and clutter were removed from the floors to improve safety and ease of transfers. Pathways were cleared to allow wheelchair access throughout the home. Nonglare lighting was added in all areas where T.S. regularly performed ADLs. 2. The bathroom was assessed for safety and appropriate equipment. Nonslip mats were added inside and out-side the tub, and a tub transfer bench was added to the bathtub. Grab bars and a handheld shower head were installed. The temperature of the water heater was low-ered to prevent scalding during bathing. 3. A bed transfer rail was added to the bed on the unin-volved side. Soft bedding was removed to reduce the height of the mattress and increase firmness, so that T.S. could comfortably sit with both feet on the floor. 4. T.S.’s favorite armchair was too low, so a firm seat cushion was added to increase the height and sup-port. A stable tray table with adjustable height was also added.

text: Dressing 1. The therapist collaborated with T.S. and her hus-band to find adaptive clothing that T.S. felt good about wearing. She selected button-­ up shirts and pants made from stretchy fabric with magnetic and Velcro fasteners that she could manage with one hand. She chose supportive shoes with Velcro fas-teners. 2. T.S. found it easier to get dressed when seated in the armchair next to her bed with her feet positioned on the floor and her trunk supported, rather than sitting on the edge of the bed. 3. The therapist trained both T.S. and her husband on one-­handed dressing techniques and provided hand-outs with simple steps so that they could practice the techniques outside of therapy sessions. T.S.’s hus-band was trained to provide appropriate cueing to help guide her through the steps of the dressing tasks and to successfully manage her left arm. With daily practice, T.S. was able to perform the techniques with fewer cues.

text: This chapter describes equipment recommendations as well as practical and creative solutions that the occu-pational therapist can incorporate to assist patients in becoming more independent when performing ADLs and IADLs. For individuals with limited functional return of the involved upper extremity, compensatory techniques are crucial during the rehabilitation process and can maxi-mize the potential to reach meaningful goals. As always, the therapist should focus on activities that the patient finds most meaningful in order to make the biggest impact on participation. For individuals with extensive paralysis resulting from stroke, family members or hired outside help may be required to assist with ADLs.

text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accomplish the following: 1. Recognize the impact of impairment on mobility tasks. 2. Analyze specific movement patterns observed during mobility tasks and common compensatory strategies. 3. Use a function-­based approach to retraining mobility patterns. 4. Understand the impact of environmental changes on mobility tasks. 5. Understand how to structure the environment to promote learning of mobility tasks. 6. Understand how to use specific strategies to promote learning of mobility tasks. 7. Understand fall risks.

text: Many terms have been used in occupational therapy (OT) practice to describe an individual’s ability to change the position of his or her body in space and move within the environment. Mobility broadly refers to movements that result in a change of body position or location. The term bed mobility has been used interchangeably with gross mobility within the rehabilitation setting and traditionally has included tasks such as rolling to both sides, rolling to side lying, moving from a sitting to a supine position and vice versa, and moving from sitting to standing. Transfer refers to movement from one surface to another such as from a bed to a wheelchair, from a wheelchair to a toilet, or from a wheelchair to a car and involves varied methods of achievement.

text: OVERVIEW OF THE LITERATURE

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, OVERVIEW OF THE LITERATURE, p. 138

text: Within the literature, numerous studies have carefully examined mobility functions of adults in relation to gait and locomotion. Unfortunately, few studies have examined functional mobility tasks. The analysis of the normal sit-­to-­ stand sequence of movement has received attention and is reviewed later in this chapter. 18,19,29,79,80 Rising from bed has been examined in relation to age differences and the most common movement strategies selected. 35 This research demonstrates that age-­related trends occur across the life span, but great variety remains evident in the selection of specific movement strategies. A limitation of this study is that the oldest age group examined was the 50-­ to 59-­year-­old group; thus, information concerning older adults most at risk for stroke was not included. A study of normal adult rolling patterns also has shown that adults exhibit great variability in the selection of movement patterns. In addition, the authors of this study have noted indications that a developmental sequence of movement patterns exists but is not inclusive of all individuals. Clearly, many aspects of functional mobility still warrant further investigation. 88

text: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: RELATIONSHIP TO ACTIVITIES AND PARTICIPATION
section_path: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: RELATIONSHIP TO ACTIVITIES AND PARTICIPATION

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition

section_path: FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: RELATIONSHIP TO ACTIVITIES AND PARTICIPATION
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: RELATIONSHIP TO ACTIVITIES AND PARTICIPATION, p. 138
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 7, p. 138
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: RELATIONSHIP TO ACTIVITIES AND PARTICIPATION, p. 138

text: Occupational therapists have always approached functional mobility from the perspective that individual elements involved in changing the position of the body were necessary to achieve competency in broad areas of occupation. Improve-ment in activities of daily living (ADLs), instrumental activi-ties of daily living (IADLs), education, work, play, leisure, and social participation has always been the ultimate goal of OT. The American Occupational Therapy Association, in “Practice Framework: Domain and Process,” describes functional mobility as “moving from one position or place to another (during performance of everyday activities), such as in-­bed mobility, wheelchair mobility, transfers (wheelchair, bed, car, tub, toilet, tub/shower, chair, floor). Performing functional ambulation and transporting objects.” 4 Within the Practice Framework, functional mobility is presented as a separate activity category of basic ADLs, in which mobility functions occur relative to taking care of one’s own body. Alternatively, in the International Classification of Func-tioning, Disability and Health, the World Health Organi-zation presents mobility as a separate domain under the broader category of Activities and Participation. Mobility “is about moving by changing body position or location or by transferring from one place to another, by occupying, moving or manipulating objects, by walking, running or climbing, and by using various forms of transportation.” 94 In this more global perspective, mobility is presented as much more than a function of personal self-­care. Instead, mobility is viewed as essential to enabling an individual to engage in a full range of life areas and is central to enabling the individual to participate in life situations. In planning comprehensive treatment programs, the occupational therapist should be mindful that functional mobility is not just relevant to performing self-­care tasks but is also necessary to permit engagement in education, work opportunities, community life, recreation, leisure, religious pursuits, and domestic life. In practice, the extent to which these areas are addressed may be limited by time constraints imposed by the venue of treatment. Clinicians working within an acute care setting often emphasize basic bed mobility tasks to prepare the patient for independence in grooming, bathing, and dressing activities (see Chapter 1). Within a rehabilitation setting, occupational therapists may have the opportunity to approach functional mobility more comprehensively in relation to more advanced tasks such as community mobility and tasks related to specific work and home-­management requirements. The occupational thera-pist determines goals of treatment with the patient, contin-gent on imminent and future plans to resume responsibility for activities demanding advanced mobility. The task-­related approach of OT to intervention to improve functional mobility is consistent with present motor learning research emphasizing the important role environment plays in the organization of movement to solve motor problems (see Chapter 3). 9,38 Impairments of body functions and structures and performance skills have been used to assess abilities in the patient with hemiplegia. Each patient has different strengths, abilities, and impairments that affect the perfor-mance of functional mobility. A patient may have strong neuromusculoskeletal and movement-­ related functions but demonstrate significant impairment in mental func-tions of sequencing complex movements (e.g., apraxia). Alternately, a patient may have several problems affect-ing the neuromusculoskeletal system, including decreased alignment and postural stability that interfere with the ability to roll efficiently toward the nonaffected side. Nev-ertheless, such a patient may demonstrate the ability to learn new strategies to sequence movement to accomplish the task.

text: INFLUENCE OF CONTEXTUAL FACTORS ON FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY
section_path: INFLUENCE OF CONTEXTUAL FACTORS ON FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.unit_title: INFLUENCE OF CONTEXTUAL FACTORS ON FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY
section_path: INFLUENCE OF CONTEXTUAL FACTORS ON FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, INFLUENCE OF CONTEXTUAL FACTORS ON FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY, p. 139
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 7, p. 139
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, INFLUENCE OF CONTEXTUAL FACTORS ON FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY, p. 139

text: Contextual factors represent a variety of interrelated con-ditions and situations that may influence an individual’s ability to become proficient in performing mobility tasks. Personal and environmental factors affect the patient with hemiplegia and may support or impede performance. Personal factors are unique to the individual’s life and living situation and influence the selection of mobility interventions. The occupational therapist considers fac-tors such as age, gender, race, and social background. When considering the age of an individual who has sustained a stroke and assessing expectations of the poten-tial for functional mobility, the therapist must use caution. Many factors besides age contribute to the differences in the abilities that older adults exhibit in functional mobil-ity. Readers are encouraged to explore the literature examining the effect of aging on postural control and life span mobility. Certainly, the patient’s stage in the life cycle more clearly guides assessment and interventions in the con-sideration of overall mobility needs. A young patient with hemiplegia who attends college has specific mobil-ity needs. Sit-­to-­stand movements must be accomplished in changing environments and under varying conditions. For example, using public transportation, which may be moving or stationary; rising from a low seat at a football stadium; sitting down in a crowded and darkened movie theater; and getting into a truck present different chal-lenges. These mobility tasks are not unique to young persons, however. A retired person who enjoys traveling frequently and visiting family members also has special mobility needs. Social and cultural variations also have an effect on the success of functional mobility interventions. The therapist must consider culturally derived boundaries of interaction, 55 because the therapist must frequently work within an intimate distance during mobility retraining. 42 The physical environment where interventions occur also affects the patient’s willingness to participate actively. Some patients prefer treatment to occur in the privacy of their hospital rooms, but others are more comfortable with these “close encounters” occurring in the open space of a therapeutic gymnasium. The patient, family, signifi-cant individuals, and therapist have perceptions and beliefs founded on their cultural conditionings. Similarities and differences of belief may occur in three areas influenc-ing the success of functional mobility retraining: the per-ceived state of health and illness, the perceived relevance of therapeutic interventions, and the belief that functional mobility is relevant to resuming previous occupations. 58 The therapist’s ability to listen to personal needs and appreciate individual values helps ensure success. 58 The degree of independence that a patient finds acceptable must be self-­determined. The therapist must remember that cultural variations influence patient participation and successful outcomes of home programs. 4,58,63 Environmental factors are external to the individual and are considered at two levels, individual and societal. Individual environmental factors include the immediate environment of the individual, which can be viewed as the hospital or clinical venue, and the natural environ-ments. Environment determines a patient’s function. A patient with hemiplegia may be able to roll to either side and come to a seated position on a mat or plinth within the clinical setting and engage in donning and doffing of upper extremity clothing. However, in bed within a home setting, the patient may not be able to roll as effi-ciently or come to a seated position without some assis-tance. Grooming and dressing tasks may not be practical because of changes in the height and firmness of the supporting surface. These occurrences and the reasons underlying the performance deficits are well represented in the current motor learning literature. The postural adjustments necessary to roll and come to a seated posi-tion to engage in self-­care tasks can be learned only in the context of task performance 1,20 and in the expected environment. 38,39 The treatment of a patient with hemiplegia often occurs on a continuum from acute care through commu-nity reintegration. Many treatment environments impose constraints that limit the therapist’s interventions. For example, in intensive care unit settings, therapists must contend with multiple lines, monitors, and alarms (see Chapter 1). Ideally, the relearning of motor skills and tasks should occur in the actual environment in which the task will be performed. 21,67 Societal environmental factors directly influence the patient’s ability to resume participation in IADLs and include systems within the community or society that can assist the individual to resume an active lifestyle outside of one’s immediate living situation.

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, FUNCTIONAL MOBILITY: THE OUTCOME OF MULTIPLE PROCESSES, p. 140

text: Functional mobility requires the successful interaction of a number of systems. Carrying out skilled rolling, sitting, and standing does not depend solely on the integrity of the neuromusculoskeletal system. Occupational therapists must be mindful of the interdependence of various sen-sory, perceptual, and cognitive functions in the execution of these tasks and create evaluation tools that respect this relationship, such as the Árnadóttir Occupational Ther-apy Neurobehavioral Evaluation (see Chapter 25). This awareness ensures more comprehensive assessment than do evaluations that look at motor behaviors in isolation. Occupational therapists’ knowledge and expertise in task analysis render them uniquely qualified to evaluate and plan treatment to improve functional mobility skills while keeping all the patient’s needs in mind.

text: Individual differences and variations in movement strategies may be related to factors such as the patient’s build (short, tall, obese, thin) and performance patterns before the stroke (i.e., the patient was a trained athlete, dancer, physically inactive, occasional exerciser, or physi-cal laborer). Additionally, each patient presents with individual habits, routines, and roles that influence move-ment. 28 The psychological state may indeed be reflected in movement (e.g., inhibitions or lack thereof and reac-tive depression about the current situation). Pain from preexisting conditions or pain as secondary impairment to the stroke may affect movement patterns. These indi-vidual differences and their effects on functional mobility have been explored in the literature. 88 The occupational therapist must be cognizant of these factors and others in assessment and treatment planning.
