text: Practice Conditions

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Practice Conditions, p. 170
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 7, p. 170
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Practice Conditions, p. 170

text: To prepare the patient to resume the previous lifestyle, the occupational therapist must consider carefully the conditions under which practice takes place. The goal of intervention is to maximize retention and transfer of acquired skills to everyday life situations the patient will encounter. 43 The therapist must increase the demands of the learning context during practice to prepare the patient to respond to unpredictable events. Chapter 3 presents an overview of factors the therapist considers when structur-ing the practice conditions in stroke rehabilitation. The following are considerations specific to functional mobil-ity retraining.

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Practice Conditions, p. 170
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 7, p. 170
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Practice Conditions, p. 170

text: Blocked and Random Practice Blocked practice in functional mobility retraining is the rote practice of mobility functions in sequence. For exam-ple, the patient initially practices rolling to the unaffected side, then to the affected side, and then to the seated posi-tion. Repetition of experiences and a degree of mastery must occur at each level before the patient proceeds to the next level of skill. This method of structuring practice ini-tially may assist the patient in gaining proficiency during the practice session but is not effective in preparing the patient to engage in self-­care tasks in which changes in the position of the body occur randomly in response to task requirements. For example, the patient rolls to the left to reach for a brush on the table; it is just beyond reach. The patient rolls back to supine and assumes a bridge posi-tion, pushing upward in bed. The patient then rolls again and is able to grasp the brush. Random practice of mobil-ity tasks improves learning, retention, and the ability to solve motor problems encountered in life situations. 77 Schmidt 73 recommends that randomized practice be incorporated throughout the intervention process. Mobil-ity tasks should be interspersed with other tasks such as ADL training in which the patient must make transitional movements in a natural context. The trial-­ and-­ error exploration of functional mobility in this context initially may prove difficult for the patient. Progress may be slow, and the therapist may be tempted to instruct the patient in a single movement strategy to speed progress. Varying the practice conditions increases the contextual interference, facilitating generalization as the patient relies on multiple processes and promoting the development of versatile motor strategies. 51,87 Schmidt notes one exception in which a part-­to-­whole method of practice may be beneficial. Early in the inter-vention process, when the patient is acquiring founda-tional skills, practicing of component movements may be necessary. For example, the patient initially may need to gain control of lateral flexion of neck and trunk muscles before these movements can be incorporated into the side lying-­to-­sit sequence. Schmidt suggested that as soon as patients are able to perform these component movements, they should be integrated immediately into programs emphasizing random practice. 73 This method of practice can be used only with mobility functions that are readily divided into natural component parts. 74,89

text: Varying the Practice Conditions for Specific Tasks Gentile’s taxonomy of motor tasks 37,38 is useful for deter-mining the most appropriate practice conditions for each mobility task. Objects, persons, and the spatial temporal characteristics of each task influence the motor strate-gies selected. Sabari 72 suggested that the OT process inherently considers the importance of the regulatory conditions to task performance. Occupational therapists frequently adapt and regulate the environment to facili-tate mobility functions, as in adjusting the height of a bed in preparation for a transfer (Figs. 7.­40 and 7.­41). Simi-larly, the amount of verbal cues and physical assistance are adjusted to foster independent performance and skill development. Sabari also directs attention to the crucial role occupational therapists assume as regulators through-out mobility retraining.

text: Closed Tasks

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Closed Tasks, p. 171

text: Early in the treatment process, most functional mobil-ity tasks may be considered closed, and the environmen-tal features are regulated easily to improve performance. Rolling over and coming to a seated position in a hospi-tal bed occurs on a stationary surface. The therapist can regulate the environment further by positioning pillows and bed linens appropriately, raising the bed guard rails, adjusting the height of the bed, limiting the number of persons moving around the patient’s bed, and position-ing the body in a fairly static position to assist the patient if needed. Another important characteristic of a closed

reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Closed Tasks, p. 171

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Closed Tasks, p. 171

text: task is that movement is self-­paced, and no temporal con-straints are placed. The therapist’s role as a regulator can be equated with the degree of assistance or handling provided. The thera-pist initially may give significant physical assistance and use a variety of adjunct techniques to promote perceptual, cognitive, and sensory processing. As the patient regains control of movements in desired sequences, physical assis-tance and the amount of cueing are reduced gradually or eliminated. 72

text: Variable Motionless Tasks

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 7: Functional Mobility, Variable Motionless Tasks, p. 171

text: Bed mobility becomes a variable motionless task if the therapist is not present to regulate certain features of the environment. Patients preparing to get out of bed inde-pendently may find the pillows and bed linens in disar-ray, making movement difficult; the bed guard rails are lowered, the top of the bed remains slightly elevated, and the height of the bed may be too high. Simultaneously, the patient may be receiving verbal encouragement to “hurry up.” Without the therapist present to structure the envi-ronment, the patient may experience difficulty and may use compensatory strategies incompatible with the res-toration of performance component deficits. The patient may hook the unaffected leg under the affected leg and use the hands to pull up to a seated position. This comparison illustrates the way overstructuring the environment does not prepare a patient recovering from stroke to develop flexible motor strategies. The patient needs to have opportunities to process information and acquire the ability to solve future problems. 2,73 Abreu 1 studied the effects of environmental regulation on pos-tural control and found that unpredictable environments elicited improved control. These findings are contrary to beliefs that occupational therapists have held concerning the grading of tasks from simple to complex and the struc-turing of environments from predictable to unpredictable. Abreu 1 postulated that the results of this study indicate that both types of environments should be incorporated concurrently in the intervention process. The thera-pist may regulate the environment, but not on all trials. Perhaps the height of the bed is adjusted and the guard rails are elevated on one trial, and the next session may require the patient to instruct the therapist verbally in the arrangement of the immediate surroundings in prepara-tion for the mobility task.

text: Many advanced mobility skills meet the criterion of an open task in which the spatial and temporal parameters of movement are determined by events occurring in the envi-ronment. Open tasks require more precise timing of move-ment, and the patient is challenged to anticipate and react to unexpected events. A sit-­to-­stand maneuver on a moving train, plane, or bus is an example of an open task. Practice of this kind of task should occur in the actual environment whenever possible. 44,72 Patients who are physically capable of attempting these advanced skills should be engaged in them while in the rehabilitation setting whenever possible. Patients who do not have adequate foundational skills while hospitalized can benefit from interventions to improve their future potential for the acquisition of advanced mobility skills. Patients need to be introduced to unpredictable environments where they have the opportu-nity to explore movement strategies and develop problem-­ solving abilities. text: The performance of functional mobility tasks should not occur in isolation, as in a gross mobility mat program. Practice of mobility skills while the patient is engaged in life tasks presents opportunities to solve unexpected prob-lems that arise as the patient manipulates different objects and encounters changing support surfaces and chang-ing temporal demands. text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Understand typical gait components. 2. Identify common gait deviations after a stroke. 3. Understand the basics of gait retraining, including common outcome measures used to demonstrate improvement. 4. Describe the relationship of bone mineral density to ambulation function after a stroke. 5. Examine the pathologic and impairment evidence along with the therapeutic suggestions for individuals who demonstrate contraversive pushing. 6. Identify and describe commonly used orthoses and assistive devices.

text: In the management of a stroke survivor, gait analysis and gait training traditionally have been the responsibil-ity of physical therapists. Because of the interdisciplinary approach used to rehabilitate the stroke survivor, much sharing of information occurs among team members regarding the patient’s functional and mobility status. Occupational and physical therapists often “cotreat” to enhance problem solving regarding specific barriers to independence in activities of daily living. Just as physical therapists have much to gain by famil-iarizing themselves with terminology and treatments used by occupational therapists (e.g., in the area of perceptual motor deficits), occupational therapists should benefit from having a basic understanding of typical gait com-ponents, common gait deviations after a stroke, and gait retraining. An integrated approach to treatment of stroke survivors necessitates a working knowledge of the termi-nology, evaluation techniques, and rationale for treatment by other disciplines.

text: The physical therapist should perform a thorough examination before gait analysis and retraining. This examination includes factors such as range of motion (ROM), posture and bony alignment, strength, motor control, coordination, sensation, and balance. The thera-pist notes any deficits in these areas and is then ready to observe and analyze gait and to speculate on which of the deficits may be contributing to a specific gait deviation. The therapist can address specific deficits with appropri-ate treatment interventions and modalities. Gait analysis is the objective documentation of gait 98 and ranges in complexity from observational assessment to quan-titative analysis using instrumented gait analysis systems. These systems can include tools such as videotaping, three-­ dimensional motion analysis, dynamic electromyograms, and force plates. A variety of such quantitative systems is available and differs widely in sophistication and price. 17,88 Kinematic analysis evaluates movement patterns, including the movement of the body, and specific angles between body segments (joint angles) as the body moves through the gait cycle. Observational gait analysis is a qualitative method of kinematic analysis. When kinemat-ics is measured by instrumented analysis, it is considered a quantitative gait analysis. 88 Observational gait analysis is the visual inspection of walking. 119 Although not as reli-able as quantitative gait analysis, observational gait analy-sis is the method most often used by practitioners. Most physical therapists do not have access to highly technical evaluation equipment, although videotaping is now more commonly available. Perry developed a systematic method for observational gait analysis that helps standardize this evaluation. 104 Observational gait analysis is an acquired skill that requires much practice and repetition. The physical therapist must learn how to look at nine different points on the body (head, shoulders, arms, trunk, pelvis, hips, knees, ankles, and feet) while simultaneously comparing the observed gait with typical gait features in three body planes. When one is first learning gait analysis, obser-vation of as many typical gaits as possible is necessary. When one is first performing observational gait analy-sis in the clinic, the recommendation is that the physi-cal therapist choose patients who can tolerate walking for several minutes. This allows the therapist to apply Perry’s approach to viewing trunk and limb excursions during the gait cycle. Observational gait analysis should take place in the sagittal and frontal planes. The frontal or coronal view must include anterior and posterior vantage points. Cer-tain motions such as leg rotation and foot abduction and adduction take place in the transverse or horizontal plane, although the therapist is usually not in a position to observe motion specifically in this plane. In typical gait, most movement occurs in the sagittal plane, but in atypi-cal gait, many of the deviations are observed as compensa-tions in the frontal (coronal) and transverse (horizontal) planes 98 (Fig. 8.­1).

text: Physical therapists must first familiarize themselves with the components of the typical gait cycle and with the ter-minology used to describe these components before they can analyze the gait of a person who has had a stroke. A cycle begins when the heel of one foot touches the ground and ends after the leg and body have advanced through space and time and the heel of that same foot hits the ground again. The cycle includes a period when the leg is in contact with the ground, which is followed by a period when it is advancing through space. Thus the gait cycle of one leg can be divided into two phases: the stance phase (in which the leg is in contact with the ground) and the swing phase (in which the leg is off the ground). The stance phase makes up to 60% of the gait cycle, and the swing phase makes up to 40% (Fig. 8.­2). In a typical gait, the opposite leg also is going through a gait cycle simultaneously (i.e., has a stance phase and a swing phase). Each leg has two periods at the beginning and end of stance when the opposite leg is also in contact with the ground. These are called the periods of double support.

text: Together, they account for 10% of the initial stance phase and 10% of the end of stance for both legs. The phases of swing and stance are further divided into substages. The language used to describe these subdivi-sions uses the traditional terms or the terms developed at Rancho Los Amigos Medical Center (Table 8.1). Because the terms are similar, physical therapists often use a mix-ture of old and new terms unless the facility in which they work advocates strict adherence to one terminology. Most physical therapists are familiar with the Rancho Los Ami-gos terminology because of the abundance of research, literature, and gait assessment forms produced by the pathokinesiology service and physical therapy department at that facility. 100 The Rancho Los Amigos definition of swing phase is divided into the substages of initial swing, midswing, and terminal swing. The stance phase is divided into initial contact, loading response, midstance, terminal stance, and preswing (Fig. 8.3). Within these substages, the physical therapist observes the joint displacements and movements occurring at the trunk, pelvis, hip, knee, ankle, and toes. Figure 8.4 illustrates the phases of the gait cycle and the corresponding joint displace-ments that typically occur as the body moves through the sagittal plane.

text: Other terms used in describing gait cycles are stride, step, cadence, and velocity. A stride is equal to a gait cycle (i.e., from heel contact of one leg to the next heel contact of the same leg). Stride can refer to distance (stride length) or time (stride time) in the gait cycle of one leg. A step is described as the distance (step length) or time (step time) from the heel contact of one leg to the heel contact of the opposite leg (Fig. 8.5).

text: RELIABLE GAIT PARAMETERS

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, RELIABLE GAIT PARAMETERS, p. 178
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 8, p. 178
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, RELIABLE GAIT PARAMETERS, p. 178

text: Cadence is the number of steps or strides per unit of time. Walking velocity equals speed: the distance walked divided by time. Because time–distance variables are the compo-nents of gait that can be measured most reliably, thera-pists can use them in assessing improvement in patients after stroke. 56,113,114 For example, persons who have had a stroke with a resulting hemiparesis typically walk with a slower-­than-typical gait. 79,94 Routine recording of the cadence and velocity of these individuals is an objective way of documenting change over time. Velocity measures are traditionally taken during a standard 10-­m walk test and show improvement for physical therapists who do not have access to the instrumented gait analysis systems men-tioned previously.

reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities

text: It is important for therapists to have reference values from the healthy able-­bodied population for cadence (100 to 120 steps/min) and velocity (1.2 to 1.5 m/s) at their disposal so a quick comparison with their patients’ values can be made if one has the goal of recovery. 31 In

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, RELIABLE GAIT PARAMETERS, p. 179
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 8, p. 179
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, RELIABLE GAIT PARAMETERS, p. 179

text: addition, comparing an individual’s cadence and veloc-ity measure at two points in time may help to document improvement objectively. Improvements in cadence and velocity also can be an indication of functional improvement, limb recovery and balance confidence. A study of patients with hemiplegia by Harro and Giuliani 60 showed positive correlations between high scores (>90) on the motor portion of the Fugl-­Meyer motor assessment scale and the ability to increase walking speeds. Richards and colleagues 113 studied 18 hemiplegic subjects divided into three subgroups: slow, intermedi-ate, and fast walkers. They found that the fast walkers had movements and muscle activations more similar to those of able-­bodied subjects than the slow or intermediate speed walkers. The significance of balance deficits on ambula-tory function should not be underestimated, as these have been associated with low ambulatory activity. 87 In addition, improvements in upright balance have been associated with a decreased fall risk, increased walking speed and increased community reintegration (Van de Port et al. 2006). 16,83,129 Conversely deficits in walking speed have consequences outside of mobility limitations. Walking speed has been identified as the sixth vital sign (Fig. 8.6) 50 and may be considered a functional indicator of health and predictor of future adverse health outcomes. 1,53,122 Walking speed is one component in Fried’s frailty phenotype classification system, 49 which has both screening and predictive capa-bilities. 10,54,78 Thus, routine monitoring of walking veloc-ity should be performed. In recent years, the 6-­minute walk test has been used in the stroke population. Although it was first used in the cardiopulmonary population to assess functional capacity, 8 its utility in the stroke population has been demonstrated. Dean and other separate investigators have consistently reported that this population’s ambulation endurance is very limited. 37,84 The initial ambulation speed is not

reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, RELIABLE GAIT PARAMETERS, pp. 179–180
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 8, pp. 179–180
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, RELIABLE GAIT PARAMETERS, pp. 179–180

text: maintained throughout the 6-­minute walk test, and an individual’s final walk distance is both lower than pre-dicted from his or her 10-­minute walk velocity and below the value used to identify heart transplant patients, 37 thus emphasizing the need to measure and train for both ambu-lation speed and endurance in this population. Shaughnessy and colleagues have shown that moni-toring step activity throughout the day using a portable microprocessor (Step Activity Monitor; Cyma Corpo-ration) is another tool for demonstrating improvement in ambulation tolerance. 118 They demonstrated an 80% improvement in step activity across a 3-­month outpatient rehabilitation period. Clinicians could monitor step activity during the course of a day by placing pedometers on their patients. However, the accuracy and placement of com-mercially available pedometers and accelerometers must be considered for individuals who ambulate at slow speeds. 47,51 Perry has shown that ambulation speed differentiates lev-els of ambulatory functioning in the home and community. She further classified levels within community (most and least limited, full) and household (limited, unlimited) ambu-lation based on speed and independence of ambulation while performing activities in the home and outside (Box 8.1). 105 Individuals classified as least limited community ambula-tors ambulate at significantly higher speeds (0.58 m/s) than individuals classified as most limited community ambulators (0.4 m/s). A most limited community ambulator is ambula-tory for all household activities and can independently enter and exit the home, manage a curb, and perform one low-­ challenge community activity (e.g., visit a friend or doctor’s appointment). The least limited community ambulators can manage moderate challenge community activities such as grocery stores and uncrowded shopping areas in addition to those identified in the most limited community ambulator. Finally, a full community ambulator can manage busy envi-ronments while ambulating at a significantly faster speed (0.8 m/s) than a least limited community ambulator. Common threads to community ambulation are increased ambulation distance/endurance, the ability to change level and terrain irregularity, obstacle avoidance, and the manual handling of loads. All of these threads are essential for successful full access community ambulation. For individuals who negotiate a metropolitan area, there is an additional requirement: faster velocities for short dis-tances (1.33 m/s for 13–27 m) are needed to cross streets safely. 81 Thus when working on gait recovery in the stroke population, therapists must routinely take quanti-fied measures of gait speed and endurance during a variety of ambulation tasks to assess household and community ambulation feasibility and reentry.

text: HEMIPLEGIC GAITS

text: The type of gait of a person who has had a stroke depends on where in the brain the insult has occurred and which systems are affected, such as motor, sensory, balance, coordination, perceptual, and visual systems. If a motor area in the cortex or a motor track is involved, hemiple-gia or hemiparesis is manifested in the contralateral limbs. The location of the infarction within these areas deter-mines whether the arm or the leg is more impaired. Not all patients after stroke are hemiplegic or hemiparetic, nor do all hemiparetic patients have the same degree of motor deficits. Unfortunately, the term hemiplegic gait is frequently applied to all individuals with hemiparesis, although many varieties and degrees of deficits exist. 56 Individuals who have had ischemia in areas of the brain supplied by the anterior cerebral artery usually have greater deficits in the leg. Those with ischemic lesions in areas supplied by the middle cerebral artery have greater arm involvement, although leg weakness is usually also present in varying degrees. Middle cerebral artery infarc-tions are the most common type of stroke. 24 The gait deviations seen with these lesions are those most often described by the generic term hemiplegic gait. Following are descriptions of some of the more common alterations.

text: During the stance phase of the hemiparetic leg, a patient may exhibit “foot flat” or even a “forefoot first” at the initial contact instead of a heel contact with adequate ankle dorsiflexion. The patient also may exhibit plantar flexion (forefoot first) and supination (in the frontal plane) at initial contact and then begin to bear weight precari-ously on the lateral border of the foot. 25,56,88,97 During the loading response, while the patient is still in double-­ limb support, weight is being “loaded,” or accepted, onto the leg. Typically, 10 to 15 degrees of knee flexion is needed to absorb the forces of momentum and body weight. This flexion may be absent, in which case the knee remains extended or even hyperextends (genu recur-vatum) during midstance as the body moves forward. In this instance, no tibial advancement occurs over the foot because no dorsiflexion is occurring at the ankle (Fig. 8.7). Midstance begins the period of single-­limb support. In addition to knee hyperextension, the therapist also may observe trunk and hip flexion as the body attempts to move its center of mass forward over a stiff knee. The

text: indicate weak hip abductors of the stance leg. A positive Trendelenburg sign is present when excessive lateral dis-placement of the pelvis occurs over the stance leg, with an excessive lowering of the pelvis on the contralateral swing leg. 91,98 During the terminal stance phase, which is still a period of single-­limb support, typical hip extension may be absent along with the ability to transfer weight onto the forefoot in preparation for push off. Dorsiflexion at the ankle joint may continue to be excessive or diminished. Lack of heel rise can occur in the sagittal plane, combined with exces-sive dorsiflexion, and the contralateral leg makes initial contact early. 4,56,88,98 The preswing phase is the final stance stage and the second double-­ support period. A lack of knee flexion (typically between 30 and 40 degrees) often occurs in the paretic leg, accompanied by a lack of ankle joint plantar flexion at the end of preswing. 4,25,97,100 Many of the deviations observed in the hemiparetic limb during stance can contribute to a decreased step length by the opposite leg. The body is not able to complete its typical excursion forward because of lack of movement, or ineffective movement, of the pelvis, hip, knee, or ankle of the hemiparetic limb. The opposite limb may “step to” instead of stepping past the paretic limb. Step length also can be reduced in the hemiparetic leg. The therapist sometimes can see the swing phase of the paretic limb as a mass flexion movement instead of a series of sequential flexion movements. 56,79 More often, the swing phase is characterized by a stiff-­legged swing, with a decrease in hip flexion and in the velocity and amount of reciprocal knee flexion and extension. The velocity of the entire paretic limb is often decreased. 56,93 The decrease in hip flexion, together with the lack of knee flexion and dorsiflexion, often results in circumduction to advance the stiff limb. 4,56,91,97,100 Circumduction occurs when the patient swings the leg through in a semicircle and is most noticeable when looking at the patient in the frontal plane (Fig. 8.­8). The patient combines external rotation and abduction at the hip to lift the leg out to the side and then adducts and often internally rotates the leg to bring it back in. 91 In a typical gait pattern, no abduction, adduction, or external or internal rotation occurs in the frontal plane during the swing phase. 100 The limited knee flexion in the preswing phase per-sists into the initial swing phase and often throughout the entire swing phase. The toe drag first seen in the ini-tial swing phase may continue because of the decreased knee swing but also may be a consequence of decreased hip flexion and decreased ankle dorsiflexion. The patient can initiate compensatory hip hiking at this stage to assist with clearing the toes as the leg advances. 4,56,88,93,97 Other

text: compensations used to counteract toe drag are increased hip and knee flexion or vaulting by the opposite (stance) leg. Vaulting occurs when the person rises up on the toes of the stance foot for better clearance of the swing leg. 4 In the midswing phase, the pelvis may remain retracted instead of rotating forward to neutral. Hip hiking and leg circumduction may continue, especially if knee flex-ion and dorsiflexion remain limited. Dorsiflexion may be decreased or absent, with the ankle assuming a plantar-­ flexed (foot-­drop) position. The foot may supinate dur-ing midswing because of an imbalance in ankle dorsiflexor muscle function (see Fig. 8.­8). 25,34,88,100 Typically, the anterior tibialis and long toe extensors dorsiflex the foot symmetrically. Some patients after stroke have overac-tive anterior tibialis muscles and weak long toe extensors, causing the medially placed anterior tibialis tendon to pull the foot into supination. 34 As the limb progresses toward the terminal swing phase, many patients are unable to extend the knee while simulta-neously flexing the hip and ankle. Instead, knee extension is decreased, and the foot initially contacts the ground with the knee flexed. 88,93 The pelvis still may be retracted or may not have rotated forward past neutral. This, in addition to the decrease in knee extension, results in a decreased step length by the paretic leg. Other subjects may exhibit knee extension with plantar flexion during the terminal swing phase instead of the typical dorsiflexion seen in preparation for upcoming heel strike. 56,100 In other persons, adduction of the hip with knee extension can be so pronounced as to cause the swing leg to cross in front of the stance foot. Patients literally end up tripping over themselves.

text: One cannot overemphasize that the causes of the afore-mentioned observed gait deviations may vary from patient to patient. For example, a common deviation at initial contact is foot flat or forefoot first instead of heel contact. atypical movement could result from weak dorsiflexor muscles, 39,40,79,86,100 excessive activity of the plantar flex-ors, 4,80,79,100 a decreased ability to perform fast reciprocal movements, 56,73,79 disruption in the central generation of preprogrammed muscle activation, 65 noncontractile soft tissue tightness in the plantar flexors, 4,28,39,100 or a patho-logic condition of the ankle joint. Even when soft-­tissue tightness and joint contractures are ruled out, hypotheses vary and often conflict about the precipitating factor. This is especially true when the issue of voluntary versus reflex skeletal muscle activation is addressed. A number of recent papers and publications provide an abbreviated review of the literature on this topic. 28,39,45,56,60,74,77,79

text: Stroke survivors have an increased risk of falling through-out their hospitalization (acute stroke unit and inpatient stroke rehabilitation), which continues to be elevated even after discharge back into the community. 133,124 While fall rates (13% to 36%) and risk factors vary across settings (Perrson 2016), 5,32,108,109,138,106 this population has an increased fracture risk. From 1.2% to 6% of falls result in fractures to the distal radius, humeral head, and hip. 23,111,135 Fractures occur predominantly on the paretic side, and hip fractures in particular accelerate the downward spiral toward increased morbidity and mortality. 110,111 Risk fac-tors for fracture include reduced mobility, strength of the paretic leg, and reduced bone mineral density (BMD). 112 In Chapter 7, falls in the stroke population are explored; however, an analysis of the bone density demineralization timeline across the first year after stroke is warranted so interventions to minimize this loss and possibly lessen the fracture risk can be developed. 13,85 In the spinal cord injury (SCI) population, bone demin-eralization occurs within the first 3 months postinjury and proceeds up to 16 months after injury. The demineraliza-tion has been attributed to prolonged bed rest, immobility, and lack of muscle contraction and gravitational loading below the level of SCI. 52,136 In the stroke population, investigations of BMD loss have been compared within a limb and between limbs (paretic vs. nonparetic) in lon-gitudinal fashion for up to 12 months after stroke. 66,67,112 The rate of bone demineralization over the first year and the factors that might alter the loss are explored next. As early as 1 month after stroke, significant BMD loss for the paretic upper limb (UL) compared with the nonpa-retic UL has been shown for the humerus (4%) and total arm (4%). 112 The paretic limb’s distal radius loss reaches significance compared with the other side at 4 months (3%). However, all three sites of the paretic UL continue to decline over the year (total arm, 3%; humerus, 14%; distal radius, 3%), which puts the paretic UL at risk for fracture if used to break a fall. The nonparetic UL’s distal radius demonstrates a 2% increase in BMD for the first year, which may be attributed to increased loading activ-ity associated with the nonparetic UL during ambulation, although this hypothesis has not been tested. Ramnemark and colleagues 112 demonstrated that at 4 months after stroke, a significant BMD loss for the proxi-mal femur had already occurred in the paretic limb (6%), and loss continued throughout the remainder of the first year (12%). The nonparetic limb appeared to lose BMD as well but at a slower rate compared with the other side (4% at 12 months). Studies reported that when BMD loss rate was analyzed across the first year, the greatest loss occurred within the first 7 months in both the paretic (10%) and nonparetic (2%) legs of stroke survivors. 66,67,112 Jorgensen et al, 66,67 has demonstrated that ambulatory status and weight-­bearing load on the paretic limb after stroke affect the rate of BMD loss. Using the six-­level ordinal scale for the Functional Ambulation Classification (FAC) (Table 8.2) to qualify ambulation status, a linear relationship of ambulation assistance to BMD loss was

text: demonstrated. Thus if subjects ambulated independently or with assistance (FAC 2 to 6) within the first 2 weeks after stroke, subjects lost less BMD at 1 year (2%) com-pared with those who achieved ambulation by 2 months (7%) and with those still nonambulatory at 2 months (10%). 67 In addition, the amount of weight on the paretic limb during 30 seconds of static standing was linearly related to walking onset after stroke. Subjects who walked within 2 weeks of stroke had a higher percentage of body weight (51%) loaded through the paretic limb versus those who walked by 7 months (43%) and those immobile at 7 months (35%). 66 In a systematic review of the literature on physical activ-ity and BMD after stroke, Borschmann and colleagues 19 found small effect sizes in favor of physical activity and bone health in individuals with chronic stroke. More recently, Borschmann and colleagues, 18 in an ongoing longitudinal study, have demonstrated that for individu-als who are initially nonambulatory after stroke, physical activity as measured by daily counts of standing up and independent ambulation resulted in less bone loss at 6 months poststroke. Furthermore, the bone density health of the proximal femur in individuals with chronic stroke has been shown to correlate with gait related parameters (Worthen et al. 2005). The Bone Density Index (BDI) is a metric that incorporates body weight, number of steps taken per day, and ground reaction force (GRF) magnitude while walk-ing. Since GRF increases with increasing walking speed or weight-­bearing load through the lower limb, a lighter individual would need to take a larger number of steps per day and increase their ambulation speed to achieve a desir-able BDI to maintain bone density. Thus BMD loss has been demonstrated for both the paretic upper and lower limb throughout the first year after stroke. The upper extremity (UE) loss occurs sooner than the lower extremity (LE) loss, but both limbs show significant loss that could contribute to fracture risk dur-ing a fall. Early ambulation after stroke has been shown to modulate bone demineralization of the paretic lower limb during the first year. Therapists should use interventions that promote independent ambulation as early as possible after stroke with the knowledge that the sooner indepen-dent ambulation is achieved, the less bone loss occurs. In addition, increasing the number of steps per day along with LE loading (standing frequency, body weight, or speed of ambulation) should be encouraged to maintain BMD.

text: The physical therapist first addresses deficits identified during the physical assessment that are contributing to the atypical gait, such as decreased ROM and strength. Interventions can include basic modalities and therapeutic exercise and a variety of approaches to address the lack of movement and voluntary control. Many interventions are based on theories that advocate facilitation of typical movement and sensory stimulation of the patient by the therapist. In this context, the patient is a passive recipi-ent of the therapist’s efforts. However, during the past 20 years, therapists gradually have shifted away from using these more traditional therapeutic approaches to using the motor control perspective. The motor control approach is based on a theoretical model, but it does not advocate spe-cific treatment techniques that are done by the therapist to the patient. In the motor control model, the main task of the therapist is not to facilitate typical movement but to structure the environment in such a way that the patient actively relearns to use the affected limbs functionally. The motor control relearning theory is based on research from a variety of fields, including neurophysiology, muscle physiology, biomechanics, and psychology. 29,59

text: Patients are believed to learn by actively trying to solve problems. Therefore, therapists should structure tasks to promote acquisition of the movements needed to solve specific motor control problems in a variety of situations (see Chapter 3). This pertains not only to individuals with a hemiplegic gait but also to those with motor control deficits described in the following sections. In the past 10 years, the research directed at improv-ing gait function in individuals after stroke has supported a basic tenet of motor skill acquisition. To improve gait functioning, the individual must practice the task of gait. The part practice intervention of weight-­shifting activi-ties in standing with both feet in contact with the ground was not superior to the conventional neurodevelopmen-tal treatment–based physical therapy intervention at improving gait, 137 thus suggesting that improvements in gait may not be amenable to part practice in standing positions in which both feet are always in contact with the ground. The question becomes if ambulation practice is required to improve ambulation, then how much prac-tice does a patient require to improve gait? The literature shows that at least 20 minutes of actual ambulation prac-tice is the minimum amount of time per session needed to note improved ambulation. Table 8.3 shows that the amount of practice for any of the ambulatory intervention groups is a considerable increase from what is presently observed in the rehabilitation clinic. This increase in time on task results in significant gains in overground walking speed and endurance. Recent ambulatory intervention advancements have been the use of body weight support treadmill train-ing (BWSTT), task-­related circuit training, task-­related training + electric stimulation (ES), body weight support (BWS) + ES, overground walking practice, obstacle train-ing, home-­based exercise programs (HEPs), and variable intensive walking training (see Table 8.3). Visitin et al. 130 first demonstrated that BWSTT was better than non-­ BWS walking for recent stroke survivors. At the end of a 6-­week inpatient rehabilitation unit stay, individuals who received BWSTT ambulated at a faster overground speed (0.34 m/s) than individuals who received the non-­BWS (0.25 m/s) (control group). At the 3-­ month retention, although both groups continued to improve, the BWSTT group was clearly superior (0.52 m/s) to the control group (0.30 m/s) (Fig. 8.­9). Sullivan’s group 123 demonstrated that the speed at which therapists train ambulation may be a critical fac-tor in enhancing ambulation recovery. Although BWSTT was performed for all groups, the training speeds for each group were different (fast vs. slow vs. variable). Although all groups improved, the fast group (2.0 m/h) made the most gains in overground walking speed. This speaks to the specificity of speed training and suggests that training should occur at the speed to which the therapist wants the individual to ultimately ambulate.

text: An additional innovation to the BWS device is the incorporation of an ES component during gait training. However, compared with overground ambulation train-ing, both groups of chronic stroke survivors made similar gains in walking velocity and endurance. 102 Ada’s group, 3 in their study of treadmill versus overground walking programs, found similar results in a community-­dwelling population of stroke survivors, and Nilsson’s group 90 cor-roborated these results in acute stroke survivors, which suggests that the practice of ambulation is the com-mon critical element for individuals already somewhat ambulatory. Dean, 36 in her pilot study, and Salbach, 116 in a larger study, found that training individuals in upright dynamic activities through a circuit system was more beneficial than no treatment or conventional treatment. The circuit included stations for walking overground at comfortable and fast speeds, walking over obstacles, transitions of sit to stand from chairs of varying heights, dynamic upright balance activities, and LE strength-ening activities performed in standing. Bassile et al. 12 demonstrated that an ambulation training program with obstacles of varying heights and widths was feasible and improved the gait and quality of life in chronic stroke survivors. Duncan’s specific HEP for subacute stroke survivors that incorporated dynamic balance and LE strengthening performed in an upright position along with ambulation and aerobic training was found to be better than standard of care. 41 The common thread for these investigations was the emphasis on incorporation of upright, dynamic balance activities along with or within the context of ambulation.

text: The results of the Locomotor Experience Applied Post Stroke (LEAPS) trial emphasizes this importance. 43 An early (2 months) versus late (6 months) locomotor train-ing program (LTP) was compared with Duncan’s HEP (2 months) for subacute stroke survivors. The LTP included BWSTT and overground walking practice. Although all three groups significantly improved their walking out-come measures after intervention, the fall rates were not similar. As expected, individuals classified with severely impaired walking function at the study start (velocity ≤0.4 m/s) fell more. However, the more impaired early LTP group fell more than the later LTP group. Both of these groups fell more than the HEP group, thus suggest-ing that falls in this population occur even with enhance-ment of gait outcomes and appear to be linked to other impairments, in particular balance deficits. Blennerhassett and colleagues substantiated the relationship of balance to ambulatory function by identifying cutoff measures for two upright, dynamic balance tests, the Four Square Step Test (≥15 seconds) and the Step Test (≤10 steps). 15 Indi-viduals who did not meet the cutoff scores self-­limited or avoided encountering specific tasks in their environments. More recently, variable ambulation has been ­performed in conjunction with high-­intensity aerobic training param-eters. Hornby and colleagues 63 stratified patients with subacute stroke to four ambulatory groups and then ran-domized them to either an experimental or a control group to receive 40 intervention sessions. The experimental group performed 10-­minute increments (total of 40 min-utes) of walking under variable contexts which included speed-­dependent TT (task training), skill-­dependent TT (pertubations occurred or walking occurred in multiple directions, over inclines or obstacles, with weighted vests or leg weights), overground walking, and stairs. Patients exercised at 70% to 80% of the heart rate reserve or at a rate of perceived exertion ≥14. The control group per-formed tasks, stretching and active exercises, balance, transfers, gait, and stair training. Their results demon-strated significant improvements compared to the control group in self-­selected and fast walking speeds, 6-­minute walk distance, and single limb stance time. In a separate analysis focusing on the aerobic exercise performance results, the experimental group’s gains in walking function were a result of improvements in VO 2submax, with changes in gait efficiency or peak capacity. 77 While these results are promising, caution should be used to determine the aerobic intensity for a patient poststroke. In conclusion to this section, some common interven-tion themes are noted. First, the task of ambulation must be practiced for much longer periods in the clinical setting if one wishes to improve this function. Results of this lon-ger practice yield improved ambulation endurance (dis-tance) and speed (velocity). Ambulation practice should occur at faster speeds to meet community ambulation activities. Both LE strength and balance (see Chapter 18) play a role in ambulation enhancement, and the literature supports the notion that performing task-­specific prac-tice in upright dynamic postures along with ambulation practice, not in place of it, contributes to enhanced loco-motion. Finally, aerobic training principles (frequency, intensity, type and time) should be incorporated into ambulation training to enhance aerobic capacity or ambu-lation efficiency in this population.

Therefore what follows are examples of atypical gaits that are particularly challenging to the physical ther-apist. Each deficit results from damage in the particular part of the brain described.

text: A person who has an infarct in the cerebellum caused by occlusion or hemorrhage of a vertebral or a cerebel-lar artery may exhibit completely different gait deviations than a hemiparetic patient. The cerebellum is composed of three parts or lobes: the flocculonodular lobe, the ante-rior lobe, and the posterior lobe. The flocculonodular lobe also is called the vestibulocerebellum because most of its input is from the vestibular nuclei in the pons. The anterior lobe also is known as the spinocerebellum because most of its input is from the spinocerebellar tracts via the inferior cerebellar peduncle and the superior cerebellar peduncle. The posterior lobe also is known as the neocer-ebellum and contains most of the cerebellar hemispheres. The hemispheres receive their major input from the cor-tex via the middle cerebellar peduncle. In addition, the cerebellum can be divided longitu-dinally into functional zones perpendicular to the hori-zontal fissures dividing the lobes. The medial structure is the vermis. Adjacent to the vermis, on either side, is the pars intermedia (intermediate section) of the cerebellar hemisphere. Lateral to this is the bulk of the cerebellar hemisphere. Gait is influenced most by the flocculonodular and anterior lobes. Consequently, infarcts in these areas lead to difficulty maintaining a proper stance and walking. 92 Damage to the flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebel-lum) causes head and neck ataxia. Truncal tremor is often severe. The patient often uses a wide-­based stance with the feet apart to increase stability. Any attempt to bring the feet together or walk with one foot directly in front of the other causes loss of balance. Ataxia or dysmetria of the limbs is not common. Damage to the anterior lobe, especially the medial aspect, causes a disruption in the sensory input (via the spinocerebellar tracts) that is related to agonist–antago-nist muscle activity. Lower limb ataxia or dysmetria is also present, but UL ataxia is usually absent. Lesions in a cerebellar hemisphere result in ipsilateral limb dysmetria

text: or hypotonia in addition to other deficits. Although the damage does not affect postural stability, the gait appears ataxic and staggering because of the limb dysmetria. 88 The cerebellum is supplied by three main arteries: the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, the anterior infe-rior cerebellar artery, and the superior cerebellar artery. These arteries are part of the posterior circulation—the vertebrobasilar system. The posterior inferior cerebellar artery is a branch of the vertebral artery, and the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and superior cerebellar artery are branches of the basilar artery. Chapter 1 describes in detail the territories supplied by these arteries and their associated areas. 6,7 In general, these arteries supply the areas of the cerebellum that their names imply in addition to parts of the brainstem. Some areas of vascularization in the cerebellum overlap because of the many free cortical anastomoses (Fig. 8.10). 7 Although one artery may supply one particular lobe predominantly, this overlapping may result in additional blood coming from the distal branches of another artery. However, as a rule, the superior cer-ebellar artery supplies the superior cerebellar peduncle, the anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the middle cerebellar peduncle, and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the inferior cerebellar peduncle. 7 A cerebellar stroke resulting from occlusion of the pos-terior inferior cerebellar artery usually is referred to in the literature as a lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) 20,55,128 because it was believed that the poste-rior inferior cerebellar artery supplied the lateral medulla and parts of the cerebellum. Recently, this term has been disputed based on evidence that the lateral medulla is sup-plied less frequently by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery than previously thought. 6 If the lateral medulla is spared, an infarct of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory is apparent as a headache on the ipsilateral side, vertigo, nausea and vomiting, nystagmus, and limb and gait ataxia. If the lateral medulla is involved, the foregoing signs and symptoms are present. In addition, interruption of the sympathetic nerve fibers can cause Horner syn-drome. Cranial nerves V, IX, and X also are affected. 6,127 Involvement of cranial nerves V, IX, and X results in ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature in the face (V), dysphagia (IX), and dysphonia (X). Pain and temperature may be decreased on the opposite side of the body because of the interruption of the ascending spinothalamic tracts. This combination of cerebellar and medullary signs con-stitutes Wallenberg lateral medullary syndrome. In either type of posterior inferior cerebellar artery infarct, the inferior cerebellar peduncle and the inferior aspect of the cerebellum are affected. The result is ipsilateral limb ataxia and gait ataxia. 6,127 In addition, the patient tends to fall to the side of the lesion (ipsilateral axial lateropulsion) and has difficulty shifting weight toward the contralateral leg. 6 Earlier texts reported that posterior inferior cerebellar artery infarcts are the most common, 20 but recent find-ings have shown that superior cerebellar artery infarcts occur as frequently. 6,7 Superior cerebellar artery infarcts have several different clinical manifestations. Dysarthria is one of the most frequent. Limb dysmetria, gait ataxia, and ipsilateral axial lateropulsion are also common symp-toms. 6 Anterior inferior cerebellar artery infarcts are the least common. In addition to vertigo and ataxia, tinni-tus and deafness are present. Auditory involvement and peripheral facial palsy are classic signs of anterior inferior cerebellar artery infarcts, which differentiate them from superior cerebellar artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery infarcts. 6,127 Gait retraining after a cerebellar stroke is focused on relearning the way to correct balance losses. Patients first must learn the point in space where their center of grav-ity is positioned optimally over their base of support for stability. Then they must relearn the way to realign their center of gravity constantly with their base of support. This task is most difficult during ambulation when the center of gravity is shifted anterior to the base of support as the body moves forward. 126 Balance retraining should encourage active prob-lem solving by the patient (see Chapters 18). Being held upright by the therapist while walking does not promote functional independence. Likewise, assistive devices that require UE weight bearing (e.g., walkers) may prevent loss of balance but do not promote functional improve-ment because they do not challenge the patient to relearn balance control. 9,21 The patient is merely stabilized exter-nally and is not required to use or integrate postural reflexes. Activities that require active weight shifting and goal-­ oriented reaching are encouraged and practiced while the

text: Contraversive Pushing or Pusher Syndrome

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, Contraversive Pushing or Pusher Syndrome, p. 190
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 8, p. 190
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, Contraversive Pushing or Pusher Syndrome, p. 190

text: An unusual motor behavior that patients with hemiple-gia sometimes display in the clinic is ipsilateral pushing. The patients tend to push away from the unaffected side in any position. Davies 34 described the syndrome in 1985 and called it the pusher syndrome. The original description of the pusher syndrome was based solely on a practitio-ner’s observation and was most often thought to be asso-ciated with left hemiplegia. 34 The behavior was seen in as many as 10% of the 327 patients after stroke in the study by Pedersen and colleagues. 101 However, the syndrome appears in both right and left hemisphere damage. 69,101 Neglect and aphasia are also highly associated with push-ing behavior. 69 Recent research activity has attempted to identify the neural correlates and mechanisms for this clinical dis-order. Unilateral lesions of the posterior lateral thala-mus have been implicated in recent imaging studies. 70,71 Also, diminished perfusion for the intact areas of inferior frontal, middle temporal, and inferior parietal lobes has resulted in pusher syndrome. 125 Karnath and colleagues have suggested through their research that the task of the brain areas damaged or receiving low perfusion in patients with pusher syndrome appears to be control of upright body posture. 69,70,125 They demonstrated that individuals with pusher syndrome show correct perception of visual vertical but a severe tilt of perceived body posture in relation to gravity. While seated in a tilting chair, individuals with pusher syndrome oriented their bodies upright when they were actually 18 degrees tilted toward the side of the brain lesion. How-ever, they were able to orient the visual world vertically appropriately. In addition, they were able to align their bodies to earth’s vertical when they used visual cues from the laboratory surroundings. In the dark, they were also able to orient to visual vertical, suggesting that both visual and vestibular inputs were unaffected. 34 Karnath and Broetz 68 have identified three charac-teristic behaviors associated with pusher syndrome (see Chapter 17 for the Clinical Assessment Scale for Contra-versive Pushing). First, the individual’s longitudinal body axis is tilted toward the paretic side when sitting or stand-ing. Second, the individual actively pushes (abduction and extension of arm or leg) with the nonaffected extremities, which results in a lean toward the hemiplegic side and loss of balance. Third, the individual resists any attempt by the examiner to correct the tilted body axis. Recently, addi-tional scales have been validated in this group to assess more activities. The Modified Scale for Contraversive Pushing includes the activities of sitting and standing transfers. 76 The Lateropulsion Scale may be particularly useful in these patients because walking and rolling are additionally scored activities (see Chapter 17 for scales). 33 The rehabilitation literature is scant on outcomes and intervention. 99,101,103 Karnath et al. 71 found that indi-viduals with pusher syndrome have a good prognosis. The behavior was rarely observed 6 months after stroke. However, rehabilitation did take 3.6 weeks longer for those individuals with contraversive pushing compared with other stroke survivors to achieve similar functional outcomes. Gait training for patients with contraversive pushing is a definite challenge, as is transfer training. During sit-­ to-­ stand activities, some individuals project themselves quickly out of a chair toward the hemiparetic side. If left unguarded, they fall. Transferring toward the stronger side is difficult because they always push away from that side. Although easier, transfers toward the hemiparetic side are dangerous because of the lack of motor control on that side. Standing requires assistance to prevent falling to the weak side. Walking with an assistive device, such as a cane in the stronger hand, is initially unproductive because these individuals tend to use the cane to push themselves toward the hemiparetic leg. They appear unable actively to shift weight onto the strong leg. The more these individuals are supported (to prevent falling to the paretic side), the more they push into the helper. Gait retraining is based on the same principles dis-cussed in the ataxic gaits section. Individuals must relearn the way to adjust their center of gravity over their base of support while standing. They must regain proper posi-tioning of their trunks in relation to gravitational forces so their center of mass stays within the limits of their strength and base of support (cone of stability). This implies a need for conscious awareness of their loss of balance. Trial and error is encouraged to promote active problem solving. Two interventions are suggested for specific use with indi-viduals who demonstrate contraversive pushing. Karnath and Broetz 68 proposed that because these individuals’ per-ception of visual vertical is intact but their perception of body vertical is inaccurate, they must use the visual verti-cal to align their bodies. They must be taught that the visual alignment information is correct and the body’s perception (feeling) of alignment is incorrect. This can be done through visual feedback of their bodies aligned to an external vertical axis. For example, individuals can align their trunks to the vertical axis in a mirror with tape along the vertical line bisecting their body halves. Individuals can also use door and window frames to align their trunks.

text: However, they may require external feedback from the therapist simultaneously with a “conscious awareness” that balance is achieved in this position. Using the visual vertical axis for postural alignment takes care of a behavior seen with pusher syndrome. During dynamic activities such as transferring sit to stand and ambulation, the unaffected upper and lower extremities are called into play to assist with the activity. Active pushing by the nonaffected extremities in a lateral direction toward the hemiplegic side occurs, and often the individual falls to this side when transferring, standing, or walking if not prevented from doing so by the therapist. The second intervention used by clinicians to alter the active pushing behavior of the limbs has not been evalu-ated systematically in the clinic. Therapists should remove all firm pushing surfaces from patient contact during activ-ities. Thus when performing sitting activities, the feet may be unsupported initially. In sitting and standing, the indi-vidual is not allowed to hold a firm external support with the nonparetic hand, so assistive devices and parallel bars are counterproductive. For example, the individual may be asked to hold a cup of water while transferring from sit to stand. When standing or transferring, the individual might be asked to simultaneously perform reach, grasp, and place activities with the nonparetic UE. The items are retrieved or placed on movable surfaces (e.g., a hospital tray table or rolling stools). This intervention eliminates the success of the pushing arm in destabilizing the indi-vidual, and the therapist can assist the individual to realign the vertical axis of the body more easily. If the individual can perform these activities while preferentially shifting his or her center of mass toward the nonparetic side while receiving external visual and verbal feedback about verti-cal alignment, then he or she can consciously be aware of what body positions create stability (e.g., objects are placed or retrieved from midline and in the direction of the nonparetic side). Relearning to maintain balance while walking is a for-midable task for individuals with contraversive pushing. The degree of difficulty in relearning to maintain bal-ance while walking is compounded by changes in somatic sensation, strength, motor control, and feedback circuits following the infarction. Individuals must regain some control of trunk in dynamic standing activities before ambulation can proceed safely. Visual and tactile goals can be helpful. Having individuals walk around a high mat table while observing themselves in a mirror verti-cally bisected with a tape may cue them where to shift their weight to avoid falling. They can be cued to have their upper arm/ribs touch the mat table. The use of par-allel bars is discouraged; these individuals must learn to weight shift through the trunk toward the nonparetic side to correct balance losses and not merely pull on a bar to remain upright. If it is safe for both the patient and thera-pist, using the mirror and ambulating in free space may be possible with the therapist guarding and stabilizing the affected lower limb and trunk side. Using a wheeled IV pole may allow the patient to use the nonparetic UE to stabilize/support the paretic leg without reinforcing the contraversive pushing behavior; the IV pole will run away from the patient if the push is lateral but will support the patient if the push is downward into the floor. Individu-als can advance to using a cane after they have mastered trunk control. Hands-­on techniques used by the therapist to facilitate movement are discouraged. These individuals will simply push into the hands of the therapist. At times, leg weakness interferes with this group’s abil-ity to relearn postural control and weight shifting. Davies 34 advocated splinting the hemiparetic knee in extension while having the individual work on active weight shift-ing during functional standing activities. Splinting the knee this way might increase loading in the affected leg while standing. One can assume that the added stability somehow reassures these individuals and gives them time to assess accurately whether they are balanced. Perhaps, the degrees of freedom have been limited, allowing these individuals to concentrate on one task, weight shifting, to achieve a functional goal without having to concern them-selves with an unstable knee. Recently, a single subject case report demonstrated an alternate method to mini-mize the effect of the leg weakness while working on trunk stability and walking all at the same time. The interven-tion used a lateral stepping activity with BWSTT. 115 On a slowly moving treadmill, the patient was positioned so that lateral stepping (abduction) occurred with the nonpa-retic leg. This required the paretic leg to bear weight and extend during the lateral movement of the strong leg. The body weight was adjusted for successful leg extension. In addition, the patient was wearing a sliding shoe for ease of adduction movement when swing phase occurred for the paretic limb. A mirror was also placed in front of the patient for visual feedback of trunk postural alignment. This was only one component of a comprehensive reha-bilitation program, but the patient was greatly improved on the Scale for Contraversive Pushing upon discharge. At this time, only speculations can be made about what mechanisms reduce the pushing tendency and why they might be effective. Although treatment techniques were suggested for gait training individuals with contraversive pushing, only one case study has been performed to verify their efficacy, with much based solely on this and other practitioners’ clinical experiences.

text: Loss of sensation after a stroke can compound motor deficits. In particular, loss of proprioception can greatly impede motor recovery after stroke. 42 Proprioception is conveyed to the cerebellum and to the cerebral cortex. Information about joint position and muscle activity is sent to both, but the information projected to the cerebel-lum is not recorded as conscious perception. The infor-mation is used to ensure coordinated limb movements. In

text: contrast, the information sent to the cortex can be per-ceived consciously and provides awareness of limb posi-tion and movement. 55 Proprioceptive input from muscle spindles, joint receptors, and cutaneous touch receptors reaches the cer-ebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle via the ipsilateral dorsal spinocerebellar tracts. The same infor-mation reaches the somatosensory area of the cerebral cortex via the ipsilateral posterior columns of the spinal cord, which cross in the medulla and ascend in the medial lemniscus to the thalamus and then to the cortex. Middle cerebral artery strokes can impair awareness of proprioception at the cortical level. Although all sen-sations can be affected, proprioception and two-­ point discrimination are usually more impaired than pain and temperature perception. 20 The deficits are manifested in the contralateral arm and leg. Cerebellar artery strokes cause loss of the unconscious, rapid proprioceptive input required for the smooth, automatic movements of gait. Loss of sensory input regarding agonist–antagonist mus-cle activity disrupts the continuous modulation of these muscles that is required for coordinated gait movements. A study by Kusoffsky and colleagues 75 found that patients with proprioceptive loss after cortical stroke were able to regain a greater amount of function in the leg than in the arm. One explanation they gave for this was that gait greatly depends on centrally generated acti-vation patterns, and these patterns in turn do not depend on peripheral sensory mechanisms. These central pattern generators originate in the spinal cord and are controlled by locomotor centers in the brainstem. These centers are influenced by the cerebellum, the basal ganglia, and the cerebral cortex. 57 The physical therapist can take advan-tage of this phenomenon by emphasizing functional gait as much as possible, as with BWSTT. Along with vestibular and visual input, proprioceptive information contributes to a patient’s ability to maintain a stable upright position. Input from muscle spindles and joint receptors provides valuable information not only about the position of a limb in space but also about the environment. 65,126 The ability to react to uneven surfaces or changes in ground texture depends on this input, and its impairment puts a patient at higher risk of falling. Coordi-nated limb movements may be decreased, and the person may be unable to judge the step length or limb joint excur-sions needed for maneuvering in the environment. Vision can help to compensate for the proprioceptive loss. 55,65,96,126 As with other deficits, the physical thera-pist should encourage a problem-­solving approach. The patient must learn consciously to use visual input, which was not necessary before. Occasionally, mirrors are useful, although the therapist should evaluate these aids individu-ally for each patient. Mirrors can hinder as often as they help patients, especially those with visuospatial deficits. The therapist’s role is to provide a variety of settings in which the person can practice using visual cues. In addition, biofeedback can be used to provide auditory cues. One type of biofeedback unit is a limb load moni-tor that can signal a person when the foot contacts the ground. Standard biofeedback units provide information about the force of muscle contraction during strengthen-ing exercises.

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, Visual Deficits, p. 193

text: Visual impairments from strokes also can affect gait. The most common visual deficit in patients with hemiplegia is homonymous hemianopsia, 128 which occurs when an infarction involves the optic tract, the lateral geniculate body, or the optic radiation to one occipital cortex. A branch of the internal carotid artery, the anterior choroi-dal artery, supplies most of the optic tract and the optic radiation, with some coverage by branches of the middle cerebral artery and the posterior cerebral artery. 128 The visual cortex is supplied mainly by the posterior cerebral artery but also is supplied by some middle cerebral artery collaterals. 26 Homonymous hemianopsia can also result from an isolated occlusion of the calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery, but in this case, no concurrent hemiplegia or hemisensory loss occurs. 48 When homonymous hemianopsia is present, visual information about one half of a person’s environment is missing. The temporal half of the visual field of one eye and the nasal half of the visual field of the other eye are absent. Loss of the left half of the visual field accompa-nies left hemiplegia, and loss of right visual field accom-panies right hemiplegia. As mentioned previously, balance is maintained by an intricate communication network among the visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive systems. If vision is impaired, one aspect of this network is func-tioning abnormally. The ability to maintain balance is at risk if the patient does not learn to use other systems for feedback about the environment. 30 Self-­ awareness of the visual deficit is crucial for patients. They must test this new awareness in a variety of situations and environments to ensure safety on discharge from the hospital and maximize functional independence (see Chapter 24).

text: Perceptual deficits such as left neglect and visual neglect are neurobehavioral deficits that can affect gait. These phenomena and their manifestations, causes, and clinical implications are discussed elsewhere (see Chapters 24 to 26). 14,48 Contraversive pushing may also be classified as a neurobehavioral deficit. Hemineglect and hemianopsia are separate entities that can often coexist. 11 Likewise, neglect and sensory loss can develop together or independently. Communication between the occupational and physical therapists concern-ing a patient’s perceptual status is a necessity and helps determine the best treatment approach to maximize func-tion and ensure consistency of treatment interventions.

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, Orthotic Interventions, p. 193

text: An orthosis (from the Greek adjective orthos, meaning “straight”) is an external device that improves a person’s function when applied to a body part. 82 The more com-monly used term for an orthosis is a brace. Orthoses now are named according to the joints they encompass. Short leg braces are known as ankle/foot orthoses (AFOs). A long leg brace is known as a knee/ankle/foot orthosis (KAFO) or a hip/knee/ankle/foot orthosis if it contains a hip joint and a knee joint. The newer terminology is more descriptive and specific and avoids confusion. Orthotic devices are prescribed by a physician and fab-ricated by an orthotist. The physical therapist provides input to the physician and orthotist about which tempo-rary devices have been assessed in the clinic before a per-manent orthosis is prescribed. The physical therapist is also responsible for gait training the individual with the orthotic device. Training includes donning and doffing instructions, skin inspections, and patient education as well as the actual gait training. Orthotic devices are classified in four categories: sta-bilizing (supportive), functional (assistive), corrective, and protective. All orthoses are used to increase function. Stabilizing and functional orthoses are the two types most often used with stroke survivors. Stabilizing ortho-ses are used to prevent unwanted motion such as plantar flexion at the ankle or knee buckling. Functional orthoses have an element that compensates for lost muscle strength by assisting with movement. Stabilizing orthoses are not intended as a way to correct a fixed deformity in an adult; they only can stabilize and accommodate a deformity. Corrective orthoses are used to correct or realign parts of a limb. They are used for infants and young children to help correct flexible skeletal deformities. These ortho-ses should not be used to correct a fixed deformity in an adult. Protective orthoses protect a portion of a limb from weight-­bearing forces (e.g., a limb with a fracture). 46 The orthotist adheres to basic physical principles when fabricating an orthosis to control a weak joint. An orthosis that provides three points of pressure is the most common type. 121 One of the three forces is directed toward the joint itself, and the other two end forces are directed opposite to the main force (Fig. 8.11). This principle is important for the occupational therapist to learn because of its relevance to adaptive shoe equipment. Figure 8.11B illustrates the three points of pressure used with an AFO that is provid-ing a dorsiflexion assist. The main point of pressure is on the dorsum of the foot. The two counterpressures are at the posterior calf and the distal plantar surface of the foot. Elastic laces, often used to facilitate donning a shoe with stroke survivors, eliminate the main point of pressure and result in loss of orthotic effectiveness. Therefore elastic laces should not be used with dorsiflexion-­assist braces. Elastic laces should be used cautiously with solid ankle AFOs that prevent dorsiflexion (see Fig. 8.11A) because the foot needs to be held snugly in the AFO and shoe. This is especially true if plantar flexion spasticity is present. Another orthotic principle states that the longer the lever arms, the less force needs to be applied at the three points of pressure. Therapists need to consider bony land-marks and superficial nerves when implementing these principles. 121 The orthotic joint axis of motion should be aligned with the skeletal joint; otherwise, abnormal pres-sures can be applied in the wrong areas, such as under calf bands, with movement or positioning. 46,121 Orthotic devices can be made of a variety of materials, the most common of which are metal and plastic. Plas-tic orthoses are in total contact with a limb and are worn inside the shoe. Metal orthoses are attached to a shoe and held in place on the limb with straps or bands. An AFO is the most commonly used orthosis for patients with a hemiplegic gait and is the most appropri-ate. 88,104,132 An AFO can affect knee motion and ankle
