text: motion. Knee buckling can be reduced, in stance, by adjusting the amount of dorsiflexion at the ankle joint. Similarly, knee hyperextension (genu recurvatum) can be avoided by controlling the amount of plantar flexion. Therefore the therapist can avoid using a heavier KAFO to control the knee. Plastic orthoses usually are made from high-­ temperature thermoplastic materials such as polypropyl-ene. They require high temperatures for molding and therefore are shaped over a model, such as a plaster cast impression of the patient’s leg. They are more resistant to continued stress than the low-­temperature thermoplastics used for UL orthoses. The simplest and most commonly used plastic AFO is the posterior leaf splint or spring 46 (Fig. 8.12A). The leaf spring is used when the main gait deviation is “foot drop” during the swing phase. The orthosis functions as a dor-siflexion assist device because of its flexibility. The plastic of the calf portion is displaced in stance and then springs back to a 90-­degree angle during swing. The ankle joint is held at this 90-­degree angle during swing. Foot drop and toe drag are avoided. This orthosis, however, does not afford any mediolateral stability at the ankle joint. If this is of concern, then the therapist can try a more substantial orthosis. A modified AFO has a wide calf upright with lateral trimline borders that are just posterior to the malleoli (Fig. 8.12B). Usually, the foot plate encompasses more of the lateral and medial borders of the foot. This results in more control of calcaneal and forefoot inversion and eversion. The increased width of the calf portion offers somewhat more resistance to plantar flexion in swing and stance. The most supportive AFO is the solid ankle AFO (Fig. 8.12C). The lateral trim lines extend even farther forward, anterior to the malleoli. Because of its construction, the solid ankle AFO is designed to prevent ankle motion and foot motion in any plane. The device controls dorsiflex-ion, plantar flexion, inversion, and eversion. A variety of hinged plastic AFOs are now available to allow certain motions and to block others. The ankle joint components are too numerous to mention, and newer components are being designed continuously. The orthotist can use different combinations of joints and stops to allow, limit, or prevent movement. For example, the therapist may wish to allow dorsiflexion past neutral (90 degrees) in stance to allow for typical tibial advance-ment over the foot but block plantar flexion at neutral to prevent foot drop in swing and knee hyperextension in stance. With the recent advent of commercially available foot drop stimulators used during ambulation, clinicians now have an additional management option for foot drop other than an AFO. In a 30-­week, randomized controlled trial of AFO to electrical stimulation, Kluding and colleagues demonstrated that although both groups significantly improved walking outcomes and activity and participation levels, therapeutic effects and user satisfaction was signifi-cantly higher in the stimulator group (Fig. 8.13). 72

text: Another group of plastic AFOs is referred to as tone-­ inhibiting AFOs. Most of these AFOs initially were designed for use with children with cerebral palsy. 38 Sev-eral types have been designed more specifically for use with adults with hemiplegia. 89 The common denominator is the flexibility allowed by these orthoses in the foot and in the ankle. In theory, this flexibility allows more typical weight-­bearing contacts on the plantar surface of the foot throughout stance, which promotes typical mobility in the foot during stance rather than having the foot held in one position. Mueller and colleagues 89 documented the foot-­ loading patterns obtained when using two different tone-­ inhibiting AFOs. They assessed biomechanical alignment and foot stability, and one orthosis—the dynamic AFO— was found to have had significant effects at the lateral forefoot with respect to force. The authors concluded that this effect might support the medial longitudinal arch of the foot and increase the stability of the forefoot as it is loaded. They theorized that this in turn might allow the forefoot to be loaded at a faster velocity. They did not investigate the effects of correct biomechanical alignment on muscle electromyographic activity. The use of this type of AFO is based on the same prin-ciples that underlie the use of serial casting. 27,38 Both were believed, by some practitioners, to reduce increased muscle activity. However, the scientific literature so far does not confirm that the prolonged stretch afforded by serial cast-ing has a central inhibitory effect. 2,22,27,35,131 Changes in sarcomere number and connective tissue caused by immo-bilization, positioning, and stretch can influence muscle contraction force. 2,22,28,58 In addition, muscle length also can influence the manifestation of hyperreflexia. 2,17,28 Per-haps, these mechanical properties of muscle are influenced by tone-­inhibiting orthoses. By promoting better biome-chanical alignment and muscle length, these AFOs may exert an effect on peripheral rather than central factors that, over time, could otherwise augment stretch reflexes. Further research is needed—especially long-­ term, controlled studies—to investigate the many variables that influence motor control and muscle function. The term tone inhibiting may have to be reconsidered until a more complete and universally accepted definition of tone exists along with what contributes to normal and increased tone. Metal orthoses were the main type of orthotic devices used before the 1970s. 46 Metal AFOs still are used for certain stroke survivors who cannot tolerate the total contact of a plastic AFO for whatever reason. The com-ponents usually consist of two metal uprights attached to an ankle joint. The metal is usually aluminum, but some-times heavier steel is needed for control. The ankle joint is attached to a stirrup that is fastened beneath the heel of the shoe. The proximal ends of the upright are attached to a calf band. The metal ankle joint is usually a single-­ or double-­ channel (chamber) type (Fig. 8.14). Other types of ankle joints are described in detail elsewhere. 28,46,79 A single-­ channel ankle joint can assist dorsiflexion with a spring placed in the channel. Plantar flexion also can be limited to prevent genu recurvatum by placing a pin in the chan-nel. A double-­channel ankle joint can prevent dorsiflexion and plantar flexion by using pins in both channels. Small screws hold the pins in the chambers. The degree of dor-siflexion or plantar flexion (i.e., the ankle joint angle) can be determined by the degree to which the pins are driven into the channels by tightening the screws. Springs and pins can be used in combination to stop one movement and assist another. The metal uprights attached to the ankle joint and stir-rup offer a certain amount of foot and ankle mediolateral control. However, if additional support is needed (e.g., to prevent severe foot inversion), a strap can be added that applies pressure to the lateral malleolus in a medial direc-tion and is secured around the medial upright. Because it prevents varus positioning of the ankle, the strap is called a varus correction strap. Force can be applied in the opposite direction with a strap to prevent foot eversion and a valgus

text: foot position. This strap then is called a valgus correction strap. A varus correction strap is more common. The simplest type of metal AFO is the Veterans Admin-istration Prosthetic Center shoe clasp orthosis, which consists of a single narrow metal upright that attaches to the heel counter of a shoe with a metal clasp and a calf strap (Fig. 8.15). The orthosis offers dorsiflexion assist only, with no mediolateral or plantar flexion control. Occasionally, a KAFO with knee locks may be pre-scribed for a patient who requires additional knee con-trol. However, the additional weight, the prevention of typical knee joint excursions during swing, and increased energy cost caused by these factors greatly limit the potential for functional ambulation. 88,104,132 In addition, donning and doffing a KAFO are difficult for patients with hemiplegia (see Fig. 8.11C). 132 A KAFO combines the features of an AFO with a knee joint and (in the case of a metal orthosis) metal uprights that extend proximally up the thigh. Thigh bands secure the KAFO on the upper leg. The simplest knee joint is a hinge, and the most common locks to maintain knee extension are drop ring locks. 46 The thigh component of plastic KAFOs usually is made of the same thermoplastic material as the AFO component. Metal and plastic combi-nations also can be used. 44,46,79 As previously mentioned, KAFOs are seldom used for hemiparetic patients. Occasionally, a preexisting knee joint deformity or ligamentous laxity is exacerbated by walk-ing because of the now weak muscular support. In such instances, no alternative may be available to using a KAFO to allow minimal household ambulation. A KAFO or a knee extension splint sometimes is used as an initial training device to enhance stability. These are used only as tempo-rary measures and not as long-­term orthotic devices. 29,88,132 The physical therapist has the responsibility of evaluat-ing the need for an orthotic device and reevaluating the orthotic device in an ongoing basis, especially in the out-patient or home therapy setting. In this era of decreased length of hospital stays, patients sometimes are prescribed an orthotic device while still in the early stages of recov-ery. As motor control improves, the orthotic device may need to be modified or discontinued to allow more active movement by the patient. Finally, clinicians should refer to the clinical practice guideline for AFO use presently in its final review stage to determine evidence based practice suggestions for orthotic use in this population. 64

text: ASSISTIVE DEVICES

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities

text: The assistive devices most commonly used with patients after stroke are canes, walkers, and occasionally two crutches. Hemiparetic patients whose balance is impaired minimally and who have functional strength in the oppo-site UE may use a cane. Two crutches or a walker requires at least some functional use of both upper extremities. Both devices provide more external stability, with the walker providing more stability than the crutches. The main function of a cane is to increase the base of support and thereby improve balance. 117 The base of support is increased by providing another contact with the floor. Canes also decrease the need for abductor muscle tension to stabilize the pelvis in stance on the paretic side. 95,117 This in turn helps to prevent dropping of the contralat-eral pelvis (a positive Trendelenburg sign) in stance when the cane is used in the hand opposite the hemiparetic leg. Using the opposite hand also helps simulate the reciprocal arm and leg movements of a typical gait. A variety of canes are on the market, ranging from a sim-ple wooden straight cane to a tripod “walk cane” (also called

text: a hemiwalker). At a level in between these two canes are the narrow-­ and wide-­ based quadruped canes (quad canes) (Figs. 8.16 to 8.19). Widening the base of support provides more stability. Physical therapists may begin training with a wide-­based cane because of hemiparesis and impaired balance. They should advance patients as quickly as pos-sible to the least amount of assistance required to ensure a safe, stable gait. Patients often are kept inadvertently on a maximally wide base of support cane when it is no lon-ger needed. This prevents the patient from maximizing functional ambulation for two reasons: (1) typical weight shifting to the hemiparetic leg is limited and (2) cadence is slower than it is with a smaller device 117 or no device. The key word is safety. Maximum use of the involved leg should be encouraged along with typical trunk and pelvic move-ment if patient safety is not compromised. Two crutches occasionally are used, axillary or (more often) forearm (Lofstrand) crutches (Fig. 8.20). Cer-tain patients after cerebellar stroke or others who have

text: impaired balance but functional use of both arms and hands may be trained with these devices. These patients require the extra postural support afforded by the sec-ond crutch but have enough motor control to be able to advance the crutches reciprocally. Therapists may use walkers for training patients after stroke who have functional use of both arms and hands but need greater outside support than that afforded by two crutches. Occasionally, a walker may allow functional use of a hemiparetic arm even though balance is sufficient with a cane. In this case, the patient also should practice gait training with a cane to promote optimum postural control. If patients have sufficient control of the paretic arms, they may also use walkers when it is necessary for them to transport objects around the house (e.g., in the kitchen). Standard walkers are the most stable assistive devices because they provide four points of contact with the ground. The base of support is greatly increased. A variety of walkers are available as well. In addition to standard walkers with four legs, rolling walkers with front wheels only, with four wheels, and platform attachments are also available. Rolling walkers allow a more typical reciprocal gait, but the therapist must take care to prevent the walker from “running away” with the patient. A stroke survivor with insufficient arm and hand strength to lift a walker may have the ability to maintain a grip on the rolling walker and push it for-ward. Some walkers have pressure-­sensitive brakes that prevent forward movement when the patient pushes down on the walker. As mentioned in the cerebellar stroke section, postural control sometimes is sacrificed for stability when a walker is used. The patient has no need to relearn balance and control if the walker provides needed support. As men-tioned, safety is the ultimate concern. If safe, functional ambulation is not possible without a walker, then safe, independent ambulation with a walker is the preferred choice. The type of gait pattern taught to the stroke survi-vor depends on a number of factors, including balance, strength, and coordination. 95,117 The therapist should also consider cognitive and perceptual deficits, including apraxias. Smidt and Mommens 120 suggested terminology for describing walking patterns. Point refers to the num-ber of contacts made with the floor, including with feet and assistive devices, during the forward progression of the gait cycle (Figs. 8.21 and 8.22). For example, a four-­point contralateral gait indicates that two feet and two assistive devices (e.g., canes being advanced one at a time) are being used (Fig. 8.22A). The more contacts on the floor at any given moment, the more stable the person is while walking. In addition, the pattern can be called a delayed pattern if the assistive device is advanced before the limbs. Delayed patterns provide more stability than moving a limb concurrently with an assistive device. Following are the most common gait patterns taught to patients after stroke.

text: Hemiparetic patients with a nonfunctional arm often are taught a two-­point contralateral gait pattern using one assistive device. A device, such as a cane, is held in the unaffected hand. The cane and the paretic leg are advanced together (one point), and then the unaffected leg is advanced alone (second point) (Fig. 8.21B). The cane may be advanced first and then the paretic limb, followed by the unaffected limb for a more stable pattern. This pat-tern is a delayed contralateral two-­point gait pattern (Fig. 8.22B). In Figures 8.21B and 8.22B, the right leg is the hemiparetic leg.

text: The devices used in a four-­point contralateral gait pattern could be canes or crutches. The therapist might choose this type of gait for patients after stroke who have func-tional use of all four limbs but have impaired balance. They require bilateral support but are able to advance each device (two points) and each leg (two points) individually and reciprocally. Although this is a stable gait pattern, it is not used often with hemiparetic patients. Sometimes a patient recovering from a cerebellar stroke will be taught this pattern to encourage coordinated reciprocal arm and leg movements and postural control.

text: Therapists may train patients with a walker if they have functional control of all four extremities but require greater trunk control than that afforded by a cane. For example, certain patients who have had cerebellar strokes may never recover adequate postural stability to be able to use two canes. A walker allows the patient to use five points of contact: the four legs of the walker and one of the patient’s legs. The patient advances the walker simul-taneously with one leg and then places all four of the walker legs firmly on the floor at the same time as the patient’s foot. This pattern is called a five-­point gait pattern (Fig. 8.23A). If the patient moves the walker first, followed by the patient’s leg, the pattern is called a five-­point delayed gait pattern (Fig. 8.23B). Other authors refer to this gait pattern as a “3-­1-­point” or “modified 3-­point” pattern. 107 The basic sequence is the same, however. Therapists may train previously mentioned patients with a rolling walker. They may choose this device for two reasons: (1) the walker is in constant contact with the floor while being advanced, therefore affording maximal pos-tural control, and (2) the walker is in constant motion, and the patient is able to take equal step lengths and to increase

text: GUARDING TECHNIQUES

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, GUARDING TECHNIQUES, p. 200
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 8, p. 200
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 8: Gait Awareness, GUARDING TECHNIQUES, p. 200

text: The goal of gait training after a stroke is to have the patient walk as efficiently, safely, and independently as possible. To promote optimum functional ambulation, it is important for the patient to experience postural insta-bility and to relearn the way to correct these imbalances. With this in mind, the therapist must be as close to patients as necessary to prevent them from falling or injur-ing themselves and yet not inhibit them from learning the way to right themselves. Therapists must allow patients to take some risks without jeopardizing the patients’ safety or their own safety. This is not an easy task, especially for new therapists. The ultimate horror for any therapist is having a patient fall. Obviously, until therapists are com-fortable with patients and know how much, if any, out-side support they need, guarding too much is better than guarding too little. Regardless, the goal always should be safe, optimal function, and the therapist needs to reevalu-ate on an ongoing basis how much guarding is needed and in what type of setting and on what type of surface activi-ties should be performed. Hemiparetic patients walking with a cane most often are guarded on the weaker side. The therapist stands slightly posterior and lateral to the affected side. 107,117 The therapist is then in the best position to assist the patient. If patients lose their balance or stumble, they may have difficulty preventing a fall to the weaker side because of decreased sensation and decreased strength and control of the paretic leg. The therapist can control patients with the hand closest to them at the hip or pelvis and can con-trol the patients’ shoulder and trunk with the other hand if necessary. The use of gait belts or guarding belts varies from ther-apist to therapist and from institution to institution, but most facilities advocate their use in the initial stages of gait training and on stairs. The patient’s safety is of the utmost concern. At times, a patient is uncontrollable with-out a gait belt. Other times, the belt can be a hindrance to patients relearning postural control if the therapist is inad-vertently tugging on the belt with every step. Therapists must evaluate each patient individually. The size of the patient in comparison to the therapist may also need to be considered. The therapist should decide which anticipa-tory actions need to be taken to protect the patient from harm based on clinical assessment and sound judgment. When guarding a patient who is ascending stairs, the therapist is positioned posterior and to the weaker side. The patient should be trained using a railing at the stron-ger side. Initially, the therapist may teach the patient to ascend one step at a time, leading with the stronger leg. When the patient is descending, the therapist stands in front of and lateral to the affected side so as to provide assistance if the patient’s knee buckles. Using the railing, the patient steps down one step at a time, leading with the

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities

text: Gait Training after Stroke This case study in no way reflects the patient’s whole treat-ment program because emphasis is also placed on increas-ing strength and function in the trunk and left arm and in the leg. In addition, frequent sessions of cotreating by the occupational and physical therapists occurred to enhance communication about specific treatment concerns (e.g., the subluxed shoulder) and functional goals. H.C. is a 54-­year-­old man who was admitted to the emergency department of a university medical center with sudden onset of left-­sided weakness. Two weeks earlier, he had undergone a mitral valve repair and a single coro-nary artery bypass with a left saphenous vein graft. He had had an uneventful postoperative recovery course and was discharged to his home and prescribed a beta-­blocker. On admission, the neurologic workup and results included (1) a computed tomography scan of the head showing early lucency in the right subcortical area; (2) noninvasive flow studies (on the second day) showing accelerated flow velocities in the right middle cerebral artery suggestive of stenosis and normal flows in the ante-rior cerebral arteries, posterior cerebral arteries, and basal artery; and (3) a transesophageal echocardiogram reveal-ing trace mitral regurgitation, normal left ventricular function, and no intracardiac or aortic mass or thrombus. The attending neurologist concluded that H.C. had sus-tained an infarct in the right corona radiata and putamen in the territory supplied by the lenticulostriate branches of the right middle cerebral artery. The cause of the infarct was probably an embolus of cardiac origin that developed after the mitral valve repair. H.C. was prescribed antico-agulant medication and was stabilized medically. Twelve days later, he was transferred to the rehabilitation unit of the same medical center. On admission to the rehabilitation unit, H.C. had symptoms of a pure motor syndrome with left UE weak-ness that was greater than the left leg weakness, minimal left lower facial droop, and no sensory loss. He was alert and oriented and most cooperative although somewhat deconditioned because of the previous cardiac surgery.

text: paretic leg. A patient who regains functional strength of the paretic leg may advance to the step-­over-­step method of stair climbing, with close guarding by the therapist. Ascending and descending stairs with only a cane or two canes are difficult and require excellent balance. Some home environments may necessitate such training, but it should be undertaken with sufficient guarding, and the therapist carefully should weigh the safety risks. Guarding techniques need to be taught to family members as soon as possible during inpatient rehabilita-tion. Family participation in gait training provides the opportunity for practice and repetition of newly learned techniques.

text: Physical assessment revealed full passive ROM of the left arm and leg, although both legs manifested tight hamstrings and could perform only a straight leg raise to barely 60 degrees. A finger-­width subluxation was pres-ent in the left shoulder. Strength testing revealed that the left arm was grossly 2 to 3 out of 5 throughout. He was able to extend the left knee completely while sitting (3 out of 5), but the hip flexors were weaker (2 out of 5). He exhibited no isolated voluntary ankle movement, although dorsiflexion was 2 out of 5 with simultaneous flexion of the hip and knee, and plantar flexion was 2 out of 5 during simultaneous extension of these proximal joints. He did not at that time (or ever) exhibit any spasticity in the limbs during passive testing by the therapist, with the exception of mild, unsustained ankle clonus. He exhibited no ankle edema despite the leg weakness and previous vein graft for the coronary artery bypass graft surgery. His gait was evaluated initially while he was walking around a high mat with his right side next to the mat, using his right arm and the mat to “unload” the left leg. During static standing, he required contact guarding and verbal cues to extend the left hip and knee actively. He had a tendency to bear most of his weight on the stronger right leg. When cued to stand with equal weight on both legs, he was unable to maintain an upright posture and would fall to the left because the knee would buckle. He required minimal assistance to maintain the hip and knee in extension when bearing weight symmetrically. Initially, he was able to take 10 steps around the mat with minimal assistance. His gait analysis was as follows: uneven step lengths were observed; the left was greater but less controlled than the right. The shorter step with the right leg resulted in a “step-­to” type of gait pattern—the right leg stepping to meet, instead of pass, the left leg. He exhibited a decrease in single-­limb stance time on the left leg. His cadence was slow—approximately 40 steps per minute. During the left leg stance, the heel did not strike at initial contact; the foot was flat. The loading response resulted in excessive knee flexion that was greater than the typical 10 to 15 degrees. To prevent buckling in midstance, the knee snapped back into hyperextension (genu recurva-tum). Instead of bringing his body forward by allowing the tibia to advance over the foot (dorsiflexion), he kept the ankle angle fixed and flexed the hip and trunk over the foot. He did not push off at the end of stance. Instead, he quickly took a short step with the right leg to unload the left one as soon as possible. Because the resulting right leg position was next to the left leg instead of beyond it, the left leg was unable to assume the typical preswing position of hip extension and 40-­degree knee flexion (Fig. 8.­5). Instead, the left hip and knee were in full extension, and he was forced to initiate swing on the left from this position. During the swing phase of the left leg, H.C. exhibited decreased hip and knee flexion and a foot drop because of the weak dorsiflexors. This resulted in his toes scraping the floor. He displayed mild lateral trunk flexion to the right in an attempt first to initiate swing from the previ-ously mentioned atypical preswing position and then to clear the toes throughout the swing phase. H.C. was put on a program of active assistive ROM and strengthening exercises for the left arm and leg. Treat-ment of the leg emphasized functional strengthening in weight-­bearing positions (e.g., sit-­to-­stand exercises for hip and knee strengthening). During the initial stage of gait training, a posterior leaf splint orthosis was used to assist with dorsiflexion during the swing phase on the left side. This splint was chosen to encourage a more efficient swing phase and to discour-age the patient from leaning to the right to clear the left leg during swing. Because of its flexibility, the posterior leaf splint did not restrict activity at the left ankle or knee during stance. Although the knee was unstable, H.C. was still in the early stages of recovery. Sacrificing mobility for stability (i.e., blocking any ankle dorsiflexion and knee flexion in stance) was not beneficial. Doing so would have forced him to move compensatorily because it is typical to dorsiflex up to 10 degrees at the ankle during midstance and terminal stance. The therapist offered close supervi-sion to contact guarding at the knee because of possible knee buckling resulting from excessive dorsiflexion. H.C. was taught to be aware of the difference between excessive knee flexion and recurvatum. He was soon able to identify correctly when he was in either of these atypical positions even if he could not always prevent them. H.C. quickly advanced from ambulation around the high mat to ambulation with a narrow-­based quad cane and then a straight cane. He had the advantage of recov-ering much of his hip extension and abduction strength, which meant he did not require a large degree of outside support from an assistive device for these muscles. Functional training included standing balance retrain-ing in single-­limb and double-­limb weight-­bearing posi-tions. Modified versions of activities that the patient previously had enjoyed (soccer) and a few new ones (golf putting and baseball) were introduced. H.C. practiced

text: ambulation in a variety of environments and on both even and uneven terrains in preparation for discharge. H.C. even practiced getting through busy revolving doors. After 6 weeks of inpatient rehabilitation, H.C. was evaluated for a permanent AFO. His left leg strength had improved enough to allow him to isolate dorsiflexion and plantar flexion in any position grossly in the 2 out of 5 range, ankle inversion and eversion in the 2 out of 5 range, and toe flexion and extension in the 1+ out of 5 range. His hip flexors improved minimally to 2+ out of 5, and knee extension also improved minimally to 3+ out of 5. During ambulation, H.C. continued to manifest knee recurvatum in stance and did not push off at the end of stance because of weak plantar flexors. During swing, he continued to exhibit a foot drop and toe drag. The phys-iatrist, physical therapist, and orthotist performed a joint observational gait analysis. Because of the continued plan-tar flexor and dorsiflexor weakness during the swing and stance phases and less than typical knee extension strength, they decided that H.C. required minimal knee control and ankle control from an AFO. In addition, the weak ankle invertors and evertors necessitated mediolateral con-trol by an orthosis. Therefore a posterior leaf splint was deemed insufficient. However, because H.C. was continu-ing to progress and did not require maximum support at the knee, a solid ankle AFO was also inappropriate. The general consensus was that H.C. should be allowed to have as much movement at the ankle as possible without jeopardizing his safety to promote development of a typi-cal gait pattern. For this reason, the team decided to order a hinged polypropylene AFO with free dorsiflexion at the ankle and a plantar flexion stop at 90 degrees. The hinged ankle with free dorsiflexion allowed him to move his tibia over his foot (dorsiflexion) in midstance and terminal stance. The plantar flexion stop at 90 degrees prevented foot drop in swing and recurvatum in stance. The orthosis improved his gait by allowing the typical joint excursions at the knee and ankle in stance while preventing atypical movements in stance and swing. The promotion of typical joint excur-sions at the ankle in stance allowed him to take equal step lengths with both legs. On discharge to his home, H.C. was able to ambulate independently indoors with a straight cane and the hinged AFO, but he required supervision outdoors. He was able to ascend and descend stairs step over step using a railing and ascend and descend curbs and ramps with the straight cane, all with distant supervision. He could perform sim-ple home exercises independently for left leg and arm strengthening. He returned to work as a full-­time uni-versity professor and continued with outpatient physical therapy three times a week for 6 months after discharge. He regained full functional use of the left UE, including finger function (albeit with decreased coordination), fine motor control, and strength. He also continued to receive occupational therapy for several months as an outpatient.

text: The aim of this chapter is to familiarize occupational therapists with processes used by physical therapists dur-ing gait evaluation and training of patients who have had a stroke. The most common types of gait disorders are those resulting from a middle cerebral artery infarction. The application of orthotic devices is not an exact science. To assume that a particular atypical gait always requires one specific type of orthotic device is not accu-rate. Therapists must evaluate devices on an individual trial basis. Use of a specific device or pattern requires indi-vidualized attention. Those well versed and experienced in motor control research 29,56,59,61,134 believe that the trend in physical therapy is moving away from earlier theoretical mod-els of treatment techniques and toward a motor control model. The emphasis is no longer on specific treatment techniques to “facilitate” movement but on active prob-lem solving by the patient to promote skilled movement and motor relearning. The practice of specific tasks is to be emphasized during intervention along with the practice amount. Treatment programs need to be based on specific motor control deficits, which may require modification or emphasis in the practice of a task that is meaningful to the patient and that takes place in numerous environ-ments. All of the gait intervention research presented in this chapter supports this model. One can no longer assume that certain treatment techniques are effective. Effectiveness needs to be vali-dated by research. As presented earlier, Weinstein and colleagues 134 examined the effect that balance-­ training and weight-­shifting activities during standing had on the hemiplegic gait. Although patients who received training improved their standing symmetry significantly, training did not translate into improved weight shifting during ambulation. This study clearly demonstrates the hazards of assuming that transfer of training occurs from a part of one functional task to another. For example, it would be convenient to assume that the techniques used to improve the standing balance of a patient with contraversive push-ing will improve the ability to walk. However, no evidence as yet supports this theory. Further research such as that of Weinstein and colleagues 134 is imperative for therapists to validate the rationales for their treatment procedures for patients after stroke. To do otherwise denies patients the most beneficial treatment approaches. The case study was unusual because the patient exhib-ited no spasticity and had voluntary, isolated control of all muscles but had decreased strength. However, several authors have questioned the role of spasticity in prevent-ing typical movement 2,28,29,61 and point to weakness as the more limiting factor. Spasticity is well known to increase the incidence of muscle contracture and thereby alter the biomechanical efficiency of a muscle. 2,28,29,39,58,61 In this respect, only the ankle joint was at risk and minimally so.

text: The patient was a model patient for other reasons. He was not cognitively impaired, and he was motivated to return to work. He was aware (although grudgingly at times) of the need for faithful adherence to a regular exercise pro-gram of repeated practice of newly learned motor skills. Therapists should always be aware of the need for careful physical assessment, individualized treatment pro-grams that are based on research findings, and ongoing reevaluation of the effectiveness of the treatment program in promoting optimum function.

text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Embrace the importance of addressing work after stroke. 2. Be aware of the barriers and facilitators related to return to work after stroke. 3. Develop the skills to find a good match between the indi-vidual and the workplace. 4. Assess the client’s work abilities and limitations. 5. Use government resources such as O*NET to assist in the rehabilitation of stroke survivors. 6. Design intervention plans to address return to work after stroke.

text: Return to work after stroke is becoming an increasingly important issue to address. The prevalence of stroke is increasing among individuals who are younger than 60 years of age. According to the Centers for Disease Con-trol and Prevention, more than 795,000 people in the United States experience a stroke each year. 7 Wolf and colleagues found that almost half of the people treated for mild stroke at their large medical center were of working age. 47 There may be several reasons for this increase in stroke, such as an increased prevalence of medical con-ditions that increase stroke risk (hypertension, obesity, diabetes, metabolic syndrome), increased drug abuse, and increased recognition of stroke symptoms, to name a few. 12 Aging Americans are choosing to work long past the traditional retirement age of 65 years, necessitating the need for many individuals to work after stroke. The labor force participation rate of people ages 65 to 74 years increased from 17.5% in 1996 to 26.8% in 2016, and it is

text: projected to increase to 30.2% by 2026. People aged 75 years or older participate in the labor force at compara-tively low rates, but participation in this group is expected to rise to 10.8% by 2026. 37 Remaining in the workforce is often a financial decision fueled by a multitude of fac-tors, including continued need for a regular salary, the increased retirement age for receiving full social security benefits, the need for health insurance, financial stress from credit card debt and mortgages, and decreased prev-alence of retirement pensions through employers. 16,28,35,39 But many people are choosing to work longer for personal fulfillment. Work provides meaning, routine, self-­esteem, quality of life, energy expenditure, and social interac-tion. 1,35 However, there can also be risks associated with work, such as work-­related injuries and illnesses, stress and anxiety from deadlines and workload, and inability to juggle work with other important home and community roles. 5 Many people who have experienced a stroke want or need to resume a worker role in the days, weeks, or months after their stroke. 14,16 The focus of this chapter is work performance after stroke. After a brief orientation to the reasoning behind the increasing need to address work in this population, this chapter will discuss how to assess work performance and design interventions to help people who have expe-rienced stroke make informed decisions regarding work, whether it is returning to work, managing long-­ term issues poststroke, or exiting the workforce via retirement or some form of disability. The chapter will present two case studies to help readers envision how rehabilitation professionals can assist stroke survivors to address work performance.

text: Other chapters in this book have described the sequelae of impairments, functional limitations, and performance and participation problems common after stroke (see Chapters 1, 17, 18, 20, 24, 25, and 28). The client must be medically stable before considering return to work, but the treatment team should not assume that return to work is not possible in clients with hemiparesis, expressive speech deficits, or impaired mobility. For example, a large study of 2500 working-­age individuals with stroke found that 74% returned to work 1 year poststroke. 11 However, the flip side is also true. In cases of mild stroke, the vast majority of stroke survivors easily passed motor, cognitive, and functional screens, so it was assumed that they could return to their prestroke activities; however, nearly 40% of clients presenting to the emergency department with mild stroke never returned to work, and another 15% remained unemployed 6 months later. 29 Other research-ers have reported similar rates of return to work after stroke. 10,32 Return-­to-­work rates after stroke are higher in other countries, including 39% in the Netherlands, 60% in Korea, 74% in Sweden, and 75% in Australia. 4,8,11,14 Many person, environment, and occupation factors have been found to support or prevent return to work after stroke. Culler and colleagues found that stroke survivors’ awareness of their limitations, insight into their need and ability to use strategies, and their motivation to work were important personal factors facilitating return to work after stroke. 9 Having a less avoidant coping style, a better pre-morbid quality of life, and scores suggesting lower levels of depression were associated with return to work. 4 Indi-viduals with depressive symptoms, pain, and low socio-economic status were less likely to return to work after stroke. 11 Factors associated with return to work include a supportive, accommodating work environment where individuals feel enabled and advocated for by colleagues and supervisors. 48 Larsen and colleagues found that poor mental health was a predictor of inability to return to work after stroke, as well as higher levels of fatigue. 22 Wang and colleagues found that individuals who were flexible and realistic in their vocational goal after stroke and who had emotionally accepted their resultant limitations were more likely to return to work. 45 Individuals with higher rates of sick leave from work prior to stroke had lower return to work rates 1 year poststroke. 46 Strong social sup-port from family and friends, a supportive workplace, and societal policies are important factors supporting return to work after stroke. 4,16 Individuals from low socioeconomic backgrounds have more difficulty returning to work after mild stroke than individuals from higher socioeconomic backgrounds. 6 Saeki and colleagues found that stroke survivors who were younger, better educated, employed in white col-lar jobs, and had a positive acceptance of their condition were more successful returning to work. 32 A large study with 2539 people with first stroke found that after adjust-ing for age, sex, and functional status (low mood, high pain, and dependency in activities of daily living [ADLs]), high income was independently associated with increased chance of return to work compared with low-­ income patients. 11 To address the occupation of work, the clinician must have a thorough understanding of the client’s medical condition; previous medical history; other health condi-tions; and limitations from physician-­imposed restrictions

text: or treatments for their health conditions, including medi-cations. As with any occupational therapy (OT) evalua-tion, the clinician begins by developing an occupational profile. 2 The procedure is similar to the development of a traditional occupational profile, except there is an addi-tional focus on education and training, work history, and the client’s return-­to-­work goal. It is essential to under-stand required job tasks, performance expectations, the work environment, and workplace routines. It is impor-tant to consider other factors about the individual and his or her life when making work decisions, such as preexist-ing and/or concomitant health conditions, other required life roles, and the importance placed on work. A good match between the individual and the workplace is the first step to optimal work performance. Because legal and financial ramifications can be associated with work and the consequences of returning to work without possessing the ability to meet requirements of the workplace, use of a taxonomy is recommended to ensure that all areas are considered. The third edition of the Occupational Therapy Practice Framework (OTPF) 2 has proven to be especially helpful in organizing these concepts; therefore, it will be used in this chapter. Use of the OTPF ensures that the cli-nician considers the tasks performed at work, the activity demands of these tasks, the performance skills and body functions required for these tasks, the client’s work abili-ties and limitations, the performance patterns (i.e., roles, routines, habits, and rituals) at the workplace and of the worker, and the context of the workplace. 2

text: Rehabilitation professionals understand the requirements of most daily living tasks and are well equipped to design assessments and interventions for these areas. Physical therapists know how to assess and rehabilitate an ath-lete with a shoulder injury, occupational therapists rou-tinely help people resume their ADLs and manage their home responsibilities, and speech pathologists are experts at helping people communicate and manage cognitive impairments. The motion necessary to swing a tennis racket, the requirements of getting bathed and dressed, and the oral motor control necessary to speak are well known to these rehabilitation professionals. With more than 867 detailed occupations in the U.S. economy, there is huge variation in what people must do at work. 38 All OT students have analyzed ADLs and understand the various ways that people perform common tasks such as tooth brushing and cooking. Clinicians may have an elementary understanding of what a construction worker must do, but it is impossible to know what all jobs involve and to have a deep enough understanding of the job in order to help a client return to work after stroke. The clinician must understand the tasks performed and the tools and equip-ment used at work in addition to the level of skill, ability, and knowledge required to perform the particular job. The clinician must understand the environmental con-ditions encountered in the workplace and the employer policies. It is important to understand the fit between the person, the job, and the workplace before the stroke. Prestroke work performance, relationship between the worker and employer, and workers’ feelings about their jobs are important factors in return to work after stroke. 9 It is important for the practitioner to consider the effect that the wide array of employment policies can have on the process of addressing work performance after stroke. Of course, the practitioner must also consider other important policies, such as patient privacy and insurance reimbursement, when helping clients return to work after stroke. Understanding the fit between the client and his or her job and employer begins with a conversation between the clinician and the client. After this conversation, the clini-cian should have a good idea of (1) the client’s satisfac-tion with his or her job and employer, (2) plans before the stroke for continued work at this job, and (3) inter-est in continuing employment in this prior work position. Even if the client does not express interest in continuing employment, the client should inform his or her employer of the need to miss work because of a health condition in order to prevent termination from employment and ben-efits associated with work, including health care coverage. Employers are not required to hold an employee’s job unless the client formally requests a medical leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA). FMLA pro-vides employees with up to 12 weeks of annual unpaid, job-­ protected leave because of a serious health condi-tion; it also requires that group health benefits are main-tained during the leave. People who have worked for their employer at least 1250 hours during the past 12 months are eligible for FMLA. All public agencies, public and pri-vate schools, and companies with 50 or more employees must provide FMLA. 40 The clinician should ensure that the client has applied for a formal FMLA to protect his or her job and health insurance even if return to work with that employer does not appear to be feasible. FMLA is also available for a client’s spouse, child, or parent to care for a family member with a serious health condition. 40 During the course of work rehabilitation, the clinician often needs to speak with the employer to get a written job description, arrange a worksite visit, and discuss return-­to-­ work possibilities. As is always the case, the clinician cannot reveal protected health information per the Health Insur-ance Portability and Accountability Act. This includes the client’s past, present, or future physical or mental health or condition and details regarding provision of health care to the client. 36 If the clinician anticipates that any protected health information will be disclosed during an interaction with the employer, such as the impairments that the client is demonstrating, written permission from the client must be secured before disclosure. text: Employment tests must be derived from a job analysis and physical demands analysis that targets critical or impor-tant job duties, work behaviors, or work outcomes. 31 Evaluations used to make work decisions must possess the following characteristics in this hierarchical order: (1) it must be safe to administer; (2) it must give reliable val-ues that are quantifiable; (3) it must predict risk of future injury or illness; and (4) it must be practical. Predicting risk of future injury is a type of validity, which means that the test measures what it claims to measure. 18 Quantify-ing the work requirements into the necessary skills and designing an assessment to measure these abilities and skills can enhance content, construct, and other forms of criterion validity. The work evaluation should be reliable, meaning that it produces consistent scores on diferent occasions (test–retest reliability) and when administered by diferent raters on the same occasion (interrater reli-ability). 17,31 Safety is the first criterion that must be con-sidered—safety must never be compromised for the sake of reliability or validity. For example, before asking a cli-ent to lift the actual object he moves from floor to over-head level at work, the clinician should know if the client can assume the required positions, maintain balance, and generate grip in the manner necessary to grasp the object. Screening of functions that underpin task performance is necessary; this should include cognitive and sensory func-tions. Monitoring for safety throughout the assessment is of utmost importance, such as vital signs, ratings of per-ceived exertion, and body mechanics and pace, as well as observing for signs of distress or maximum tolerance. A work evaluation can be considered an employment test; therefore, Uniform Guidelines on Employment Selection Procedures developed and issued by the Equal Employ-ment Opportunity Commission must be followed. The work evaluation must not discriminate based upon race, national origin, religion, sex, origin, age, and disability. 41 Payne and Harvey’s framework for physical employment tests and standards outlines this topic well. 31 The Occupational Information Network (O*NET) is the U.S. Department of Labor’s (DOL’s) system for describing characteristics of the job, worker, and the work environment for every job in the U.S. economy. O*NET replaced the Dictionary of Occupational Titles in 1998. O*NET identifies the work tasks required for each job and ranks these tasks by level of importance and relevance.

text: Requisite knowledge, skills, abilities, and work activities are identified and ranked for importance and level of function. Other work interests, work styles, and work val-ues associated with the job are identified, as well as work context, tools and technology, and educational and voca-tional preparation. Wages, employment trends, and job openings by state are included, as are videos about the job and related jobs. 30 O*NET has a wealth of information about jobs; it is a good starting point for understanding the generic requirements of a job. After understanding this generic information, the clinician can work with the client and his or her employer to understand the require-ments of the client’s actual job. Table 9.­1 describes the categories within O*NET and lists examples of elements within each category. text: her ability to perform the required job tasks. 21 The cli-ent’s perceptions of his or her abilities and limitations may not always be accurate, especially after experiencing a new stroke, but it is prudent to understand the client’s beliefs before performing the actual work tasks. After identify-ing the job title(s) that most closely matches the client’s job, the clinician consults O*NET to identify tasks that are commonly performed by people who hold this spe-cific job title. 30 This task list serves as a starting point for understanding the specific tasks that are required of the job. Tasks that are not required are deleted, and other tasks not identified by O*NET are discussed. It may be necessary to search other job titles because the client’s job may not neatly fit into one job on O*NET. The clinician converses with the client about these tasks to identify the manner in which they are performed and tools or equip-ment needed to perform these tasks. To understand the frequency of performance, each task is rated on a 7-­point rating scale designed by the DOL. This scale ranges from once or less each year to every hour or more. After the JPM has been used to identify the job tasks, the client is asked to identify his or her current ability to perform each job task on a 10-­point scale, ranging from not able to extremely well. The JPM uses methods and rating scales from the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure with approval from the authors. 23 The JPM was devel-oped by our team at Washington University in St. Louis; it has been used clinically with hundreds of clients at the Rehabilitation Institute of St. Louis and in research stud-ies performed at Washington University School of Medi-cine. Although the psychometric properties have not been formally measured, the JPM has proven to be one of the best predictors of return-­to-­work outcomes in clients with mild to moderate stroke. 21 By comparing the activities listed in O*NET (Table 9.­1) with the functions commonly affected by stroke that are well known to all clinicians and outlined in other chap-ters of this book, it is apparent that there is a wide range of constructs that potentially will need to be assessed when addressing return to work with a client with stroke. The clinician may have already performed standardized assess-ments that measure various body functions (e.g., sensa-tion, strength, memory, and executive function) and ADL and instrumental ADL (IADL) performance; these can be very useful when assessing ability to work (see Chapters 5, 25, and 26). However, clinicians need to be careful not to assume that a specific score on a standardized test or a manual muscle test grade equivocate a certain level of ability to work because this is not supported by the litera-ture. There are many standardized assessments to measure client’s work ability and limitations, as well as workplace exposures, social climate, and work policies that can be useful when evaluating a client after stroke. Table 9.­2 out-lines many of these assessments. There is also a role for nonstandardized assessment when addressing ability to work. Job simulations are especially useful; however, the clinician must ensure that the methods used are safe and reproducible; job simulations are inherently valid, but they may not be practical because of the equipment, space, and time required. When designing a nonstandardized assessment using job simulations, the clinician begins by identify-ing construct(s) that need to be measured, designing a simulation that mimics that job task, acquiring tools and supplies necessary for the simulation, deciding the measurement methods that will be used (e.g., time, rep-etitions, number of items dropped, weight lifted), and setting up the environment to match the work envi-ronment that the client appears able to tolerate (e.g., physical environment, people to interface with, noise level). Before performing job simulation testing, it is important to screen the client’s ability to perform skills embedded in simulation; for example, standing, balance, ambulation, and vision should be assessed before asking

text: a client to perform a job-­simulated climbing task. The client should be involved to help make the simulation as real life as possible and he or she should understand mock-­ups before testing, such as using soft theraputty to simulate ground meat for a chef. During the simulated nonstandardized assessment, the therapist observes for each construct that is being measured, recording behav-iors, methods, and self-­management. The Assessment of Work Performance (AWP) is a standardized assessment by Jan Sandqvist that assesses 14 skills while a client per-forms a work activity, including five motor, five process, and four communication/interaction skills. 33 The clini-cian rates the client’s performance on a 4-­point ordinal rating scale (1 = incompetent performance, 2 = limited performance, 3 = unsure performance, and 4 = competent performance). Tiering the AWP over a job simulation assessment allows the therapist to gather objective data that can be used to measure changes over time. There are also work performance assessment proto-cols that cluster standardized and nonstandardized assess-ments into a battery that has standardized administration procedures and has been validated. As always, when using standardized assessments or batteries, it is critical to abide by the directions in the manual or protocol. It is important to use both qualitative and quantitative approaches when performing an assessment of work ability, with the client’s beliefs and concerns about work ascertained and strongly considered. Use of the JPM before actual performance testing familiarizes the clinician with the client’s percep-tions of his or her abilities to perform work tasks before actually performing these tasks with the client. Screens of functions that are required components of a work task are performed first to ensure that the client is safe to perform the performance-­based assessment. For example, before measuring ability to climb a ladder, the client’s ability to hear, see, follow directions, ambulate, and balance should be measured. After administering standardized assessments, work simulations that are similar to the work requirements can be tested, ensuring that safety is always maintained. The client must be a close partner with the clinician, advising the clinician when the simulation is as real life as pos-sible. To be able to know work tolerances and to track progress, work simulations should include objective measurements, whether it is tracking repetitions, tim-ing tolerance, counting the number of errors, describing prehension patterns, observing nonverbal communica-tion skills, or the ability to manage frustration. Because these assessments are being administered to make a return-­to-­work decision, Title 1 of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) applies both in the workplace and in the therapy clinic. Clients with qualified disabili-ties who request reasonable accommodations should be provided with these during the assessment. Testing pro-tocols, equipment, environments, and facilities used in the rehabilitation setting should not discriminate against individuals with disabilities. 20

text: If the client does not possess the ability to return to work after the assessment but wants to return to work and there is potential to do so, a treatment plan can be initiated. The profession of OT defines the occupation of work as (1) employment interests and pursuits, (2) employment seeking and acquisition, (3) job performance, (4) retire-ment preparation and adjustment, (5) volunteer explora-tion, and (6) volunteer participation. 2 Much of the work rehabilitation that has occurred in the professions of occupational and physical therapy over the past 25 years has been directed at returning people with work-­related musculoskeletal disorders to their jobs through services such as work hardening, work conditioning, and post-­ offer preemployment testing. Historically, people who have strokes are at or above working age, so return to work has not been a major focus of treatment. Some individuals who experience a stroke may be focused on returning to their previous job, others will need to iden-tify residual abilities and seek new employment, others will choose to pursue volunteer work experiences, and others will decide to retire. It is important to understand

text: that rehabilitation to address work can focus on one or more of these levels of participation. For example, the initial focus may be on returning to the previous job (i.e., job performance); however, if that does not appear to be realistic, the client may choose to seek alternative employment, pursue volunteer work, or retire from the workforce. The intervention plan should address work as defined by the client at the time point that he or she is involved in rehabilitation. After the assessment, if there is a major mismatch between a client’s abilities and the requirements of the job, return to the previous job is most likely not pos-sible. Depending on the client’s goals, treatment may or may not be warranted. For example, a client with major expressive communication deficits who negotiated con-tracts for a Fortune 500 company may choose to explore alternative careers at the company that do not hinge on expressive communication, or a 60-­year-­old construction worker who cannot climb and lift may choose to retire and focus on his passion for mission work. When a client who was employed at the time of stroke is no longer able to work competitively, the financial ramifications need to be discussed. The OT practitioner should refer the client to social work of a social service agency regarding both the finances and health insurance. In some cases, the OT practitioner’s documentation regarding limitations in the client’s work abilities may be used to help the client qual-ify for long-­term disability. If the client demonstrates the ability to safely per-form the job demands at a competitive level and appears capable of tolerating the work schedule and environmen-tal demands, discussions with the employer are recom-mended. A work trial may be warranted before a full return to work. The OT practitioner can be involved in negoti-ating this and can even go to work with the client on the first day to observe the client’s performance in context. It is important to ascertain that the client is able to perform at the levels of performance for the entire work shift and that this can be dependably performed on a regular basis. A client may be able to perform most of the job functions, nearly meet the productivity requirements, or fall just short of the required work schedule. In these cases, the therapist should work with the client and the employer to identify the best course of action to address the short-comings, whether it is treatment to restore loss functions, learning compensatory strategies, providing accommoda-tions at the workplace, or a combination of these strategies. A supportive and accommodating work environment is an important factor supporting return to work after stroke. 16 Conflicting institutional practices can contribute to dif-ficulties individuals have when attempting to return to work after stroke. 27 Fatigue often interferes with return to work after stroke. 3,13,22 Some employers may consider a graduated work schedule to manage fatigue, but others will require that the client return to the customary work schedule. As with other areas of practice, the occupational therapist addressing return to work after stroke must be a creative problem solver who is capable of negotiating innovative solutions. When assisting a person with return to work after stroke, the client must follow certain procedures, begin-ning with disclosure of the disability. The client must be able to perform the essential functions of the job with reasonable accommodations, which must be specifically requested from the employer. It is important for the cli-nician to address all of these areas with the client before recommending that the client return to work. The Job Accommodation Network (JAN) is an online resource that provides free, expert, and confidential guidance on workplace accommodations and disability employment issues, including determining if a client has a disability under the ADA. JAN consultants provide individual online and phone guidance for workplace accommodations, and the website provides accommodations for various dis-abilities. 19 Clinicians can refer employers to JAN to learn about their role in providing reasonable accommodations. Often, employers are willing to allow the client a work trial at the workplace; it is important to protect the cli-ent, employer, and yourself when performing work trials. The clinician must have a good feel for the client’s ability to reenter the workplace environment, ensuring that the client is not exposed to injurious conditions, physiological stress, cognitive overload, emotional turmoil, or the risk of being terminated from work. Assisting a client to return to his or her previous job can be a challenging task; however, helping the client under-stand his or her work abilities and limitations in order to identify and search for a new position is often a more dif-ficult task. Clients who attempt to return to their same job at the same employer are usually the most successful. The client can draw on knowledge, skills, relationships, work-place norms, routines, and other familiar environmental characteristics when returning to the same job with the same employer. The employer is also familiar with the employee and his or her worker behaviors and prior per-formance; however, if changes in the client’s skills, execu-tive functions, workplace tolerances, stamina, interaction abilities, affect, or work ability have occurred, these will most likely be evident to an employer who knows the client before stroke. Nearly half of the individuals who returned to work after mild stroke reported that they were performing at 75% or less of their prestroke work abilities, and nearly one-third were not satisfied with their initial poststroke work performance. 29 Often, people with stroke are able to return to work with accommodations, but changes from their premorbid status may impact suc-cess in the workplace. Reduced work speed, organization and concentration problems, and fatigue were reported 6 months after return to work in a large cohort of patients after stroke. 29 Clinicians need to be sure that individuals with stroke not only return to work but that they are able to stay at work. text: stroke were found to be more likely to continue to be working 1 year after stroke, suggesting that focusing on the IADL of health maintenance and management may help individuals who have had a stroke maintain employ-ment on a long-­term basis. 22 Although returning to the prior job is preferred, some employers will offer a new or modified position to workers who have been exceptional employees in the past. This may be preferred over seeking new employment, but if the client can perform duties of the previous job, performing the same job title with a dif-ferent employer is a viable option. Changing to a different job title with a new employer is commonly the most diffi-cult thing to do. Relationships may be an important driver behind this phenomenon. It has been established that the requirements of each client’s job vary significantly; however, some require-ments of working are generic to all workplaces and jobs. Many of these issues are temporal in nature: workers must arrive to work on time, consistently work their required schedule, perform assigned work tasks for a specified period of time, take and return from work breaks on time, and tolerate working the number of hours they are sched-uled to work. Workers must obtain required productiv-ity levels and complete all assigned work. Work must be performed accurately, and the quality of the output must be acceptable. In most work settings, workers must have good hygiene, be well groomed, and wear clothing and personal protection equipment that is required of the workplace. Workers must be able to accept direction from their supervisors, modify behaviors based on feedback, interact with coworkers in an acceptable manner, and maintain socially appropriate behaviors in the workplace. It is important for the occupational therapist to address these generic work requirements in addition to the spe-cific abilities necessary to perform required job tasks.

text: Stroke can impair a wide range of functions that result in limitations in a client’s ability to meet these generic worker requirements. This may be directly tied to physical, physi-ological, cognitive, emotional, social, sensory, or motiva-tional changes after stroke, or it could be a combination of a constellation of limitations. Interventions to address some of these generic worker requirements may be novel to clinicians who treat in traditional outpatient settings. For example, clients participating in OT to address return to work may be required to punch a time clock or sign in and out, with methods used in therapy similar to those at the worksite. Treatment sessions may need to be longer in length to simulate a normal work day. The clinician may need to assume a supervisory role when addressing some of these generic work requirements, which is quite differ-ent from the enabling and helping role that the therapist is accustomed to. Interventions may need to occur in groups rather than individually, allowing a client to interact and work collaboratively with others as is common in work groups. Clinicians set goals and coach their clients to per-form the required repetitions needed to remediate their deficit, but therapists do not traditionally counsel their clients who are not performing to the level of productivity that is needed. Outside of psychiatric settings, it may be rare for a clinician to discuss grooming and hygiene with a client; however, this is common when addressing work performance. If return-­to-­work decisions are based solely on the client’s ability to competently perform required job tasks (e.g., lift heavy boxes, address customer service calls, design creative artwork) and his or her ability to con-sistently achieve these generic work requirements is not considered, the client may have an unsuccessful return-­to-­ work attempt. Clinicians assisting clients with return to work must be able to assume new roles with their clients and integrate novel treatment activities into their reper-toire to ensure their clients’ success when reentering the workforce. When rehabilitating other areas of occupation after stroke, the client may adjust his or her expectations regarding an activity (e.g., a homemaker with limited abil-ity to bend and stoop may choose to purchase vegetables rather than garden; a retired man with limited dexterity may ask his wife to floss his teeth). However, a client who is attempting to return to work cannot decide not to do a required job task (the butcher will cut meat but not oper-ate the grinder, or the medical transcriptionist will type short evaluations but not extensive surgical reports). If it is apparent that the client cannot perform the required job duties, return to work can be supported by working closely with the employer to adjust the work expectations or provide increased assistance. 44 The client must meet the ADA’s definition for disabled, must disclose his or her disability to the employer, must be able to perform the essential functions of the job with accommodations, and must request these accommodations from the employer. The OT practitioner can assist with this process. The employer is required to make accommodations for the worker if he or she is indeed capable of performing these essential functions with accommodations and the accom-modations are reasonable for the employer. Clinicians who are familiar with ADA’s requirements for accessibil-ity may assume that an employer must accommodate an employee after stroke if he or she is able to do much of the job, but there are strict guidelines and case laws that guide employer’s decisions in these types of cases. The Job Accommodation Scale (JAS) is a 21-­item employer self-­ report measure recently developed to assess the likelihood that the employer would support temporary job accom-modations. 34 Although it was developed for workers with musculoskeletal back conditions, many of the items are relevant to individuals after stroke or other health condi-tions. The five factors identified through factor analysis of the JAS are (1) modify the physical workload, (2) modify

text: the work environment, (3) modify the work schedule, (4) find alternate duties, and (5) arrange for assistance. 34 Clinicians use many of the same models of practice and frames of references when addressing work performance. A simple model by the author, the Kaskutas Model of Work Performance, combines characteristics from Law-ton and Nahemow’s Ecological Model of Aging (i.e., personal competence, environmental press, and the docil-ity theory) with Kurt Lewin’s Field Theory, which sees human behavior as a result of the function of the person and the environment. 24,26 In the Kaskutas Model, work performance is viewed as a result of interaction between the personal competence of the individual and the envi-ronmental affordances. Interventions address personal competence, environmental affordances, and job require-ments until a match is reached between these three fac-tors. In the visual of this model depicted in Figure 9.­1A, there is a mismatch among these three factors; the job requirements are well outside of the personal competence of the client and the environmental affordances fall short. Figure 9.­1B demonstrates how the job demands have been adjusted through employer collaboration and an adequate number of environmental affordances have been put in place to allow the client to meet his job demands. In Figure 9.­1C, the job demands remain the same, and increases in both personal competence and environmental affordances have occurred, allowing the client to be able to meet the job demands. Treatment planning for return to work after stroke has many similar components to treatment planning to address other areas of occupation. The clinician develops interventions to address body functions or performance skills that appear to be deficient for the area of occupa-tion; these may be restorative or compensatory in nature; in some cases, they will be to modify or maintain perfor-mance. A mix of preparatory, purposeful, and occupation-­ based interventions can be used in rehabilitation to return to work. Similar methods to those addressed in other chapters in this book apply, whether it is design-ing strengthening programs using the biomechani-cal approach, modifying the environment or providing adaptive equipment, or using the Cognitive Orientation to Daily Occupational Performance model to improve cognitive performance. 25 Advocacy, education, and self-­ management can be useful intervention approaches to address return to work. Clinicians can consult the JAN to identify equipment that may support employment at the worksite; JAN’s searchable online accommodation resource tool is especially helpful. 19 People who have had a stroke do not usually experience pain because of the stroke; however, they may experience pain because of shoulder instability, gait abnormalities, or abnormal movement patterns. They may also be experi-encing pain because of other health conditions common in aging Americans, such as arthritis or peripheral neu-ropathy. In addition to limiting physical tolerances, pain can impair an individual’s ability to concentrate and main-tain vigilance, leading to inattention and errors. Many individuals who have had a stroke have a constellation of other health conditions that they are managing, such as arthritis, depression, and diabetes. These conditions may result in physiological, emotional, or physical limitations that can affect ability to work. Medications can affect indi-viduals’ ability to perform, attend, and process. Individu-als who want to work must learn to manage the multitude of impairments that they may be experiencing because of stroke and other health conditions. OT can help clients learn to self-­manage their symptoms, manage their health, and improve their function and participation. 15 Clinicians addressing work performance should under-stand the public policies, laws, and standards regarding employment. These policies can impact delivery of OT services, including assessment, intervention, and return to work. Each state has an agency that administers state-­ funded vocational rehabilitation services. Although ser-vices differ by state, funds for retraining, job coaching, adaptive equipment, and other services may be available. It is important to help individuals with stroke maintain their employment status, health insurance coverage, and income source during the period of time that they are unable to work. The OT practitioner should discuss tak-ing a medical leave through the FMLA and accessing short-­ or long-­term disability insurance policies that they may have; often, people forget about them.
