text: Joan Joan is a letter carrier with 23 years on the job. She expe-rienced a stroke, and her occupational therapist began addressing work performance while Joan was in day treat-ment. Joan is the divorced mother of two children; the youngest is still in high school. She is also the caregiver for her elderly mother who lives across town in her own home. At the time of referral, Joan had left-­sided weak-ness and was not able to perform bathtub transfers inde-pendently. Before the stroke, she loved her work, and her coworkers loved her. To understand the job demands, the clinician got a written job description from the employer and initi-ated a discussion with Joan’s supervisor. Because Joan was required to drive a mail truck to get to her walking route, a computerized driver’s screening was performed, which revealed impairment with leg strength and mobility and mild impairments on all visual subtests. Treatment included a lot of job-­ simulated tasks, including stuff-­ bundling mail, walking a paved “route” inside and outside of the clinic, and performing a simple delivery task, which was somewhat similar to her work but different enough to require new learning. Joan required cueing to attend to details and compensate for decreased working and short-­ term memory. A mail satchel from work was used, and her tolerance built up to 1 hour. During a worksite visit, Joan walked through the procedures she did at work with help from her supervisor, and practiced performing some of the physical tasks. It was apparent that she was remember-ing details of her job with some help. The therapist dis-cussed job transition with Joan’s boss. Even though Joan was unable to drive her car, she believed that she would be able to drive the mail truck. She did not understand her limitations and remained optimistic. The therapist used a computerized interactive driving program that required Joan to think about what she was attending to, problem solve, and attend to visual and auditory stimuli. The pre-driving Dynavision training protocol for driving was used, and the roadwise driving screening was readministered. Despite failing this screening for a second time, Joan began driving with her family against the therapist’s direc-tions. Joan’s ability to tolerate mail delivery simulations involving multiple steps increased, as did her awareness of her capabilities and limitations. She was independent

text: in ADLs but still had problems with vision, processing speed, and working memory. Joan sustained a second stroke during treatment. After the second stroke, she had bilateral upper extrem-ity weakness, decreased fine motor skills, limited endur-ance, increased dependence in ADLs, and deteriorations in cognition and memory. When she came back to OT, she noted that her thinking was slow, her left hand felt like pins and needles, and she was under a 10-­lb doctor-­ imposed lifting restriction. She was concerned about going back to driving but remained motivated to return to work. To see what she recalled about the mail deliv-ery task she had done in therapy, the clinician had Joan instruct the therapist in the task; she needed cueing and reminders with about 50% recall. After several days of performing the mail delivery sequence again, she could tolerate 1 hour of work with good mental and physical endurance but had some problems with attention to detail and way finding. She was sorting mail for the departments in the rehabilitation hospital with supervision from the therapist despite limited left-­hand function. Cueing was required to decrease conversation while working because of breakdowns in performance. She continued to perform the computer-­based driving program for visual tracking, field of view, and reaction time. After the restriction was lifted, mailbag carrying tolerance increased from 18 lb and then 28 lb. She demonstrated good initiative and appro-priate interaction skills with mail delivery. She continued to need intermittent cueing with the computer driving program; her field of view had improved 50%. The therapist referred Joan to the state vocational reha-bilitation, which provided funding for a driving evaluation and adaptations for work. She was able to pass the driving evaluation and identify steps for return to work. The team explored ways for Joan to get back to work in a graded manner, increasing physical and cognitive demands as per-formance improved, working with the physician to do this. The essential functions of the job were closely compared with her current functioning, and the employer’s medical health office was contacted to obtain guidelines for return to work. After receiving the physician’s approval, Joan was allowed to return to work with walking and driving limited to 1 hour at a time and the use of a notebook for memory and reminders. She was assigned a new mail route, which combined two routes she had performed previously. The clinician went to work with Joan on her first day back; the clinician explained the return-­to-­work limitations to Joan’s supervisor. She began sorting mail and learning the proce-dure for a new handheld scanner as well as the new mail route. The therapist visited Joan at the worksite 20 days later; Joan was very slow at the mail casing activity, and she was constantly fatigued. The clinician went with Joan on her mail delivery route. She was able to ambulate on vari-ous terrains in a slow manner, keep her mail well organized, and interact appropriately with patrons. text: Eric is a land surveyor for a small surveying and engineer-ing firm. He experienced a small stroke and was able to return to work; however, only part-­time work was avail-able. Several months later, he experienced a second stroke and was seen by OT. The JPM was used to identify the required work tasks, tools used, and common environ-mental conditions encountered. The requirements of his job included ability to walk, climb, and carry tools for extended distances over even and uneven terrain; work in reaching, squatted, and bent positions; prolonged standing; use of a machete to clear brush; operation of a hand-­based computer; and the ability to work outdoors in all types of weather conditions. He had to be able to work safely on busy roads and highways, attend to details, accurately perform mathematical functions, and follow detailed procedures. On the JPM, Eric perceived that he could perform these work tasks at a level 8 to 10. The therapist spoke with Eric’s employer, who confirmed the job description; the employer allowed the therapist to borrow some back-­up equipment that they had to per-form some job simulations in OT. Because Eric worked on a survey crew with one man, the therapist and Eric walked around the grounds near the clinic and performed portions of a survey task with the therapist acting as the survey assistant. They performed this for several sessions, with increased tolerances noted. Eric was able to operate the equipment and perform the physical demands well. He consistently demonstrated safe work behaviors when per-forming simulated surveying in the clinic’s busy parking lot. He was able to talk through the procedures required at work and accurately perform mathematical computations. After several OT visits, the therapist spoke with Eric’s employer again as he was doing well with the simula-tions in the clinic. The employer questioned Eric’s abil-ity to accurately record numbers, stating that when he was working he had “some kind of dyslexia” that caused him to make errors. He would write down incorrect numbers his coworker called out during the survey, rendering the survey inaccurate. The employer was concerned about the liabilities associated with a surveying error, which could result in contractors building roads in the wrong spot, land

The union intervened because the productivity requirements had recently been reconfigured; it was found that she was actually perform-ing 6 or 7 hours of work. Fortunately, the post office had a float position that routinely handles the overflow of work, so they were picking up the work that Joan could not per-form. The therapist helped Joan rearrange her workspace and her route, and she gradually increased her productivity to the required level. She has been working full time with-out problems for the past 9 months.

text: being incorrectly split, or other errors with legal and safety ramifications. The management team wanted to be com-pletely convinced that Eric could perform tasks regarding numbers consistently correct. Eric had not mentioned this problem, and it had not arisen during the OT evalu-ation or treatment. He was not aware that he was making errors. The occupational therapist began working with Eric on measurement activities, reading numbers that he had measured aloud, and listening to and recording num-bers the therapist said in a tape recorder. His abilities to perform these number tasks accurately improved, and it was apparent that he could perform all essential functions with accommodations. Eric and the therapist listed each essential function of the job, Eric’s current abilities to per-form them, and accommodations that were needed. Eric increased awareness of his deficits and ability to advocate for his accommodations. A discussion with the employer and Eric’s coworker revealed that the problem occurred when he was performing the laborer duties on the two-­ man crew and not the operator duties (these did not involve reading numbers aloud). Initially, Eric returned to work performing operator duties only, which he consis-tently performed accurately. The occupational therapist performed several worksite visits to work with Eric on resuming the laborer’s duties in the field. They identified the “just right” combination of factors that supported his performance with number citation. He began to use these strategies and gradually resume laborer’s duties (e.g., use of voice recorder, repetition, accuracy checks). Eric began to ask for feedback and help if needed, and he was eager to accept feedback and guidance. As he gained confidence to begin performing the laborer’s duties, his work was checked several times. When he was accurate 100% of the time, he was allowed to rotate duties with the other sur-veyor on the crew. He learned about the effects of fatigue and was able to recognize early signs of fatigue and request to switch roles with his coworker if fatigue was interfering with accuracy. Because Eric worked in all types of weather and was required to physically exert himself, this was an essential lesson for him to learn. Eric continues to work his regular duty job and he has not had any instances of errors.

text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Understand the instrumental activity of daily living (IADL) of driving and community mobility as a highly valued but complex occupation. 2. Identify the risk factors for the IADL of driving and com-munity mobility and appropriately implement evaluation and intervention strategies. 3. Addressing this IADL either through interventions to prepare for the resumption of driving, make an appropriate referral to a driver rehabilitation specialist, or assist with a compre-hensive community mobility plan.

text: For most individuals, the world becomes a larger place when one acquires a driver’s license. Driving a motor vehicle allows people to move beyond their neighborhood, community, state, province, or country to visit, explore, and join activities outside the home and immediate envi-ronment. Although public transportation in communities provide some of the same destinations, driving a motor vehicle allows for the spontaneity and freedom to move beyond the boundaries of train, subway, or bus stations. After a driver’s license has been acquired, there is an expectation that a person will be always be able to drive, and although there may be other methods of transport available, driving is the most accepted form of community mobility in the United States. 76 Moreover, because com-munity mobility is recognized as the means to participate in other occupations, it is considered an occupation enabler. 69

text: Thus, persons who do not drive, whether because of dis-ability, function, finances, or choice, face consequences that affect their ability to participate in some aspects of life. 76 Accordingly, when a stroke survivor is told that driv-ing is no longer an option, it comes as a shock and viewed as untenable. 55 Many individuals consider continuing to drive regardless of the medical recommendation. 33,55 Driving is and will be for the foreseeable future one of the most valued instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). One of the changes in the updated Occupa-tional Therapy Practice Framework: Process and Domain (OTPF) 5 is that driving has been elevated to driving and community mobility as the identified IADL rather than simply community mobility. The definition of this IADL remains basically the same, clearly positioning driving as one means of community mobility along with walking, biking, and other transportation systems. This change— identifying driving first—reflects the importance driving has to our clients and the recognition that the majority of adults use their own personal motor vehicle as a means of community mobility and will continue to do so in the foreseeable future. 19 Evidence of clients’ desire to resume this valued occu-pation after a major medical event such as a stroke has been well known among occupational therapy (OT) practitioners but only recently documented. A study was undertaken to examine how chronic conditions impacted valued IADLs from the perspective of the client and their caregivers. 28 Thirty older adults with a mean age of 68 years were interviewed during their outpatient rehabilita-tion program. A primary caregiver was also interviewed. Although several diagnoses were included in the inclu-sion criteria, almost all of the participants were recover-ing from a stroke and had significant impairment that required continued outpatient services. With the excep-tion of three participants who had already ceased driv-ing, all remaining participants identified driving as the most important IADL over all others. When questioned further, it was clear for many that driving was viewed as primary in order to be successful at other IADLs (e.g., shopping, getting to social events, banking, and manag-ing medication). 28 For some individuals in this study and others, the loss of the occupation of driving led to feelings of depression and isolation. 46,55,59 This is particularly true for younger persons with stroke, who need to drive to continue to work, provide services for family members, and continue to participate in an active lifestyle. However, stroke primarily affects those individuals older than the age of 60 years. And because persons with stroke repre-sent the largest impairment group of Medicare beneficia-ries receiving inpatient medical rehabilitation services in the United States, 60 occupational therapists should be the experts in providing services to assist clients in restoring their daily occupations, particularly activities of daily liv-ing (ADLs) and IADLs. Moreover, the clients are going to be changing as the next generation, the Baby Boomers, becomes the majority of our client base.

text: The generation born between 1945 and 1964 is affection-ately known as the Baby Boomers. News media, politicians, insurance companies, and advertisers have spent significant resources and time researching this generation because the numbers of individuals in the age group overwhelmingly outnumber other cohort groups. Currently, as the Boom-ers move into later stages of adulthood, the unique aspects of this generation will continue to change OT practice over the next several decades. For example, there will be a shift from the Depression-­era seniors, fearful to spend too much money on near necessities, to the Boomers, who overspend on luxuries. The Boomers will demand adaptive equipment that is both useful and attractive because they will not take “no” for an answer but want solutions. The Boomers’ work ethic and drive will demand that therapists find better ways to adapt work environments (see Chapter 9); modify efficient home environments (see Chapter 30); and address occupations beyond dressing, eating, and bath-ing. Since the development of improved contraception, cohort groups have fewer children, and working mothers are more the norm. Thus, working adult children (i.e., the “sandwich” generation) cannot be expected or relied on to meet the transportation needs of their aging parents. The Boomers want and will demand their independence, and for this generation of people, nothing means indepen-dence more than getting behind the wheel (BTW) of a vehicle to drive. Matching problems or impairments with options, the Boomers will demand access to the solutions that can keep them on the road. Just as the present young generations are growing up using fingertip technology to access their needs, the Boomers grew up with the development of motor vehi-cles. In the 1940s and 1950s, the new shiny car was the status symbol of independence, the method of interacting with others, and provided the “vehicle” to engage in occu-pations outside the home. Although some cities supported or promoted public transportation, for most of America’s cities, towns, and villages, and the expansion of suburbia, neighborhoods were designed around the personal vehi-cle. For those living in the urban sprawl or rural areas, the

text: personal vehicle became a necessity rather than a luxury in order to meet daily needs. As teenagers, most Boomers counted the days until they could take the driver’s test and be able to explore beyond their immediate neighborhood. Although the telephone was available and used, driving a car was the social network of the Baby Boomer generation (i.e., the car was the equivalent to the newest tablet or smartphone). Teenagers drove to their local gathering places, whether it was a high school sports game, concert, or swimming pool. Boys worked and saved so they could be seen driving their Ford Mustang or Chevy pickup down the town’s main street. With the building of the interstate highways and improved roadways during the 1950s and 1960s, individuals could live and work well beyond their immediate communities. Suburban communities became the norm, with going for a Sunday drive an important occupation for immediate and extended families well into the 1970s. Drive-­in theaters allowed families to gather with a picnic and watch a movie from the comfort of their own station wagon for a reasonable price. Why the history lesson? Because on the whole, driving for the generation of Boomers is not just about community mobility and getting to where they want and need to go, but it is also about the occupation of driving. Regardless of whether alternative transportation is available or not, when an older adult is at risk of losing his or her ability to drive, occupational therapists must understand and con-sider that for these individual clients, it may not be just about losing an option of community mobility but losing their only valued option for community mobility, the car. Furthermore, it is recognized that driving is crucial to engaging in other occupations.

text: As discussed throughout this text, the role of occupational therapists in evaluation and intervention with stroke survi-vors differs by setting as well as the severity of the stroke. After the stroke event, the survivor is typically treated ini-tially in acute care (see Chapter 1), where the therapist is concerned with evaluation of client factors and performance skills to prevent further deterioration (e.g., spasticity, con-tractures) and enhance recovery from functional disabilities. Moving quickly into the subacute phase, evidence is clear that interdisciplinary stroke rehabilitation improves the outcomes of stroke survivors when rehabilitation resources, including OT, are devoted to these stages of recovery. 72 In terms of services, it is the role of the occupational therapist to address each occupation, as identified by the OTPF. What is not always clear to practitioners is that the occupation of driving and community mobility is related directly or indirectly to all other occupations (Table 10.­1). Consequently, it is critical that practitioners consider driv-ing and community mobility in their intervention and/or discharge plans and not assume that someone else (e.g., the physician, outpatient therapist) will address it later in the therapeutic process. viduals, occupational therapists start with the basic ADLs, focusing on the individual’s sense of dignity to be able to perform his or her daily tasks of self-­care. As the indi-vidual improves, attention can be addressed in areas of IADLs or other occupations (e.g., work, leisure). With stroke survivors receiving an average of 16 days for inpa-tient therapy, 52,60 OT practitioners have limited time and thus must work with their clients, caregivers, and teams to address essential unmet needs with appropriate discharge planning. Driving and community mobility will likely be one of the areas that may not be directly addressed dur-ing initial rehabilitation services but will be essential to the continued recovery of function and quality of life for stroke survivors. Therapists must understand that many of the ADLs and most of the IADLs are affected by whether the client is able to be mobile in his or her community. Clients face many challenges as they begin the recovery after a stroke and return home. It is therefore important to ensure that clients and families have the information needed to effectively engage in valued occupations and be able to make future plans, necessitating being able to get

text: activities in the community. During the rehabilitation process or in planning for discharge, when the question of driving arises, the occu-pational therapist must acknowledge and respond to this critical IADL without hesitation. That does not mean the practitioner is making a decision about licensure, but as with all other complex IADLs, he or she has the best per-spective in terms of functional performance to determine if any functional deficits will impact the activity of driving. Table 10.­2 illustrates some examples of deficits associated with stroke that may affect the activity of driving. Identifying potential risk for clients when considering driving is not significantly different from identifying risk with other complex tasks. When an occupational therapist observes a client having difficulty independently organiz-ing a meal or managing the household budget, the thera-pist informs the client and family or caregivers of the risk, implications of risk, and strategies that might be used to mitigate any unwanted outcomes. With driving, that process is not more complex, but it is more complicated. This is because the potential risk does not just involve the driving outcome proves negative (a crash). This is often the reason OT practitioners do not have the confidence to address driving. 30 However, driving and community mobility are well within the scope of OT practice, and furthermore, it is the ethical obligation of the practitioner to identify risk. 39,66 Additionally, occupational therapists have been identified as the “go to” profession for driver evaluation and rehabilitation. 12 Unless all OT practitioners step up to address this IADL with all clients, it will be a practice area lost to other less qualified service providers who are already devising certificate programs that purport to be able to evaluate older adults effectively. 22,23 Unlike normal aging individuals, stroke survivors have specific visual, perceptual, motor, and cognitive issues that are best addressed by a medical professional. text: Recently, Dickerson and Schold Davis 29 identified the four categories of stakeholders and their essential functions when considering driving—state licensing authorities, researchers, practitioners, and consumers (i.e., drivers, caregivers, family members) (Fig. 10.­1). This model holds true for the stroke survivor wanting to resume driving. Although coming from different perspectives, the four stakeholder groups fulfill essential roles for determination of driving privileges for stroke survivors. State licensing agencies make the legal determinations about the status of all drivers. Within the United States, federal guidelines may influence laws and practices, but each individual state develops its own policies. Under ideal circumstances, licensing authorities use recommen-dations from practitioners, who evaluate the specific indi-vidual client and use the most current and valid evidence from the researchers to render an appropriate licensing decision. The researchers provide the evidence needed for mak-ing decisions about fitness to drive, particularly related to screening and assessment. Providing evidence about the validity and reliability of the tools as they relate to diagnoses such as stroke, researchers establish the appro-priate constraints and limitations when used by clini-cians in practice and by the licensing authorities. In other words, researchers help translate the research outcomes into practical criteria for an objective decision about fitness to drive. Researchers may be psychologists, occupational therapists, physicians, or other professionals with research degrees. Practitioners are able to provide professional screening and evaluation of drivers and provide the recommendations to the licensing authorities. In the case of stroke, OT practi-tioners are uniquely qualified to use their evaluation tools and clinical reasoning to provide the most accurate pic-ture of the stroke survivors’ ability to perform complex IADLs, including driving. This category of the model

text: might include a generalist OT practitioner or the driver rehabilitation specialist (DRS) who can provide an expert evaluation and recommendation based on tools supported by the best evidence provided by the researchers. The prac-titioner must interpret research evidence on older driv-ers and, if possible, specifically using stroke populations. In some cases, the definitive decision is the responsibility of the primary physician who, based on knowledge of the consumer (client), will recommend cessation to the client or caregiver, will pass the information (reporting form) on to the licensing authority, or may refer for a specialized driving evaluation. However, it is clear that physicians are not always comfortable with this decision-­ making process 76 and should look to occupational therapists for insight into the client’s level of risk. Finally, the consumers are the drivers (stroke survivor), caregivers, or family members at the center of the issue. In the effort to retain their driving privileges, consumers attempt to understand and manage the complexities of the evaluation and the licensing process. Consumers seek ser-vices that will assist them in this process and, conversely, avoid services that do not offer a desired outcome or are not worth the investment of time, money, or effort. Ideally, this framework illustrates a process that is inte-grated and responsive to each of the stakeholder groups with the consumer as the beneficiary of services. Unfortu-nately, this process depends on communication and coop-eration among stakeholder groups. Communication is built on common knowledge and language, and although progress has been made in this process, 31 continued work is needed to facilitate a common nomenclature in order to benefit our clients. Box 10.­1 provides definitions for important terms in driver rehabilitation. Since being rec-ognized as an issue, the goal of a unified taxonomy for use by practitioners, licensing authorities, and researchers has been under development by leaders in the transpor-tation field. 31 Although not officially established, the box offers a reflection of current driver rehabilitation terms and definitions.

text: The profession of driver rehabilitation is a multidisci-plinary field that plans, develops, and implements driver rehabilitation services for individuals with disabilities. The driver rehabilitation specialist is also a general term that encompasses a diverse group of providers. Because the requirements for certification and education for the field are vague and inconsistent from state to state, the back-grounds of providers who use the initials DRS include engineers, driving instructors, and health care profession-als. It is important to understand that the driver rehabili-tation field developed soon after the proliferation of the automobile. 56 As early as the 1920s, adaptations to vehicles have been created to allow individuals to continue to drive despite physical impairments. 40 Occupational therapists, driver educators, and engineers collaborated to provide

text: Fitness to drive: a driver characteristic, defined by the absence (or the extent to which) of any functional (sensory, perceptual, cognitive, or psychomotor) deficit or medical condition that significantly impairs an individual’s ability to competently operate a vehicle while conforming to the rules of the road or that significantly increases crash risk Driving competency: the demonstration of fitness to drive that meets criteria recognized by a body responsible for driver licensing Driving skill: the demonstration of vehicle control decisions at operational and tactical levels in a range of traffic and environmental conditions that a driver may be exposed to in everyday experience Driving ability: the necessary sensory, perceptual, cognitive, or psychomotor skills needed to control a motor vehicle for a designated range of traffic and environmental conditions plus a knowledge of rules of the road that meets jurisdiction requirements Clinical driving evaluation: a health care professional obtaining, interpreting, and documenting data to determine fitness to drive through assessment of sensory, perceptual, cognitive, or psychomotor abilities using specific tools or instruments. On-­road assessment: a driving evaluation in a motor vehicle to examine a person’s driving abilities and skills at the operational, tactical, and strategic levels using a method of scoring or determining attainment levels Comprehensive driving evaluation: a complete assessment of an individual’s driving knowledge, skills, and abilities by a health care professional that includes (1) medical and driving history; (2) clinical assessment of sensory, perceptual, cognitive or psychomotor abilities; (3) on-­road assessment, as appropriate; (4) an outcome summary; and (5) goals and recommendations for inclusive mobility plan including transportation options Behind the wheel: performing driving maneuvers using a vehicle or simulated vehicle for purposes of instruction/training on public roads or off-­road settings On road: driving on roadways that are private or streets, roadways, or highways Driving test: an examination of driving maneuvers and knowledge of the rules of the road performed in a motor vehicle on a public highway or street Off road: a component of the on-­road assessment that is conducted on roadways or areas that are not publicly managed as roadways (e.g., private road, parking lot, closed course). It should be noted that in some areas or disciplines, this refers to the clinical assessment done before the on-­road assessment. Closed course: a driving venue separate from publicly traveled roadways, with known and controlled driving parameters, that is used for evaluation of skills or abilities or practice of driving maneuvers Naturalistic driving (study or assessment): a methodology to monitor or evaluate driving behavior using instruments installed unobtrusively in a driver’s own car that (1) provide an objective driver ID and driving data for each trip and (2) require no interaction from the driver Standardized road test: a road test with specific components always performed (e.g., right turns, highway, intersections) to establish a score on a scale with at least interval data properties that are comparable across individuals

text: driver rehabilitation based on medical and vocational rehabilitation service models. 56 The focus was evaluation and rehabilitation through vehicle modification and adap-tive equipment for individuals with physical impairments (e.g., spinal cord injuries, amputations, spina bifida, dwarf-ism). It has only been in recent years that programs have been expanding to include older adults with physical and cognitive disorders because of the increasing numbers of older adults (i.e., Baby Boomers) living longer with accom-panying chronic conditions who want to maintain their independence through driving. In fact, the first National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) collab-orative agreement with the American Occupational Ther-apy Association (AOTA) was initiated in 2003 with the recognition that expansion of driver rehabilitation services programs, policies, and strategies was required to meet the need for services to maintain safety on public roadways. From the historical perspective, the diverse roles of the DRS functioned well. Determining fit of hand controls and teaching an individual with a spinal cord injury their use by a DRS with an engineering or driver instructor background are practical. However, when the individual is a stroke survivor, the medical background of a health pro-fessional becomes essential. Thus, the differentiation of what driving evaluation and rehabilitation should be and who has the qualifications becomes much more compli-cated. The general practice occupational therapist needs to recognize and understand that individuals who describe their credential as DRS and practice driving rehabilitation can be as diverse as the practice areas of OT (e.g., school-­ based therapists, mental health practice, long-­term-­care therapists). Unlike OT, however, individuals using the title of DRS may include individuals with an educational background that did not address medical conditions, such as engineering or psychology.

text: A DRS who is also an occupational therapist typically performs a comprehensive driving evaluation to determine an individual’s driving knowledge, skills, and abilities. The comprehensive driving evaluation is defined as “a complete assessment of an individual’s driving knowl-edge, skills, and abilities by a health care professional that includes: (1) medical and driving history; (2) clinical assessment of physical, cognitive, vision, and/or percep-tion abilities; (3) on-­road assessment, as appropriate; (4) an outcome summary; and (5) goals and recommendations for inclusive mobility plan including transportation options.” Specifically for older adults with medical conditions such as stroke, the individualized plans may include recom-mendations for rehabilitation of skills (e.g., increase scan-ning skills through designed intervention), compensation through training (e.g., learn to drive a roundabout, learn to use hand controls), compensation through adaptation of the vehicle (e.g., using a steering knob for one-­handed turning), cessation of driving, or a combination of these. A wide range of options and innovations makes it possible to compensate for physical disabilities through technol-ogy. For example, bioptic telescope systems for individuals with low vision, hand controls for individuals with lower limb amputations, a left foot accelerator for an individual who has had left-­side stroke resulting in right-­side hemi-plegia, or joystick steering for an individual with a high-­ level spinal cord injury are all technological advances for individuals with significant physical impairments. How-ever, although rehabilitation or compensation through training or adaptation is the ideal goal, the individual must have the capacities for new learning and skill development. Technological advances are not yet able to compensate for executive functioning skills, a key determinant of driver strategies, tactics, and safety. 61 Additionally, individuals with decreased insight 6 or poor cognitive abilities, 11 in addition to their physical impairment, no longer have the ability to voluntarily limit or adapt their behaviors to be deemed fit to drive. See Chapters 25 and 26.

text: As described, the profession of driver rehabilitation is evolving with the changing needs of clients, state licens-ing authorities, and families and the fast-­paced changes of technology. To complicate matters, frequently, physi-cians are asked about driving and may not know about the services of driver rehabilitation or that a general practice occupational therapist can screen for driving risk. Under-standably, consumers are confused or complain about cost because they do not understand the level of service that is needed for completing a medically based comprehensive driving evaluation. Consumers may not understand why the licensing authorities may simply withdraw a license based on a diagnosis and where to go for help if that happens. Understanding this dilemma and in an effort to clarify services, the two professional associations most closely related with driver rehabilitation, the Association for Driver Rehabilitation Services and the AOTA, adopted a document describing the spectrum of driver services. 43 The development of this seminal document was completed over an 18-­month period through funding by the NHTSA and it is the first time the diverse types of services related to driving have been described and differentiated. 43 The document has two sections. The first section illus-trates the range of services from community awareness to specific services of driver rehabilitation (Table 10.­3). The second section breaks driver rehabilitation programs into three general groupings according the levels and com-plexity of services (Table 10.­4). The significant features of Table 10.­3 include: 1. The differentiation among community-­based educa-tion; medically based assessment, education, and refer-ral; and specialized evaluation and training with driver rehabilitation programs

text: 2. Under each of five different program types (driver safety programs, driving schools, driver screening, clinical IADL evaluations, and driver rehabilitation programs), the typical providers are described with their creden-tials. This assists in determining which programs use providers with a medical background, making it an appropriate service for individuals with stroke. 3. Under each program type (as listed earlier), the required providers’ knowledge and typical services will assist readers in being able to differentiate preventive services (i.e., updating driving skills or acquiring a driv-er’s license) from medically based assessment. These sections also articulate the differences among screening at a physician’s office, a clinical (or IADL) assessment that might be done by a generalist occupational thera-pist, and the specialized services provided by the DRS. 4. The outcome of each program type is clearly stated. Because driver safety programs provide education and awareness and driving schools enhance skills for healthy drivers, these two categories should not be the inter-vention resource for individuals with stroke. The medi-cally based assessment, education, and referral programs that indicate risk or the need for referral to the specialized programs are the appropriate programs for individuals recovering from stroke. Table 10.­4 illustrates the different levels of driver reha-bilitation programs. The development of this table is also the first work toward differentiating levels of programs within the professional field of driver rehabilitation. The significance is that all health care providers referring to driving programs (e.g., physicians, neuropsychologists, medical licensing boards, occupational therapists) should understand that not all driver programs are the same. Specifically for stroke clients, the differentiation may be critical. For example, if the client has any upper or lower extremity paresis, he or she should be referred to a low-­ tech program because adaptive equipment may be needed to compensate for operation of primary or secondary controls of the vehicles. The basic program would not be appropriate because the typical evaluation vehicle does not have any modification, and therefore the most effec-tive and efficient evaluation could not be completed.

text: SCDCM, Specialty Certified in Driving and 2014; 28(2):177–187. coupled with the diversity of impairments from a stroke, any single assessment tool purported as being the only tool needed to determine driving risk for a person with stroke should be suspect. Instead, groups of tools are being analyzed together to capture some of the skills and abilities needed (e.g., vision, cognition, perception, and motor function). 8,17,49,75 Studies have focused on assess-ments that increase predictive validity for fitness to drive in older adults, and others have examined tools in samples with specific medical (or clinical) conditions, 18 including stroke. Specific tools valuable for assessment of stroke and driving are discussed later in this chapter. The point is that the activity of driving, as a complex IADL, needs to be considered within a performance-­based context, not according to the scores of a computer-­based or pencil-­ and-­paper test. In his Slagle lecture, 37 Gillen argued for a return to performance-­based assessment tools, stressing the need to “…use them to maintain our professional identity” (p. 650). With driving being a complex IADL that needs to be evaluated within its context, all OT practitioners need to step up and become the profession that stake holders (e.g., physicians, consumers, caregivers, licensing authorities) seek for driving and community mobility recommenda-tions and referrals. Although all DRSs who complete driving evaluations use an array of assessment tools, it is the data gathered in the BTW or on-­road assessment that are primarily considered when making a recommendation of fitness to drive. 24 However, not all clients need the BTW compo-nent. When the clinical assessment indicates that the indi-vidual does not meet the minimum capacities to be able to safely operate a motor vehicle (e.g., significant visual deficit, moderate or severe dementia), there is no justifica-tion for a specialist’s referral. For example, if the occupa-tional therapist is working with a client who has sustained a significant cerebrovascular accident and is confident in recommending moderate assistance in order to prepare a meal because of visual-­perceptual or cognitive deficits, it is not a leap of faith to make the connection to driv-ing performance. General practice occupational thera-pists already familiar from observing and working with their clients should recognize that when a stroke survivor struggles with other complex IADLs, the therapist can make a driving recommendation with confidence. This is because the same abilities and skills the client needs to perform most complex IADLs are the same needed for driving. The recommendation “to refrain from driving at this point in the recovery process” can be stated with con-fidence without a referral to a DRS. This issue is explored further later in this chapter.

text: of lower exposure to the risk factors of being on the road during rush hour and avoidance of high-­speed interstates. With normal aging, a person has slower information pro-cessing and motor responses, and as with most activities, older adults compensate for this slowing by driving more slowly and more conservatively. In a recent study, 65 crash risk was examined among drivers in their 60s, 70s, and 80s. It was evident from this work that when data group all older adults into one group, they exaggerate the risk for drivers who are in their 60s. The statistics show that the fatality rate increases for drivers over the age of 70 years, especially at intersections. Figure 10.­2 illustrates the issue. 70 When drivers are older than 70 years of age, as a group, the type of intersection influences the crash risk. For intersections that require information process-ing and immediate decisions (e.g., yield signs, flashing sig-nals), the risk significantly increases for those older than the age of 70 years. In fact, in their analysis, 26 of the 27 crashes were fatal at yield signs for individuals older than 70 years, which is why the line goes off the chart on Fig-ure 10.­2. However, it is very important to remember that older adults are individuals, and driving decisions should be made on an individual basis. That is, this information does not “prove” that all drivers older than 70 years of age are at-­risk drivers. What it does is allow us as therapists to consider that when we have clients older than 70 years of age who are frail or have slower processing, informing the client and his or her family that specific types of intersec-tions have associated risks might assist them in avoiding these types of intersections and begin considering a plan for driving retirement. The other important factor to understand about age and driving is that the numbers and implications of medi-cal conditions increase as one ages. Individuals with a stroke often also have diabetes, high blood pressure, arthritis, or other conditions that may affect their driving ability. Thus, unfortunately, some individuals who were driving independently before their stroke may not be able to return to driving because of the significant impairment in the areas of cognition, motor, vision, or perception on top of previous medical conditions. Consider Figure 10.­3. This is a framework for general practice occupational therapists to use for evaluation and referral for driving risk. A person with a severe stroke on top of other multiple medical conditions represents an individual is in the “high risk” area of Figure 10.­3. When the generalist occupational therapist recognizes that the client’s impairments exceed the thresholds in one or more areas, it means that driving is a high-­risk activity; thus, informing the client, family, and rehabilitation team is appropriate. Sending the client or family to a DRS is unwarranted in terms of cost for a specialized evaluation or the emotional turmoil of a negative outcome. That is not to say the therapist informs the client that he or she will never drive again. Similar to all other important and valued occupations, therapists can use the desire to return to driving as motivation to work toward improvement. The critical issue is that driving and community mobility should be part of the overall goal-­setting and intervention plan with the client and family in order to preserve mobil-ity by implementing a plan for supportive transportation until a final driving decision might be made. Timing is important because more studies are showing that recov-ery can continue far beyond the time clients receive OT intervention. 7,72 Conversely, clients who recover quickly from the stroke and demonstrate no impairment with other com-plex IADLs likely have no need to see a DRS either. In other words, when evaluation results show no impairment identified in vision, cognition, perception, or motor abil-ity, driving is not flagged as a concern. However, this does not mean the therapist is reporting that “the client is a safe driver.” The client may actually have poor habits and be

text: a poor driver; however, the evaluation results do not war-rant further investigation. When there is any question about fitness to drive, it would be the right time to select appropriate (and evidence-­ based) screening tools for driving to ensure there are no red flags that would indicate risk for driver fitness. For a general practice occupational therapist, using the screening tools also offers an opportunity to educate clients and their families by approaching the topic of driving from a mobility preservation perspective. Sharing strategies for maximizing skills and abilities, promoting self-­awareness information, sharing websites illustrating valuable consumer resources, and discussing making a transportation plan for the future are as important as retirement planning. Offering resources for future planning is the type of preventive action that occupational therapists need to promote (see the resources at the end of this chapter for examples). The middle or risk (i.e., caution) group in Figure 10.­ 3 is designed for individuals who are frequently referred to as being in the gray area. These are individuals who are recovering from stroke and demonstrating gains in the functional areas of cognition, motor, vision, and percep-tion, so they are likely to return to many previous roles and functional abilities. These clients are the ones for whom a general practitioner cannot definitively make the decision about fitness to drive and thus need to be referred to a specialist. Research has shown that an outcome of assess-ment of complex IADLs validly predicts how someone might do on a driving evaluation. 27 Specifically, using a standardized assessment such as the Assessment of Motor and Process Skills (AMPS) 35 (see Chapter 5) differenti-ates between drivers who pass and drivers who fail a driv-ing evaluation. Thus, when an individual recovering from stroke wants to return to driving, the general occupational therapist can play a critical role in contributing informa-tion to the specialist.

text: In North America, there are specialized occupational therapists skilled in assessment of fitness to drive. Nev-ertheless, a general practice occupational therapist can assist in the process by referring to the right services (e.g., if needing adaptive equipment, referring to a DRS with an adaptive vehicle) at the time when the client is deemed ready to perform at an optimal level. The gen-eral OT practitioner should develop a referral pathway to the specialist, providing valuable referral information, specifically including results of assessment tools or evalu-ation outcomes that can allow the specialist to specifically target the questionable areas rather than having the client undergo a lengthy, broad-­based evaluation. DRSs are currently using more than 100 different assessment tools for determining fitness to drive in the areas of vision, perception, cognition, and motor abili-ties. 24 Interestingly, although it is recognized that cogni-tion is the most important aspect to evaluate for driving, the most consistent evaluations between DRSs include visual screening for acuity, range of motion (ROM) of the extremities and neck, and strength of the arms and legs. Furthermore, when considering the cognitive tools used by the DRS as a tool to evaluate driving (e.g., Trail Mak-ing Tests, Motor Free Visual Perception Test, Mini Men-tal Status Examination, Short Blessed, letter cancellation, clock drawing), generalists certainly can and probably do use many of these same assessment tools with their cli-ents. A report to the specialist with assessment results that include ROM, strength, specific vision testing, and results of cognitive tests would allow the specialist to incorpo-rate the results, not repeat the same tests, and therefore be more efficient and cost effective for the client paying for a specialized evaluation. Even more important, generalists can and should use their astute observational skills during ADLs and IADLs to judge functional abilities in an activ-ity rather than with paper-­and-­pencil tasks. Together, the generalist and specialist can determine what information would be most helpful to avoid duplication of services but provide the specialist with an adequate understanding of performance in order to provide an appropriately focused on-­road driving assessment. It has been argued that there are not nearly enough DRSs in the United States to provide comprehensive driv-ing evaluations for every client who wants and needs to resume driving after a medical condition or every client with developmental or physical disabilities who wants or needs to learn to drive. 22,23,27 This is particularly true in some areas of the country, but the focus needs to be on increasing capacity of DRSs and OT generalists who col-laboratively meet the needs. In fact, the goal of the Gaps and Pathways Project, a joint collaboration of the NHTSA and the AOTA, is to build and expand the pathways or referral links between general practice therapists and DRSs. 29 General practitioners have the skills, knowledge, and abilities to observe and describe their clients’ func-tional performance and prepare their clients for referral

text: Assessment tools currently used by DRS for determin-ing fitness to drive span all functional areas, and selection in each of the areas shows significant diversity. 24,42 Over the past 10 years, research has attempted to determine which tool has the best predictive validity and reliability for driving performance. Some tools have been used for many years (e.g., Trail Making A and B, Mini Mental Sta-tus Examination, Useful Field of View), and others are relatively new or new to the application of driving (e.g., AMPS), but all fall short of being the only tool that can be used for prediction of driving performance. For stroke, there have been specific studies designed determine the usefulness of specific tools for prediction of driving per-formance (Table 10.­5). It is not a surprise that there is no clear finding that supports the use of one specific assess-ment tool. With the complexity of stroke (i.e., depending on the lesion area, severity), many areas (e.g., peripheral vision, processing speed, executive functioning, self-­ awareness) clearly need to be assessed, with most studies concluding that an on-­road assessment is warranted to realistically determine who is fit to drive. 50 Thus, most researchers now appreciate that the search for one perfect assessment tool is not likely because it is not possible to capture all the complexities of driving in a brief measure or clinical tool, 10,26 especially for stroke, which has such diverse outcomes, as opposed to dementia with cognitive impairment being the primary hallmark. Instead, researchers focused on fitness to drive are ana-lyzing groups of tools together to capture the skills and abilities (e.g., vision, cognition, perception, and motor function) needed to safely control and navigate a vehi-cle. 8,17,49,74 Some studies have focused on assessments to determine for fitness to drive for older adults, 78 and groups of researchers have examined tools for specific medical (or clinical) conditions. 18 Akinwuntan and col-leagues have contributed greatly to driving assessment of persons with stroke. In a prospective study of 68 stroke clients evaluated on 15 individual assessment tools (including on-­road evaluations), the researchers found that

text: 86% of the participants were correctly predicted accord-ing to three tests, visual neglect, figure of Rey, and on-­ road assessment. 1 A follow-­up study with an additional 43 stroke survivors confirmed results, showing that this short assessment battery (i.e., two clinical assessments and an on-­road assessment) is a good predictor for fitness to drive in stroke survivors, especially those without severe deficits. 2 Another assessment battery designed specifically for stroke is the Stroke Drivers Screening Assessment (SDSA). 51 Developed in the United Kingdom, it has been adapted for use in the United States and Scandinavia. The SDSA consists of four component tests: dot cancellation, square matrix direction, square matrix compass, and road sign recognition. The dot cancellation is similar to other tests asking the client to differentiate elements on a page across the field of vision. The square matrix tests are two visual perceptual and cognitive tests that require the client to accurately perceive a matrix that has identified directions or highlighted compass parts across the top and side of 16 squared rectangles and match correct pictures to the appropriate square in the matrix (Figs. 10.­4 and 10.­5). The road recognition does not include just recognizing signs but also identifying where the signs belong in traffic situations. Studies have compared SDSA and road perfor-mance for stroke survivors and control subjects. 51,3 Akin-wuntan et al. 3 used the adapted U.S. version and found that stroke and healthy participants’ driving performance was predicted with 87% and 88% accuracy, respectively, concluding that it has the potential to be a good predictor of driving performance for mildly impaired stroke survi-vors. Importantly, although studies have shown that the SDSA has potential for clients with stroke, other studies have demonstrated that it is not a good tool for diagnoses other than stroke, specifically dementia 48,63 or traumatic

text: brain injury. 58 As clinicians, it is critical to remember these two important points. First, the SDSA shows validity for stroke survivors and has clear evidence that it is not use-ful for other diagnoses and should not be used with other clients with neurologic conditions until future research deems otherwise. Second, although these studies support the predictive validity of the SDSA, it was developed as a screening tool; therefore, based on the results, a stroke sur-vivor should not have his or her license taken away based on this screening tool. As mentioned previously, in an important study com-paring the AMPS with the results of the outcome of a driv-ing evaluation, 27 the AMPS demonstrated the ability to differentiate the drivers who passed the driving evaluation and those who failed the driving evaluation. The princi-pal investigator (PI) was only evaluating clients using the AMPS as the calibrated rater for the first half of the study. For the second half of the study, the PI switched roles, completing the clinical and on-­road assessment while two other independent and calibrated raters completed the AMPS. As a researcher, the PI understood it was critical to keep the outcome of the AMPS blind to the other compo-nents as to not bias the outcome of the research. However, as a clinician getting in the vehicle to drive with the client, the PI sorely wanted the knowledge of the outcome of the AMPS more than any other clinical testing result. What the PI discovered is that watching the client perform tasks such as cooking eggs, toast, and coffee; making a salad; making a bed; or making a sandwich revealed more about what to expect on the road than any pencil-­and-­paper or computer test. When the person made a different sand-wich than agreed upon or struggled to manage multitask-ing, he or she would likely have difficulty with traffic or an intersection decision. The study bore out this clinical understanding; that is, the outcome of the study is that the AMPS accurately differentiated the clients who received a pass and those who failed for the comprehensive driving evaluation. 27 Recently, the conceptualization that generalists can appropriately determine driving risk was supported by a study in Ireland with 46 stroke survivors over a 22-­month period. 67 In his study, Stapleton completed a compre-hensive driving evaluation on the stroke survivors and observed the on-­ road assessment component from the backseat. Because Ireland does not yet have DRSs, the on-­road component was completed by a driving assessor (with no medical background) who actually made the final determination as to whether the client passed or failed the driving test. Except for 11 participants who did not take the on-­road assessment for a variety of reasons (e.g., no suitable car, medical deterioration, relocated, refused or cancelled appointments), all of the other participants in the study passed the assessment (100% pass rate). Because this finding was exceptionally unusual for this type of research, Stapleton investigated the outcome with a quali-tative study interviewing occupational therapists, physi-cians, and driving assessors. text: therapists and physicians developed their own methods of reasoning and decision making for clients with stroke. Although there are likely several combined reasons for the 100% pass rate, one of the influences was the thera-pists’ knowledge that, if referred for a driving assessment, the client would likely pass within the present legal sys-tem. Therefore, occupational therapists mindfully and skillfully used clinical judgment and observations of the client’s performance in daily activities to make a determi-nation of whether the client should be referred for assess-ment. 67,68 In other words, the therapists used their clinical reasoning skills based on their observation of performance in therapy to determine the best time to refer for the on-­ road examination, confident that their clients were ready to pass the examination and return to driving. This find-ing supports the concept that observation of functional tasks by an occupational therapist is valuable for judging fitness to drive. Obviously, a drawback in the process is that therapists might be overrestricting (i.e., not referring clients who might need training or adaptation to be suc-cessful drivers). With nonmedically based driver rehabili-tation, the adaptation of a vehicle is not a simple process. Fortunately, in North America, adaptation to vehicles by driver rehabilitation for one-­handed or one-­footed use is common practice. Regardless of the limitation, with this study and future publications on performance-­based evaluations, this work may lead to unique insights for the successful return to driving based on recommendations of the appropriate time of recovery for different levels and types of strokes. Accordingly, because recovery from stroke is ongoing, one of the significant contributions of the occupational thera-pist to the client, caregiver, and health care team is the understanding of an individualized timeline advising cli-ents of the preliminary steps and recovery milestones on which to base the timing of advanced services such as the on-­road evaluation. Functional performance with other IADLs offers valuable guidance as a measure of potential for a positive on-­road assessment outcome. OT practitioners observe, analyze, and describe func-tional performance through their clinical reasoning. OT documentation can contribute greatly to recommenda-tions that include driver risk and referral for additional services through astute documentation and analysis from their observation of regular everyday activities of clients. Recently, Dickerson and Bédard 25 developed a decision tool for clients with medical issues, specifically a general-ist’s framework for identifying driving risk as well as the potential to return to driving. Although not stroke spe-cific, the tool can be used with any diagnosis, including stroke. The framework is based on Michon’s three levels of driving behaviors: strategic, tactical, and operational. 47 The strategic or highest level is the decision-­making pro-cess of planning trip goals, mode of transport (e.g., vehi-cle, walking, biking), and mapping out how to get there. In terms of stroke, it includes the decision of whether the driver is competent to drive the vehicle on a specific route or at a specific time. Although not in Michon’s original hierarchy, strategic planning is also needed when a driver comes upon construction or an accident and has to make the strategic decision of whether to cancel the trip or find an alternative route. 32 The second level consists of tactical behaviors, the behaviors related to decisions made during driving maneu-vers such as slowing for weather, when to pass a vehicle, making a turn based on gaps between traffic, using a turn signal, and other maneuvers. The lowest level, operational behaviors, includes the overlearned human–machine interactions necessary to control the vehicle. These include using the brake, turning the steering wheel, and pressing the accelerator. There are the skills one does automatically, for example, driving a familiar route every morning and not remembering the actual drive because you were thinking about something else. The frame-work was designed to assist therapists with the “process of extrapolating from client’s OT performance of tasks they have previously completed (i.e., evaluations already done) to identifying fitness to drive” (p. 196). 25 In other words, this framework is used to identify risk, and therapists need to use their clinical reasoning skills to decide the degree of impairment (i.e., none, mild, moderate, severe) and how many checks or red flags warrant making a recommenda-tion. At this point in time, there are no answers to that question because more research is needed. However, with stroke, an important determination is about the type and level of impairment. reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 10: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living, Interventions to Facilitate Returning to Driving, p. 238
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 10, p. 238
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 10: Driving and Community Mobility as an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living, Interventions to Facilitate Returning to Driving, p. 238

text: As discussed earlier, driving is a highly valued IADL, and clients may not ask if they can return to driving in order to avoid the answer no. Families or caregivers may not recog-nize that it is an issue or may also avoid the repercussions of dealing with a spouse, parent, or sibling who will need assistance with transportation for an indefinite period of time. Because of possible reluctance on the part of the cli-ent or family, it is critical for the occupational therapist to bring up the issue of mobility with the client as well as the primary caregiver. This is especially true when the client is recovering function and gaining independence in per-sonal ADLs with the natural progression to continue into IADLs. As an occupation, community mobility is essential to maintain connections to community and quality of life; therefore, addressing this in stroke rehabilitation is a part of the occupational therapist’s ethical obligation. 66 If the client does ask about returning to driving, the obvious question becomes what therapies improve func-tion in the areas needed for driving. Because driving is a complex task that requires the integration of sensory, motor, visual, and perceptual skills with good executive functioning, it is not a simple answer with cookbook-­ specific activities to practice. An associated example is a recent study using a case study design 57 of a stroke survivor who wanted to return to previous occupations, including driving, but had little right upper extremity (UE) function. In this case, occupa-tional therapists illustrated the complexity of therapeutic intervention to regain movement of the UE. The therapists argued that intervention cannot be about just stabilizing the scapula to get functional arm and hand motion. They developed an algorithm that focuses on the analysis of the client’s alignment along with movement of the trunk, rib cage, and scapula because dynamic interaction of the pel-vis, trunk, and lower extremities contributes to postural stability. 64 Because trunk alignment, stability, and mobil-ity are all key factors in control of the UE, 53,62,71,77 they argued that therapists need to facilitate postural muscle activity that will assist in improving UE recovery poten-tial. 64 This same concept might be applied to frame how to maximize cognitive function. Doing exercises on paper to improve scanning skills, block sorting for facilitating perceptual skills, or computer rehabilitation may improve discrete skill sets, but using actual complex activities is necessary to challenge the integration of the neurologic system and facilitate the reorganization process. Other chapters in this book expand on many of these processes and specific therapeutic interventions. The main point here is that the occupation of driving uses all of the same underlying processes used in other complex IADLs. Thus, therapeutic interventions to assist the client in regaining his or her driving skills and abilities are not any dif-ferent from other ADL or IADL tasks. As a client practices making a meal in the kitchen, he or she is also working on the same component skill sets for driving. The generalist can facilitate these and use all other therapeutic interven-tions before sending the client for a comprehensive driving evaluation or driving test at the right time; that is, when the client has recovered functionally and is able to pass the on-­road assessment task. That said, there is one possible exception of a therapeutic activity that might be contextu-ally unique for driving, the interactive driving simulator.

text: There have been some recent systematic reviews about interventions used to improve fitness to drive after a stroke. In a recent Cochrane review, 36 George et al. inves-tigated the literature to determine if “any intervention, with the specific aim of maximizing driving skills improves the driving performance of people after stroke.” The primary outcome was on-­road performance; assessments of vision, cognition, and driving behavior were considered sec-ondary outcomes. Although there was no clear evidence of improved on-­road scores after training in any of the four studies’ randomized controlled trials (RCTs), there was some limited evidence that the use of a driving simula-tor may improve visuocognitive abilities, such as road sign recognition related to driving. Classen et al. 16 also conducted an evidence-­based review of intervention studies for improving driving outcomes.

There was some support for driving simulation versus cognitive train-ing to improve on-­road driving skills in clients with mild stroke. Classen et al 16 also recommended using on-­road interventions with traffic theory knowledge tests to improve driving abilities with drivers with stroke but found insuffi-cient evidence for providing interventions with Dynavision, Useful Field of View, or general visual-­perceptual training.

text: An interactive driving simulator is defined as a computer-­ controlled environment that represents selected aspects of the driving experience considered to be representational of real-­world driving and allows objective measurements of users’ responses to designed driving tasks and scenar-ios and the users’ responses influences subsequent events within the limits of the parameters of the simulation pro-gram through accelerator, brake, and steering compo-nents. There is a wide range of simulators, from desktop computer programs with one screen to the totally immer-sive ones in which the person sits in a motor vehicle with a widescreen projection of a driving scene. Despite the diversity, for functional clinical use, a handful of models have been designed and developed specifically for clinical occupational therapists. With technology costs decreas-ing, companies have worked hard to develop ready-­made systems for therapists to literally put in the key and use. Most of the systems have developed a way to report the findings in clinical terms rather than the engineer speak that has been used in the past. Specifically, the systems have evolved from the therapists or researchers needing to develop their own scenarios (i.e., individualized driving runs that unfold with designed events) and determine how to evaluate the behaviors and outcomes to reporting pro-grams that document critical errors and response times. With increasing development and use of driving sim-ulators, there is beginning evidence for the efficacy of using driving simulators for both assessment and inter-vention in driver rehabilitation. Two related studies are worth expanding on here. In Belgium, data were further analyzed from a previous RCT investigating the effect of driver simulation on driving with stroke survivors. In this analysis, Devos et al. 21 compared two types of inter-ventions. One group of 42 participants received 15 hours of simulator-­based driving training and 41 participants received cognitive training for 15 hours. Twelve tailor-­ made, interactive driving scenarios were used from the STISIM drive system (version 1.03, System Technology, Inc., Hawthorne, CA) to train on specific driving skills (e.g., lane maintenance, speed maintenance, hazard per-ception and judgment, passing, and responding to road signs). For the cognitive training, participants received cognitive training using commercially available games that involved cognitive skills reported as necessary for driving (e.g., Rush Hour from Binary Arts). The results measured at 6 months poststroke found that performance on the on-­road test improved significantly more in the simulator group than in the cognitive group, supporting the argument that “rehabilitation of driving skills after stroke should focus on direct training of functional skills rather than its component parts” (p. 703). 21 These results also support other studies that suggest driving simulator skills can be generalized to real-­world driving. 4,41,45 The second study was a 5-­year follow-­up to the above study. 20 In the 5-­ year follow-­ up, 61 participants were reassessed using medical, visual, neuropsychological, and on-­road assessments. Results found that 18 of the 30 par-ticipants (60%) in the simulator group were considered fit to drive compared with 15 of the 31 (48%) in the cognitive training group (p = 0.36; no significant difference between the two groups). Thus, the advantage of simulator train-ing faded after 5 years, with no lasting difference between the two groups. Although one of the reasons for nonsig-nificance between the two groups was likely due to low power (i.e., not enough of the participants to compare), the researchers proposed another possibility. Because measurement of the outcome was at 6 months, some of the participants were not able to be assessed; specifically, they had not recovered enough from the stroke to return to driving. This did not increase the number of participants in the simulator group because the maximum number that returned to driving was achieved. However, it did increase the percent of eligible drivers in the cognitive group (from 42% to 48%). text: negative outcome at 6 months were cleared to drive before the 5-­year follow-­up. The authors suggested that this was likely due to these stroke survivors having further recov-ered, and gaining real-­life experience in contextual train-ing (driving in a real vehicle) allowed them to improve enough to return to driving to be reassessed at 5 years. 20 These findings have two major implications for OT practice. First, these two studies support the OT con-cept that performing occupation-­based activities provides greater rehabilitation potential for recovery from stroke. That is not to say that component-­based therapy is not useful but that the integration and use of functional tasks at the right level of challenge will improve function over component-­based exercise. The second implication is the recognition of recovery of function well past the 6-­month time frame. As OT practitioners, we must monitor fitness to drive with stroke survivors throughout rehabilitation and ensure they have the adequate resources and infor-mation for pursuing driver evaluation and rehabilitation beyond the time they are in short-­ term rehabilitation services. In summary, driving simulators appear to have a great potential for occupational therapists, including and espe-cially generalists, to work with stroke survivors in a con-textually rich environment. Classen and Brooks 14 have recently suggested that OT practitioners may use driving simulators to detect underlying impairments in driving performance, identify driving errors (e.g., yielding, speed-ing, maintaining correct lane position), and differentiate between driving behaviors of healthy and impaired indi-viduals. However, there are significant barriers. First, the cost of driving simulators is significant. However, with increasing research to show the benefit of outcomes and the fact that simulators can be used across disabilities and the lifespan as a superior contextual environment, the cost can be substantiated through reimbursement as a thera-peutic modality. Another barrier of driver simulators is simulator adap-tation syndrome or simulator sickness. Simulator sickness is similar to motion sickness, 38 a physical discomfort expe-rienced when “driving” a simulated vehicle because of the incompatible sensations of visual, auditory, and motion systems. Symptoms include dizziness, restlessness, cold sweats, nausea, and vomiting. In a review of the literature, Classen and colleagues 13 found that the client factors of being older (older than 70 years) and female, as well as context and environment such as the scenario design (e.g., curves and turns) and duration, simulator configuration, and calibration of the brake and accelerator, contribute to the rate of simulator sickness. Mitigation strategies can be effective and include diet, room temperature and airflow, and keeping turns to a minimum. 15 Finally, the other barrier to driving simulators is training. The driving simulators developed today are deceptively easy to use: turn the key, and run a scenario. However, using a driving simulator is complex, and the occupational therapist wanting to use it “needs to seek and obtain the appropriate education and training to use this tool effectively, appropriately, and with the knowledge to minimize simulator sickness.” 14
