text: All persons are sexual, and sexual activity is important to most persons throughout their lives. Interest in or desire for sexual activity does not necessarily diminish as persons grow older. Stroke may interfere with sexual expression by affecting the survivor’s desire; libido; erectile or lubrication response; orgasm or ejaculation; and sensorimotor, cognitive, psychoso-cial, ADL, and role function. Stroke also may affect the part-ner’s response or the patient’s ability to find a sexual partner. Research has shown that sexual desire most often is affected; however, prestroke sexual activity is the strongest predic-tor of poststroke sexual activity. Occupational therapists can use a holistic approach and training in activity analysis and adaptation to assist persons who have had strokes to regain their desired sexual function. A team model is best for sexual rehabilitation, with each team member knowledgeable about sexuality and providing special expertise. The PLISSIT model helps the practitioner identify the type of sexuality interven-tion required. All occupational therapists should be able to provide patients with permission, limited information, and specific suggestions and should be able to make appropriate referrals for sexual concerns related to stroke. Therapists must be sensitive to the multiple components of sex.

text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Define leisure, types of leisure, and functions of leisure activities. 2. Discuss the changes in an individual’s ability to engage in leisure tasks after a stroke. 3. Describe problems that may interfere with a patient’s par-ticipation in leisure tasks. 4. Present possible solutions to these problems. 5. Discuss research addressing leisure participation and oc-cupational therapy interventions after stroke. 6. Outline ways occupational therapists can adapt leisure tasks to allow partial or full participation by someone with a disability caused by a stroke.

text: Comprehensive stroke rehabilitation must include the con-sideration of leisure. This is particularly true because there is a renewed focus on decreasing activity limitations and participation restrictions and on improving quality of life as a critical outcome to measure after stroke. Rehabilitation professionals are obligated professionally to address changes in patients’ leisure roles and to use patients’ leisure interests to plan treatment sessions. This area of functioning is criti-cal in the assessment of patients’ motivation, quality of life, and self-­esteem. Effective approaches to improving leisure skills and participation usually require a team approach to meet the complex needs of stroke survivors. This chapter provides a conceptual framework to help therapists evaluate the leisure skills and improve the lei-sure participation of patients who have survived a stroke. It focuses on increasing the ability of occupational thera-pists to improve the leisure skills and the quality of life of this population. Readers are encouraged to review Chap-ter 2 with this chapter.

text: The Occupational Therapy Practice Framework (OTPF) 1 of the American Occupational Therapy Association includes leisure under the heading Performance in Areas of Occupation. Leisure is described as being “nonobliga-tory behavior, intrinsically motivated, and engaged in during discretionary time, that is, time not committed to obligatory occupations such as work, self-­care, or sleep.” 36 The OTPF includes the following two subcategories: 1. Leisure exploration: identifying interests, skills, oppor-tunities, and appropriate leisure activities 2. Leisure participation: planning and participating in appropriate leisure activities; maintaining a balance of leisure activities with other areas of occupation; and obtaining, using, and maintaining equipment and sup-plies as appropriate The OTPF also includes the following related definitions:

reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities

text: • Play: “any spontaneous or organized activity that provides enjoyment, entertainment, amusement, or diversion.” 36 Play is further broken down into play exploration (identifying appropriate play activities) and play participation, defined as “participating in play; maintaining a balance of play with other areas of occu-pation; and obtaining, using, and maintaining toys, equipment and supplies appropriately.”

text: • Social participation: “organized patterns of behavior that are characteristic and expected of an individual or a given position within a social system.” 33 Social partici-pation can include community (engaging in activities that result in successful interaction at the community level), family (engaging in required or desired family roles), and peer or friend (engaging in activities at dif-ferent levels of intimacy including engaging in sexual activity). See Chapter 12. Leisure attitude is defined as the expressed amount of

reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 13: Leisure Participation after Stroke, DEFINITION OF LEISURE, p. 280

text: affect toward a given leisure-­ related object. According to Feibel and Springer, 16 “this attitude is a multiplicative function of a person’s beliefs that an object has certain characteristics and a personal evaluation of these charac-teristics.” Many factors affect an individual’s leisure atti-tudes. These factors include social influences, personality, past experiences, and motivation. Leisure attitudes play an important role in the choice and pursuit of leisure activi-ties. A positive experience during an activity usually results in the person continuing to engage in this pursuit. A leisure role is defined as a perceived identity associated with a leisure task. Changes in a person’s roles throughout life are accompanied by shifts in leisure participation. Role changes resulting from disability may cause role strain and role conflict: “Role strain refers to the difficulty an individ-ual experiences when attempting to meet role obligations. Role conflict occurs when the occupant of a position per-ceives that he or she is unable to meet role expectations.” 23 Use of time is an important factor in leisure participa-tion. It is well documented that individuals have impov-erished time use after stroke, including leisure and social participation. The therapist should analyze the person’s schedule to determine whether intervention is necessary. In an inpatient rehabilitation unit, those with stroke spend more time inactive and alone than those without stroke. 6 Additionally, at 1 month postdischarge, survivors struggle with establishing routines in their day and coping with an increased amount of idle time. Subjects’ strategies for man-aging increased idle time include “passing time,” “waiting on time,” and “killing time.” 41

text: • Barriers to leisure participation A strong, well-­coordinated person may prefer physi-

text: cal leisure activities such as baseball, soccer, and basket-ball. Persons with less developed physical skills may be interested in more intellectual leisure tasks such as read-ing, playing chess, and working puzzles. They also may be interested in creative leisure pursuits such as painting, photography, and quilting. Geographic location also may affect participation in leisure activities. If a person lives in a rural environ-ment, leisure activities may include hiking, horseback riding, swimming, and fishing. Someone in an urban environment may go shopping or to theaters, lectures, and museums.

text: Leisure assumes various forms throughout life. The amounts and types of leisure activities depend on the per-son’s developmental stage. 21 During adulthood, leisure pur-suits are important for establishing and maintaining social networks. A balance between work and play is important. Factors that influence participation in active leisure activi-ties include financial constraints, decreases in functional skills, and decreases in social supports. Many older individ-uals replace active leisure tasks with more passive ones after experiencing decreases in physical and cognitive abilities. A recent study by Tang et al. (2019) aimed to char-acterize environmental barriers to leisure participation among individuals living with stroke, examine relation-ships between environmental barriers and leisure interest and satisfaction, and investigate participant factors associ-ated with the perception of environmental barriers. The authors found that individuals with stroke report frequent and large physical and structural environmental barriers to leisure participation, which may be associated with the presence of depressive symptoms.

text: Occupational therapists working with patients who have had a stroke are concerned with the way these individuals spend their time. Often, leisure and play interventions are considered secondary during the rehabilitation process as therapists focus on self-­care and instrumental activities of daily living. However, leisure activities can be equally meaningful to patients as they redefine their life roles. 2,43 Occupational therapists can integrate leisure activities into the rehabilitation process in two ways: occupation as end and occupation as means. 45 Occupation as end 45 refers to activities and tasks that comprise a role. The patient chooses the occupation as a meaningful activity he or she wants to perform, needs to perform, or has to perform. Therapists may become aware of these activities (e.g., bowling, crossword puzzles, and making jewelry) via an interview process or a semi-structured interview such as the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM). 28 When a (leisure) activ-ity is defined by the patient, the therapist collaborates with the patient to accomplish the goal through a vari-ety of interventions, including adaptation (e.g., enlarged print on books), education (e.g., providing information regarding transportation methods to and from a local pool), using remaining abilities, or remediation. Trom-bly 45 pointed out that when a therapist uses occupation as ends, the therapist is not focused on using leisure activities to make a change at the impairment level (e.g., improve scanning ability), although this may occur as a secondary gain. Trombly suggested that the therapist use the follow-ing principles to implement occupation as end:

text: (leisure) occupations as a treatment to improve body system and body structure impairments. The (leisure) activity is the change agent. The therapist may use lei-sure activities such as the Nintendo Wii to remediate impairments such as weakness 34 postural dyscontrol, poor endurance, 20 and neglect. Valued leisure activities may be incorporated into the treatment plan to improve other functional areas. For example, the patient may achieve postural and motor goals in a standing position while engaging in a game of air hockey. See Chapter 20 for examples of using occupation as means to remediate upper extremity motor control dysfunction and Chap-ter 26 for examples to improve cognitive-­perceptual dysfunction (Box 13.­1). Therapists should be cautious about relying too much on using occupation as means during treatment sessions; patients should be given a clear explanation related to why the activity was cho-sen. For example, when a patient has mild neglect, the therapist might say, “As we’ve both discovered, you are forgetting to look for items on your left, such as not finding your toothbrush on the left side of the sink or the juice in the left side of the refrigerator. We are going to try to get you to look left more often. We are going to play dominoes, and I will put all of your domi-noes on the left side. Try to look left as often as possi-ble, and I will remind you as needed.” After the activity, processing should occur related to whether the patient met the goals of the session (see Chapter 26). If patients are not given this information, they will not be able to make the connection between the therapeutic activity and their functional goals.

text: When evaluating the leisure roles of patients, thera-pists must consider seven factors that can affect leisure performance: 1. Evaluation findings related to impairments and perfor-mance in areas of occupation 2. Types of leisure activities that interest the patient

text: 3. Patient’s stage in the life cycle 4. Physical, social, and cultural environments 5. Patient’s previous leisure attitudes, roles, and satisfac-tion 6. Patient’s past and present use of time 7. Premorbid barriers These factors can guide therapists in identifying leisure activities that must be modified and in assisting patients with leisure exploration. A checklist (Fig. 13.­1) can assist therapists in determining the types of leisure tasks patients enjoyed before their stroke. 19,31 Other usual and customary assessments can assist therapists in making decisions regarding leisure inter-ventions. For example, information regarding range of motion, skeletal muscle activity, strength, endurance,

text: postural control and alignment, motor control, praxis, fine motor coordination, and visual-­ motor integra-tion is critical. The complete cognitive and perceptual assessment provides necessary information regarding the level of arousal, orientation, recognition, atten-tion span, initiation and termination of activities, memory, sequencing, categorization, concept forma-tion, spatial operations, problem solving, learning, and generalization. Therapists should review the types of leisure activities the patient performed before the stroke. For instance, someone who mostly participated in individual leisure tasks may have been content with little social contact. If the person enjoyed relational leisure tasks, social interac-tions may be important.

text: The therapist must consider the patient’s stage in the life cycle because participation in leisure changes during the aging process. During adulthood, an individual’s par-ticipation in leisure activities decreases because of demands such as work, household maintenance, and childcare. The importance and meaning of leisure also change as a person matures. The physical, social, and cultural environments are critical in the development of leisure practices and the pursuit of leisure activities during adulthood. Informa-tion on the patient’s social and cultural networks helps the therapist focus the treatment plan. The patient’s leisure attitudes, roles, and satisfaction before the stroke are important factors to consider after the stroke. The therapist should identify the importance

text: of the selected leisure tasks and the patient’s level of sat-isfaction with them. Identifying the specific aspects of the activity the patient finds enjoyable is helpful. The thera-pist also should document the patient’s leisure roles by discussing topics such as family expectations. The therapist can address past and present use of time by asking patients to describe the way they spent their time before the stroke, whether they achieved a balance between work and play, and whether they now require additional time for nonleisure activities. The therapist must address premorbid barriers to lei-sure participation, which are obstacles that kept patients from participating in the full scope of leisure activities before their stroke and include intrinsic, environmental, and communication barriers (Box 13.­2).

text: Interventions to Improve Leisure Skills

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 13: Leisure Participation after Stroke, Interventions to Improve Leisure Skills, p. 285
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 13, p. 285
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 13: Leisure Participation after Stroke, Interventions to Improve Leisure Skills, p. 285

text: The intervention process begins with obtaining the patient’s leisure history. The therapist then reviews the results of the evaluation and determines the patient’s strengths and limitations in relation to the performance components. Leisure tasks may be used to achieve the goals of OT treatment. Leisure activities may be used dur-ing treatment sessions to remediate impairments, enhance the skill itself, or adapt the leisure activity itself. Thera-pists must identify the skills necessary to perform the tasks and modify them according to each patient’s ability. The occupational therapist may provide treatment for neuro-muscular, psychological, and cognitive deficits that will enable the patient to engage in the leisure activity. The National Therapeutic Recreation Society proposes a continuum model of leisure service delivery. According to one description, “the ‘Leisure Ability Model’ serves as a guide for community recreation professionals to facilitate the movement of individuals with disabilities from more intrusive, specialized recreation services into integrated leisure environments.” 42 This model consists of a contin-uum with four levels: 1. Noninvolvement 2. Segregated 3. Integrated 4. Accessible At the first level, noninvolvement, the person who has the disability does not participate in any leisure tasks. At the second level, segregated, the patient participates in structured activities developed for group members with the same disability group. Examples include community activities through local stroke organizations, stroke sup-port groups, and specialized sports programs (aquatics). The third level, integrated, “provides persons with dis-abilities the opportunity to be mainstreamed into regular community recreation programs and to participate along-side nondisabled participants. This approach appears to go a long way toward helping to change the nega-tive attitudes, stereotypes, stigmas, and myths associated with persons with disabilities and the systems that serve them.” 42 The occupational therapist can instruct patients in the use of adaptive equipment and methods to pursue leisure activities successfully in the community.

reference.source_title: Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition
reference.part_title: Maximizing Participation in Everyday Activities
reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 13: Leisure Participation after Stroke, Interventions to Improve Leisure Skills, pp. 285–286

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 13: Leisure Participation after Stroke, Interventions to Improve Leisure Skills, pp. 285–286

text: The fourth level, accessible, occurs when the individ-ual with a disability “is able to select and access preferred recreation programs with no more effort than his or her counterpart who is not disabled..... The participant is able to realize his or her ultimate goal of achieving a satisfy-ing leisure lifestyle, free of any significant individual and external constraints.” 42 The therapist can use these levels to improve an indi-vidual’s involvement gradually. For instance, if a patient enjoys bowling and wants to return to this activity, the therapist may locate or form a specialized bowling pro-gram. When the patient develops skills, he or she may join an integrated bowling program and eventually an acces-sible bowling program. This model can serve as a guide for occupational therapists when introducing resources for leisure services. Occupational therapists can assist patients in exploring alternative types of leisure tasks that fulfill their needs. This may include expanding their lei-sure activity repertoires to improve the quality of their lives. Occupational therapists educate patients on avail-able services. Treatment also can focus on helping patients and fam-ily members overcome barriers to leisure participation. Common barriers are intrinsic, environmental, and com-munication related. Intrinsic barriers are the results of the disability. These barriers may include lack of knowledge about leisure activities and programs, decreased educational activities, health problems related to the disability, psychological and physical dependence, and decreased skills. 24 Occupational therapists can address intrinsic barriers in a variety of ways. Remaining informed about current community resources, support groups in the area, and professional leisure organizations designed to serve indi-viduals who have a physical disability is essential. 9 These organizations include stroke support groups, wheelchair sport leagues, and the American Heart Association. Environmental barriers include attitudes, architectural and ecological obstacles, transportation, rules and regula-tions, and barriers of omission. 24 The attitudes of others are a serious problem for persons who have disabilities. Attitudinal barriers result in negative behaviors, stigmas, and decreased acceptance and participation in leisure tasks. Occupational therapists can suggest strategies that patients can use to address social prejudices. Architectural barriers prevent individuals who have physical disabilities from participating in leisure activities. The main problem is accessibility because many buildings and sport facilities are not wheelchair accessible. Occupa-tional therapists can consult with architects, builders, and contractors to determine necessary modifications, such as installing a lift for a swimming pool. See Chapter 30. Transportation barriers are another issue. Many per-sons with disabilities cannot drive or take public trans-portation independently. Public transportation is not always wheelchair accessible, and when it is accessible, it does not always foster independence because a driver may be required to operate the lift for the person to enter. The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) is cor-recting this problem gradually by requiring wheelchair-­ accessible transportation. Occupational therapists can educate patients about the ADA and alternate methods of transportation. See Chapter 10. Economic barriers also play a role in preventing indi-viduals with disabilities from performing leisure activi-ties. For example, gym memberships are too costly even for many able-­bodied persons. Disabled individuals often live on fixed incomes and have many medical and liv-ing expenses. Occupational therapists can educate their patients about available resources and community groups and encourage participation. The final barrier involves communication. Disabilities that affect the ability to speak, listen, or respond lead to

text: of interventions are most successful in improving engage-ment in leisure activities after a stroke. At this point, clini-cal trials focused on this issue are limited with conflicting results. Dorstyn and colleagues conducted a systematic review aimed at synthesizing and evaluating the empirical evi-dence examining leisure therapy in stroke rehabilitation. 11 The authors reviewed eight trials with 615 participants. They concluded based on their review that leisure therapy contributed to significant short-­ term improvements in psychological outcomes (quality of life and mood) in addi-tion to leisure-­ specific outcomes, including increased participation in and satisfaction with leisure activities. The authors could not determine longer-­term effects of treatment. Corr and colleagues evaluated the effectiveness of a day program for stroke survivors. The authors used a randomized crossover design. 8 The program aimed to offer participants the opportunity to identify meaning-ful and realistic opportunities within the community. Activities included creative activities and social outings. The authors found improvement in self-­rated perfor-mance and satisfaction, with performance averaged across areas of self-­care, leisure, and productivity as measured by the COPM. In addition, there was a trend toward an increase in leisure activities conducted regu-larly as measured by NLQ. Desrosiers and colleagues 10 evaluated the effect of a leisure education program on participation in and satis-faction with leisure activities (leisure-­related outcomes) and well-­being, depressive symptoms, and quality of life (primary outcomes) after stroke via a randomized con-trolled trial (RCT). Experimental participants received the leisure education program at home once a week for 8 to 12 weeks. Control participants were visited at home at a similar frequency. Participants were evaluated before and after the program by a blinded assessor. The leisure education program was carried out by an occupational and recreational therapist for a maximum of 12 sessions. text: assessments were carried out on admission to the study and at 3 and 6 months after discharge from hospital by an evaluator blind to the trial. The results showed an increase only in the leisure scores for the leisure reha-bilitation group despite an age imbalance in the study. The authors also concluded that subjects receiving lei-sure rehabilitation performed significantly better in mobility and psychological well-­being than the subjects in the other two groups. Parker and colleagues 38 evaluated the effects of leisure therapy and conventional OT via a multicenter RCT using the outcomes of mood, leisure participation, and independence in ADL. Subjects included stroke survi-vors 6 and 12 months after hospital discharge. In total, the study included 466 patients from five centers in the United Kingdom. The standardized assessments used in the trial included the General Health Questionnaire (12 items), the Nottingham Extended ADL Scale, and the NLQ, assessed by mail and with telephone follow-­up for clarification. Eighty-­five percent of survivors and 78% of survivors responded at 6-­ and 12-­month follow-­up, respectively. At 6 months and compared with the control group, those allocated to leisure therapy did not have sig-nificantly better General Health Questionnaire scores, leisure scores, and extended ADL scores. The group assigned to ADL did not have significantly better General Health Questionnaire scores and extended ADL scores and did not have significantly worse leisure scores. The results at 12 months were similar. The authors concluded that in contrast to the findings of previous smaller trials, neither of the additional OT treatments showed a clear beneficial effect on mood, leisure activity, or indepen-dence in ADLs measured at 6 or 12 months. A post hoc analysis by Logan and colleagues 30 of the previously mentioned study by Parker and colleagues 38 further examined the ADL and leisure groups. Whereas the ADL group received significantly more mobility train-ing, transfer training, cleaning, dressing, cooking, and bathing training, sport, creative activities, games, hob-bies, gardening, entertainment, and shopping were used significantly more in the leisure group. Fifteen items from the outcome measures were identified as specific to these interventions. The authors found no evidence that specific ADL or leisure interventions led to improvements in spe-cific relevant outcomes. Gilbertson and Langhorne 17 evaluated a short post-discharge home-­based OT service for stroke patients, including an assessment of the patients’ satisfaction with occupational performance and service provision using a single-­site, blind RCT. A total of 138 patients were assigned randomly to a conventional outpatient follow-­ up or conventional services plus 6 weeks of home-­based OT. The data were collected before dis-charge and at 7 weeks and 6 months after discharge using the COPM, the Dartmouth Cooperative (COOP) Charts, the London Handicap Scale, and a patient satisfaction questionnaire. At 7 weeks, the intervention group reported significantly greater changes in per-formance and satisfaction (COPM), better emotional scores (Dartmouth COOP Charts), and improved work and leisure activity scores (London Handicap Scale). text: home-­based OT service could improve patients’ per-ceptions of their occupational performance and sat-isfaction with services but may not have a long-­term effect on subjective health outcomes. Gladman and Lincoln 18 reported findings of the Domiciliary Stroke Rehabilitation (DOMINO) study that compared home-­ based and hospital-­ based reha-bilitation services for stroke patients via an RCT, with 327 subjects enrolled after discharge from the hospital. No difference between the services had been found at 6 months, but home therapy was better than outpatient therapy related to improving household ability and leisure activity in the subjects who originally were dis-charged from a stroke unit. Jongbloed and Morgan 22 designed a study to deter-mine the efficacy of OT intervention related to the lei-sure activities of stroke survivors. The study included 40 discharged stroke patients who were assigned randomly to an experimental group, which received OT interven-tion related to leisure activities, or to a control group. An independent evaluator assessed the patients’ involve-ment in activities and satisfaction with that involvement on three separate occasions. The authors found no statis-tically significant differences between the experimental and control groups in activity involvement or satisfaction with that involvement. The authors point out that the lack of significant differences may be due to the interven-tion’s being limited in scope (five therapist visits) and the observation that many environmental factors strongly influence activity participation and satisfaction.

text: Leisure Skills after Stroke R.S. is a 74-­year-­old woman who sustained a right-­sided stroke 4 months ago. After completion of the central ner-vous system assessment, interest checklist, time log, and activity analysis form, the occupational therapist estab-lished goals with R.S. Briefly, the results of the central nervous system assess-ment were as follows. Right upper extremity function was within normal limits. Left upper extremity function revealed poor motor control with stereotypical patterns present and impaired sensation throughout. Ability to shift weight anteriorly and laterally while in a seated posi-tion was fair. Sustained attention skills were limited. She had a minimal left-­sided inattention to self and environ-ment and minimal impairments with spatial relations.

To select the most effective adaptive aid, the occupational therapist analyzes the skill components necessary to perform the chosen activity. After identifying the components that limit performance, the therapist selects and introduces an appropriate adaptive device. Occupational therapists provide patients with information about various organizations, adap-tive methods, and adaptive equipment that enhance and pro-mote participation in leisure activities. Use of these resources enables patients to lead meaningful and productive lives. Many types of adaptive equipment enable patients who have use of one hand to participate in leisure tasks (e.g., card holders, knitting-­needle holders, fishing-­pole hold-ers, and needlepoint holders). These products are avail-able from the Internet, catalogs, occupational therapists, and specialized organizations and stores.

text: Leisure is a complex phenomenon. A review of the litera-ture reveals that leisure may be defined in various ways. Many factors influence an individual’s participation in lei-sure activities, such as roles, attitudes, satisfaction, stage in the life cycle, and intrinsic and extrinsic barriers. The role of the occupational therapist is multifaceted, including assessment, intervention through techniques and adap-tive equipment, and patient and family education, with an emphasis on community resources. Leisure activities may be used to improve a patient’s motivation, quality of life, and self-­esteem and as means to treat impairment.

text: It has been estimated that 43.5 million Americans (19.2%) are informal caregivers and 39.8 million Americans (16.6%) are informal caregivers for adults (18 and older). 65 Informal caregivers are defined as individuals who assist others with self-­care, home care, and medical tasks with-out receiving additional time, pay, or other resources. They are differentiated from formal caregivers or those who are trained and paid to provide care in a home or care setting. 33 The term caregiver is used to indicate the infor-mal or unpaid caregiver throughout this chapter. Stroke is a leading cause of long-­term disability, which may include physical, cognitive, communication, or psy-chological impairments. It is among the top 18 diseases

text: contributing to years lived with a disability. 12 Approxi-mately 74% of people who have had a stroke are cared for by family or friends after being discharged to their homes. 64 In a survey, caregivers identified stroke as one of the most frequently occurring conditions that require caregiving. 26,65 Many policymakers and health care providers have the perception that long-­term care is provided in nurs-ing homes. However, 80% of adults who receive care rely exclusively on informal caregivers. 34 These care-givers are the foundation of long-­term care and the key to keeping medical costs down. They often operate as extensions of health care systems and professionals by performing activities of daily living (ADLs), instrumen-tal activities of daily living (IADLs), complex medical tasks, ensuring the care recipient’s adherence to thera-pies, and coordination of care. 72 Even with this recogni-tion in the literature, the work that caregivers perform in the home and in health care settings remains largely unseen and undervalued. Caregivers have been referred to as a “shadow workforce” in the care of persons with disabilities. 14 In 2013, the economic value of their unpaid contributions to the economy was estimated to be $470 billion. 70 As a reflection of the undervaluing and unseen nature of their work, caregivers do not receive adequate training, preparation, or support from health care sys-tems or professionals to do the tasks that they commonly perform. 65,72

text: The typical caregiver may be described as a married woman with some post–high school education or a college degree and a full-­time employee earning less than $50,000 per year. The median age of a caregiver is 48 years old and of a care recipient is 79 years old 26 (see Table 14.1). On the other hand, spousal caregivers are split evenly between male and female, with a median age of 64 years. On aver-age, spousal caregivers have lower educational levels, less income, and are less likely to be employed than nonspousal caregivers. 72 With these characteristics, spousal caregivers are more susceptible to experiencing the negative effects of caregiving.

text: The support from family and friends has been judged as the most important environmental factor affecting recov-ery for a person after stroke. 64 The tasks that family mem-bers and friends perform range from ADLs and IADLs to complex medical tasks. 64 At least one ADL is performed by a majority of caregivers of adults, with the most com-mon being assistance with transfers. (See Fig. 14.1 for the percentages of caregivers assisting with certain ADLs.) The three most common IADLs that caregivers of adults provide are “transportation,” “housework,” and “grocery shopping.” (See the percentage of caregivers assisting with IADLs in Fig. 14.2.) Long-­distance caregivers per-form many of the same IADLs as those who live with or near the care recipient and nearly three-fourths of them provide financial management; medication assistance; and coordination of transportation, meal preparation, and other services. 16 In addition to ADL and IADL care, half of family care-givers are performing physical, cognitive, or behavioral health tasks in medical or nursing domains. 71 For help with medical or nursing tasks, adult care recipients and their caregivers receive few home visits from health care provid-ers; spousal caregiving dyads receive even less help from outside sources or other family members. 72 An important report, “Home Alone Revisited: Family Caregivers Provid-ing Complex Chronic Care,” details the results of a sur-vey of 1084 caregivers who performed medical and nursing tasks. 71 (See Fig. 14.3 for the percentage of caregivers pro-viding specific medical or nursing tasks.) Eighty percent of the 1084 caregivers reported managing their care recipi-ent’s medications and 70% reported that they also man-age pain. 71 Caregivers reported these as the most stressful tasks they perform because of their fear of making a mistake and hurting the care recipient. Over half of the caregivers who administered medications said they had never received training in medication management from any medical pro-fessional. If they performed more complex tasks, such as catheterization, ventilator use, or ostomy care, they were more likely to have received specialized training although they stated that it was insufficient. Relevant for all health professionals, caregivers requested that they receive better instruction with additional exposure to medical or nursing tasks and equipment; supervised practice; consistent writ-ten, visual, and video instructions; and a phone number to call with questions. 71

text: caregivers, when compared to noncaregivers, had reduced mortality and increased longevity. 77 Some research-ers argue that to find ways to buffer caregivers from the negative effects, the positive aspects of caregiving should receive more examination. 63 Caregivers of persons who have had a stroke have reported that their experiences had given them an appreciation and purpose in life, posi-tive emotions such as feeling good about themselves, and stronger relationships with the care recipient and other family members or friends. 63 For long-­distance caregiv-ers, it helped them to fulfill a personal obligation to their loved ones, to receive a sense of personal satisfaction by ensuring good care, and to spend more time with the care recipient. 16 Caregivers reported that improvement in the stroke survivor’s condition, learning new skills, and suc-cessfully coping and mastering their situation improved their self-­esteem and were positive aspects of caregiving. 63 Caregivers of persons with stroke report positive experi-ences at different times during rehabilitation. Health pro-fessionals can facilitate this by emphasizing the caregivers’ contributions to the rehabilitation of their family mem-bers, acknowledging the uncertainty of the stroke progno-sis, and helping caregivers to adopt problem-­solving and coping strategies throughout the continuum of care. 63 The majority of caregiver research has found nega-tive employment, financial, physical, and emotional consequences for caregivers. One study found a small drop in employment of spousal caregivers of stroke survivors within 1 year after the care recipient had a stroke, with male caregivers more likely to return to work. 80 Over half of caregivers of adults with all condi-tions are employed full-­ or part-­time. 26,65 A majority of employed caregivers reported a negative impact to their employment as a result of caregiving duties, including cutting back work hours, taking on fewer responsibili-ties, taking a leave of absence, using vacation and sick days, receiving a performance warning, quitting the job,

text: or retiring. 26,65 Women suffer more from lower income as a result of the impact of caregiving on their employ-ment. 95 In addition to the financial costs related to the effect on employment, financial burden is also often due to out-­of-­pocket medical expenses (e.g., co-­pays, home modifications, medical equipment/supplies) and travel costs and is estimated at a median of $150 per month. 26,81 Long-­distance caregivers had the highest annual expenses compared with coresident caregivers or those who lived near their care recipient. 33,81 Between 17% and 20% of caregivers report that care-giving has caused their physical health to deteriorate. 26,65 Negative physical effects for the caregiver may be a result of physical strain or exertion, poorer self-­care, physiologi-cal effects of psychological conditions, and changes in cardiovascular function. 34 Physical exertion in caregiving increases the potential risk for muscle strain and injury. Poorer caregiver self-­ care may result in an unhealthy diet, decreased exercise, and poorer self-­ management of chronic diseases. 34 Finally, changes in cardiovascular function may lead to greater incidence of heart disease and hypertension. 34 In fact, caregivers of persons poststroke, particularly African American or male, with high levels of caregiver strain themselves have a higher estimated stroke risk. 46 Caregiver factors that are associated with reporting poorer physical health include higher-­ hour caregiving; being in the caregiver role for a longer length of time; caring for a spouse; lower income and lower education levels; performing medical/nursing tasks; and caring for someone who has a mental health condition, cognitive impairment, greater physical impairment, or behavioral problems. 34,65 Between 12% and 55% of caregivers of persons who have had a stroke have emotional distress. 97 An estimated 40.2% have depressive symptoms and 21.4% have anxiety symptoms. 61 Predictors of depression in caregivers of per-sons with stroke included these caregiver factors: female gender, Caucasian ethnicity, concern for the future, fewer social contacts, and poor health. 48,61 The factors of care recipients with stroke that were predictors of caregiver depression included female gender, more physical disabil-ity, care recipient depression, poor cognitive function, and more abnormal behavior. 22,48,61 Being the spouse or child of the care recipient with stroke predicted lower incidence of depression for the caregiver. 61 When a caregiver experiences unrelieved stress, there are significant negative effects on the stroke survivor. Greater caregiver stress is associated with more frequent institutionalization, poorer rehabilitation outcomes, and more frequent and longer hospitalizations for the stroke survivor, thus incurring greater costs for the health care system. 7

text: Another predictor of depression and anxiety in caregivers is a high level of caregiver burden. 91 Caregiver burden, a subjective state reflecting the individual caregiver’s per-ceptions, is a widely accepted feature of many caregiving studies that measure the effects of caregiver stressors and emotional symptoms. 13 Zarit and colleagues defined care-giver burden as “the extent to which caregivers perceive the adverse effect that caregiving has on their emotional, social, financial, and physical functioning.” 98 In caregiv-ing for adults with any condition, Adelman and colleagues found that caregiver burden was greater in caregivers who were female, had less education, resided with the care recipient, had depression, were socially isolated, incurred financial stress, spent more time caregiving, and lacked the choice to be a caregiver. 1 There were similar findings for caregivers of stroke survivors. 93 After stroke, caregiver burden was also found to be greater when the stroke survi-vors had depression, poor mobility, verbal comprehension deficits, upper limb spasticity, dysphagia, and lower scores on a neurologic assessment. 28,30,42,93 A meta-­analysis by Zhu and Jiang examined the predictive factors of caregiver burden specifically related to stroke survivors and their caregivers. They found that of caregiver factors, depres-sion, anxiety, and a sense of coherence (an individual’s ability to cope successfully with stress) had large effect sizes on caregiver burden. The care recipient or stroke survivor factors that had large effect sizes on caregiver burden were the ability to perform ADL, psychological health, and anxiety. 100 Because few longitudinal studies of caregiver burden after stroke have been conducted, it is uncertain if the level of burden a caregiver experiences changes over time poststroke. 73 However, caregivers have identi-fied the time just after the stroke, including the initial

text: hospitalization and the transition to the home, as the most difficult in the first 2 years. 50 One study examined the first 4 months poststroke and found three categories of problems that caused the most stress for caregivers of stroke survivors: (1) interpersonal disruption, including poor communication, family conflict, loss of lifestyle, and survivor negativity; (2) sustaining the self and the fam-ily, including financial problems, lack of time for self-­ care, and uncertainty about the recovery of the stroke survivor; and (3) stroke survivor functioning, such as the survivor’s cognitive, communication, and emotional issues; functional losses and plateaus; falls; and noncom-pliance with therapy. 50 Up to 2 years after stroke, stroke survivor depression, cognitive deficits, behavioral problems, and memory problems pose significant challenges for caregivers and contribute to the caregivers’ emotional distress. 17,20,45 Burden has been found to decrease over the first 3 years after stroke, but caregiver depressive symptoms, less har-mony in the relationship, and poorer social relations in their social network may have long-­term negative conse-quences for caregivers’ quality of life. 94 Occupational loss or decreased participation in mean-ingful activities has a negative impact on stroke caregivers’ quality of life and level of burden. 17,49,54,55 A scoping review found that immediately after a stroke, caregivers most often abandoned activities in social, leisure, work, cultural, recreational, exercise, shopping, household, cooking, sex-ual, outside, and traveling categories. 49 Younger caregiv-ers stated that child-­rearing tasks suffered. 49 Specifically, female spousal caregivers who reported occupational loss as a result of caregiving within 6 to 24 months of their hus-bands’ stroke also had high caregiver burden scale scores and lower quality of life scores. 54 Occupational losses for caregivers whose spouses had aphasia from stroke had a negative effect on family life, participation in social activi-ties, low-­demand leisure activities, and activities they did not enjoy doing alone. 55 Caregivers who were especially at risk for occupational loss were spouses or partners of the stroke survivor, younger caregivers, those who remained employed, and those who provided higher levels of care to stroke survivors because of greater disability. 49 Neverthe-less, over time, stroke caregivers were able to develop new routines or resume many former activities. 49 Most ben-eficial for stroke caregiver quality of life was found to be doing mutual activities with the stroke survivor and main-taining high activity levels. 49 Occupational therapy (OT) practitioners should support caregivers in participating in valued activities or, if necessary, help them to identify alternate ones. Researchers have found many potential negative con-sequences of caregiving, but a small, but growing body of research has found positive benefits. Understanding both how to mitigate the negative consequences and enhance the benefits of caregiving will lead to better quality of life for the caregiver and care recipient.

text: Stroke rehabilitation care guidelines include family, friends, and caregivers as integral members of the reha-bilitation team. 97 The Occupational Therapy Practice Framework (OTPF) goes further and defines caregiving as “a co-­occupation that involves active participation on the part of both the caregiver and the recipient of care” (p. S6). 2 The OTPF states that we must consider co-­ occupations in an integrated and complete view of the cli-ent in context. It guides us to include caregivers in our interventions because they are part of the context and environment within which clients of OT must function. In fact, the OTPF states that caregivers should also be identified as clients. 2 OT practitioners may provide services to caregivers either indirectly or directly. Consultation with agen-cies and advocacy to improve services for the caregiver and care recipient are means of providing services indi-rectly. 2 In settings where the care recipient who has had a stroke is receiving services such as inpatient facili-ties, outpatient clinics, and home health, occupational therapists interact with caregivers directly. In addition to nurses or social workers, occupational therapists may be the primary interface between the health system and the family who will be caring for the stroke survivor at home. 87 As outlined by the OTPF, when working with caregivers, occupational therapists should follow the process that includes evaluation, intervention, and tar-geting of outcomes.

text: Caregiver assessment is an essential first step in acknowl-edging, valuing, and understanding the caregiver. It has been defined as a “systematic process of gathering infor-mation about a caregiving situation to identify the specific problems, needs, strengths, and resources of the family caregiver, as well as the caregiver’s ability to contribute to the needs of the care recipient.” 36 Among leaders in care-giving research, there is a consensus on the fundamental principles to guide caregiver assessment policy and prac-tice (Box 14.1). 34 There are differing opinions on when a caregiver assessment is warranted. Adelman and colleagues 1 sug-gested that caregivers receive a referral for assessment of burden if they have around-­the-­clock responsibilities for recipients with high health needs or if they are dealing with an impending care setting transition. The recom-mendations of the Family Caregiver Alliance are broader and more inclusive, stating that anyone who self-­identifies as a caregiver should be offered a screening followed by an assessment if indicated. 34 The Caregiver Self-­Assessment Questionnaire is a valid and reliable screening tool recom-mended by the American Medical Association for use by health care professionals. 32

text: 1. Because caregivers are a core part of health care and long-­term care, it is important to recognize, respect, assess, and address their needs. 2. Caregiver assessment should embrace a family-­centered perspective, inclusive of the needs and preferences of both the care recipient and the family caregiver. 3. Caregiver assessment should result in a plan of care developed in collaboration with the caregiver that indicates the provision of services and intended measurable outcomes. 4. Caregiver assessment should be multidimensional in approach and periodically updated. 5. Caregiver assessment should reflect culturally competent practice. 6. Effective caregiver assessment requires assessors to have specialized knowledge and skills. Practitioners’ and service providers’ education and training should equip them with an understanding of the caregiving process and its impacts, as well as the benefits and elements of an effective caregiver assessment. 7. Government and other third-­party payers should recognize and pay for caregiver assessment as a part of care for older people and adults with disabilities.

text: At the most basic level, an assessment must identify the primary caregivers and improve their understanding of the caregiving role and tasks. The assessment must collect enough information so that the caregiver’s needs will be understood, appropriate services can be identified, and the caregiver’s eligibility for the services can be determined. 35 At a more comprehensive level, seven caregiver domains may be considered when developing an assessment proto-col for a health care setting: (1) context; (2) caregiver’s per-ception of health and functional status of the care recipient; (3) caregiver values and preferences; (4) well-­being of the caregiver; (5) consequences of caregiving; (6) skills, abilities, and knowledge to provide the recipient with needed care; and (7) potential resources that the caregiver could choose to use. 35 Administering measures of all seven recommended domains may not be necessary in each caregiver assessment (e.g., initial versus reassessment versus a change in care recipient health status), but the measures should be avail-able in all health care settings and staff members should be familiar with them. 35 Table 14.2 lists the seven domains and provides examples of measures in each domain. 35 (Measures not specifically developed for caregivers were not included in Table 14.2 but are commonly used with this popula-tion, e.g., depression or anxiety screenings and quality of life measures.) A much more comprehensive and detailed list of available measures has been compiled by the Fam-ily Caregiver Alliance. 35 The multidimensional caregiver

Lutz et al. 62 stated that after stroke in the rehabilita-tion phases of the stroke trajectory, all stroke survivors’ needs are thoroughly assessed as standard-­of-­care. They argue that what is lacking in order to successfully transition a stroke survivor from the inpatient setting to the home are caregiver readiness assessments, similar to the Family Caregiver Alli-ance 35 recommendations, in the following two categories: (1) caregiver commitment (relationship strength and caregiver willingness); and (2) caregiver capacity (preexisting physical and mental health concerns, prestroke roles and responsibil-ities, accessibility of the home environment, transportation, internal and external resources, the ability to sustain caregiv-ing, and to respond to crises). 62 Identifying the gaps between the stroke survivor’s needs and the readiness of the caregiver will lead to the development of a plan to prepare the care-giver before discharging the stroke survivor to the home. One OT intervention that may reduce caregiver burden is providing home modifications to reduce the environ-mental barriers that caregivers face in the home. With the In-­Home Occupational Perfor-mance Evaluation for Providing Assistance (I-­ HOPE Assist), the occupational therapist and caregiver identify caregiving activities that are the most problematic. It also measures the caregiver’s self-­efficacy in performing these problematic activities. Results of the I-­HOPE Assist guide the occupational therapist in recommending home modi-fication interventions to improve caregiver performance and self-­efficacy in caregiving tasks. The I-­HOPE Assist has been found to have good content and construct valid-ity and was rated as displaying the best properties for prac-tice use and flexibility in real-­life OT practice. 66 A caregiver evaluation is a positive step in meeting the needs of the caregiver and the care recipient, but the attention to the caregiver must not end there. The plan of care and interventions should be based on the needs iden-tified by the caregiver evaluation, and reassessment should be performed as needs or challenges for the caregiver or care recipient change.

text: According to the Improving Stroke Caregiver Readiness Model, after matching the needs of the stroke survivor with the caregiver commitment and capacity, a plan for inpatient preparation of the caregiver must be developed to make the transition to home as smooth as possible. 62 Caregiver preparation may include activating resources (financial, social), readying the home environment (installing ramps, grab bars), providing skills training for stroke survivor care at home (transfers, medication man-agement), training for the case management role (coordi-nating care, negotiating with insurance, managing work schedules or leave), and planning for caregiver self-­care (respite, counseling). Rehabilitation services outside of inpatient settings have been shown to benefit both the stroke survivor and the care-giver. Home health services have been found to have mod-est positive effects on caregivers’ mood, levels of strain, and knowledge of stroke. 42 Outpatient rehabilitation services improve functional outcomes for persons with stroke and thus reduce caregiver burden; but only about 36% receive outpatient rehabilitation, a figure that is lower than is rec-ommended by practice guidelines. 6 Inpatient rehabilitation occupational therapists must follow practice guidelines and recommend home health or outpatient rehabilitation for more stroke survivors. Newer communication technology, such as telehealth and telephone video or web-­based video visits, allow for alternative rehabilitation services for both the stroke survivor and the caregiver. 97 A systematic review of telehealth interventions’ effect on caregiver outcomes found significant improvement in caregiver outcomes and caregiver satisfaction with such telehealth interventions as education, psychosocial and cognitive behavioral therapy, and clini-cal care delivery. 24 Home health, outpatient, and telehealth methods of service delivery will afford opportunities to assess caregivers, provide interventions for them, or make referrals to other professionals to address unmet needs. Education and training are fundamental caregiver interventions performed by occupational therapists in all treatment settings. The OTPF defines education as a type of intervention that involves imparting knowledge and information to the client and caregiver to enhance their understanding and training as facilitation to enhance performance of concrete skills. 2 Although the OTPF 2 dif-ferentiates between education and training, much of the caregiver literature uses the terms information, education, and training interchangeably. Many health professionals perceive the social worker as the interdisciplinary team member who is designated to interact with the client’s caregivers, but each team member gives information, education, and training to caregivers within their scope of practice. Unfortunately, these interventions are often delivered to caregivers by overloaded therapists “on the fly” and as the result of the caregiver’s “effortful seeking” for information (i.e., determined efforts by the caregiver to obtain information from the interdisciplinary health care team). 75 Involving caregivers as active members of the interdisciplinary team and including them in team meet-ings have been found to be effective ways to both assess the caregivers’ needs and deliver information to them. 75,97 A systematic review found studies in which provision of stroke information resulted in significantly greater

text: education to address the needs that caregivers identified because of our preparation in both the physical and psy-chological realms. In a survey of occupational therapists, physical therapists, and speech-­ language pathologists who treated people with stroke across practice settings (acute care, acute rehabilitation, subacute, outpatient, home health, and nursing facilities), Lawson et al. 59 found the percentage of occupational therapists who provided caregiver training in the following areas: ADL training (98%), transfers and mobility (93%), rehab techniques (88%), stroke education (78%), community resources (76%), cognitive strategies (72%), and problem-­solving skills (50%). Less than 50% of occupational therapists referred them to a support group (46%) or provided communication strategies (46%), time management (27%), stress management (29%), or financial manage-ment (14%). 59 When the survey results of all three disci-plines were combined, they reported that their methods of caregiver training were primarily hands-­on, face-­to-­ face instruction, and providing written materials. They also reported providing 45 minutes to 1 hour of training to each caregiver, an amount of training that may not be adequate for caregivers to be confident in caring for the stroke survivor. 59 Therapists stated that the greatest barrier to caregiver training was that the caregivers were not present in therapy for training and the greatest facil-itator was a positive attitude by the caregiver. Lawson et al. 59 recommended that therapists move beyond basics such as ADL and transfers to more important caregiver needs such as managing stress, managing finances, creat-ing more opportunities for caregiver training and dem-onstration of skills, delivering group interventions, and following-­up postdischarge. Regarding caregivers’ desire for education about health promotion and prevention of future stroke, other researchers have found that many occupational therapists are unaware of practice guidelines to provide this educa-tion and do not address it with stroke survivors and their caregivers. 78 Training caregivers to assist stroke survivors with ADLs, IADLs, or complex medical tasks is still critical and must be individually tailored to the capabilities and wishes of the caregiver and the stroke survivor. Occupational therapists should offer every patient treatment session as an opportunity for the caregiver to learn techniques and problem-­solving strategies. 64 Because caregivers are likely to be overwhelmed with complex information from all stroke interdisciplinary team members, training and home programs must be repeated, demonstrated, and written to accommodate different caregiver learning styles. Use of the teach-­back method has been shown to improve the understanding of caregivers in IADL training such as medication management. 69 The therapist should also ask the caregivers to demonstrate their skills rather than sim-ply verbalize an understanding. Guidelines for working with the caregiver in stroke rehabilitation recommend counseling interventions that focus on improving problem-­solving behaviors and com-munity support groups for both the stroke survivor and the caregiver. 64,97

text: Cameron and Gignac 18 developed a comprehensive framework, Timing It Right (TIR), to identify the focus and unique support needs for caregivers in each of five phases after stroke. The TIR model may assist OT prac-titioners and researchers to identify the phase-­ specific caregiver support needs in the categories of information, training, emotional support, and appraisal or feedback

reference.citation_text: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 14: Caregiving after Stroke, Intervention Timing and Outcomes for the Caregiver, p. 304
reference.short_form: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation, 5th ed., Ch. 14, p. 304
reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 14: Caregiving after Stroke, Intervention Timing and Outcomes for the Caregiver, p. 304

text: and the outcomes to determine the efficacy of caregiver interventions. Intervention needs for caregivers in phase 1, the event and diagnosis phase, include basic stroke information and the emotional support. In phase 2, the stabilization phase, caregivers require more stroke infor-mation, emotional support, and initial training by inter-disciplinary health professionals (e.g., ADLs). Phase 3, or preparation, requires information about community resources, emotional support for anxiety, social support, and continued training in skills to assist the stroke survi-vor. Implementation, or phase 4, begins when the stroke survivor returns to the home. In this phase, caregivers begin to understand how caregiving impacts them person-ally. They may require additional training to manage care in the home and emotional support for fear and anxiety. Finally, in phase 5, adaptation, the caregiver and the per-son who has had a stroke have adjusted to living at home and turn their attention to community reintegration. In this phase, caregivers need information for participa-tion in valued activities for themselves, community par-ticipation for the care recipient, and planning for future crises or events. Support groups and emotional support for relationship changes are essential for the caregiver at the adaptation stage. The TIR framework also provides phase-­ appropriate outcome categories to determine if caregiver needs have been met (e.g., stroke knowledge, knowledge of community resources, community reinte-gration, social support, emotional distress, participation in activities) (see Table 14.4). In addition to having a foundation in the stroke caregiving literature, Cameron and Gignac 18 stated that the TIR model is consistent with the transtheoretical model of behavior change. By provid-ing phase-­appropriate supports to caregivers, they will be more prepared to receive the supports and to benefit from them, a similar concept to the transtheoretical model’s stages of behavior change. 68 Cameron and colleagues 19 conducted a qualitative study of caregivers of persons with stroke and found evi-dence to reinforce the TIR framework premise that care-giver support needs change over each phase and time. Caregivers reported that their information needs were greatest in phases 3 and 4, preparation and implemen-tation, respectively; the need for emotional support was greatest in phases 1, 2, and 4, event and diagnosis, sta-bilization, and implementation, respectively; and hands-­on training needs were most important in phases 3 and 4, preparation and implementation, respectively. Peer support groups were deemed most important in phases 3, 4, and 5, preparation, implementation, and adapta-tion, respectively. During phases 4 and 5, implementation and adaptation, respectively, they felt that they no longer received information or support from health care profes-sionals and decreased support from family and friends. In phases 3 and 5, preparation and adaptation, respectively, caregivers stated that they wanted a greater focus on the family from the health care team.

text: A study examining the TIR phase needs of caregivers of people with aphasia after stroke also found that informa-tion about aphasia throughout all phases was desired but was provided consistently only in phase 2, stabilization. These caregivers reported that they primarily obtained information about aphasia on their own. 76 Using the TIR framework, Cameron and colleagues developed the Timing It Right Stroke Family Support Program (TIRSFSP) to guide how health care profes-sionals provide specific types of information, education, training, and support to meet the changing needs of care-givers. 20 Preliminary results have shown that the TIRS-FSP may be effective in improving caregivers’ perceived support and mastery. 21 Further study is needed to use the TIRSFSP as a model for stroke family education to deliver caregiver interventions and improve outcomes for caregivers.

text: Stroke is a leading cause of long-­term disability and is one of the primary health conditions that caregivers identify as the reason why their care recipient requires assistance. 12 The broad and complex nature of stroke may include physical, cognitive, emotional, or behavioral impairments. Thus, caregivers of persons who have had a stroke face daunting challenges. Although there is some recognition of their value in providing long-­term care and in reducing medical costs, caregivers remain a “shadow workforce.” 14 To bring caregivers out of the shadows and value their contribution to the health of our clients who have had a stroke, we must understand who the caregivers are, the tasks that they perform, and the effect that caregiving has on their lives. Occupational therapists are charged by the OTPF to consider caregivers as clients. 2 The first step in the OT process of assisting the caregiver as client is to perform a screening and a comprehensive assessment if warranted. Many assessments are available to determine the needs of caregivers in different domains. After assessment and com-parison of the needs of the stroke survivor with the com-mitment and capacity of the caregiver, providing caregiver intervention is the next step in the process. Caregivers of adults who have had a stroke may need to perform ADLs, IADLs, and complex medical and nursing tasks at home for which they are often ill prepared. The “Improving Stroke Caregiver Readiness Model” provides a framework of intervention topics to prepare the caregiver for the transition from inpatient to home. 62 In addition, inpatient therapists must follow stroke guidelines and advocate for further therapies along the care continuum, such as home health, outpatient, or telehealth interventions. These have positive outcomes for both stroke survivors and their care-givers. Occupational therapists who work in the stroke continuum of care are well positioned to provide infor-mation, education, and training needed by caregivers to

text: effectively assist their care recipient. Moreover, occupa-tional therapists have the training to assess and treat the psychological, emotional, and physical effects of caregiv-ing and may be one of the primary liaisons between the health care setting and the caregiver, particularly during stressful transitions. 87 Providing the types of interventions that the caregiver of a stroke survivor will be ready for and benefit from may depend on the timing or phase after the stroke. One model addressing caregiver needs along the stroke care continuum is the TIR framework. 18 In the TIR frame-work, phases include diagnosis and event, stabilization, preparation, implementation, and adaptation. The TIR framework and the corresponding stroke family sup-port program, the TIRSFSP, may offer OT practitioners and researchers a systematic structure to provide phase-­ appropriate support to caregivers. 18–21 Stroke practice guidelines emphasize that caregivers are essential team members and are the most important envi-ronmental factor for the person who has had a stroke. 64,97 Stroke practice guidelines urge health care professionals to support caregivers throughout the rehabilitation con-tinuum by including them as members of the interdisci-plinary team; assessing their needs; providing information, education, and training; providing counseling focused on problem solving and social support; and attending to their emotional and physical health. 64,97 By including and sup-porting their caregivers, not only will the caregiver benefit, but also the person who has had a stroke will have better physical, functional, and psychosocial outcomes.

text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Understand the psychological manifestations of stroke in both children and adults. 2. Understand how a variety of psychological impairments affect the recovery process. 3. Understand the effect of stroke on family members and those in the caregiver role. 4. Include attention to psychological needs during occupa-tional therapy intervention.

text: Understanding the relationship between psychologi-cal factors and stroke is a complex undertaking. Anxiety, depression, aggression, and emotional lability are com-monly seen in persons who have sustained a stroke, and each takes its toll on adjustment and each affects func-tional outcome. Psychiatric conditions restrict recovery, quality of life, and participation, making assessment and treatment of paramount importance. When considering the psychological consequences of stroke, observing phys-iological changes, and emotional reactions to this life-­ altering event, one’s personality constructs and cultural background play a role in recovery and outcome. The pur-pose of this chapter is to review the relationship between stroke and its psychological consequences in adults and in children, discuss the impact on the family’s and on the caregiver’s well-­being, and consider treatment approaches that occupational therapists and the rehabilitation team can incorporate into their intervention process. It is well documented that nearly 800,000 persons each year have a stroke, and of those, it is the first attack for almost 600,000. 2 These statistics are especially significant when considering that there is a decrease in both stroke

text: incidence and stroke fatality, particularly in high-­income countries, because of attention to cardiovascular risk fac-tors. 32 Even though stroke is the fourth leading cause of death in the United States, there are more than 4 mil-lion survivors (more than 25% of whom have sustained functional limitations, including difficulty with activities of daily living [ADLs]). 2 Stroke is a leading cause of dis-ability and has a major impact on participation because it compromises ADLs and social roles. 29 Stroke survivors, even in this climate of health care change, continue to receive and to benefit from services offered by occupa-tional therapists. 92 Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death in indi-viduals older than 65 years old, but 22% of those with stroke are between 20 and 60 years of age 2 because stroke can occur at any age. In addition to stroke afflicting adults, it has been estimated that stroke affects children at a rate of at least 6 per 100,000, with a 10% chance of recurrence for children with nonperinatal ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke. 2 These statistics are further compounded by the significant psychological impact of stroke on the survivors and their families. It is well established that adults who have sustained a stroke are at high risk for psychological consequences. As many as 30% to 50% of stroke survivors have been estimated to have had some significant psychological dis-order after stroke 113 even in the absence of a disabling condition. 107 At least one-third of the stroke survivors experience depression, 52 nearly 30% experience negative cognitions such as feelings of worthlessness, 53 and between 20% and 38% experience some degree of anxiety. 7 In fact, the risk for developing a psychological disorder persists long after the stroke event. 1,3,156 Table 15.1 identifies the prevalence of some of these disorders. Given the profound impact that psychological disor-ders have on recovery, understanding the relationship, the range, and the effect that these disorders have on indi-viduals with stroke is paramount because psychological factors may be antecedents, consequences, or reactions to the traumatic neurologic experience. Clearly, a complex relationship exists between psycho-logical factors and medical conditions. Undesirable psycho-logical features may have an adverse effect on recovery and outcome. Specific psychological symptoms, such as anxiety or depression; specific personality traits or coping styles, such as aggressive personality traits 38,157; maladaptive health behaviors, such as tobacco or alcohol abuse; and stress-­related physiological responses 138 have been linked to stroke. 86 The stress of illness and disability affects not only the person but also his or her family. 77 An unexpected serious and disabling illness results in the need for all family mem-bers to cope and find new ways of relating to one another. Previously established roles, authority relationships, family-­ based activities, and occupations may change, resulting in a structural shift that puts the entire family at risk for sig-nificant distress. Because of the disability, the potential for increased alienation of the individual and of the family adds to the psychological distress already being experienced. 48 When a stroke happens to a child, the implications can be devastating for the family 108 and can result in increased mental health disorders in the child’s parent. 47

text: One study identifies it as a risk factor for younger study participants and for those with high high-­density lipopro-tein cholesterol values 157; another found that participants with a pattern of outward expression of anger were twice as likely to sustain a stroke compared with even-­tempered individuals. 38 In a more recent study in which data were pooled from three large cohort studies, personality fac-tors, including sensitivity to negative emotions, anxiety, and depression, did not predispose one to fatal stroke, but experiencing positive emotions and being generally extroverted did increase one’s risk for stroke, possibly as a result of being exposed to high-­risk behaviors. 61 Psychological distress or intense levels of perceived stress have been linked with risk of stroke. 86,138 Stressful life events, such as bereavement or health-­related issues, have also occurred within 1 week or month of an ischemic stroke, suggesting a triggering effect. 50 When stress was examined as a predictor of (any) stroke within specific age categories, however, psychological distress emerged for those younger than 44 years and older than 65 years. 152 Behavioral factors may be implicated for those two groups. Some research is emerging suggesting that personal-ity traits may also be protective against stroke. There is a decreased risk of fatal stroke in individuals whose per-sonalities reflect task orientation, persistence, and ability to plan ahead, suggesting that these traits might be asso-ciated with better health behaviors. 61 There is evidence that having a “purpose in life” may reduce the incidence of stroke. 66 Even one’s ability to express anger in a moderate way may actually be protective. 36 Personality traits are not the only predictors of stroke. Although some studies have suggested that depression is a predictor of stroke, other studies did not share this finding. A meta-­analysis and systematic review were conducted to determine whether an association exists. 102 It was found that depression indeed puts one at risk for not only stroke in general but also for fatal stroke and for ischemic stroke. Although this may be a result of the physiological mecha-nisms associated with depression, poor health behaviors, or comorbidities, 102 depression is a disease with wide-spread implications.
