text: Therapists can use placement of objects in reaching activities as a way to place a variety of demands on the trunk. The key to eliciting a trunk response is to place the object slightly beyond the arm’s reach. Fisher 26 observes that when subjects with-out brain injuries reach, they anteriorly tilt the pelvis, slightly extend the upper back, and move the trunk in the direction of the arm. Patients with brain injuries do not incorporate trunk movements into arm movements and reach only to arm’s length as they maintain a slumped posture. Therapists have the ability to control the desired response by the way they set up the activity. Setting up the activity includes placing items required during ADL in specific places, choosing the appropriate environment (e.g., kitchen with upper and lower shelves, bookcase, desk space, meal table), deciding how far beyond the arm span the activity should be placed, and deciding on the characteristics of the objects the patient is reaching for (number of objects, weight of the objects, and whether objects require one or two hands). Table 17.­11 includes examples of activity placement and resulting trunk response. Dean and Shepard 19 investigated, via a randomized placebo-­controlled trial of task-­related training after stroke, the effect of a training program designed to improve the ability to balance in sitting after stroke. The training pro-gram was designed to improve sitting balance and involved emphasis on appropriate loading of the affected leg while at the same time practicing reaching tasks using the unaf-fected hand to grasp objects located beyond arm’s length. The reaching tasks were performed under varied condi-tions. Changing the location of the object that the subject was reaching for varied the distance and direction of reach. Seat height, movement speed, object weight, and extent of thigh support were also varied. Increasing the number of repetitions and complexity of the tasks advanced the train-ing. The authors found that after training, subjects were able to reach faster and farther, increase load through the affected foot, and increase activation of affected leg muscles compared with the control group (highlighting the critical contribution of the lower extremities in promoting sitting balance). The experimental group also improved in sit to stand. The control group did not improve in reaching or sit to stand, and finally, neither group improved in walking. See Tables 17.­9 and 17.­11 for suggestions to grade reach-ing tasks.

text: Supine Use “log roll” technique to test patient’s response. Roll first toward the affected side then toward the unaffected side. Circle the side to which the resistance is most prominent. Score below the maximum resistance felt and add one point if resistance is noted in both directions. (Patients with marked lateropulsion may resist rolling to either side; hence, an extra point is added if resistance is noted with rolling both toward and away from the affected side.) 0 = No resistance to passive rolling 1 = Mild resistance 2 = Moderate resistance 3 = Strong resistance 1 = Add one point if resistance noted in both directions

text: Sitting Score with the patient seated, feet off floor, with both hands in lap. The expected hemiplegic response is for the patient to carry his or her weight toward the unaffected side. Some patients will passively fall toward their paretic side when placed in true vertical position by the examiner. This will not be scored as “lateropulsion.” Position the patient with their trunk 30 degrees off true vertical toward their affected side, then score the patient’s response to your attempts to bring them back to vertical. The “lateropulsion” phenomenon is an active attempt by the patient to keep their center of gravity toward their impaired side as they are brought to true vertical. 0 = No resistance to passive return to true vertical sitting position 1 = Voluntary or reflex resistive movements in trunk, arms or legs noted only in the last five degrees approaching vertical. 2 = Resistive movements noted but beginning within 5 to 10 degrees off vertical. 3 = Resistive movements noted more than 10 degrees off vertical.

text: Handling is a common technique used in the clinic. This intervention commonly is associated with neurodevel-opmental therapy 8 and may allow the patient to feel the desired movement pattern, gain range, assist weak move-ment patterns, and provide external support to prevent falls. To be effective, the patient must be aware of the goal associated with handling, and the therapist should use handling within the context of a functional task. In addi-tion, the handling from the therapist should be graded to allow the patient to perform as much of the movement pattern as possible. text: balloon volleyball and catch). During the initial stages of treatment, the therapist sat behind S.G. in a straddle posi-tion, which increased feelings of security and allowed the therapist to provide outside assistance with difficult pat-terns and to prevent falls. S.G. was observed while eating, and the therapist noted that she did not shift her weight anteriorly when bringing food to her mouth. Instead, she kept her trunk supported against the back of the chair. Because of the increased distance the food had to travel to reach her mouth, spillage was considerable, especially of liquids on a spoon (e.g., soup and cereal milk). S.G. was trained to shift her weight forward as she brought food to her mouth. Although spillage still occurred, it happened less frequently, with the food falling to the plate or table and not in her lap. As S.G. progressed, the therapist was able to sit next to or in front of her during activities. She engaged in graded reaching activities in which the distance S.G. was required to reach was increased progressively. Activities included reaching to lower shelves in the refrigerator and reaching for objects positioned at specific levels (e.g., knee level, midshin level, and floor level). On discharge from inpatient rehabilitation, S.G. was able to perform all basic ADL with distant supervision and without assistive devices, reach to the floor when she propped her upper trunk with her more affected forearm against her knees, and eat independently by using a rocker knife to cut her food, with spillage occurring only 10% of the time.

text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Define postural control and understand its role in supporting functional independence. 2. Identify the systems involved in postural control and the standing postural control impairments that are typically seen after stroke. 3. Understand the assessment of component standing balance skills and balance during functional activity. 4. Provide examples of interventions that target specific standing balance impairments in order to address these impairments as part of a comprehensive treatment plan.

text: Our ability to maintain an upright standing posture and to control our posture while standing is instrumental to almost everything we do during daily life. For example, when cooking a meal, our ability to walk around the kitchen or retrieve needed items from cabinets, drawers, and the refrigerator is, in part, dependent on our ability to control our body’s position in space (aka postural control). text: comprehensive occupational therapy (OT) treatment plan aimed at restoring function after stroke. The purpose of this chapter is to provide an overview of how to address standing postural control impairments after stroke. After a brief discussion of terminology and identification of the systems involved in standing pos-tural control, common standing balance impairments seen after stroke will be discussed. This will serve as a basis for the remainder of the chapter, which focuses on assess-ments and interventions designed to address standing bal-ance impairments. Finally, a case study illustrating the application of assessment and intervention principles to address standing balance impairments will be presented. The reader is referred to Chapters 7, 8, and 17 for further information regarding postural control with respect to functional mobility, gait, and trunk control, respectively.

text: In the literature, various terms (e.g., postural control, bal-ance, equilibrium, postural reactions, balance reactions, etc.) are used interchangeably to describe a person’s abil-ity to control their body’s position in space in order to maintain postural orientation and stability. 60,66 Accord-ing to Shumway-­Cook and Woollacott, “postural control involves controlling the body’s position in space for the dual purposes of stability and orientation.” They further define postural stability as the ability to control the cen-ter of mass (COM) with respect to the base of support (BOS), and postural orientation as the ability to maintain appropriate relationships between body segments and between the body and the environment for task perfor-mance. 60 Postural control responses can be reactive (i.e., in response to an external threat to balance) or anticipa-tory (i.e., planned in advance of a movement that may destabilize balance. 60 Many theories have been proposed to explain the abil-ity to maintain postural control. In the now outdated reflex or hierarchical model, balance was considered the interac-tion of reflexes and reactions, which are organized hier-archically, that result in the support of the body against gravity. 60 In this model, postural control deficits result from eliminating higher central nervous system (CNS) control, resulting in the release of spinal and supraspinal reflexes. This model is no longer tenable as it is clear that the nervous system is not organized as a distinct hierarchy. It is now generally accepted that postural control emerges from complex interactions between the person, task, and environment and involves both parallel and serial pro-cessing among multiple structures within the CNS. 59,60,63 The systems or distributed control model introduced by Bernstein describes balance as a complex interaction of musculoskeletal and neural systems. 59 According to Bar-ros de Oliveira et al., important resources required for postural control include 6: (1) the processing of various sensory modalities; (2) the ability of the CNS to integrate and “reweight” sensory information; (3) biomechanical constraints of the musculoskeletal system; (4) cognitive and perceptual (verticality) processing; and (5) movement strategies; the ability to maintain balance is specific to and modified around the constraints of the environment and task. Within this system, a disruption of balance (or insta-bility) results from a malfunction in or disruption of any one or more of the elements of the postural control sys-tem. 6,60 The subsequent section will highlight key systems that interact to influence postural control.

text: The integration of information from three sensory modalities is used for maintaining balance. The systems of importance are the 6,60 (1) visual system; (2) vestibular system; (3) somatosensory system.

text: Visual System The visual system (see Chapter 24) provides information regarding vertical orientation and visual flow. Visual or optical flow information, which describes movement of an image on the retina, is important input that aids detection of personal and environmental movement. Information provided by the visual system can be ambiguous and must be compared with other sensory information to determine accuracy. 6 For example, a person sitting in a stationary car next to another stationary car at a red light may receive optical flow information that indicates the other car is moving backward. This information alone is not adequate for determining which vehicle is moving; it only reveals relative movement. The information must be compared with other sensory information (i.e., somatosensory and vestibular) to determine whether self-­motion or object motion has occurred. 6

text: the support surface and the relationship of one body seg-ment to another (e.g., lower limb position relative to the trunk). Evidence suggests that somatosensory information from all parts of the body plays an important role in pos-tural control. 60 However, like visual input, somatosensory input can be ambiguous. For example, dorsiflexion at the ankle indicates that the body is displaced anteriorly over the BOS. However, when standing on an incline, this ankle position may coincide with midline posture. Thus, the individual must consider other senses to determine which position is accurate.

text: Vestibular System Information from the vestibular system (see Chapter 19) helps determine the position and motion of the head in space relative to gravity. The vestibular receptor appara-tus consists of the otolith organs and semicircular canals. The semicircular canals (horizontal, anterior, and poste-rior) sense angular accelerations, allowing the transduc-tion of rotational movements of the head (e.g., shaking or nodding the head). 23 Each canal is oriented in a way that allows it to be sensitive to movements that are made within a specific plane of three-­dimensional space 23 (Fig. 18.­1). The otolith organs include the utricle and saccule. They are responsible for detecting translational move-ments of the head (i.e., linear accelerations) or the orien-tation of the head with respect to gravity. 23 Specifically, the utricle responds to head tilt and translations along the horizontal plane. The saccule appears to be instrumental in detecting vertical translations of the head. 23 This system provides important information for the maintenance of postural control, the generation of com-pensatory eye movements, and the cognitive perception of motion and spatial orientation. 23 However, vestibular signals alone are insufficient in determining how the body is moving in space. 60 For example, information from the vestibular system alone would not allow one to distinguish between laterally flexing the head on a fixed trunk versus laterally flexing the trunk to one side.

text: Summary As indicated earlier, integrated sensory information from these three systems plays an important role in standing postural control. However, the CNS is able to “reweight” this sensory information (CNS increases reliance on one type of sensory input while decreasing reliance on another type) based on the constraints of the task and environ-ment. 6,60 For example, when visual cues are unavailable (eyes closed, dark room) or inaccurate (the environment is in motion), reliance on visual information is reduced, and the CNS will rely heavily on somatosensory and vestibular input. 6,60 The ability of the CNS to modify how sensory information is used is essential in allowing a person to maintain standing balance under varying task and envi-ronmental constraints. Deficits in the ability to modify how sensory information is used can lead to impairments in standing balance. 6,60

text: According to Barros de Oliveira et al., 6 in order to main-tain postural stability, one must keep the center of gravity within the limits of the BOS, or stability limits (the area about which the COM can be moved over the BOS without disrupting balance). 6 Stability limits (aka limits of stabil-ity) take into account the biomechanical constraints of the individual, and they can be modified to cope with chang-ing task and environmental demands. 6 Therefore, an indi-vidual’s ability to maintain standing balance depends not only on accurate evaluation and use of sensory information but also on appropriate body alignment, muscle tone, and the implementation of effective movement strategies. 6,60 The ideal standing posture is one in which the vertical line of gravity falls within the midline of the body (Fig. 18.­ 2). This body alignment allows an individual to maintain an erect position with the least amount of muscle activity. In order to maintain this standing posture, there needs to be an appropriate level of muscle tone in multiple muscle groups. Examples include the following 60: (1) plantar (gas-trocnemius and soleus) and dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior) of the ankle, (2) hip abductors (gluteus medius and tensor fascia latea, (3) hip flexors (iliopsoas), (4) back extensors (erector spinae), and (5) trunk flexors (abdominals).

text: Movement strategies are stereotyped or synergis-tic patterns used to maintain the COM over the BOS; they are characterized as automatic, general sensorimo-tor solutions to maintain postural control. 6 Synergistic movement patterns are useful in that they reduce the degrees of freedom, thus decreasing the response time. Automatic postural responses include ankle and hip strat-egies and strategies that change the BOS (i.e., stepping and reach and grasp strategies 6,60) (Fig. 18.­3). These pos-tural responses are reduced or absent when an individual uses an external support such as a cane or countertop to help maintain postural control. An ankle strategy is used to maintain the COM over the BOS when movement is centered on the ankles and appears to depend on ade-quate somatosensory information. 6 Knee, hip, and trunk stabilities are necessary for this strategy to be effective. Ankle strategies are used to control small, slow, swaying motions. They are effective when the surface area is firm and long in relation to foot length. Muscular activation while using the ankle strategy occurs in a distal to proxi-mal sequence. 6 Timing of muscular contractions is impor-tant to generate sufficient torque about the ankles and to maintain adequate stability at the hips, knees, and trunk. Ankle strategies frequently are used during “quiet” stand-ing. For example, this strategy is effective in controlling the small, slow, swaying motions that occur when a person stands in line (e.g., at a bank or grocery store).

text: Hip movement that maintains or restores standing bal-ance is a hip strategy. 6,60 This strategy is most effective in maintaining stability when the support surface is short in relation to foot length or is compliant. This strategy appears to rely on adequate vestibular information and is used to cope with faster and larger COM movements or when an ankle strategy is ineffective (i.e., unable to occur rapidly enough or generate adequate torque). 6,60 Muscle activation while using hip strategies occurs in a proximal to distal sequence. This strategy is used more frequently than ankle strategies when the COM approaches the outer limits of the BOS. 6,60 An example of a situation in which persons would use a hip strategy would be a circumstance that requires them to stand on a narrow beam. When ankle and hip strategies are or are perceived to be ineffective, strategies are employed to change the BOS. This involves movement of the limbs to produce either a stepping strategy or a strategy that involves reaching to grasp an object for support. 60 In the case of a stepping strategy, the person takes a step to adapt the BOS to the COM movement. 6 This is the strategy used effectively when taking each step while walking. The person shifts weight outside the existing BOS and takes a step to bring the BOS back under the COM (see Fig. 18.­3). In the case of a reach and grasp strategy, upper limb movement brings the hand in contact with an object that can be grasped for stability. Environmental factors, such as space constraints or the availability of appropriate support objects, appear to play a dominant role in whether a stepping or reach and grasp strategy is utilized. 60 For example, when standing and riding on a crowded subway, it may be more com-mon for an individual to use a reach and grasp strategy as opposed to a stepping strategy due to the space constraints (limiting the ability to step) and the presence of handhold loops or bars (affording grasp). Regardless of the movement strategy used, each is a reactive response to the displacement of the COM. These reactive responses are important as they allow us to main-tain stability when there are external threats to our balance. However, much of the time, we are engaged in activities that require us to compensate in advance for movements that will displace our COM. The organization of postural muscle activity that proceeds voluntary movements (e.g., a destabilizing arm movement when reaching for a bottle or a destabilizing leg movement when attempting to kick a ball) is termed anticipatory postural control. 60 Previous experience and sensory cues weigh heavily in the determi-nation of the appropriate sequence and degree of muscle activity required to maintain stability when anticipating a perturbation. 60 Because anticipatory postural adjust-ments precede destabilization, misperceiving the needed amount of muscle activity may result in too much or too little correction. 60 For example, when persons pull a door open, they initiate a posterior weight shift to counteract the weight of the door. If the weight of the door is lighter than anticipated, too much correction might occur and may result in a posterior perturbation of balance.

text: In addition to sensory and motor processing, postural control is also influenced by cognitive and perceptual pro-cesses, such as the allocation of attentional resources 60,74 and the ability to perceive an upright orientation of the body with respect to gravity (aka subjective postural verti-cal [SPV]). 11 The role of attention in postural control was brought to light by studies utilizing dual-­ task paradigms (e.g., maintaining postural control while engaged in a complex cognitive activity). The results of these studies suggest that postural control is attentionally demanding and that attentional demands required for postural control vary as a consequence of the interaction between the person, task, and environment. 74 With respect to SPV, healthy indi-viduals are able to determine the upright orientation of the body with respect to gravity in standing within a very narrow range (normality values range from –1.7 to 2.3 degrees in the sagittal plane and from –1.6 to 1.2 degrees in the frontal plane) without the aid of vision. 11 Disruptions in this internal frame of reference of vertical have been associated with standing balance impairments after stroke, particularly those with pusher behaviors (see “pushing” or “pusher syndrome” in the subsection on common postural control impairments). 4,12

Specific CNS structures are responsible for performing these complex tasks, regulating both reactive and anticipatory postural control responses (see Table 18.­1).

text: Cerebral Cortex The cerebral cortex is thought to play an instrumental role in mediating postural control. Recent evidence suggests that cortical structures, such as the supplementary motor area, premotor areas, primary somatosensory cortices, prefrontal cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and the ante-rior cingulate cortex play an important role in modulating subcortical postural control centers (e.g., brainstem [BS] centers) in order to maintain upright standing posture and standing balance under varying task and environmental demands. 62,63 It is thought that these areas work in a coor-dinated fashion to integrate sensory information, moni-tor ongoing postural stability, detect stable from unstable postures, and generate coordinated postural responses to cope with potential and actual threats to standing balance. Thus, damage to the cerebral cortices can have a nega-tive impact on standing balance (see “Common Stand-ing Postural Control Impairments after Hemispheric Stroke”). text: Cerebellum The cerebellum is thought to be an important structure underlying postural control. 32,77 The cerebellum receives information from structures such as the cortex, basal ganglia, spinocerebellar tract (somatosensory informa-tion), vestibular nuclei, and vestibular pathways. Input is modulated, interpreted, and sent out to the cortex; basal ganglia; thalamus; fourth, fifth, and sixth cranial nerves; vestibular nuclei and pathways; and indirectly to the spi-nal cord, providing the regulatory input needed to modify postural muscle tone and postural response to cope with changing task and environmental demands. 77 Damage to the cerebellum can result in difficulties with both reac-tive and anticipatory standing postural control. An indi-vidual with damage to the cerebellum may present with increased body sway, exaggerated postural responses, and an ataxic gait (see Chapter 8), and they may use a wide BOS in an attempt to increase stability when standing. 46,77

text: Basal Ganglia The basal ganglia are also involved in integrating infor-mation used for postural control. 70 The basal ganglia receive information from multiple sources, including the cortex and cerebellum, and then output information to the motor cortex via the thalamus. The basal ganglia work closely with the cerebellum and are believed to influ-ence sensory reweighting, postural flexibility (adapting to changing circumstances), and the sequencing of automatic postural reactions including the ankle, hip, stepping, and reach and grasp strategies previously discussed. 70 Dam-age to the basal ganglia may result in postural inflexibil-ity, impaired scaling of automatic postural responses, and an inability to modify postural responses according to the demands of a given task. 70

text: Brainstem The BS houses several centers (e.g., areas in the midbrain, vestibular and raphe nuclei, and the pontomedullary reticular formation) that are important for the regulation of postural muscle tone and postural responses and gen-eration of compensatory eye movements. 45 Many of these areas have reciprocal connections with the basal ganglia and cerebellum and are also modulated by the cerebral cortex. These nuclei output to lower motor neurons in the spinal cord via the vestibulospinal, raphespinal, and reticulospinal tracts, respectively. 45 Thus, damage to the BS can result in impairments in the regulation of postural muscle tone and the execution of appropriate postural responses.

text: When conducting a subjective interview, the clinician must keep in mind that patients who have had an acute stroke may not be able to provide accurate information during the interview process due to cognitive and/or language impairments. Clinicians may need to use other sources of information, including family members, signifi-cant others, and information from the medical chart, to supplement, clarify, or verify information that a patient provides. Patients may improve in their ability to provide information as cognitive and language deficits improve. Patients often also demonstrate a greater awareness of their situation and surroundings as they improve and become more fully integrated into the home and commu-nity environments. Subjective patient interviews allow patients to describe in their own words and from their own perception just how the stroke has affected their level of functioning. The interview should allow the therapist to obtain the follow-ing information about the patient: 1. Premorbid health history: The patient’s premorbid health history can have a significant impact on prog-nosis and, thus, appropriate goals. Having a thorough understanding of any premorbid conditions that could affect a patient’s balance functioning is important for the therapist. Examples include diabetic neuropathies, vision disturbances, vertigo, prior stroke or head inju-ries, prior lower extremity range of motion or strength problems, or other orthopedic issues such as lower back dysfunction. 2. Prior lifestyle: As more details are added to this portion of the interview, the therapist will be better equipped to create an individualized treatment plan to meet the individual patient needs. Attention should be focused on life roles the patient was engaged in (e.g., spouse, caregiver, parent, grandparent). 4. Patient’s perspective of current functioning: This area may be difficult for patients who have just had a stroke, but understanding what patients consider as problems resulting from balance deficits and what goal areas are relevant for the patient is important for the therapist to grasp. Early in the rehabilitation process, patients may cite self-­care and mobility as problem areas. Later, when patients are receiving home health or outpatient services, they may no longer experience difficulty in these basic areas but may cite problems with household or community activities. This portion of the interview is important for determining patients’ awareness level about the way their balance deficit limits their partici-pation in normal activities and for determining appro-priate and meaningful goals. In addition to a subjective interview, standardized self-­ report measures that ascertain the patient’s per-ceptions with respect to balance may provide valuable information. The Activities Specific Balance Confidence Scale 14,48,51,52 attempts to capture the patient’s view of his or her disability related to functional activities and perceived fall risk. It is a 16-­item test that asks patients to score their perception of their risk of falling when engaging in a particular task. This test is best used in an outpatient or home health setting. Research suggests that perception of fall risk may be positively related to functional mobility and greater community reintegra-tion. 14,48 The Falls Efficiency Scale is also a confidence assessment scale used in much the same manner. 47

text: Assessing balance in the context of function is an impor-tant part of a comprehensive evaluation as it allows the therapist to determine if standing balance is adequate for safe and effective task performance. This can be done using both nonstandardized and standardized methods. Regardless of the method used, safety must be a top pri-ority when assessing balance. In order to properly assess balance, patients must be engaged in tasks that will result in instability; thus, there is always a risk of a loss of balance (LOB). 60 The therapist must be cognizant of this and pro-tect the patient from falling at all times. Nonstandardized methods for evaluating balance typically involve the ther-apist observing the patient during engagement in typical activities of daily living (e.g., grooming while standing at the sink, dressing, or emptying the dishwasher) and not-ing whether balance is interfering with task performance). During observation of task performance, the thera-pist should note the following: (1) postural alignment, (2) BOS (narrow or wide), (3) stability limits, (4) movement strategies used to maintain standing balance, (5) presence or absence of anticipatory postural adjustments, and (6) LOB. The specific functional tasks used during evalua-tion depend on what the patient’s goals are at the time of intervention, the setting in which treatment is being received (e.g., inpatient rehabilitation, skilled nursing facility, home, outpatient clinic), and the discharge plan. For example, acute and inpatient therapists may evaluate balance in the context of the performance of basic self-­ care activities because independence in those areas tend to be a top priority of patients receiving care in that setting. Conversely, therapists working in the home environment or outpatient clinic may be more likely to evaluate balance in the context of instrumental activities of daily living. After the therapist has had an opportunity to observe the patient during functional activities, he/she should

text: begin to develop hypotheses about the reasons why the patient is having a LOB during various activities. The component evaluation (presented in subsequent sections) and the diagnostic information can assist the therapist in determining whether these hypotheses are substanti-ated. For example, a patient may experience a LOB when attempting to put on pants while standing. The therapist may hypothesize that the LOB resulted from an asym-metrical postural alignment, an inability to shift weight toward the affected side, and/or lack of an effective lat-eral hip strategy when attempting to stand on one leg. These hypotheses can be supported by assessing postural alignment, stability limits, and the use of an available hip strategy. With respect to standardized assessments, there are several assessments that are appropriate for use with patients after stroke. 8,25,43,57 The most commonly used assessments are highlighted below. The Berg Balance Scale (BBS) 8 is by far the most com-monly used balance assessment. This assessment tool can assist with predicting fall risk, determining lengths of stay, and determining adaptive equipment and discharge plan-ning recommendations. 2,13,27,40,42,61,68,72 The test does not help the therapist in determining why patients might lose their balance and therefore is limited in its ability to assist with treatment planning. The test examines a number of factors, such as unsupported sitting and standing, trans-fers, reaching forward, picking objects up from the floor, turning 360 degrees, and standing on one foot, and each is graded on a five-­point scale. The assessment outlines the specific scoring criteria. This test examines many aspects of balance and has been shown to have high interrater reli-ability and validity in older adults. 9,13,18,42,61 This test has been developed primarily for and used with the older pop-ulation and stroke patients. 10,18,61 The Berg can be time consuming, however. A new, shorter version of the Berg, referred to as the BBS 3P (seven item) Test, has been developed. Tasks in the shortened version include reach-ing forward with outstretched arm, standing with eyes closed, standing with one foot in front, turning to look behind, retrieving an object from the floor, standing on one foot, and sitting to standing. Available research sug-gests that this shortened version demonstrates similar psy-chometric properties as the original Berg assessment. 18,71 The timed up and go (TUG) test is another common, highly used evaluation. The TUG has three subtests. The TUG Alone requires the patient to stand up from a chair with armrests, walk a short distance, turn around, return to the chair, and sit again. 43 The TUG Cognitive requires the same activity while the patient counts backward from 20. The TUG Manual again requires the same basic activ-ity while the patient carries a full glass of water. These three subtests have established cutoffs to assist the thera-pist in predicting likelihood of falls under different condi-tions and therefore can be useful in recommendations. 2,55 Performance is rated on a somewhat nonspecific five-­point scale. This test is used with the older adult population, and because of its varying rating criteria, the criteria should be evidence based and consistent in use within a facility if used as an assessment tool. 49 The functional reach test 25 requires the patient to stand next to a wall with a yardstick placed parallel to the floor. The patient is asked to reach as far forward as possible, and the reach length is measured. This test is quick and easy to perform and does not require expensive equipment. Test-­ retest and interrater reliability is high. 25,61,73 The test has been used with a variety of populations spanning children through the elderly. 24,25,73 The disadvantage of this test is that it measures only one functional task and assesses skills in the anterior direction only. 7 The Postural Assessment Scale for Stroke Patients (PASS) 14,40,42 tests the ability of patients to maintain a given posture as well as to maintain balance while chang-ing positions, including lying, sitting, and standing. It consists of 12 items, several of which assess standing bal-ance (i.e., sit to stand and stand to sit, standing with and without support, standing on nonparetic and paretic leg, picking up a pencil form the floor) and uses a 0–3 ordinal rating scale. Research indicates that this test has high con-struct validity, high correlation with functional measures such as the Functional Independence Measure, and good reliability. This test is most predictive in the first 30 days poststroke and takes approximately 10 minutes to admin-ister. A short form of the PASS has been developed and tested, and it contains only five items and uses the 0–3 scale for scoring; initial research indicates that the short form may also demonstrate high interrater reliability and validity. 16,71 The Brunel Balance Assessment Scale (BBAS) is a scale that measures balance at three levels: sitting, stand-ing, and stepping. The entire assessment scale can be administered at the same time, or it may be adminis-tered in sections. The advantage of this assessment is that it can be used repetitively as the patient progresses in mobility; because of this, the assessment easily lends itself to use across an entire continuum of care and across a wide range of patients with varying levels of mobility. Research suggests that this assessment tool demonstrates high reliability and validity and has potentially useful predictive validity. 67,69 The Rivermead Mobility Index can be administered using self-­report or proxy report. It consists of the follow-ing 15 questions. 29,30 1. Turning over in bed: Do you turn over from your back to your side without help? 2. Lying to sitting: From lying in bed, do you get up to sit on the edge of the bed on your own? 3. Sitting balance: Do you sit on the edge of the bed without holding on for 10 seconds? 4. Sitting to standing: Do you stand up from any chair in less than 15 seconds and stand there for 15 seconds, using hands and/or an aid, if necessary?

Transfer: Do you manage to move from bed to chair and back without any help? 7. Walking inside (with an aid if necessary): Do you walk 10 m, with an aid if necessary, but with no standby help? 8. Stairs: Do you manage a flight of stairs without help? 9. Walking outside (even ground): Do you walk around outside, on pavements, without help? 10. Walking inside, with no aid: Do you walk 10 m inside, with no caliper, splint, or other aid (including furni-ture or walls) without help? 11. Picking up off floor: Do you manage to walk 5 m, pick something up from the floor, and then walk back without help? 12. Walking outside (uneven ground): Do you walk over uneven ground (grass, gravel, snow, ice, etc.) without help? 13. Bathing: Do you get into/out of a bath or shower to wash yourself unsupervised and without help? 14. Up and down four steps: Do you manage to go up and down four steps with no rail but using an aid if neces-sary? 15. Running: Do you run 10 m without limping in 4 sec-onds (fast walk, not limping, is acceptable)? A score of 0 = a “no” response; a score of 1 = a “yes” response. A total score is determined by summing the points allocated for all items. A maximum score of 15 is possible: higher scores indicate better mobility perfor-mance. There is a modified version of the tool that includes eight items that are directly observed by the rater. 39 The Motor Assessment Scale is a relatively lengthy assessment (15 to 60 minutes depending on the patient’s participation) that focuses on supine to side-­lying, supine to sitting edge of bed, sitting balance, sit to stand, walking, and effect of upper arm function, hand movements, and advanced hand movements on balance. It uses a one-­ to six-­point scale. This assessment is reliable, valid, and sen-sitive to change over time. 27,31,68 Disadvantages include the amount of time needed to administer the test, espe-cially with more mobile patients and a more in-­depth training needed for consistent therapist use. Advantages are similar to the BBAS. If standing balance impairments are noted during task performance, it is likely the occupational therapist will need to complete an assessment of component skills to determine the subsystems (sensory, motor, or cognitive) that may be contributing to the balance impairment. The component areas that should be assessed related to standing postural control are highlighted in the subsequent section.

text: An evaluation of the visual, somatosensory, and vestibular systems is considered to be an important part of component assessment related to standing postural control. 6,60 An evaluation of the visual system typically includes visual acuity and an assessment of oculomotor function (reflexive and voluntary—see Chapter 24 for details). An evaluation of the somatosensory system should include an assessment of light touch, pressure, proprioception, and kinesthesia, particularly of the lower extremities. Finally, assessment of the vestibular system should be performed if deficits in this system are suspected (see Chapter 19). In addition to assessing the basic functioning of these systems, an evaluation of the ability to integrate and use these sensory modalities for standing postural control must be assessed. This is addressed later in this section on evaluation. As part of a component assessment, it is important to determine if there are any biomechanical constraints that might interfere with standing postural control. 6,60 Muscle tone, active and passive range of motion, and strength, particularly of the trunk and lower extremities, should be evaluated. 60 An evaluation of postural alignment should be conducted with the patient in standing; the posture for static standing or the “starting or ready position” should be symmetrical; the head should be in midline, centered over the shoulders; the shoulders should be centered and aligned over the pelvis; under “normal” conditions, the feet should be approximately hip distance apart; and the pelvis should be centered over the BOS created by the feet (see Fig. 18.­2). Asymmetries in alignment or bias over the BOS should be noted. The width of the BOS can be mea-sured by measuring the distance between the medial mal-leoli with the use of tape measure. 60 Having the patient stand on two scales can assist with determining asymme-tries in weight bearing. 60 In addition to assessing standing postural alignment, it is important to determine the movement strategies that are used to maintain stability (see Fig. 18.­3) and the patient’s stability limits (Fig. 18.­4). Movement strategies and sta-bility limits are commonly evaluated during self-­initiated body sway (patient voluntarily shifts weight forward, backward, and side to side), in response to external pertur-bation (therapist displaces the patients weight in multiple directions), and in anticipation of potentially destabilizing movements of the extremities (patient is asked to quickly lifting a heavy object, reach to grasp an object placed out of reach, step onto a curb, or to stand on one leg). 60 The following section describes examples of testing procedures designed to elicit ankle, hip, and stepping strategies, and the testing of stability limits. An initial assessment of the use of ankle strategies can be conducted with the patient standing on a firm support surface that is long in relation to foot length. The patient’s feet should be placed approximately hip distance apart. The therapist should note oscillations about the ankles. If the patient is able to perform this task effectively, increas-ing the demands of the task by narrowing the BOS may be necessary. The therapist may ask the patient to place his/her feet together to decrease the size of the BOS, narrow

text: the limits of stability, and increase the need to control COM oscillations. The therapist should note increased use of ankle strategies, and if swaying increases in speed or magnitude, the patient may initiate a hip strategy. 57,60 Individuals should be able to maintain their balance in this position with an ankle strategy and perhaps with minimal use of a hip strategy. Not using ankle strategies or using stepping strategies in this position indicates a disturbance in the ability to generate automatic postural responses. 57,60 Several methods exist for assessing hip strategies. As indicated earlier, hip strategies are used when the sup-port surface is short in relation to foot length, the support surface is compliant, or when ankle strategies are (or are perceived to be) ineffective. Simulation of each of these conditions should result in the use of a hip strategy. For higher-­level patients, the therapist may ask the patient to stand on a 4-­inch balance beam so that only the middle of the foot receives support. 57,60 Ankle strategies are ineffec-tive under these circumstances because adequate torque cannot be produced around the ankle when the support surface is this short. The therapist should note use of primarily anterior/posterior hip strategies. Attempts to use ankle strategies only or any use of stepping strategies indicates a dysfunction in the ability to generate an appro-priate hip strategy. 57,60 Compliant support surfaces also result in use of hip strategies in “normal” subjects. The therapist can simulate this condition by having the patient stand on a 4-­inch-­thick piece of medium-­density foam. Adequate torque around the ankles is not possible under this condition, and the patient uses hip strategies in all planes/directions. As stated previously, excessive attempts to use ankle strategies or exclusive use of stepping strate-gies indicates dysfunction. 57,60 The therapist may assess lateral hip strategies by hav-ing the patient assume a tandem stance (a heel–toe posi-tion in which one foot is directly in front of the other). This position significantly narrows the lateral limits of the BOS; because ankle strategies have a limited lateral range of effectiveness, the patient uses hip strategies. 57,60 This position on a firm support surface would not be chal-lenging enough to elicit hip strategy use in some patients. These patients could perform the same task on a 4-­inch balance beam to further narrow the BOS. When one assesses use of hip strategies in any of these conditions, observation of strategy sequence is important. The therapist also should note the effectiveness of the tar-get strategy. Use of ineffective strategies (i.e., LOB) indi-cates that a particular strategy has failed. The therapist may elicit use of the stepping strategy 57,60 by further chal-lenging the postural control system (e.g., by combining all of the previous test conditions). For example, the therapist may ask patients to stand with feet together or in tandem on a compliant surface. A delay in or lack of a stepping strategy that results in a LOB indicates dysfunction. As indicated earlier, each individual possesses stabil-ity limits (aka limits of stability). An assessment of the patient’s ability to move within his/her stability limits and noting the symmetry and extent of those limits are nec-essary. Because of the biomechanical constraints of the foot and ankle, the limits are greatest in the anterior/pos-terior direction and smaller in the lateral direction. The greatest degree of movement usually occurs anteriorly. The area created by the limits of stability is in the form of an ellipse (see Fig. 18.­4). Therapists need to assess both actual and perceived stability limits. Actual stability limits are the true ellipse that a patient can achieve relative to foot length and available motor control. Perceived stabil-ity limits are the ellipse in which a patient perceives he or she can move; patients may underestimate or overestimate this area. If patients underestimate the limit, usually due to fear of falling, it results in an inability to weight shift normally to complete the activity. If the patient overesti-mates this area, usually due to sensory or perceptual defi-cits, it results in a fall. 57,58,60 Stability limits may be measured in a number of ways. An experienced evaluator with a strong understanding of typical limits of stability might ask patients to shift their

Several computerized pressure plate systems on the market are able to compute an individual’s “normal” stability limits based on height by force plate analysis. 57–60 The therapist then can compare normal and actual figures. text: Evaluating the Influence of Sensory Organization on Postural Control Assessing the ability of the CNS to evaluate, integrate, and appropriately weight sensory information is an impor-tant part of a component assessment of standing balance. Computerized tests of sensory organization are available commercially and often are combined with force plates that can measure motor responses to test conditions (to a degree). The sensory organization portion of the appa-ratus usually consists of a safety harness, a movable foot plate, and a movable visual screen that surrounds the sub-ject. Test conditions also have been simulated in the clinic by using 4-­inch medium-­density foam as a compliant sur-face and a visual “dome” that encompasses the patient’s visual field and is worn on the head. 6,19,56 The Clinical Test of Sensory Organization and Bal-ance uses six test conditions to assess an individual’s abil-ity to access, use, and organize sensory information. 6,19,56 Within this formalized procedure, the therapist times the tests, measures the amount of sway, and records complete LOB falls. This formalized assessment provides specific informa-tion to the therapist about why patients may lose their balance and is therefore very useful in developing indi-vidualized treatment plans. text: list, set goals, and plan a course of treatment designed to achieve those goals. Naturally, many factors must be considered when developing goals and planning targeted interventions. First and foremost, the therapist must con-sider what the patient wants or needs to do during daily life. In addition, factors such as prognosis, service delivery setting, length of stay, social supports, and the eventual discharge environment must be taken into account. The therapist will often have to consider these factors when deciding whether to target remediation of standing bal-ance impairments or whether to introduce compensatory strategies for engaging in meaningful activities despite these impairments. These are important decisions because prescribing equipment too soon to a patient who has the potential for remediation may limit potential recovery of standing postural control. For example, issuing a cane or walker increases the BOS and decreases the need for the patient to cope with COM changes. Similarly, prescribing a tub bench or shower chair may limit the opportunities for prac-ticing standing safely in the shower. This is not to suggest that devices should not be considered or recommended— numerous patients are able to function only because of their adaptive equipment and devices. It is only to suggest that when planning treatment, therapists should be aware of the appropriateness and implications of using each device. Therapists may consider training patients to use devices outside of therapy that provide greater independence but limit their use during actual therapy sessions. Patients then can maintain their independence while still working toward improving their standing balance. Compensatory strate-gies, environmental modifications, and the use of adap-tive devices designed to facilitate engagement in daily and instrumental activities of daily living after stroke are dis-cussed in detail in several chapters in the text (Chapters 6, 9, and 30) and will not be repeated here. The following sec-tions highlight key intervention principles for remediating standing postural control impairments.

text: Using functional activities and emphasizing functional outcomes are basic principles of OT, and they are being embraced by many other disciplines. Hsieh and col-leagues 36 stated that using added-­ purpose occupation is motivating during performance. Currently, available information supports the use of repetitive functional tasks and engagement in activities as primary intervention tools for retraining standing balance. 1,3,26,33,44,53,65 In addition, adjuncts to task training such as exercise, 35 motor imag-ery, 17 and virtual reality training 50 have also been shown to be effective for improving balance (see Table 18.­4). The tasks chosen should be client centered and specifi-cally address the balance component disturbances that have been identified during evaluation, so that occupa-tional therapists can provide individualized and functional treatment (see Boxes 18.­1 and 18.­2 and Fig. 18.­6).

Wu and col-leagues 75 indicated that one functional goal in rehabili-tating persons with hemiplegia should be “to improve symmetrical characteristics of postural control.” The most common forms of treatment for asymmetrical weight bearing and poor standing postural control are to expose the patient to a variety of conditions that require

text: Retraining Symmetrical Postural Alignment A variety of strategies can be used to help patients develop a symmetrical standing posture. For example, therapists often utilize verbal cues (e.g., “shift your weight a little more to the left”) or manual assistance (shifting patients weight through the pelvis) to help patients find their optimal postural alignment. 60 Once this alignment is achieved, the patient is encouraged to maintain it for a period of time. Therapists may also make use of feedback mechanisms to improve symmet-rical standing alignment. For example, visual feedback can be provided using a mirror or force-­plate biofeed-back devices. 60 In and colleagues found that providing visual feedback via a mirror improved standing balance ability during quiet standing on an unstable surface. However, a nonsignificant effect was observed with respect to a stable surface. 37 Using a mirror to pro-vide visual feedback may be most appropriate in con-texts that normally involve the use of a mirror (e.g., when performing self-­care tasks such as grooming or dressing). The use of force-­plate biofeedback devices has also been investigated; although there is some evidence that this type of feedback may improve standing symmetry, improve-ments do not appear to carry over to improved balance dur-ing functional activities. 5 Additionally, many clinics do not have these types of devices available. An alternative to the use of these types of devices is to have the patient stand on two standard scales placed side-­by-­side. The weights dis-played on the scale provide the patient with clear informa-tion regarding weight-­bearing discrepancies. 60 In addition to the use of visual feedback, therapists can instruct patients to use somatosensory information (if sen-sation is intact) about pressure they receive through their feet while weight shifting to achieve symmetrical align-ment. For example, a therapist can cue a patient with an anterior or posterior bias to locate foot pressure in rela-tion to the balls of the feet.

text: Retraining Effective Movement Strategies As discussed previously, part of a comprehensive bal-ance assessment is evaluating what patients do to main-tain their balance. Three strategies were outlined as normal movement strategies: ankle, hip, and strate-gies that change the BOS (i.e., stepping and reaching). Information from the component assessment allows the therapist to determine whether a strategy is being used, the amount of delay in strategy use (and therefore its effectiveness), and whether the strategy is appropriate. Therapists can use external perturbations (e.g., pas-sively moving the patient through the hips or using a moveable surface to cause weight shifting in various directions) in an attempt to retrain standing balance responses. 60 In these situations, patients must be able to initiate and execute a motor response that is appro-priate to the perturbation experienced to maintain bal-ance. The therapist can use informa-tion gained during the patient interview to determine in which performance areas a patient is experiencing balance deficits (e.g., washing hair while standing in the shower, donning pants while standing, or reach-ing into a high cabinet during meal preparation) and which activities the patient values. Incorporating active weight shifting into a specific activity or using weight shifting that is inherent to successful completion of an activity allows the patient to learn more normal pos-tural responses that are appropriate for engagement in that specific activity. This is important given that there is evidence that postural response vary in accor-dance with task and environmental demands (see Fig. 18.­6). 6,60 Therapists must be able to complete skilled, accu-rate task analyses to determine which strategy should be used in accordance with specific activities. text: should see a correlation between functional activity obs­ ervations and the results of component testing. This information can be used to determine which functional activities may place patients at risk for LOB. The iden-tified activities then may become part of the treatment plan (see Table 18.­3). For example, therapists can elicit ankle strategies by asking patients to engage in tasks requiring small weight shifts on solid support surfaces that are larger than their feet. For example, patients could wipe down a table or arrange fruit in a bowl while standing. They could begin the task training with upper extremity support, which would gradually be removed to further challenge standing balance (Fig. 18.­7). Therapists can elicit hip strategies by asking patients to engage in tasks requiring larger weight shifts on narrow BOS. These tasks could include playing toss and catch while the feet are close together or while standing on compliant surfaces. Therapists also can promote the use of hip strategies by asking patients to reach into drawers or cabinets without locking their knees in extension; hip flexion is necessary to counteract the resulting anterior weight shift (Fig. 18.­8). Therapists can elicit strategies that change the BOS by engaging patients in activities that require them to make weight shifts that are well outside of their BOS, such as hitting a tennis ball against a wall or reaching out of their BOS to pick up work boots off the floor. Activities can be graded by the changing the direc-tion, speed, and magnitude of body and limb move-ments that are needed to complete the task, changing the size of the BOS, or changing the complexity of the task. For example, when placing food cans into a cabi-net, the task can be graded up by having the patient place cans on the second as opposed to the first shelf (Fig. 18.­9), and when practicing, carrying items while standing the task can be graded by holding the item close to the body and gradually increasing the distance from the body at which the item is held (Fig. 18.­10). Breaking down activities into a hierarchy of tasks rang-ing from simple to more complex is advisable.

text: As stated previously, the CNS uses integrated infor-mation from the visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems to maintain balance. Given this, it is impor-tant that patients be provided with activities that allow them the opportunity to adapt to changing sensory conditions. 6,60 Results of sensory testing and the test of sensory organization can help guide the therapist with respect to activities that may place the patient at risk for LOB; these activities can become part of the treatment plan (see Table 18.­3). For example, patients who perform poorly under testing conditions forc-ing them to maintain balance on uneven surfaces may lose their balance while standing on carpet or while

Patients who perform poorly under testing con-ditions forcing them to maintain their balance while receiving conflicting visual input may lose their bal-ance while scanning items on a grocery store shelf or when rinsing shampoo out of their hair while standing in the shower. Therapists also must determine possi-ble compensations or strategies patients may use when one or more systems are impaired. 60 Patients with somatosensory dysfunctions usually become visually dependent, whereas patients with visual disturbances usually become dependent on somatosensory infor-mation (i.e., information obtained from contact with surfaces). Patients with vestibular dysfunctions may become visually or somatosensory dependent. These compensatory strategies can work for patients in iso-lated environments but prevent true independence and result in a higher risk for falls for patients who are active in the home and/or community. text: stop going out into the community to compensate for balance deficits, which can result in social isolation or depression. The inclusion of the manipulation of sensory infor-mation into treatment of stroke survivors has been shown to increase functional balance. 7 Generally, this is done by exposing the patient to activities that pro-gressively challenge standing balance while altering the availability and accuracy of sensory information. 60 For example, patients who rely heavily on vision may be challenged to maintain a standing balance while performing an activity with their eyes closed (e.g., rinsing shampoo from the hair while standing in the shower) or under low light conditions (reaching for an item from a medicine cabinet with only a nightlight available). Conversely, a patient who is overreliant on somato-sensory information may be challenged to maintain bal-ance while performing tasks when standing on carpet or uneven surfaces as opposed to a solid surface. Tasks should be graded to increase postural demands. For example, the therapists can develop a treatment plan that initially requires the patient to practice holding an item while standing on an uneven surface. The next step would be to have the patient reach for an item while standing on an uneven surface. Then, the patient would carry an item as they transitioned from an uneven sur-face to an even surface and vice versa. Patients also may lose their balance during func-tional activities if they have difficulty with head-­eye coordination and gaze stabilization. Activities such as walking in a busy mall, scanning the grocery store shelves for items, and placing groceries on various shelves can cause LOB. The CNS is unable to over-ride the false visual information that results from these tasks, and thus, patients feel like they are losing their balance. Patients then institute postural reactions that are incongruent with the actual events that are occur-ring. Therapists can develop treatment plans that chal-lenge patients’ ability to maintain gaze stability during functional activities requiring coordinated head-­ eye movements. Patients with impaired vestibular function are gen-erally visually and somatosensory dependent, although they usually rely more heavily on one system. Patients with premorbid health issues may be more reliant on one system for a predetermined reason. For example, patients with diabetic neuropathies may be more visually dependent because they do not have access to somato-sensory information through their lower extremities. Most traditional treatment approaches to address ves-tibular dysfunction have relied on graded, repetitive head movements in the form of exercise to improve ves-tibular functions. 15,21 Cohen and colleagues 20 outline a treatment approach that incorporates this basic premise into functional activity. They stress that treatment activities must include head movements and positions that elicit the vestibular dysfunction during assessment. They also stress that activities must be interesting to patients; their use may assist patients with relating to real-­ life experiences. Suggested activities include retrieving towels in a basket on the floor and hanging them on an overhead clothesline, ambulating in the hallways while scanning and describing objects placed at various heights, playing badminton, and dribbling a basketball back and forth across the room. A thorough and accurate assessment of the specific impaired bal-ance deficit is necessary to design the most efficacious treatment plan (see Chapter 19). Throughout this process, careful consideration of safety and fall risks must also be considered, especially when treatment occurs in home care or on an outpatient basis. Thorough patient and family education outlining the reasons for particular difficulties and safety modifica-tions to reduce the risk of falls while treatment is ongo-ing is essential. text: Other Factors Affecting Treatment Planning As indicated, earlier deficits in attention and perceptual deficits may impact standing postural control. Therefore, addressing these deficits in treatment is an important part of improving standing balance. Treatment of these types of deficits is covered extensively in Chapters 25 and 26 and will not be repeated here. However, it should be men-tioned that there is emerging evidence suggesting that dual-­ task training may improve both standing balance and gait parameters after stroke. 34,60 He and colleagues 34 conducted a systematic review and meta-­analysis investi-gating the effects of dual-­task balance and mobility train-ing in people after stroke. The review included 13 articles involving 457 participants. Dual-­ task mobility training improved single-­ task walking function as compared to single-­ task mobility training, and cognitive-­ motor bal-ance training improved standing balance. The authors concluded 34: “There is some evidence that dual-­task train-ing can improve single-­task walking and balance function in individuals with stroke.” The researchers cautioned against definitive recommendations for the use of dual-­ task training secondary to the weak methodological qual-ity of the studies. 34 Finally, medical factors such as fluctuating blood pressures, fluctuating blood sugar levels, infections, metabolic disturbances, and medications also can affect a patient’s balance skills. Therapists should remain cognizant of these factors and report any sig-nificant changes that they observe to the physician (see Chapter 1).

An understanding of the systems involved in postural control and the application of appro-priate assessment and treatment of standing balance dys-function is an important component of comprehensive OT treatment for stroke survivors. The subsequent case study provides an example of the implementation of these principles.

text: Improving Function through Balance Retraining M.J. is a 58-­year-­old female who was diagnosed with a right middle cerebral artery stroke. She was assessed first by an inpatient rehabilitation occupational therapist, who determined that the patient had difficulty control-ling her balance during bathing, grooming, and dress-ing. The patient stated that she wanted to perform all of these activities independently. The therapist noted that M.J. had a postural bias to the right in standing, used a wide BOS when standing during functional tasks, and was unable to control her center of gravity when shift-ing her leg to the left to complete a task. M.J. was able to support weight on her left lower extremity. Sensation was impaired but not absent in her left lower extremity. M.J.’s perceived stability limits were not congruent with her actual stability limits. She underestimated her ability to shift weight to the left and thus could not complete tasks that required her to shift weight to the left. When assisted with a left weight shift, M.J. was not able to con-trol the shift because of poor coordination and timing of muscle activation. Because she lost control whenever she shifted weight to the left, M.J. compensated by maintain-ing an asymmetrical postural alignment. When asked to shift her weight actively to the left, M.J. altered her postural alignment by attempting to shift her shoulders rather than her COM. Inpatient rehabilitation treatment initially centered on assisting M.J. in relearning appropriate motor responses in sitting. Activities that involved reaching and intrinsically incorporated weight shifts to the left were used. Activities of daily living were incorporated with facilitation of mid-line posture, and weight shifts during this functional task were used. She progressed to standing tasks, and these same principles were incorporated into standing tasks. text: and visual feedback via a mirror to aid M.J. in achieving an optimal standing position. The therapist selected parts of self-­care tasks that did not require large weight shifts (e.g., combing her hair, washing her face, and selecting clothing from her closet) and had M.J. perform these tasks while trying to maintain a midline position. The therapist helped M.J. learn to use visual and somatosensory infor-mation when possible to provide information about her position in space during task performance. In addition, M.J. was provided with an audiotaped motor imagery script designed to guide M.J. in visualiza-tion of engagement in standing activities while focusing on maintaining a midline position. She was encouraged to use the tapes outside of scheduled therapy sessions. M.J. was discharged home with continued needs in the areas of functional balance skills. Patient and family education focused on appropriate use of adaptive equipment, envi-ronmental modifications, and safety in the home. Following discharge from acute rehabilitation, home care and outpatient therapy services continued. As M.J. improved her ability to achieve and maintain midline dur-ing additional static standing tasks, the therapist began to introduce tasks requiring a more significant weight shift from right to left (e.g., putting on her shirt while standing, reaching for objects on the sink, and getting objects out of the closet that were placed to elicit a left weight shift). Emphasis was placed on assisting M.J. with developing an awareness of her actual stability limits. As M.J.’s control improved, the therapist also focused on narrowing her BOS to the more normal site dictated by particular activi-ties. M.J. improved to the point that she could maintain midline and actively shift weight laterally during self-­care activities without assistance from the therapist. Upon dis-charge from outpatient therapy, M.J. was provided with a comprehensive home program designed to continue to challenge and improve motor control involved in balance skills.

text: The vestibular system is one of the special senses; it has receptors on the head and signals the brain via a cranial nerve. The end organs for the vestibular system, the ves-tibular labyrinths, detect head acceleration, or a change in the rate at which the head is moving. This information is converted to a velocity signal (velocity is speed plus direc-tion), so the signal received by the brain really represents the speed and direction at which the head moves. The laby-rinths are located within cavities inside the temporal bones of the skull on either side of the head, so the end organs are inaccessible from the outside world; they cannot be seen or otherwise examined without drilling into the temporal bone to expose them. Because the end organ is not obvious and because the roles of the vestibular system—contributions to postural control, oculomotor control, and spatial orientation, and modulation of some autonomic function—are subtle, the vestibular system was the last of the special senses to be dis-covered, and many people still do not understand it.

text: vestibular system has been reviewed many times in journal articles and textbooks. For excellent reviews, the reader is encouraged to examine other texts. 3,5,7,9,10,22 To put the topic of this chapter in context requires brief reviews of some main points about the vestibular system. The vestibular labyrinth has two sets of motion detec-tors: three semicircular canals (lateral, posterior, and superior) that act as rotatory accelerometers to detect turning motions of the head and two saclike otoliths (utri-cle and saccule) that act as linear accelerometers to detect linear acceleration of the head (Fig. 19.1). Since gravity is a fixed linear acceleration, the otoliths also detect static tilt with reference to gravity. This gravitational signal is very important for spatial orientation because it acts as an earth-­fixed reference. This information, and the complex anatomic structures associated with it, is needed to keep the head erect and see where one is going as one moves through space, plots a course toward a particular location or target, and generates appropriate autonomic responses when one encounters a perturbation; that is, when one is inadvertently thrown off balance for some reason. These motor skills help some lower animals capture and eat their prey and help other animals avoid becoming prey. These skills serve similar purposes in humans as they move through space, while avoiding or encountering obstacles, performing purpose-ful activities that involve manipulating objects while they move their heads in all planes. People with impaired ves-tibular systems complain of vertigo and poor spatial navi-gation skills, blurred vision, impaired postural control, and nausea and other signs of autonomic involvement.

text: Inertial Mechanism The mechanism of the vestibular labyrinth is based on the principle of inertia, that is, that an object remains at rest until an asymmetrical force acts on it, and then it contin-ues to move until another asymmetrical force acts on it to stop it. The semicircular canals are narrow (imagine a curved tube approximately the width of a hair on your head), so they provide a large amount of resistance to any fluid that fills it. The canals are then filled with a thick fluid known as endolymph. Endolymph has a high spe-cific gravity, so it has high inertia. The inertial properties of endolymph and the high resistance of the canals, com-bined, mean that the vestibular system is not sensitive to extremely slow head movements. It is somewhat respon-sive to slow head movements, but it responds most accurately to moderate to rapid head movements in the range of 0.1 to 7.0 Hz. Not surprisingly, this frequency bandwidth is the range of most normal head movements. When an individual rotates his or her head, while shak-ing his or her head “no,” tiny cilia attach to specialized hair cells, located on a minuscule hillock that blocks one end of the canal, and bend backward in response to movement of the endolymph over the gelatinous cup or cupula into which they protrude. This motion of the cilia starts a chain of events within the hair cells in which ions are exchanged; the cell membrane either hyperpolarizes or depolarizes. If the cell membrane depolarizes, then neurotransmitter is released, and the adjacent vestibular nerve fires, which signals to the related neurons in the vestibular nuclei, located in the medulla, that the person turned his or her head. In the otoliths, the hair cells are located in patches either in the base of the utricle or on the side of the saccule. Their cilia protrude into the oto-conial membrane, which is a protein matrix containing many microscopic crystals of calcium carbonate known as otoconia. The otoconia act as an inertial mass. The otoconial membrane slides back and forth over the cilia in response to linear acceleration. For example, when a person accelerates his or her car going forward, the otoconial membrane virtually slides backward over the underlying cilia, bending them backward and commenc-ing the transduction process described in the preceding paragraph.

text: Innervation and Blood Supply All of this hardware in the temporal bone is supplied by nerves and arteries. The vestibular labyrinth is innervated by the vestibular nerve, which is half of cranial nerve VIII. The vestibular nerve has two branches. The superior branch innervates the superior and horizontal semicircu-lar canals and the utricle, and the inferior branch inner-vates the posterior canal and the saccule. The arterial supply to the vestibular labyrinth is similar to the innervation. The entire labyrinth receives its blood supply from one artery, the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), which is a branch off the basilar artery. A major branch from the AICA, the labyrinthine artery, sup-plies the entire inner ear. Inside the inner ear, it bifurcates to form the common cochlear artery and anterior vestib-ular artery (AVA). The AVA supplies the area primarily innervated by the superior vestibular nerve—the superior and horizontal semicircular canals and the utricle. These areas drain into the anterior vestibular vein. The common cochlear artery bifurcates and forms the cochlear artery and the posterior vestibular artery (PVA). The PVA innervates the posterior semicircular canal and the sac-cule. These areas drain into the posterior vestibular vein. Both veins join with the vein from the round window, elsewhere in the inner ear, and form the vestibulocochlear vein, eventually draining into the cochlear aqueduct and then the inferior petrosal sinus. Other small veins from the semicircular canals join to form the vein of the vestib-ular aqueduct, eventually draining into the lateral venous sinus (Fig. 19.­2). Interruption to the blood supply to the vestibular lab-yrinth can cause the usual manifestations of vestibular weakness, including vertigo, disequilibrium, blurred vision, and nausea. The blood supply can be interrupted by ischemia or infarction. When the AVA is involved, the patient does not have hearing loss, since the loss of blood supply is distal to the bifurcation of the labyrin-thine artery. When the labyrinthine artery is involved, hearing loss is more likely. During the acute phase of sudden, dramatic, and incapacitating symptoms, which may last hours to days, patients are treated with pal-liative care. After the acute phase is over, patients who have not compensated spontaneously may be referred for vestibular rehabilitation. These patients are often rehabilitated successfully.

text: The vestibular nerve projects to the vestibular nuclei in the rostral medulla (Fig. 19.­3). The projection has some spatial specificity in that different nerves project to differ-ent areas of the vestibular nuclei. From there, projections project to the dentate and fastigial nuclei of the cerebel-lum. Eventually, those signals make their way to the floc-culus, nodulus, and ventral uvula in the cerebellar vermis, the so-­called vestibulocerebellum. Projections out of the cerebellum return to the vestibular nuclei. From there, some signals descend the vestibulospinal tracts to cervi-cal and lumbosacral levels of the spinal cord. Those path-ways are involved in postural control and are especially important in the absence of vision. Patients with vestibu-lar weakness caused by peripheral or central lesions often have impaired balance.
