text: arobotics.com/en/) allow the user to compensate for lost skills when the potential for motor recovery is poor. The purpose of this chapter is to review a second class of robots that provide repetitive, task-­ specific training to help restore lost motor function. Unlike constraint-­ induced movement therapy (CIMT), robot-­assisted technologies are appropriate for persons with moderate to severe motor impairments. Rehabilitation robots to restore lost motor function can be categorized by how the device is controlled or acti-vated and how the user interface is designed. Robots for the upper limb can be broadly classified into three types: active systems with actuators that provide movement assistance along a defined trajectory; passive systems that support the limb during movement attempts; and interac-tive systems in which actuators or motors are combined with impedance and control strategies that allow the robot to react to the patient’s movement attempts. The way in which the robot assists with movement affects how the robot “feels” to the user during therapy. Low-­impedance interactive robots such as the InMotion ARM are highly “backdrivable” and compliant to a client’s attempts to move, allowing precise and objective measures of motor performance. Active robots that use pneumatic actuators or “muscles” to power the device (e.g., Hand Mentor) are not as responsive to the patient’s movement attempts because the mechanics of the robot create a more viscous response, similar to moving through honey. Pas-sive robotic systems offer varied forms of nonpowered assistance with elastic bands or springs that support the limb against gravity during movement attempts. An exam-ple is the Armeo®Spring device described later. The user/robot interface is another consideration when selecting rehabilitation robots for clinical use. End-­ effector robots, such as the InMotion ARM, are typically attached to the person’s hand or forearm at a single point of contact. These robots are easily adjusted to different limb lengths but do not control movement torques (rotary motions) at individual joints. In contrast, the structure of exoskeletal robots more closely resembles human anat-omy and allows separate control of the torques applied to each joint. Exoskeletal robots, such as the interactive Armeo®Power, require extra time for set up between patients because the components that support the arm and hand must be adjusted to assure proper fit and use of the device. The therapeutic games used to visually direct the patient’s movement attempts during robot-­assisted ther-apy also vary in complexity, ranging from simple stimuli to interactive games and virtual environments designed to simulate functional task performance. During this review, readers are encouraged to consider needs specific to their patient mix and clinical setting as well as potential goals for intervention. The robotic technology discussion that follows is arranged from higher to lower tech, with more complex, low-­ impedance robots preceding simpler wrist/hand orthoses.

text: The most widely studied rehabilitation robot is the MIT-­ MANUS and its clinical successors, the InMotion2 and InMotionARM robots (https://www.bioniklabs.com/). During therapy, the client is seated at the robot worksta-tion and the paretic hand is positioned in a customized arm support attached to the end-­effector (i.e., handle) of the robot arm. Therapy involves repetitive goal-­directed, planar reaching tasks that emphasize shoulder and elbow movements. As clients attempt to move the robot’s handle toward designated targets, the computer screen in front of them gives visual feedback of the target location and movement of the robot handle (Fig. 21.1). The low-­impedance controller of the InMotionARM is highly compliant during paretic arm movements, simi-lar to hand-­over-­hand assistance from a therapist during conventional therapy. Although the InMotionARM is capable of providing passive, active-­assistive, active, and resistive modes of therapy, the majority of studies have investigated the effects of active-­assistive robotic therapy on motor recovery after stroke. The adaptive control-ler allows the robot to adjust the amount of guidance or assist provided to the patient based on his or her indi-vidual needs. Proof of concept studies began in the mid-­1990s, with a focus on the effects of intensive robot-­assisted sensorimo-tor therapy for individuals in inpatient rehabilitation dur-ing the first weeks post stroke. 4 Since then, investigations have primarily included persons with chronic, moderate to severe motor impairments more than 6 months after stroke. In early studies, participants typically received 1 hour of robotic therapy three times per week for 6 weeks to align with conventional rehabilitation practice. These early studies indicated that task specificity and intensive practice (approximately 18,000 repetitive reaching move-ments over the course of therapy) play a critical role in upper limb robot-­assisted therapy, with the largest reduc-tions in motor impairment after robot training observed in the exercised shoulder and elbow versus the unexercised wrist and hand. 26,66 Since these initial trials, many studies with MIT-­MANUS and InMotionARM have examined the effects of intensive robot versus clinician-­delivered therapy, potential benefits of proximal or distal robotic training, and changes in upper limb motor control follow-ing robot therapy. Here we highlight the results of this work, with attention to how principles of motor learning dependent neuroplasticity 40 inform the and experience-­ interpretation of results.

text: The development of wrist and hand modules for the InMotion robotic system enabled the training of multiple degrees of freedom (DOFs) that was not possible during earlier studies. The multisite VA ROBOTICS study 45 compared the effects of therapy delivered by multiple InMotion robot modules (planar shoulder-­elbow, verti-cal shoulder, wrist, and hand) with (1) an intensive com-parison therapy (ICT) delivered by research clinicians and (2) usual care. The ICT was experimentally designed to match the intensity of robot practice and included assisted stretching, shoulder-­stabilization activities, and functional reaching tasks. This multisite randomized control trial involved 127 participants with moderate to severe chronic motor impairments: the mean baseline upper extremity (UE) Fugl-­Meyer score was 18.9 (±9.5) of a possible 66 points. Robot-­assisted therapy consisted of four 3-­week training blocks in which the different InMotion modules were used. Participants in the active treatment groups received 1-­hour therapy sessions, 3×/week over 12 weeks. Results showed small longitudinal improvements for both the robot and ICT groups compared with usual care. No significant differences between these active therapy groups were found on the Fugl-­Meyer Assessment (FMA) or Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), reinforcing the motor learning principle that intensity matters. 40 It is impor-tant to note that the intensity of ICT was much greater than conventional UE therapy and likely not possible to imple-ment in clinical practice. This multisite trial demonstrated that highly repetitive multi-­joint robotic exercise is feasible long after stroke and may be a cost-­effective alternative to intensive conventional therapy for the paretic arm and hand. 67 The higher cost of these intensive interventions was recuperated 36 weeks post randomization, as participants in the intensive treatment groups had lower health care utili-zation expenses than those who received usual care during this time. 67 While the VA ROBOTICS study supported use of intensive therapy for the paretic upper limb, its inclusion of persons with chronic motor impairments and longer treatment duration (36 visits over 12 weeks) limits its clin-ical application and generalization to individuals recently diagnosed with stroke. A number of smaller studies have tested effects of robot-­assisted therapy for individuals in the subacute phase of recovery less than 6 months post stroke. While these studies varied with regard to the dura-tion of treatment, comparison interventions, and outcome measures, they provide valuable information regard-ing potentially important treatment ingredients and the importance of measuring outcomes across ICF domains. text: 481 improvements on FMA after the completion of 30 treat-ment sessions, the potential of robot-­assisted therapy to accelerate the rate of motor recovery in subacute stroke is an important area for continued research and an impor-tant consideration for robot use in clinical settings. Kinematic measures derived from InMotionARM eval-uations showed improved active ROM (AROM), move-ment velocity, and smoothness when reaching toward robot targets as soon as 1 month post-­ therapy onset, while gains in motor accuracy (straightness of move-ments) improved only after 2 months of intervention. 51 These kinematic measures are surrogates for cortical plas-ticity related to spontaneous and rehabilitation-­related recovery during the first 6 months post stroke and pro-vide a glimpse into motor recovery processes that are not detected by clinical outcomes. Pila et al. questioned whether the planar point-­to-­point reaching tasks prac-ticed during InMotionARM training are an optimal exer-cise to promote recovery of the paretic arm and hand for everyday tasks, which involve the control of multiple DOFs to transport the arm and actively grasp, stabilize, or manipulate objects. The transfer of robot-­trained move-ments to UE use during daily activities requires further exploration before widespread clinical use of rehabilita-tion robots is expected. While progressive staging of smaller studies is essen-tial to the planning of large, multisite trials, 19 variations among studies in the timing, duration, intensity of prac-tice, and reported outcome measures limit our ability to identify the treatment ingredients essential to improved

text: motor function, activity performance, and participation after stroke. The planning and completion of large, mul-tisite confirmatory trials can take many years, and while the planned interventions may be “state of the art” at the beginning of the trial, innovative hybrid approaches often continue to be developed during this period. An example is the recently published study of robot-­ assisted training for the upper limb after stroke (RATULS), in which 770 participants with moderate to severe UE impairments were randomly assigned to receive either robot-­assisted training, enhanced upper limb ther-apy (EULT) delivered by clinicians, or usual care between 1 week and 5 years after their first stroke. 53 Robot-­assisted training with three InMotion robots (InMotionARM, InMotionWRIST, and InMotionHAND) was provided during 45-­minute sessions, 3×/week for 12 weeks, similar to VA ROBOTICS. 45 An evidence-­based EULT program of the same frequency and duration emphasized func-tional task practice to address participant-­centered goals. The primary outcome measure, the Action Research Arm Test (ARAT), was selected to assess upper limb function, specifically grasp, grip, pinch, and gross movement. Sec-ondary measures across ICF domains evaluated changes in body functions (FMA), activity performance (Barthel Index [BI] for activities of daily living [ADL]), and par-ticipation (Stroke Impact Scale [SIS]). While RATULS participants in all groups showed improved ARAT scores, findings did not support routine use of robot-­ assisted training, as there were no significant between-­group dif-ferences for any outcome measure at the end of interven-tion or at the 6-­month follow-­up assessment. Although the intensity of practice was held constant across inter-ventions, the “direct target” of therapy differed. The robot-­assisted therapy was directed toward a reduction in paretic UE motor impairment via repetitive cursor-­driven movements toward targets on a computer monitor, with little to no attention to the salience of trained tasks or transfer to daily UE use. The EULT targeted participant-­ centered goals to improve functional use of the paretic arm and hand via repetitive task practice (RTP). It is quite possible that the BI and hand items on the SIS were not sensitive to measuring changes in paretic arm and hand function following these interventions. While hind sight is 20/20, review of this large multisite trial highlights the importance of progressive staging of research studies, clear delineation of treatment ingredients and targets, and careful selection of outcome measures. Further develop-ment of treatments that utilize the distinct strengths of robot-­ assisted technology and embrace principles of motor learning and exercise-­ dependent neuroplasticity may optimize motor outcomes, activity engagement, and participation in meaningful daily activities after stroke.

text: The Haptic Master is a three-­DOF robot that provides gravity assistance for the paretic arm while the user sits at a workstation to complete therapeutic tasks. A free-­ moving elbow splint attached to an overhead frame sup-ports the arm, and a passive mechanism supports the hand and allows for supination, pronation, and wrist flexion and extension. Force and position sensors enable interaction with virtual tasks such as reaching to a supermarket shelf or pouring a drink. The Haptic Master has been used for task-­oriented training (TOT) in a three-­dimensional vir-tual environment, as in the GENTLE/s project, 18 and during grasp and manipulation of real objects. 63 Depend-ing on the user’s movement abilities, three therapy modes can be selected: passive, active-­assistive, or active. Haptic feedback from the robot provides the user with the feeling of increased resistance when movements stray from the programmed trajectory. The use of individualized TOT in natural environ-ments is gaining greater attention in the rehabilitation technology literature. A randomized trial (n = 22) that compared TOT with and without Haptic Master assist illustrated the importance of providing the “just right challenge” during therapy. 63 Participants with chronic motor impairments were randomly assigned to receive technology-­ supported task-­ oriented arm training with the Haptic Master robot 4×/week for 8 weeks. Treatment involved breaking down tasks into functional components, grading levels of difficulty, and encouraging motor learn-ing and endurance through the use of different objects and weights. While participants in both groups improved significantly after training, no between-­group differences were found on any of the outcome measures, including the ARAT and Motor Activity Log (MAL). Median scores on the UE FMA at baseline were 50 to 53 of a possible 66 points, indicating very mild motor impairments at study onset. The highly functional chronic participants in this study did not appear to benefit from the addition of Hap-tic Master assist. These results corroborate findings by Lo et al. who found no additional effects of robot-­assisted therapy over a nontechnology-­supported control inter-vention. 45 The authors proposed that individuals with lower functional abilities after stroke may benefit more from Haptic Master guidance to provide support and min-imize execution errors during TOT. A recent pilot study demonstrated that proximal weight support from the Haptic Master helped individuals with moderate to severe motor impairment and synergistic movements after stroke to reach more quickly and accurately toward targets. 68 Taken together, this research reinforces the importance of providing technology-­aided interventions that deliver appropriate levels of support and challenge based on the individual’s upper limb motor capacity.

text: games focused on proximal control of the shoulder and elbow while the paretic hand is attached to the robot handle, similar to the InMotionARM. The ReoGo pro-vides upper limb assistance and feedback while the user performs progressively challenging reaching movements toward spatial targets from a seated position at the work-station (Fig. 21.2). A small, single-­group study with 19 chronic stroke par-ticipants reported statistically significant gains on the UE FMA, Box and Block Test (BBT), and Frenchay Arm Test (FAT) following 20 1-­hour sessions with the ReoGo 5 days a week for 4 weeks, which were retained at a 1-­month follow-­up assessment. 8 Distal improvements in hand func-tion evidenced by the BBT in this chronic patient sample were not observed in a recent study of individuals only 4–8 weeks post stroke 60 The aim of Takahashi and colleagues’ subacute study was to examine the effects of conventional therapy plus self-­guided interventions with or without the use of the ReoGo robot. 60 While significant improvements in proximal scores on FMA were found for the ReoGo group, no between-­group differences were found for the WMFT or MAL—assessments that evaluate both proximal and distal motor function. The gains noted only in proximal scores for the FMA in this subacute study could be attributed to the specificity principle discussed by Kleim and Jones that predicts the greatest improve-ments in motor performance for practiced limb segments and tasks. 40 Although additional research is needed to clarify these outcome differences, initial work indicates that ReoGo training is well tolerated and may contribute to positive motor outcomes and improved quantification of upper limb performance post stroke. 23 A multisite trial is underway to further examine the effectiveness of self-­ training with the ReoGo-­J robotic device when combined with conventional occupational therapy (OT) or CIMT compared with a control intervention without a robotic device. 61

text: The Armeo®Power (https://hocoma.com) (Fig. 21.3) and its predecessor, the ARMinIII, are exoskeletal, low-­ impedance robots designed for repetitive, task-­ specific upper limb therapy after stroke. The interactive assistance it provides is based on “patient-­cooperative” control strat-egies that allow patient-­driven movements while the robot gives support only as needed, versus preprogrammed levels of assistance. This form of control is expected to increase the intensity of practice while computer gener-ated training tasks enhance patient motivation to engage in repetitive training. Haptic, visual, and auditory feed-back are provided during patient use. The increased DOFs afforded by the Armeo®Power and other exoskeletal devices such as the Armeo®Spring more closely mimic TOT provided by rehabilitation cli-nicians. Although passive nonmotorized devices support the arm against gravity and are intrinsically safer and less expensive, they cannot assist movements that the patient is unable to perform (e.g., elbow extension). The exoskel-etal Armeo®Power can apply and control torques at each joint individually when assistance is needed because of increased muscle tone or poor isolated movement. Randomized trials have compared robot-­ assisted ARMinIII training to conventional therapy for individuals with chronic moderate to severe upper limb impairments after stroke. In a large multisite randomized trial (n = 77), individuals more than 6 months post stroke were assigned to receive 24 45-­ minute sessions of either ARMinIII training or conventional therapy over an 8-­week period. 39 Three modes of ARMin training (mobilization, games,

text: and ADL training) were delivered during each session. When compared to those who received conventional therapy, participants in the robotic therapy group had modest but significantly greater gains on the FMA at the end of treatment. This study established the safety of task-­ specific training with the ARMinIII device and provided additional evidence that training with an upper limb exo-skeletal robot can improve body functions and activity performance, even in persons with severe, chronic upper limb impairments. In a crossover design trial, 10 participants were ran-domized to receive a 12-­hour block of either robot or conventional therapy over a 1-­ month period. Robot-­ assisted therapy involved simultaneous reach/grasp of virtual and real-­world objects while using a combination of the ARMInIII and HandSOME hand devices. 9 Assess-ments were administered at the end of this first treatment block, following a 1-­month washout period, and again after a second 12-­hour block of the alternative therapy. At the end of training, significant improvements were found across groups on the FMA and BBT. A significant between-­group difference was found for the ARAT: gains after robotic therapy were significantly larger than those after control therapy, independent of the order of the treatments. Despite the small sample size, clinically sig-nificant results were apparent across groups. This study suggests that robot-­assisted therapy provides a stimulus for recovery that differs from and complements conven-tional therapies. This combined treatment approach to address reach and grasp movements allows for greater integration of patient-­centered interventions while tak-ing advantage of the high intensity and reproducibility of practice afforded by robotic devices. To understand whether improvements in clinical outcome measures after robot-­ assisted therapy repre-sent improved cortical processing and plasticity, Cal-abro et al. used transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to measure cortical excitability and elicit motor evoked potentials (MEP) pre and post intervention in a pro-spective cohort study. 12 Thirty-­five individuals at least 2 months post stroke received 40 training sessions with the Armeo®Power robot. Calabro et al. found positive effects of robotic training, as indicated by a significant increase in MEP amplitude and improved interhemispheric inhibi-tion in the affected hemisphere. 12 These indicators of cor-tical plasticity were associated with clinical gains on the FMA and kinematic improvements in ROM of the paretic shoulder and elbow as measured by the Armeo®Power. Advances in rehabilitation technologies for assessment and intervention contribute to a greater understanding of the active treatment ingredients and mechanisms of action that contribute to the restitution of function after stroke.

text: The Armeo®Spring (https://hocoma.com), predecessor of the Armeo®Power described earlier, is a body-­powered exoskeletal orthosis to support upper limb training after stroke. The robot size and spring tension are adjusted to provide a safe method of gravity assist to support the paretic arm and hand during interactive therapy games. The Armeo®Spring enables naturalistic movement across two-­thirds or more of a normal workspace while the user attempts virtual reach and grasp tasks, such as moving items to a shelf or throwing a frisbee. DOFs can be con-trolled by the clinician to allow for whole-­arm training or isolated practice of forearm and wrist motions. Electronic sensors detect arm movement and hand grasp, allow the user to interact with the therapeutic games, and provide quantitative feedback about upper limb performance. (Fig. 21.4). Several studies have investigated effects of Armeo®Spring training for individuals in the subacute phase of stroke recovery. Chan et al. stratified 48 indi-viduals receiving inpatient rehabilitation less than 6 months post stroke into three groups based on their level of functioning on the Functional Test for the Hemiplegic Upper Extremity (FTHUE). 14 The Armeo®Spring pro-tocols were customized to provide one-­, two-­, or three-­ dimensional therapy activities based on this stratification (see Table 21.1). In addition to conventional rehabilita-tion services, all participants received 45 minutes of sup-ported upper limb training 5 days/week for 3 weeks. This protocol was unique because the intervention was specifi-cally planned to provide the “just right challenge” based on each individual’s baseline functioning. Within-­group analyses revealed that individuals with the highest level of functioning did not benefit from Armeo®Spring therapy on clinical outcomes, including the FMA and AROM scores, pre-­post intervention. This suggests that either the Armeo®Spring training was not sufficiently chal-lenging or that the assessments were not sensitive enough to detect improvements in this high functioning group. However, Armeo®Spring training did produce targeted gains in proximal control for individuals with the great-est impairment at admission (only initial voluntary move-ment of shoulder and elbow) and improved hand control

text: for those with moderate impairments and AROM in the shoulder and elbow at the start of therapy. 14 Safety of the Armeo®Spring for semiautonomous robot-­assisted therapy was demonstrated in a small fea-sibility pilot study for individuals presenting with severe upper limb paresis less than 3 months post stroke. 10 Access to the Armeo®Spring robot was offered to indi-viduals receiving conventional inpatient rehabilitation during evenings and weekends 6 days/week over 4 weeks. Enrolled participants were provided a treatment program from the research occupational therapist and encouraged to exercise on their own with the Armeo®Spring, given help only for device set-­up from a research assistant. Semi-­ structured interviews revealed that additional upper limb therapy with the Armeo®Spring was feasible and satisfy-ing to participants but limited in some cases by a lack of transportation from the therapy unit to treatment room and participant fatigue due to a rigorous daily therapy schedule. On average, participants attended 13 of the 24 training sessions, receiving an additional 33 ± 8 minutes of targeted paretic upper limb training per session that resulted in significant improvements on proximal items of the WMFT. Although the lack of a control group limits interpretation of results, further research of semiautono-mous robot-­assisted therapy to increase treatment dose may reveal a faster rate of motor recovery as reported by Sale and colleagues. 56 In a separate study conventional inpatient rehabilitation was combined with either Armeo®Spring or Kinect virtual reality training 45 minutes/day for 10 sessions. 1 Outcome measures across ICF domains, includ-ing cognitive assessments, depression and anxiety scales, and the Functional Independence Measure (FIM), evalu-ated group differences at the end of training. Although stroke participants in both groups significantly improved in upper limb isolated control and coordination as mea-sured by the FMA, some effects of training differed based on the type of intervention provided. Individuals who received Armeo®Spring therapy demonstrated higher functional recovery in shoulder and elbow ROM, muscle tone, hand dexterity, and grip strength, as well as statisti-cally higher visuospatial abilities, attention, and memory, and decreased anxiety level. Self-­care abilities on the FIM were significantly higher for the Kinect-­based training. Further studies to tease apart the active ingredients of these technology-­based interventions will better inform clinical decisions when choosing treatments to address a client’s specific needs. The efficacy of Armeo®Spring training for individuals with mild to moderate chronic impairments following stroke has also been explored. 17 Participants received 36 1-­hour therapy sessions, three times a week, focused on active reach and grasp in three-­dimensional space during virtual games. The Armeo®Spring exercise program, workspace, and angle of suspension were modi-fied regularly according to the person’s progress and level of ability. Significant improvements were found on ICF-­ related measures of body functions (FMA and Motricity Index [MI]) and activity performance (Motor Assessment Scale [MAS], WMFT, and Manual Function Test) with-out significant changes in muscle tone. Also, gains in motor function were clinically significant, as evidenced by an average 5-­point change on the FMA at the end of train-ing. 17 While performance improvements were sustained at the 4-­month follow-­up assessment, it is unclear whether the retention of scores was related to the Armeo®Spring training or to other therapies that participants engaged in after the experimental protocol had ended. Although larger, well-­controlled studies are warranted, this research suggests that persons with mild to moderate chronic upper limb impairments may benefit as much from intensive training via a passive suspension system as from higher cost, low-­impedance machines such as the InMotionARM or Armeo®Power.

text: The MyoPro® myoelectric orthosis, successor to the Myomo e100 (http://myomo.com) is a portable, wearable device that assists with elbow flexion and extension and gross hand function during daily activities (Fig. 21.5). It consists of a motorized elbow brace powered by recharge-able batteries and a control system that detects and ampli-fies surface electromyographic (EMG) signals generated by muscles of the paretic arm. Surface electrodes are placed over the bicep and triceps muscles to assist with elbow motions, and forearm flexor and extensor muscle groups to assist grasp and release. Forearm positioning is achieved by passively moving the forearm component of the orthosis to the desired degree of supination or prona-tion needed for task performance. Continuous monitoring of muscle activity by the surface EMG sensors allows the device to assist with the desired movement (e.g., elbow flexion) and return to the starting position when the EMG stimulus subsides as the person relaxes. The amount of force generated by the MyoPro® device is based on the amplitude of the EMG signal, resulting in movement assistance that is proportional to the patient’s effort. 50 Unlike robotic devices attached to a fixed work sta-tion, portable Myomo myoelectric orthoses can be used in everyday settings and allow for the training of basic functional tasks, such as pushing up from an armchair or stabilizing an object during bilateral activities. A small randomized controlled trial (RCT) for persons with chronic hemiparesis compared the efficacy of task-­specific practice with and without the Myomo e100, as mea-sured by the FMA. 48 Participants in both groups received 1-­hour therapy sessions, 3×/week for 8 weeks in which four functional tasks were practiced: lifting a laun-dry basket, sit to stand transfers, drinking from an adapted cup, and turning a light switch on/off. Small equivalent gains of ≈2 points on the FMA were found post training in both treatment groups. Subject perceptions of upper

Sub-jects positively viewed the Myomo as helpful during real-­ life ADL tasks, reinforcing its utility as a portable assistive device to aid paretic arm use after stroke. Peters et al. reported that individuals with chronic mod-erate upper limb paresis (n = 18) showed statistically and clinically significant gains in upper limb function during a single session in which clinical outcome measures were administered pre/post donning of the MyoPro Motion-­G orthosis. 50 Use of this myoelectric orthosis signifi-cantly increased scores on the FMA by an average of 8.7 points and resulted in significant reductions in the time to perform gross manual tasks such as grasping a cup or transporting blocks during the BBT. The need for stan-dardized training of MyoPro control for functional use was identified for future research. A separate case report 20 and focus group survey 24 indicated user acceptance and desire for wearable actuated orthoses to compensate for lost motor function and improve functional bilateral task performance after stroke.

text: The development of robots to assist with wrist and hand retraining has lagged behind that of shoulder and elbow devices, largely due to the complexity of control needed to assist with grasp and release motions. Although the num-ber of robots designed for hand rehabilitation after stroke has grown significantly in recent years, few are commer-cially available. 2 The subsequent sections will focus on two empirically tested devices that are available for clinical use: the Hand Mentor and the Amadeo robots.

text: The Hand Mentor (https://motusnova.com) is a com-mercially available repetitive motion device designed for home and clinical use (Fig. 21.6). It uses a pneumatic arti-ficial muscle to extend the wrist and fingers and provides EMG biofeedback of muscle activation via light-­emitting diodes displayed on a small screen. Its purpose is to inhibit flexor tone of the wrist and fingers, provide neuromuscu-lar reeducation, and increase ROM and strength of the paretic wrist and fingers. In two early single case studies, Hand Mentor training was combined with RTP to improve upper limb function in persons 7-­ and 22-­months post stroke. 29,55 Interven-tion occurred 4 hours/day, either 3 or 5 days a week, over a 3-­week period. During 2 hours of each session, Hand Mentor training included use of EMG biofeedback to reduce abnormal muscle tone in the wrist and fingers and two active control modes to elicit wrist flexion and exten-sion. If the user could not reach the target position dur-ing active training, the pneumatic muscle inflated to assist wrist movements. In addition, study participants spent up to 2 additional hours doing functionally-­oriented RTP with the paretic arm. The level of difficulty was increased gradually, and participants selected activities for training. Gains reported at the end of intervention included faster speed of performance on some WMFT items; increased AROM in the shoulder, wrist, and thumb; better isolation of upper limb motions; and a slight increase in maximum grip force. 29,55

text: One RCT further examined the effects of Hand Men-tor training and RTP on perceived quality of life, as mea-sured by the SIS. 43 Seventeen participants, 3 to 9 months post-­ stroke onset, were assigned to receive either 60 hours of therapist-­supervised RTP or 30 hours of RTP combined with 30 hours of Hand Mentor robot-­assisted therapy. While significant SIS gains were found for both groups, participants who received combined RTP and Hand Mentor therapy reported a higher level of stroke recovery post-training. These findings suggest that the integration of robot-­assisted therapy with conventional RTP may enhance motor recovery while decreasing therapist labor, potentially reducing rehabilitation costs. Well-­controlled empirical studies are needed to further delineate the potential contribution of this technology to the recovery of upper limb function after stroke.

text: The Amadeo (https://tyromotion.com/en/) is a commer-cially available end-­effector device that provides robot-­ assisted therapy for paretic finger flexors and extensors after stroke. The user’s hand is attached to the robotically controlled slides by small magnetic discs that are taped to the distal phalanx of the thumb and each finger. This robotic system contains passive, active-­assistive, resistive, and isometric modes. Visual feedback is given during computerized games that direct practice of either whole hand or individual finger flexion/extension movements (Fig. 21.7). One potential benefit of the Amadeo is the low impedance, actuated control of finger motions that allows for consistent measurement of participant-­ generated forces and ROM during training. Studies with the Amadeo robot have provided evidence of its effectiveness during subacute and chronic phases of stroke recovery. One RCT for participants enrolled 30 ± 7 days after stroke onset (n = 20) compared effects of 40-­minute sessions of either Amadeo robot-­assisted train-ing or personalized OT in addition to 3 hours of inpatient rehabilitation daily. 57 Amadeo training consisted of pas-sive, active-­assistive, and active exercises during computer-­ generated games to elicit collective and individual finger movements. OT interventions were specific to the indi-vidual’s needs and focused exclusively on the recovery of hand function. The duration of training was 4 to 5 days per week for 4 or 5 weeks. Significant improvements were found in both groups on the FMA, MI, Medical Research Council strength scale, and BBT immediately post inter-vention and at the 3-­month follow-­up assessment. The sustained benefits of these focused, repetitive interven-tions are highly relevant to clinical practice, providing further support for the delivery of intensive therapy to restore motor function during the early phase of stroke recovery. Of note, the target of this intervention, as indi-cated by the reported outcome measures, was a reduction of motor impairment rather than improved functional use of the paretic hand during daily activities.

text: The effects of passive and active-­ assistive Amadeo training were tested in participants with mild impairment within the first year post stroke. 36 Following 20 sessions of therapy (5×/week/4 weeks), significant dose-­ related improvements were reported for wrist and hand items on the FMA and Jebsen Hand Function Test. Individu-als who received active-­assistive Amadeo training during the entire 4-­week trial experienced greater improvements at the 8-­week follow-­up assessment than participants who received early passive Amadeo therapy (first 2 weeks) fol-lowed by active-­assistive training (last 2 weeks). This small study illustrates how the treatment ingredients, namely the dose and type of robot training, can impact the desired outcome or target of therapy. Research on the effects of robot-­assisted therapy for the paretic hand is still in its infancy, with a need for progressively staged trials to identify which intervention approaches are most beneficial to an individual’s recov-ery after stroke. It is difficult to compare the effects of Amadeo training across studies because of variability in the number of treatment sessions, types of exercise pro-vided, and selection of clinical outcome measures. Recent studies have trialed the addition of surface EMG signals to detect the participant’s intention to move and respond with needed robotic assistance, 22 and have compared changes in cortical activation resulting from intensive Amadeo training or OT. 11 This research is instrumental for exploring how treatment ingredients impact perfor-mance at multiple levels and the mechanisms of action that contribute to improved functional use of the paretic arm and hand.

Lower cost, nonrobotic technologies to exercise the paretic hand also are being marketed for clinical and home use. Two of these novel devices, the MusicGlove 30 and RAPAEL SmartGlove system 59 have earned initial empir-ical support. These instrumented gloves engage users in virtual, computer-­driven tasks that provide opportunities for individualized and engaging repetitive task-­ specific training of gross grasp and release and isolated finger motions/pinch. Collaborations between rehabilitation cli-nicians, engineers, and end-­users are critical to the devel-opment of these new technologies and provide exciting opportunities for interprofessional partnerships in the coming years.

text: Research on the use of bilateral arm training, in which both upper limbs perform the same movements simultaneously and independently, has shown bimanual practice to have a facilitating effect on paretic arm function after stroke, with movement of the nonaffected upper limb stimulating ipsi-lateral corticospinal projections to the paretic arm. While the neural correlates of bilateral arm training are not well understood, reported changes in cortical activation mea-sured by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), TMS, and EEG include significantly higher cortical acti-vation bilaterally 67 and a shift toward greater ipsilesional EEG activity in sensorimotor cortex after training. 31 Two rehabilitation devices have been empirically tested: the Bi-­ Manu-­Track and Bilateral Arm Training with Rhythmic Auditory Cuing (BATRAC).

reference.formatted: Gillen, Stroke Rehabilitation: A Function-Based Approach, Fifth Edition (2021), Chapter 21: Rehabilitation Technologies to Promote Upper Limb Recovery After Stroke, Bi-Manu-Track, p. 488

text: The Bi-­Manu-­Track (https://reha-­stim.com/) is a computer-­assisted arm trainer that allows bimanual prac-tice of supination and pronation and wrist flexion and extension (Fig. 21.8). Exercises can be performed pas-sively or actively, and resistance can be added based on the patient’s ability level and needs. Wu et al. compared the effects of Bi-­Manu-­Track bilateral robotic arm ther-apy (RBAT) to therapist-­generated bilateral arm training (TBAT) and a conventional occupational therapy control. Individuals with chronic paresis (n = 42) received 90-­ to 105-­minute therapy sessions, 5 days a week for 4 weeks. Both experimental treatment groups participated in 15 to 20 minutes of unilateral and bilateral functional training and 5 minutes of tone normalization at the end of each therapy session. The higher intensity RBAT and TBAT groups significantly outperformed the conventional ther-apy group on a range of outcome measures, but in differ-ent ways. TBAT led to greater kinematic improvements in temporal efficiency, movement smoothness, trunk con-trol, and distal motor function, while those in the RBAT group had increased shoulder flexion and quality of life as reported by the SIS. 69 In order to better understand the contributions of RBAT versus activity-­ based treatments for the paretic upper limb function after stroke, Hsieh et al. compared effects of a sequential protocol of Bi-­Manu-­Track and modified constraint-­ induced training (mCIT) to Bi-­ Manu-­Track training alone. 34 The frequency and duration of sessions was consistent with the study by Wu et al. 69 However, individuals randomized to the sequential pro-tocol received 10 sessions of Bi-­Manu-­Track training fol-lowed by 10 sessions of mCIT. Persons in this group wore a mitt on the unaffected hand for 6 hours/day and strate-gies to facilitate transfer of function and daily use of the paretic upper limb (e.g., behavioral contract, home diary, problem solving) were applied. Outcome measures across ICF domains included the WMFT, kinematic measures of reaching performance, and the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living (NEADL) measure. Participants who received sequential training with Bi-­Manu-­Track and mCIT achieved significantly greater improvements on the functional ability scale of the WMFT and NEADL total score as compared to the Bi-­Manu-­Track only group.

text: Kinematic outcomes revealed different patterns of change in motor control strategies for each group, with better res-toration of motor control and less compensatory move-ments following sequential training, and greater force generation when initiating movements in the Bi-­Manu-­ Track only group (see Table 21.1). 34 The use of shaping, graded task difficulty, and modeling of real-­life activities during task-­oriented mCIT training is likely to have con-tributed to the activity-­based improvements, as may be predicted by the specificity principle of motor learning and exercise-­dependent neuroplasticity. 40 To delineate effects of different forms of robot-­assisted therapy, the same Bi-­Manu-­Track training protocol was compared to unilateral robot-­ assisted therapy via the InMotion 3.0 robot (now known as the InMotionWRIST) and an OT control intervention that consisted of muscle tone normalization, motor training, strengthening, and functional activity practice. 35 At the end of each session, participants in the two robot-­ assisted therapy groups practiced 20 minutes of functionally-­based activities to facilitate the transfer of robot-­trained motions to daily tasks such as turning a doorknob or dressing. Findings revealed that participants who received unilateral training with the InMotion 3.0 robot outperformed the other two groups, with a large and statistically significant 8-­point gain on FMA post intervention. Group differences on secondary outcomes, including MAL reports of perceived amount and quality of paretic upper limb use during daily activities, were not significant. The authors proposed that benefits of this intervention were associated with the use of unilateral robot-­assisted training to “prime” the motor system for the consolidation and transfer of robot-­trained motions to functional use of the paretic arm and hand (see Table 21.1). These results mirrored those reported earlier by Yang et and colleagues, who also found large and sig-nificant differences in group outcome based on the type of Bi-­Manu-­Track training. 70 Compared with bilateral arm training and control interventions, Yang et al. found that unilateral Bi-­Manu-­Track training led to significantly greater improvements on the FMA (overall and proximal items) and distal strength scores. These outcomes were attributed to the greater proportion of active training for the paretic arm in the unilateral group. 70

text: The BATRAC trainer is another device for repetitive bilateral upper limb therapy. BATRAC therapy involves moving two unyoked handles forward and backward in a reaching motion, both symmetrically and asymmetrically in response to auditory cues set at individually deter-mined rates. In an RCT, Whitall et al. compared the effects of BATRAC training with dose-­matched thera-peutic exercises (DMTE). 67 A total of 111 persons with chronic upper limb paresis received therapy 3×/week for 6 weeks. BATRAC training outcomes were not superior to DMTE: both groups had small but significant improve-ments on the FMA and WMFT (time) that were retained at the 4-­month follow-­up evaluation. Functional MRIs administered to a subgroup of participants showed that BATRAC training led to significantly greater increases in cortical activation bilaterally, with changes in the contral-esional superior frontal gyrus correlated with improved time on the WMFT. Although no significant group dif-ferences were found on clinical measures, greater adap-tation of brain activation was associated with BATRAC robot-­assisted training. Continued studies that examine changes in function across ICF domains are essential to our understanding of how variations in treatment ingredi-ents, including unilateral versus bilateral arm training and motor priming, contribute to the mechanisms of action and functional recovery post stroke. Research studies that include bilateral task analysis and assessment of interlimb coordination will continue to play an important role in clarifying ways in which motor function of the paretic arm changes over the course of intervention.

text: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) is a method to facilitate limb movement after neurological injury, such as stroke or acquired brain injury, by apply-ing electrical current to paretic muscles. NMES may be applied under passive conditions to prevent muscle atro-phy and at low levels to provide sensory input through afferent pathways. 54 Functional electrical stimulation (FES) is a subcategory of NMES and is defined as elec-trical stimulation to facilitate muscle contraction during active, voluntary movement attempts. FES is a techno-logical advancement designed to facilitate motor recovery during functional activities, like holding a glass to drink. Although the effects of FES during post-­stroke rehabili-tation have been widely researched, methodological limi-tations including heterogeneity of study participants and lack of consistent measures across studies limit the inter-pretation and application of research findings to clinical practice. A brief review of the NESS H200 and systematic review findings 25 follow.

text: The Handmaster, marketed as the NESS H200 Hand Rehabilitation System (Bioness, Valencia, CA) is a non-invasive, advanced neuroprosthesis used for the treatment of upper limb paresis following stroke, traumatic brain injury, or C5–­C6 spinal cord injury. It contains a custom-­ fit orthosis that uses FES to provide neuromuscular reedu-cation, sequentially activate muscle groups in the forearm, and elicit active grasp and release in the paretic hand. Research studies over the past 15 years have shown potential benefit of FES for persons with subacute and chronic upper limb paresis after stroke. For example, an

text: RCT that examined dose effects in persons with moderate, chronic impairments (n = 32) revealed that 120 minutes/day of RTP augmented by the NESS H200 5 days/week for 8 weeks elicited large and consistent improvements on the FMA, Arm Motor Ability Test (function and quality scales), and ARAT scores. In this study, the dose effect was significant, as individuals who practiced only 30 or 60 minutes/day did not show significant or consistent gains during the treatment protocol. 49 Although several system-atic reviews have been completed, 13 the effects of FES on motor function and ADL performance over the course of stroke recovery are not clear. The aims of a recent sys-tematic review and meta-­analysis were to clarify the effec-tiveness of FES compared to standard therapy on ADL performance and motor outcomes, based on the time post stroke that FES was initiated. 25 Time mattered for several of the primary and secondary outcome measures reported. When FES was initiated an average of 2 months after stroke, research participants demonstrated significant improvements on ADL and FMA that were not evident in the control groups or in those receiving FES one or more years post stroke. Variations across reviewed studies included participants’ baseline function and FES stimula-tion parameters, such as current, frequency, and duration of stimulation. None of the included studies administered the same stimulation protocol, which is likely related to differences in residual motor abilities, degree of spastic-ity, and treatment duration across study samples. While Eraifej et al. were the first to provide evidence that the timing of FES treatment matters, they did not find suf-ficient empirical support for routine use of FES in clinical practice due to the lack of high-­quality research trials. 25 Despite the need for large, prospective RCTs to delineate the optimal therapeutic window and FES parameters, FES with the NESS H200 is often recommended by clinicians and is well tolerated by persons with mild to moderate upper limb dysfunction. As with all present rehabilita-tion technologies, the high cost of the NESS H200 may present an additional barrier to its widespread use after stroke. Novel approaches to integrate FES with forms of robot-­assisted therapy are in their infancy and may further enhance multijoint coordination and functional upper limb performance following stroke (see Table 21.1). 52,54

text: The SaeboFlex is a high-­tech, dynamic orthosis developed to address the difficulty that many stroke survivors have in opening their paretic hand after stroke. This orthosis con-sists of a forearm cuff attached to a dorsal hand platform that anchors two spring attachments. Individual finger sleeves are placed over the distal phalanges and attached to the spring attachments via a high-­tensile line to assist with finger and thumb extension (Fig. 21.9). Several small trials have tested the feasibility of SaeboFlex training and found positive effects for persons with moderate to severe upper limb impairments after stroke. 28,38,44 Training pro-tocols based on systems theory and motor learning prin-ciples have emphasized RTP, active problem solving, and use of the paretic hand to promote motor recovery of the upper limb. SaeboFlex therapy has included strengthen-ing exercises, ROM, and electrical stimulation to wrist and finger extensors. Lannin et al. found that SaeboFlex train-ing in an inpatient rehabilitation setting was feasible with regard to treatment compliance, safety, and opportunity to engage in massed upper limb practice. 44 Participants randomized to the experimental group were instructed to use the SaeboFlex orthosis at least 45 minutes/day in addi-tion to their usual post-­stroke interprofessional program. Assessments were administered at the beginning and end of the 8-­week training program. Participants in both the experimental and control groups demonstrated small but positive trends in hand function as indicated by pre/post changes on upper limb items of the MAS and SIS (see Table 21.1). 44 Patients and therapists reported benefits of SaeboFlex training to include quick results and translation to functional use of the paretic hand that increased moti-vation and hope for recovery. Potential barriers included challenges with donning the device and fit, particularly for persons with increased muscle tone. 5 A small pilot study to explore the effects of SaeboFlex and FES exer-cises for persons with chronic stroke impairments showed modest gains in grip strength, AROM, and grasp release. While larger, well-­ controlled confirmatory studies are

text: While it is apparent that the focus of many robot-­assisted therapy protocols has shifted toward TOT and ICF activity-­level outcomes, little progress has been reported in recent years on the development of devices specifi-cally designed for RTP. Two of these, the AutoCITE and ADAPT work stations, provide TOT through the manipulation of real and functional objects. The AutoC-ITE was developed to automate CIMT for individuals with mild to moderate motor impairments after stroke. 47 The training tasks derived from those used in therapist-­ mediated CIMT include reaching, tracing, pegboard use, supination/pronation, threading, and finger tapping (Fig. 21.10). Instructions are given via a computer monitor, and device sensors monitor performance and track the num-ber of successful repetitions and time for task completion. Taub and colleagues reported semiautonomous AutoC-ITE training with therapist supervision for 25%, 50%, or 100% of the treatment time was safe and as effective as one-­on-­one therapist-­delivered CIMT. 62 Participants with chronic impairments had significant gains in motor ability and real-­world use of the paretic arm and hand, as indicated by the WMFT and MAL. The Adaptive and Automatic Presentation of Tasks (ADAPT) system provides active and individualized training via a number of real-­world functional tasks that involve different grasp patterns (power, overhand, pinch) and reach. 15,58 Unlike other systems in which the robot modifies the assistance provided based on the user’s ability, ADAPT allows highly intensive assistance-­free training that is prescribed by the rehabilitation therapist. Task difficulty and complexity are increased as learn-ing progresses so that the individual actively engages in achievable but challenging tasks without physical assis-tance. Preliminary testing of the ADAPT system was well tolerated, with time for task completion signifi-cantly improved after a 1-­hour session. 15 The AutoCITE and ADAPT systems provide an alternative approach to RTP for persons with mild to moderate paresis after stroke, allowing therapists to focus on the translation of robot-­trained skills to daily activities in the home and community.

text: The rehabilitation technologies described in this chap-ter offer a wide range of treatment options for persons with upper limb paresis after stroke. Choosing the “right” technology for a particular patient during clinical practice involves an appreciation for key features of the device, the patient’s level of function, and therapeutic goals.

text: Key considerations when choosing technologies for patient treatment after stroke include the type of assistance and DOFs afforded by the device, whether it is portable or sta-tionary (e.g., requires treatment space for a workstation), and the amount of training needed to safely and effec-tively administer movement therapy. The device should be easily programmed to meet the patient’s needs as motor recovery occurs and allow for semiautonomous training, which can enhance therapist productivity while the patient engages in intensive movement therapy. Many robotic devices provide quantitative measures of motor functions such as movement speed, accuracy, and forces generated. These objective measures can complement activity and participation-­focused clinical evaluations and can be used when documenting treatment plans and progress toward goals. Ease and time of treatment setup are other important considerations when selecting these tools for the clinic. At present, rehabilitation technologies are most appro-priately used as an adjunct to therapist-­rendered interven-tion. They are best at providing intensive practice while the therapist emphasizes use of the paretic arm during valued everyday tasks. Because individual devices do not assist with all DOFs needed for TOT, some researchers have proposed the benefits of multiple robotic workstations or

text: robotic “gyms”. 33,42 The therapist’s expertise in upper limb function and task analysis is essential when selecting reha-bilitation technologies and establishing treatment plans that effectively combine technology-­driven and therapist-­ rendered interventions. A novel intervention that combines robot-­assisted therapy with the training of cognitive strat-egies to facilitate transfer of robot-­trained motor skills to functional task performance is in pilot testing. 27 Certainly, the organization’s rehabilitation agenda, patient caseload, and cost strongly influence decisions to purchase rehabilitation technologies for clinical use. Cli-nicians may find the Rehabilitation Technology Evalua-tion (see Appendix A) useful for appraising device features and clinical applicability and identifying financial and marketing considerations when comparing rehabilitation technologies for their institution. Barriers to therapist and physician acceptance deserve attention; specific concerns may include treatment efficacy, equipment expense, and lack of time to evaluate technology options for stroke rehabilitation. In terms of efficacy, research studies have indicated that rehabilitation technologies can offer ben-efits not easily achieved by additional conventional ther-apy. For example, patients who had robot-­assisted therapy early after stroke showed an accelerated rate of motor recovery when compared to a control group that received conventional treatment. 56 While confirmatory studies are needed to replicate this finding, accelerated motor recov-ery during inpatient rehabilitation could contribute to improved functional use of the upper limb and positively impact self-­care performance and patient satisfaction at hospital discharge.

text: Many factors influence a patient’s ability to benefit from rehabilitation of the paretic arm after stroke. Critical factors include the level of neurologic damage and resulting motor impairment and the individual’s ability to engage success-fully in therapy aimed to improve motor function. Reha-bilitation technologies can be easily programmed to ensure a certain level of success for patients with a wide range of motor abilities. This feature can enhance patient motivation and independent carryover of exercise programs. Although researchers are working to identify essential active ingredi-ents for the learning and acquisition of motor functions after stroke, the best rehabilitation and technology choice for a given ability level is not well established. It is not safe to assume that one treatment approach or one form of rehabili-tation technology is optimal for all patients with hemiparesis. Clinical practice illustrates the need to use differ-ent techniques and treatment strategies for patients with mild versus moderate to severe levels of motor impair-ment (see Chapter 20). Unfortunately, therapist-­rendered interventions are difficult to quantify or reproduce across treatment sessions. Rehabilitation robots can objectively measure the amount and type of assistance provided dur-ing therapy and track changes in motor functions that occur during the course of treatment. Clinicians can use these measures to judge the effectiveness of treatment and learn more about how changes in motor functions may translate to activity-­level performance. Although the availability of rehabilitation technologies to deliver TOT across multiple DOFs has increased, it is not known whether this approach is as effective for persons with mild versus moderate to severe motor impairments after stroke. Krebs and colleagues proposed that modular robotic systems are particularly well suited for addressing this question. 42 Modular systems can deliver training to individual limb segments or can combine robot components to allow practice of tasks that involve greater DOFs. How-ever, current modular systems are limited in their ability to provide true TOT because they do not allow the practice of contextually rich virtual or actual tasks. While these modu-lar tools may be the key to identifying what form of move-ment therapy is best for which patient, clinicians should use a combination of empirical evidence, clinical experience, and practice theory when deciding which technology fea-tures are best suited for their rehabilitation patients. When selecting rehabilitation technologies, the thera-pist also should assure that the feedback provided by the device is clear, easily interpreted by the patient and cli-nician, and pertinent to the patient’s goals for improved motor function. The therapeutic device should offer a variety of metrics relevant to functional task performance. text: the efficacy of movement attempts. 16 Conversely, patients with higher levels of motor functioning could expect to benefit more from feedback concerning movement accu-racy or force control. 16 A patient’s therapeutic goals may be better addressed when the clinician has a clear under-standing of the types of feedback and forms of interven-tions that best promote functional motor recovery. As research unfolds, specific treatment protocols to more efficiently and effectively address patient needs across levels of function will help to guide the integration of technology-­ driven and therapist-­ rendered rehabilitation. Thoughtful treatment planning for technology-­ driven rehabilitation is not different from that of conventional therapies. It just requires an understanding of the therapy options made avail-able by these technologies and the rationale for their use.

text: The focus of conventional therapies has shifted from ana-lytical training methods directed at impairments in motor function to an emphasis on TOT for the upper limb. The development of rehabilitation technologies is following a similar trend. Potential benefits of these devices include controllable treatment intensity, high repetition, task-­ specific practice, and sensory-­motor feedback to enhance knowledge of performance and results. The research presented in this chapter generally supports the use of rehabilitation technologies to improve upper limb motor functions after stroke. Although systematic reviews of robot-­assisted therapies have substantiated task-­specific training effects at the ICF impairment level, these have not generalized well to arm and hand use during ADL. 7,65 As technology-­ aided distal training and task-­ oriented inter-ventions are further developed and therapists become more experienced with integrating technology-­driven and therapist-­ rendered interventions, the effects on activity-­ and participation-­level functions are expected to improve. Ultimately, rehabilitation technologies are anticipated to provide cost-­effective treatment options and may inform clinicians about the “active ingredients” that are key to effective and efficient rehabilitation for persons after stroke.

text: After completing this chapter, the reader will be able to accom-plish the following: 1. Describe the proposed three theories of types of stroke hand edema and relate them to appropriate criteria for clini-cal treatment technique selection. 2. Provide neurologic and anatomic rationales for treatment selection. 3. Be familiar with current research outcomes of treatment techniques for stroke hand edema reduction, and be able to implement and expand data for clinical application prob-lem solving. 4. Integrate realistic edema reduction expectations into treat-ment planning from material read in the case studies.

text: Research indicates that post­ stroke hand edema can range from 16% 21 to 82.8% 50 depending on the defini-tion of edema, length of time since stroke occurred, and study design and methodology. Research also reports a broad range of time during which edema may develop, often from 2 weeks to 2 months poststroke. 43 There are numerous theories regarding the development of edema. Boomkamp-­Koppen and colleagues found that the loss of muscle activity, hyposensibility, and hypertonia link to edema, with hypertonia being the most significant predic-tor of hand edema. 7 There is no consensus on the etiology of poststroke hand edema 38 or on the most effective management tech-nique. 7,23 Therefore, there are few guidelines for occupa-tional therapists to employ with their clients. It is widely acknowledged that edema, particularly in the subacute and chronic stages, affects a client’s range of movement, sensa-tion, dexterity, and function. There are also correlations

text: between edema and joint fibrosis, and, in stroke, there is increasing evidence on the relationship between edema and chronic regional pain syndrome (CRPS). 30 Occupa-tional therapists need to maximize their input into the multidisciplinary team to prevent CRPS and to minimize these barriers to rehabilitation. 43 It is also imperative to consider the impact of stroke on movement, cognition, perception, communication, and psychological aspects of individuals. These areas form the basis for most rehabili-tation poststroke, with edema and sensation often being lower priorities. However, given the limitations imposed by stroke on the aforementioned areas, one must con-sider how these impairments may interplay with edema management and functional outcomes, such as neglect, strength, and learned nonuse (Fig. 22.1). This chapter will focus on exploring available research regarding the etiology and treatment of post­stroke hand edema and will present it in a format to enable the thera-pist to apply research data to clinical problem solving.

text: The edema that therapists treat is defined as an excess accumulation of fluid in the interstitium. It occurs on the capillary level (microcirculation level) when there is an imbalance of pressure between the arterioles, venules, and interstitium or an obstruction of the lymphatic sys-tem. 17,51 This is also known as an imbalance in Starling equilibrium. It is important to note the vascular system refers not only to the venous and arterial capillaries but also to the lymphatic capillaries. All these structures influ-ence post­stroke arm edema. A review of the literature has resulted in two major the-ories of post­stroke hand edema: sympathetic vasomotor dysfunction due to the stroke and venous congestion. The concept of vasomotor dysfunction as part of the stroke autonomic disturbance theory was proposed as early as 1930. 56 This theory has been expanded on in light of more recent research 34; however, the role of the sympa-thetic vasomotor dysfunction deletion of post­stroke hand edema formation remains unclear. 38 The second theory proposes that post­stroke hand edema results from venous congestion due to lack of, or decreased, limb motor func-tion and dependency positioning. 38 Aspects of both of these theories will be presented in the chapter when rela-tive to a specific treatment technique.

text: The venous congestion and limb dependency theory is most relevant to the treatment techniques this chapter will present. Thus, it is important to take an anatomic look at the vascular system, which consists of both arterial and venous structures and the lymphatics. Both vascular struc-tures, the venule and lymphatic capillaries, remove excess fluid from the interstitium and can be simultaneously acti-vated in specific instances. Yet depending on the type of edema, in certain instances, each system must activate in its own unique way in order to reduce edema. Both the venous and lymphatic systems are neurologically controlled by the autonomic nervous system. 17,35 However, both systems rely on the muscle motor pump to remove tissue fluid from the interstitium. 17,35 Thus, with total or partial lack of motor function to an arm poststroke, swelling occurs. Venous and lymphatic absorption of tissue fluid occurs on the microcirculation level. In the interstitium (inter-stitial spaces), the arterial and venule histologically join in an arc. The initial lymphatic (also called a lymphatic capillary or lymphatic net) is independent from the venule arterial arc; it is a “netlike” structure in the interstitium and is much larger than the venule. 17,28 On this micro-circulation level, plasma proteins, fluid, electrolytes, nutrients, and a few other elements are excreted from the arteriole because it has a pressure of 35 mm Hg. 6 These are the substances needed for surrounding cell metabo-lism. Thus, 90% of what remain from the metabolism are small molecules that enter the venule via the processes of osmosis and diffusion. 27,28 The remaining 10% of the molecules, such as plasma proteins, are too large to be absorbed by the venule and must be absorbed by the lym-phatic capillaries. The artery system via arteriole filtration and diffusion excretes tissue fluid into the interstitium. 28 From the interstitium, there are two structures—venules and lymphatic capillaries—that join with larger veins and

text: lymphatic structures to bring fluid back to the heart (Fig. 22.2). 17 The absorption process by the venule and lymphatic capillaries differ from each other. The wall of a venule is thin and absorbs small molecules via osmosis and dif-fusion. 17 Thus, elevation, light retrograde massage, muscle contraction, and compression will facilitate this absorption. Lymphatic molecule absorption in the interstitium begins in the one-­cell initial lymphatic capillary that, most superficially, is part of a netlike structure located in the dermis layer of tissue. This initial lymphatic capillary is pencil shaped (tube closed on one end) and lined with one layer of overlapping endothelial cells (Fig. 22.3). 28 Ana-tomically, fluid cannot be physically “pushed” into the lymphatic capillaries, nor does it move from the intersti-tium by osmosis into the lymphatic capillary. Tissue fluid and large molecules can only be absorbed by the lymphatic capillary when changes occur in interstitial fluid pres-sure or by movement of the elastic anchor filaments that extend from an endothelial cell to connective tissue. 28,35 Then, the junctions of these overlapping endothelial cells open like a trap door admitting large molecules from the interstitium into the pencil-­shaped lymphatic capillary. 28,35 These pressure changes occur with move-ment of skin, light compression, muscle contraction, and respiration. 14,28 The elastic anchor filaments extending from connective tissue to endothelial junctions open the junction flaps when pressure is put on their elastic fila-ments, such as from fluid congestion in the interstitium. 17 Lymphatic absorption is stimulated by respiration. The deepest and largest lymphatic structure is the thoracic duct. It lies anterior to, and parallels, the spinal column running from L2 to T4. 57 Changes in thoracic pressure cause a proximal negative pressure vacuum and draws fluid proximally from the periphery. This is also called the pulmonary pump. 17 The thoracic duct operates accord-ing to hydrodynamic laws. 35 Therefore, inhalation and exhalation from diaphragmatic breathing cause changes in the thoracic duct pressure, drawing the lymph within the duct toward the subclavian veins. These pressure changes in the thoracic duct then create a vacuum (suction), pull-ing lymph from peripheral structures centrally. 14,35,36 The result is that fluid from the periphery moves out of the area, and edema is reduced distally in a domino effect. Once the lymph enters the subclavian veins, it then becomes part of the venous system and continues on to the lungs, heart, and other parts of the body. The differences and similarities of the venous and lym-phatic system of fluid absorption from the interstitium should be considered when choosing the appropriate edema reduction technique for poststroke arm and hand edema.

text: Dependency Edema Theory Dependency edema is due to a combination of the involved flaccid or hemiparetic upper extremity hanging in a dependent position, plus potentially the impairment of sympathetic controlled muscle function. 38,56 Thus, tis-sue fluid pools distally. Often consistent elevation, daily light retrograde massage, and a light compression glove and/or elastic stockinette tube on the arm will reduce this edema. However, even after diligently following these methods, edema can persist. How much does this persis-tent edema relate to prolonged trunk immobility, lack of scapular movement, and lack of thoracic pressure changes? This initial edema consists of small molecules that are readily absorbed by the venous system. However, the venous system has a maximum volume capacity. When this capacity is reached, the lymphatic system will carry off the excess. Often, the lymphatic system is referred to as the overflow system. Dependent venous edema has a soft “spongy feel” when pitted, rebounds quickly, and often reduces easily with elevation. This type of edema is often seen when post­stroke edema first becomes evident.

text: When the lymphatic system acts as a safety valve or over-flow system for the venous system, it carries out of the interstitium both the small molecule products that the venous system usually absorbs and the large molecules only removed by the lymphatic system. The lymphatic system also has a maximum load capacity. When the sys-tem reaches this capacity, there will be lymphatic conges-tion. Clinically, lymphatic congestion presents as viscous and has a very slow rebound time from being pitted of 20 to 30 seconds or more. At this point, the stroke edema is a combined venous and lymphatic edema that minimally reduces with elevation. Elevation alone will not reduce lymphatic congestion because the large molecules do not go into the lymphatic capillary via osmosis and the overlap-ping endothelial cells surrounding the lymphatic capillary have to be stimulated to open and close. With combined edema, the reduction treatment has to be a combination of lymphatic proximal trunk stimulation (muscle contrac-tion, diaphragmatic breathing), superficial tissue stimula-tion (creating absorption into the initial lymphatics), and elevation to aid in venous (low protein) return.

text: Minor Trauma Edema (Inflammatory Subacute Edema) Theory Minor trauma to tissue is often caused by the arm or hand being bumped, getting caught on something, or from overzealous and improper exercise by the client or care-giver. 8,18,30,33 This accidental trauma often occurs due to an impaired visual field or perception, neglect, lack of limb position in space awareness, decreased sensation, and from learned nonuse once motor function returns. Inflammation from trauma becomes a third component to persistent edema. On a microvascular level, trauma causes high capillary permeability leading to a wound healing sequence in the involved joints and tissue. If the limb is already congested due to a dependency and/or a combined venous and lymphatic overload, there is an increase in the colloidal osmotic pressure in the intersti-tium. This causes an imbalance in Starling equilibrium resulting in an excess of plasma proteins trapped in the interstitium for a prolonged period. Casley-­Smith and Gaffney found that when excess plasma proteins stayed in the interstitium 64 days or longer, they caused chronic inflammation. 16 Fibroblasts are activated by the proteins trapped in the tissue and produce collagenous tissue. 32 This in turn can lead to the eventual shortening, scar-ring, and possible fibrosing of soft tissue and joints. 12,15 Only the lymphatic system can remove the excess plasma proteins. Thus, the lymphatic system has to be specifi-cally activated to reduce the trapped plasma proteins and break the cycle to pain, scarring, and possible fibrosis of tissue.

text: Chronic Regional Pain Syndrome Edema Reflex sympathetic dystrophy (RSD), the original term used in literature but now known as CRPS type I, may be seen poststroke (central lesion damage). 41,53 In the literature, shoulder-­hand syndrome (SHS) is used syn-onymously with CRPS type I. 41 CRPS type II has the same clinical symptoms but occurs because of peripheral nerve involvement. 41 It is defined as an exaggerated pain response to injury characterized by intense pain, trophic changes, and vasomotor changes in the involved limb. 53 CRPS progresses through three phases, each causing increased hand dysfunction. Clinically, in the first phase the hand presents as edematous, hyperesthetic, warm, perspiring, having burning pain, tenderness at the wrist and finger joints, and an increased blood flow to the extremity. 30,53 Poststroke edema occurs most frequently between 2 and 4 months after the stroke, as does the occurrence of RSD (CRPS type I). 30,31 However, clients who developed RSD during this period showed a greater degree of edema than the non-­RSD edematous stroke hands. 30 Another possible predictor of RSD research-ers found was hand swelling occurring during the first month poststroke. 30 The statistics for development of CRPS poststroke range anywhere from 1.56% 53 to 25% 50 of stroke hand edema cases, using both clinical evidence and a three-­ phase triple bone scan. This great range of statistics occurs because of timing of inclusion factors, methods of evalu-ation, when treatment began, and the type of treatment

The researchers documenting the 1.56% inci-dence concluded that their incidence of CRPS was low because rehabilitation poststroke began early at 16 days after the first stroke, and treatment included proper posi-tioning, early mobilization, and sensory stimulation. 53 Therapists can play a critical role in early identifica-tion and possible prevention or reversal of CRPS type I. When evaluating and treating clients, occupational therapists should scan for neglect, sensory impairments, shoulder subluxation, and decreased visual field aware-ness. Pertoldi and Benedetto found that the presence of these increased the risk of CRPS. 41 Also, early initiation of a treatment program to prevent trauma (proper posi-tioning, functional use, and mobilization) to the involved shoulder and extremity is critical to preventing CRPS I (see Chapter 20). In a detailed review of research from 1973 to 1998 on the etiology and treatment of post­stroke hand edema and SHS, it was found that the shoulder was involved in only half the cases with a swollen painful hand. 23 Thus, the new term wrist-­hand syndrome has been coined. 23 This same study found that in SHS, trauma causes aseptic joint inflammation. 23
